Doctor: yeah
Patient: having an ambulance ride and and i've never done that before so not an experience i wan na do again either
Doctor: i'm sure you do n't yeah i see that your blood pressure was high also it was two hundred over ninety have you been
Patient: yeah i guess is that really high
Doctor: yeah that's
Patient: i feel really bad
Doctor: yeah that's pretty high are you taking your medications or you missing some doses
Patient: i do n't know i might miss one now but i try to take them all time
Doctor: yeah yeah you really need to take them very consistently now you also said you were watching your diet did you did you have some slips with that you said your ankles were swelling

Doctor: are you eating a lot of salty foods and pizza or
Patient: i like potato chips

Patient: i like the salt and vinegar potato chips they're really good so
Doctor: well so do you do you go out to eat a lot or do you where you where where are you eating those potato chips or is that just the home snacking or

Patient: well i'm i'm doing better
Doctor: mm-hmm and they

Doctor: okay good alright have you had any chest pain

Patient: okay
Doctor: and i also want you to see a nutritionist to give you some education about what foods you can eat okay now for your second problem for i know this sounds like this is just for you and so for your second problem for your hypertension i want you to continue on the cozaar one hundred milligrams daily continue on the norvasc five milligrams once daily also and i'm going to order a renal artery ultrasound just to be sure we're not missing anything and then like maybe you know some renal artery stenosis or something and so so for your third problem for your kidney disease i wan na get some more labs to make sure you tolerate this the new medications and then i'll see you again in three months do you have any questions
Patient: no i do n't think so not today
Doctor: alright it's good to see you and i hope we'll just keep getting you feeling better
Patient: okay
"""

SUBJECTIVE:
The patient reports ongoing difficulty controlling high blood pressure despite medication adjustments. She has been taking Norvasc 10 mg daily and carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, and previously took lisinopril. She measures her blood pressure at home using an electronic cuff and recently recorded a reading as high as 170/90. She notes mild headaches when her blood pressure is elevated but denies chest pain, shortness of breath, or regular headaches. She occasionally experiences mild bilateral lower extremity swelling after prolonged standing. She reports a family history of hypertension and kidney disease in one parent. She consumes alcohol, including a couple of beers during the week and one or two on the weekend. She occasionally uses nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for knee or back pain.

OBJECTIVE:
Vitals: BP 169/74, HR 88 bpm, SpO2 98%. Physical exam: No jugular vein distension or carotid bruits. Clear lungs. Grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur heard on heart auscultation. 1+ pitting edema in bilateral lower extremities.

ASSESSMENT:
Uncontrolled hypertension.

PLAN:
1. Order renal artery ultrasound to evaluate for renovascular hypertension.
2. Order urine collection, morning aldosterone levels, and 24-hour urine to assess for secondary causes of hypertension.
3. Recommend reduction in alcohol intake to one or two drinks per week.
4. Advise significant reduction in salt intake.
5. Recommend discontinuation of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; suggest acetaminophen for pain.
6. Prescribe Cardura 4 mg once daily to help control blood pressure.
7. Refer to a nutritionist for dietary counseling.
8. Instruct patient to monitor and record blood pressure at home daily for the next three weeks, preferably at the same time each day.
9. Schedule follow-up in three weeks; request patient bring blood pressure log to the appointment.

SUBJECTIVE:
The patient presents for evaluation of high blood sugar. She reports increased consumption of sweets during the holidays, which has led to lightheadedness, visual spots, and dizziness over the past week. She was treated in the emergency room with IV fluids and advised to return to a routine diet. She is currently staying with family and finds it difficult to adhere to dietary restrictions. The patient denies fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, dysuria, joint pain, or muscle aches. She has a history of osteoarthritis, atrial fibrillation, and reflux. She notes that her heart races when anxious but is otherwise asymptomatic. She is currently taking metoprolol 25 mg twice daily and Protonix 40 mg daily, both of which she reports are effective.

OBJECTIVE:
The patient appears in no distress. Her thyroid is slightly enlarged but non-tender. No carotid bruits are noted. Heart rate is irregular. Lungs are clear. Abdomen is soft. No lower extremity edema. Glucose and hemoglobin A1c levels are elevated.

Diabetes mellitus, elevated blood glucose and hemoglobin A1c. Atrial fibrillation, asymptomatic and well-controlled. History of reflux, well-controlled on current regimen.

PLAN:
1. Order a complete metabolic panel for further evaluation of diabetes.
2. Initiate metformin 500 mg twice daily.
3. Provide a glucometer and instruct on home blood sugar monitoring.
4. Continue metoprolol 25 mg twice daily and refill as needed.
5. Continue Protonix 40 mg daily.
6. Encourage dietary modifications to reduce sugar intake.

The patient is a 31-year-old female with a history of type 2 diabetes, asthma, and gastritis. She presents with a one-week history of gradually increasing upper abdominal pain, described as occurring on both sides of the upper abdomen. The pain worsens with physical activity such as jogging. She reports intermittent nausea and vomiting, occurring three times and a couple of times, respectively, in the past week. She denies fever or diarrhea. The patient attributes the onset of symptoms to increased coffee consumption and spicy food intake. She is currently taking metformin 500 mg twice daily, Flovent twice daily, and albuterol as needed. She has a history of moderately heavy alcohol use.

OBJECTIVE:

ASSESSMENT:
1. Acute gastritis likely related to increased caffeine and spicy food intake. 2. Well-controlled type 2 diabetes. 3. Stable asthma.

PLAN:
1. Reduce caffeine and alcohol intake.
2. Reduce consumption of spicy foods.
3. Prescribe Zantac twice daily for gastritis.
4. Order urinalysis, urine pregnancy test, CBC, and comprehensive metabolic panel.
5. Adjust metformin to 1000 mg in the morning and 500 mg in the evening.
6. Continue home blood sugar monitoring.
7. Continue Flovent twice daily and albuterol as needed for asthma.
8. Schedule follow-up in 4 weeks.

SUBJECTIVE:
The patient presents with a one-month history of intermittent, throbbing headaches at the top of the head, which are partially relieved by Tylenol. She also reports occasional dizziness and blurry vision. She has a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes. She is currently taking chlorthalidone and metformin, but admits to taking them only every other day due to forgetfulness. She does not follow a low-sodium diet and consumes fast food regularly, including McDonald's. She recently consumed a significant amount of Easter candy, which she suspects may have contributed to elevated blood sugar.

OBJECTIVE:
Blood pressure is 172/98. Oxygenation is within normal limits. No jugular venous distention or carotid bruits are noted. Lungs are clear bilaterally. A 2/6 systolic ejection murmur is present, unchanged from prior. Slight edema is noted in bilateral upper extremities, and 1+ pitting edema is present in bilateral lower extremities.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Uncontrolled hypertension. 2. Type 2 diabetes.

PLAN:
1. Continue current medication regimen, including chlorthalidone and metformin (increased to 1500 mg).
2. Encourage daily medication adherence, with the suggestion to use reminders.
3. Recommend home blood pressure monitoring three times per week; provide guidance on selecting a home monitor.
4. Schedule a follow-up in one month to reassess blood pressure and diabetes control.
5. Refer to a nutritionist for dietary counseling, with a focus on reducing sodium intake and adopting a DASH diet.
6. Advise continued monitoring of blood glucose levels to assess the effectiveness of the medication change.
7. Educate on the importance of diet and medication adherence in managing hypertension and diabetes.

reference:
SUBJECTIVE:
The patient reports vision changes in the right eye, particularly difficulty adjusting in dimly lit environments and noticing crooked or wavy lines, especially in door frames and paneling. These symptoms have been present for approximately three to four months and are worsening. The patient has a history of high blood pressure and is currently not taking his prescribed blood pressure medication. He reports smoking one pack of cigarettes daily and has tried various methods to quit without success.

OBJECTIVE:
Eyes: Posterior chamber intraocular lenses present bilaterally. Right eye cornea is clear without NVI, cup-disc ratio is 0.2. Fundus of right eye shows retina intact 360 degrees without holes or tears, with RPE changes in the fovea. Posterior segment reveals drusen in the macula, retinal thickening, subretinal fluid, exudate accumulation, and positive hemorrhage. Left eye cornea is clear, no NVI, cup-disc ratio is 0.3, RPE changes in the fovea, no hemorrhage or subretinal fluid noted, and retina is attached appropriately. OTC shows drusen deposits under the RPE, SRF accumulation, and choroidal neovascular membrane. Fluorescein angiography reveals focal leakage in the right eye consistent with neovascular age-related macular degeneration.

ASSESSMENT:
Neovascular age-related macular degeneration (wet macular degeneration).

PLAN:
1. Administer Lucentis injections monthly, with the first injection scheduled today.
2. Educate the patient on the nature of wet macular degeneration, including the risk of severe vision loss and the benefits of ongoing treatment.
3. Counsel the patient on the importance of adhering to prescribed blood pressure medication.
4. Encourage the patient to continue efforts to quit smoking.
5. Schedule follow-up appointments for ongoing monitoring and treatment.

The patient is a 56-year-old male presenting with a four to five-week history of difficulty swallowing. He describes a sensation of something being stuck in his throat, primarily with solid foods, which occasionally causes discomfort or pain. He denies hematochezia, hematemesis, coughing up blood, weight changes, chest pain, or shortness of breath. 7. Provide refill for Norvasc.
8. Schedule follow-up in one month for lab results and reassessment.
9. Educate patient on eating slowly and chewing food thoroughly to reduce dysphagia risk.
10. Advise patient to contact office if symptoms worsen or if emergency care is needed.

The patient is a 34-year-old female with a history of diabetes mellitus type two who is here today with a headache. The headache started about a week ago and is a dull pain in the back of her head. She has flushing in her ears, which get red and hot, and sometimes feels a little dizzy. She has taken Tylenol and Advil, but the headache is not going away and keeps coming back. It comes and goes and is worse in the evening. The headache started around the time she began experiencing stress. She denies fever, visual changes, or the worst headache of her life. She has a history of similar headaches. She is currently taking metformin 500 mg twice daily but has not been checking her blood sugars. She has not been eating well or exercising due to the headache and stress. She is a golfer but has not played recently. She works on the computer a lot and does not take breaks.

OBJECTIVE:
Physical exam is normal and unremarkable for the most part. HEENT exam is normal with intact extraocular motions and no pain. Funduscopic exam shows no papilledema. Neck exam reveals some posterior mild posterior paraspinal muscular tenderness in the cervical spine and bilateral trapezius musculature, with some tightness in those muscles. Heart exam shows a grade three out of six systolic ejection murmur, unchanged from prior exam. The rest of the physical examination is normal.

ASSESSMENT:
Tension-type headache and diabetes mellitus type two.

PLAN:
1. Continue Tylenol for pain.
2. Prescribe Flexeril 5 mg three times a day to help relax the muscles in the neck.
3. Order hemoglobin A1c, CBC, and chem-12 blood tests.
4. Continue metformin 500 mg twice daily.
5. Follow-up in four weeks or sooner if the headache worsens or does not improve.
6. Encourage the patient to check blood sugars daily and to resume exercise.

Doctor: hello , mr . ward . nice to meet you . i'm dr. flores .
Patient: hi , doc . nice to meet you .
Doctor: i was just reviewing your records from dr. howard and he's referred you because the workup for headaches revealed a mass on your pituitary gland . i did review your mri images and you have a significant mass there . can you tell me about the issues you've been experiencing ?
Patient: yeah sure . so i'm really getting fed up with these headaches . i've been trying my best to deal with them but they've been going on for months now and i'm really struggling .
Doctor: where are the headaches located and how would you describe that pain ?
Patient: located behind my eyes . it's like a dull nagging ache .
Doctor: okay . was the onset gradual or sudden ?
Patient: well it started about three months ago . and they've been getting worse over time . at first it was like three out of 10 severity , and it just gradually worsened . and now it's about six out of 10 severity . the headaches do tend to be worse in the morning and it feels like a dull ache behind the eyes . they last a few hours at a time , nothing makes them better or worse .

Doctor: okay . have you noticed any change in your vision or with your balance ?
Patient: no i do n't think so . my eyes were checked in the fall .
Doctor: okay . let's see , do you have any other medical problems that you take medicine for ?
Patient: no i do n't have any medical problems and i do n't take any medicines . i tried tylenol a few times for the headaches but it did n't work , so i stopped .
Doctor: i see . anyone in your family have any history of diseases ?
Patient: i was adopted so i really have no idea .
Doctor: okay . um , what kind of work do you do ? and are you married ?
Patient: i work as a computer programmer and i've been married for 25 years . we just bought a small house .
Doctor: that's nice . um , do you drink any alcohol , smoke , or use recreational drugs ?
Patient: nope . i do n't do any of those and never have .
Doctor: okay . um , well let me take a good look at you . um , now you'll hear me calling out some details as i perform the examination . these will be noted for me in your record and i'll be happy to answer any questions you have once we're done .
Patient: sounds good , doc .

Patient: yeah i never noticed that i could n't see out of the side until you did that test , and you closed one eye with both eyes . i really could n't tell .
Doctor: no because you're having this vision loss from the mass compressing the optic chiasm , the only option we have is to do surgery .

Patient: all right .

Patient: well i guess we have to do it regardless .
Doctor: okay . so i will have you see our surgery scheduler , [NAME] , on the way out to get you set up . we will get this scheduled fairly quickly so i do n't want you to be alarmed . um , she'll also get you set up today or tomorrow to have the visual field test and you may not be able to see the eye doctor until after surgery . but we have the pre-surgery visual field test for comparison after surgery .
Patient: okay . i look forward to these headaches going away . i never thought it could be something like this going on .
Doctor: yeah . come this way , we'll get your things lined up . please call if you think of any questions .
Patient: thanks , doctor .
Doctor: diagnosis will be pituitary adenoma . mr . ward is a very pleasant 52-year-old male who has benign appearing pituitary adenoma , incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches . he is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression , therefor surgical intervention to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa is indicated . end of note .
"""

- Write 3 to 6 sentences of plain prose (maximum 120 words), in the third person.
- Cover the patient's age/sex and reason for the visit, the key history and findings, the assessment, and the plan.
- Use only information stated in the note. Do not use headings or bullet points.

"""

Patient: hey , good to see you .

Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: i'd like to tell dax about you-
Patient: sure .
Doctor: okay ?
Doctor: so [NAME] is a 60 year old male , with a past medical history , significant for depression , type two diabetes and hypertension , who presents for followup of his chronic problems .
Doctor: so , [NAME] , i saw you a couple months ago-
Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: how are- how are you doing ?
Patient: it's been a crazy year and a half and i think the uh the anxiety , the pressure of getting ready for thanksgiving was really starting to wear on me .
Doctor: okay .
Doctor: did you have a nice holiday ?
Patient: i , i did but it was uh , it was great to see everybody after about two years but it was just a lot of work .
Patient: a lot of stress .
Doctor: yeah . yeah . and what do you have to look forward for like , the new year and that type of thing . are you- more gatherings like that ?
Patient: um planning to take a vacation . so hopefully somewhere nice and warm .
Doctor: okay . all right . um , well how are you doing in terms of your depression . i know that we've kind of talked about this in the past .
Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: and we have n't put you on medication because you're on other meds and you- you have n't really wanted to do that , so what strategies are you using ?
Patient: yeah . over the summer we tried something new . i started going for long walks outside every morning. the weather was so nice and all the plants were in full bloom that i loved to start my day that way. on the weekends, it even encouraged me to do a little in the yard myself which was a nice way to be active and get some sun. but with the seasons changing and it getting so cold out, i have not been able to keep doing it and need to find something new to do. . i'm not ready yet to try any meds , so i think i'd like to look into some alternative options .
Doctor: okay . so yeah . so we can talk about some therapy and-
Patient: sure .
Doctor: that type of thing .
Patient: sure .
Doctor: all right . and no ... you do n't wan na harm yourself or others ?
Patient: no .
Doctor: any thoughts like that .
Patient: no .
Doctor: no , okay . and then in terms of your diabetes , how are you doing , you know especially with the holidays managing your- your sugar intake and that type of thing ?
Patient: uh , got through halloween okay . did n't stick to the diet too much through the thanksgiving week but it's a little bit better . so i've been trying to really monitor it .
Doctor: okay . and are you ... you're still taking the metformin , correct ?
Patient: yes .
Doctor: okay . all right . and then in terms of your high blood pressure , did you buy the blood pressure cuff that i recommended ?
Patient: yes .
Doctor: okay . and how have they been running . i have n't received any you know notes from you in the portal .
Patient: nothing out of the ordinary . it's been pretty moderate .
Doctor: it's been pretty good . and you're still taking the lisinopril , no problems with that ?
Patient: mm-hmm . correct .
Doctor: okay . all right . i know you did a review of system sheet when you checked in .
Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: um , do you have any symptoms . chest pain , shortness of breath , belly pain-
Patient: no .
Doctor: blood in your stool .
Patient: no .
Doctor: weight loss . anything like that ?
Patient: no .
Doctor: okay . all right . i wan na go ahead and do a quick physical exam .
Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: hey dragon . show me the vital signs .
Doctor: so here in the office . i agree . your blood pressure looks good . uh , i think you're doing a good job with that so keep up the good work . i'm gon na go ahead and take a listen to your heart and lungs , i'll let you know what i find .
Patient: sure .
Doctor: all right . so on physical examination , everything looks pretty good , so on your neck exam , i do n't appreciate any carotid bruits . on your heart exam i do appreciate a slight two out of six systolic ejection murmur heard at the left base , which we've heard in the past .
Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: your lungs are nice and clear and you do have uh one plus non-pitting edema bilaterally in your lower extremities . so what does all that mean ?
Doctor: it just means i heard a little sound in your heart , which you know is n't anything clinically significant . we had looked into that last year .
Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: you do have a little swelling in your legs but that might just be from your your diet recently , okay .
Patient: sure .
Doctor: i wan na just take a look at some of your results . hey dragon , show me the ekg .
Doctor: so i just had the nurse do an ekg on you before you came in just to make sure we were n't missing anything . you're in your 60's we have some risk factors . everything looks good .
Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: there's no evidence that i'm concerned about anything at this time . hey dragon , show me the diabetes logs .
Doctor: so on your diabetic labs , your hemoglobin a1c is elevated . it's at eight . i'd like to see it closer to six .
Doctor: now some of them might be having to do with the holidays that type of thing but i still think that we need to get that under better control .
Patient: sure .
Doctor: so lets talk a little bit about my assessment and plan for you so for your first problem of your depression i'd like to just go ahead and refer you to uh psychiatry not for medications , but just for some talk therapy that type of thing , okay ?
Patient: that's fine .
Doctor: um , for your second problem of your type two diabetes i'd like to go ahead and order a hemoglobin a1c in the next couple months . i want to increase the metformin to 1000 milligrams twice a day . and we're gon na go ahead and order a lipid panel , okay .
Patient: mm-hmm .
Doctor: uh , lastly for your third problem for your hypertension i'm gon na go ahead and order an echocardiogram just to recheck it . just that heart murmur . and i'm going to go ahead and keep the lisinopril at 20 milligrams a day . do you have any questions ?
Patient: no questions .
Doctor: okay the nurse will be in soon , she'll get you checked out , okay ?
Patient: you got it .
Doctor: hey dragon , finalize the note .
"""

reference: The patient is a 60-year-old male with a history of depression, type two diabetes, and hypertension who presents for follow-up of his chronic problems. He is managing his diabetes with metformin and has been monitoring his blood sugar. His blood pressure is stable on lisinopril. A physical exam shows a mild heart murmur and mild bilateral lower extremity edema. His hemoglobin A1c is elevated at 8%. The plan includes increasing metformin, ordering a lipid panel, referring him for talk therapy, and ordering an echocardiogram.

SUBJECTIVE:
The patient presents with right foot pain that began 2 days ago after falling on the dorsal aspect of the foot while playing tennis. She twisted her foot while trying to catch herself and was unable to continue playing or bear weight. She wrapped the foot, iced it, elevated it, and took ibuprofen for pain, which provided partial relief. She denies numbness or tingling and reports intact sensation. The patient has a history of a left leg injury.

OBJECTIVE:
Physical examination reveals bruising and swelling of the plantar and dorsal aspects of the right foot. Tenderness to palpation of the midfoot and a positive piano key test of the first and second metatarsals. The right foot is warm to touch. Neurovascular examination is intact with capillary refill less than 3 seconds and strong dorsalis pedis pulse. The left foot examination is normal. X-ray of the right foot shows subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal, a 3 mm separation of the first and second metatarsal bases, and a bony fragment in the Lisfranc joint space.

ASSESSMENT:
Right foot pain consistent with a Lisfranc fracture.

1. Proceed with surgical intervention (right foot ORIF) to realign and stabilize the fracture.
2. Order MRI to further assess the fracture and evaluate for ligamentous injury.
3. Schedule follow-up in the clinic in 1 week post-surgery.
4. Recommend crutch use and non-weight bearing for 6 to 8 weeks post-surgery.
5. Prescribe formal physical therapy to strengthen the right foot and facilitate recovery.
6. Provide preoperative education and discuss risks of the procedure including bleeding, nerve damage, infection, nonunion, and hardware failure.
7. Arrange for postoperative follow-up and monitoring for complications.

7. Continue lisinopril at 20 milligrams daily.
8. Schedule a follow-up appointment in four months.

[ID]-8-4-9-2-0 . she's here for a new visit with her mother for acne located on the face , which started about two years ago and is present most every day . she has been using persa-gel and washing regularly , which is somewhat helpful . there are no associated symptoms including itching , bleeding , or pain . no additional past medical history . she lives with her parents and sister . they have a dog , bird , and bunnies . she is in 7th grade . she plays basketball and volleyball and tap . she wears sunscreen in the summer , spf 30 . no additional family history . hi [NAME] , i'm dr. Patient: yup .

Patient: mm , i think about two years .
Doctor: okay .
Family member: the biggest flare , probably , was when she started school sports in the fall , just with all the sweating .

Patient: okay , so is there anything we can do to help it ?

Patient: okay , i can do that .
Doctor: you also have multiple benign moles on your arms , legs , back and abdomen . this means they all look normal with no worrisome features . we will see if you have any progress over the next six months and follow up at that time .
Patient: okay , that sounds good . thank you .
Doctor: do you have any questions for me ?
Patient: no , i do n't think so .
Doctor: okay . if you have questions or concerns before your next visit , please call the office .
Patient: thank you , doctor , we will .

Doctor: Yes, I see that here, he also has shortening bayonet apposition.

Guest_family_1: Will he be asleep for the surgery?
Doctor: Absolutely, he won't feel a thing. Other risks include bleeding, changes in sensation and motion of the extremity, hardware failure, and need for later hardware removal, and cast tightness. I would not worry about these risks. We have great results with these surgeries.
Guest_family_1: Then yes, we'd like to do the surgery.
"""

Doctor: Good evening, and welcome to A B C D General Hospital E D.
Patient: Thank you, Doctor, I've really messed up this ankle.
Doctor: Before we begin, how old are you? And which gender do you identify?

Patient: I fell off my liner, and I landed right onto my left foot.

Patient: Um, it was really about ten feet.

Patient: What does that mean, exactly?
Doctor: I don't see any ankle dislocation, which is good.
Patient: Oh, that's good news.

Patient: No, the ankle really took all of the weight of the fall.
Doctor: Okay, I think we should do surgery in order to repair this ankle.

Patient: Okay, you're right. What are the risks of this infection with this surgery?

Patient: Will I be asleep for this?

"""

He has a history of spinal stenosis and neuropathy in his legs and reports tingling in both feet, which the doctor attributes to his known conditions. He has no signs of infection and has left the nursing home to return to his own house.

diagnoses: percutaneous screw fixation of a Schatzker I V tibial plateau fracture
procedures: percutaneous screw fixation of a Schatzker I V tibial plateau fracture

note:
Doctor: Hello, sir. So, remind me, how long ago was your procedure?
Patient: Let me think. Now, it's been about four months. I just turned fifty nine.
Doctor: Okay, and just to refresh your memory, we did a percutaneous screw fixation of a Schatzker I V tibial plateau fracture, and we've managed those toe fractures nonoperatively.
Patient: Which toes did I break?
Doctor: You broke your second and fifth toes.
Patient: Do you have the x rays? Can I see where the breaks are?
Doctor: Absolutely, if you look here, right here is where the breaks are. These are called the metatarsal heads.
Patient: Wow, that's right where it hurts.
Doctor: Yep, and where are you living now?
Patient: Thankfully, I left the nursing home, and I'm back in my own house now.
Doctor: That's really good. Are you in any pain today?
Patient: No, not today.
Doctor: Great, have you been going to P T?
Patient: Yeah, I've been going about two or three times a week.
Doctor: Are there any signs of infection, like drainage from the incision?
Patient: Nope, the wound healed up nicely. I'll be able to wear shorts again.
Doctor: Great, are you having any fever symptoms, like cough, runny nose, sore throat, fatigue, anything like that?
Patient: No, but I have had some tingling in both my feet. I don't know if its related to surgery. If I'm remembering the names right, um, I have a history of spinal stenosis and neuropathy in my legs.
Doctor: With your history of spinal stenosis, the broken toes, and the surgery, that's a pretty normal side effect.

Doctor: Welcome in, sir.
Patient: Thank you.

Patient: No. I will probably look for a place back in Coolidge.
Doctor: Back in Coolidge? Have you lived there before?
Patient: I recently separated from my wife. We lived in Coolidge together. Sacaton is too far away from everything, but it is fine for now.

Patient: Not when we were growing up but now that we are older, we have become very close. She has been a great support for me in these hard times.
Doctor: That's wonderful. Are you a tobacco user?
Patient: I smoke cigarettes. I only smoke a little bit.
Doctor: How much do you smoke per day?
Patient: I only smoke about one or two cigarettes a day.
Doctor: Do you or have you ever used drugs or alcohol?
Patient: I have never used drugs. I used to be a heavy drinker. I quit drinking a year ago.
Doctor: That's great. Do you attend A A meetings?
Patient: No, but I might start. Things have been very stressful lately with the separation and being on unemployment.
Doctor: I think it could be beneficial to you.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: I have a list for different support groups in the area that I can give you.
Patient: Great. Thank you.
"""

Plan, I will order a CBC, a comprehensive metabolic panel, a TSH, an albumin level, and a chest x-ray. Start an oral nutrition supplement twice daily between meals. Doctor: Good morning. I have you down as a 48-year-old male here about trouble hearing. What's been going on?
Patient: It's my right ear. Everything sounds muffled, and it crept up slowly over about four months. I really noticed it after I got back from a trip overseas.
Doctor: Where did you travel?
Patient: Southeast Asia, about three weeks ago. It was a fourteen-hour flight each way, and my ear felt blocked with a lot of popping the whole way home.
Doctor: Any pain in the ear or drainage?
Patient: No pain, no drainage. No ringing either, and I haven't been dizzy.
Doctor: Did you swim or put anything in your ears while you were away?
Patient: I swam a couple of times in the hotel pool. I use cotton swabs every day. And I took pseudoephedrine 60 mg three times a day for the stuffy nose on the flights.
Doctor: Okay. Anything going on with your eyes?
Patient: Yes, both eyes have been itchy and red since I got back, with watery tearing. No eye pain, and my vision is the same as always.
Doctor: Any fever or sore throat?
Patient: No fever. Just the stuffy nose.
Doctor: Any medical problems or allergies to medicines?
Patient: Seasonal allergies, that's all. No drug allergies.
Doctor: Alright. Your vitals today are blood pressure 126/78, heart rate 72, and temperature 98.4. Looking in the right ear, there is a plug of wax against the drum. The left canal is clear and the left drum looks normal. We did a wax removal with a curette today, and afterward the right drum is intact and a little retracted, with no fluid and no redness. Inside your nose the lining is pale and boggy. Both eyes show mild redness of the white part with no discharge, the corneas are clear, and your vision is 20/20 in each eye.
Patient: Is the hearing loss from the wax?
Doctor: Mostly. The audiogram we did before you came in shows a mild conductive loss on the right and a normal result on the left, and tympanometry shows reduced movement of the right drum. So my impression is cerumen impaction with eustachian tube dysfunction from your allergies and the flights, plus allergic conjunctivitis.
Patient: What should I do?
Doctor: Stop the cotton swabs and stop the pseudoephedrine. Start fluticasone nasal spray, two sprays in each nostril once a day. Start olopatadine 0.1 percent eye drops, one drop in each eye twice a day. We will repeat the hearing test in six weeks, and come back sooner if you get ear pain, drainage, or a sudden change in your hearing.
Patient: Sounds good, thank you.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Geriatrics progress note, hospital day 3. The patient is an 86-year-old female admitted after her third fall in two months, this time at night when she stood up from a chair to go to the bathroom. She denies loss of consciousness, chest pain, palpitations, and new weakness, and she did not strike her head. She does report lightheadedness when she stands and gets up three to four times a night to urinate because of bladder urgency. A CT of the head on admission showed no bleeding, and a wrist X-ray showed only a bruise and no fracture.

Her home medication list was reviewed in detail because she takes nine medications. The ones most relevant to her falls are zolpidem 5 mg at bedtime for sleep, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily for bladder urgency, and amlodipine 10 mg daily for hypertension. She also takes acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for knee pain.

Vitals this morning: lying blood pressure 146/80 with heart rate 72; after standing for three minutes blood pressure 112/64 with heart rate 76 and lightheadedness. Temperature 36.7 C and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. On exam she is alert and oriented, lungs are clear, heart rhythm is regular, and there is no leg edema. Her gait is slow and wide-based and she needs a walker. Strength and sensation are intact and there are no focal deficits. Labs show creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, sodium 139, hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, a normal vitamin B12, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 18 ng/mL. ECG showed sinus rhythm without block, and urinalysis was negative.

My impression is that these are recurrent falls that are multifactorial, with orthostatic hypotension, sedating and anticholinergic medications, bladder urgency causing nighttime trips to the bathroom, and vitamin D deficiency all contributing.

For management, stop zolpidem and use sleep hygiene measures. Stop oxybutynin and use timed voiding with fluids limited after dinner. Reduce amlodipine from 10 mg to 5 mg daily and repeat orthostatic vital signs in two days. Start vitamin D3 1000 units daily. Continue acetaminophen 500 mg as needed. Physical and occupational therapy will work on gait, transfers, and walker training, and a home safety evaluation will be done before discharge. Plan discharge once her orthostatic drop improves. Geriatrics clinic follow-up in two weeks.
"""

Telephone visit (audio only). The patient consented to a phone visit, and his identity was confirmed verbally.

Reason for visit: Follow-up of irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea in a 32-year-old male, with review of test results.

History: He reports loose stools five to six times a day, with urgency and crampy lower abdominal pain that settles after he passes stool. Symptoms started about eight months ago after a stressful job change and have been worse over the last month. He also has bloating. He has been taking loperamide 2 mg most days and says it helps only partly. He denies blood in the stool, black stools, fever, nighttime diarrhea, and unintentional weight loss. He also reports ongoing worry and trouble falling asleep, which he links to the stomach symptoms. He takes sertraline 50 mg daily, started by his primary care doctor three months ago for anxiety. Impression: Irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea, with negative infectious, celiac, and inflammatory screening. Anxiety, on sertraline, is likely worsening his bowel symptoms.

Taking OTC ibuprofen 400 mg BID x 1 wk for low back pain - told NSAIDs bad for HF, STOP.
Denies CP, palpitations, syncope, fever, cough w/ sputum, calf pain.

NKDA.

Tx: furosemide 80 mg IV x1 -> UOP 1.8 L over 4h. O2 2 L NC, weaned to RA. Post-tx SpO2 96% RA, ambulates w/o desat (94%), HR 88. Sx much improved.

- Resume sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg BID (K 4.6, Cr 1.3, SBP 118)
- Furosemide inc to 80 mg PO daily x 5d, then reassess at HF clinic
- Continue carvedilol 12.5 mg BID, spironolactone, empagliflozin

- Daily wts, fluid 1.5-2 L/day, 2 g sodium diet
- Meds filled before leaving ED (meds-to-beds), pictogram schedule in Spanish

"""
Hospital day 2 for a 54-year-old female admitted with palpitations. She describes a racing, irregular heartbeat that started the evening before admission and lasted several hours, along with fatigue. She denies chest pain, syncope, lightheadedness, and shortness of breath. Since then she has remained in sinus rhythm with rates in the 60s and 70s and had no further palpitations overnight.

Her history includes HTN and known paroxysmal atrial fibrillation diagnosed last year. On direct questioning she admitted that she has been taking her metoprolol succinate 50 mg only every other day for the past few months because of cost, and that she stopped apixaban 3 months ago because the copay was too high. She continues to take lisinopril 20 mg daily, which is a low-cost generic.

Vitals this morning are BP 126/74, HR 68, RR 16, temperature 98.2 F, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Heart is regular without murmur, lungs are clear, and there is no peripheral edema. Admission potassium was 3.4 and was replaced with potassium chloride 40 mEq by mouth, and this morning it is 4.0. Magnesium is 1.9. Troponin was negative twice, TSH is 1.9, hemoglobin is 13.1, and creatinine is 0.8. ECG this morning shows sinus rhythm. Echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 60%, mild left atrial enlargement, and no significant valve disease.

Impression is paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate, likely triggered by hypokalemia and by inconsistent beta-blocker use because of medication costs. Her stroke risk score is 2 from female sex and HTN, so anticoagulation is indicated.

Plan: Restart apixaban 5 mg twice daily. Change metoprolol succinate to the low-cost generic metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily. Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily. Case management and pharmacy have been asked to enroll her in a medication assistance program and to review a monthly cost estimate before discharge; if apixaban remains unaffordable, warfarin with INR monitoring is the alternative. We discussed that skipping doses can cause her atrial fibrillation to recur and raises her stroke risk. Continue telemetry, anticipate discharge tomorrow if she stays in sinus rhythm, repeat BMP in 1 week, and cardiology clinic follow-up in 2 weeks.
"""

Convert the following clinical encounter note into a structured SOAP note.
Requirements:
- Use exactly these four section headers, each on its own line and in this order: SUBJECTIVE:, OBJECTIVE:, ASSESSMENT:, PLAN:
- SUBJECTIVE: chief complaint, history of present illness, pertinent positives and negatives, and relevant history, medications, allergies, and social history as reported.
- OBJECTIVE: vital signs, examination findings, and test results that are documented.
- ASSESSMENT: the clinician's diagnoses or impressions.
- PLAN: a numbered list of management steps (medications, tests, referrals, education, follow-up).
- Include only information stated in the note. If a section has no documented information, write "Not documented."

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 2 for a 54-year-old female admitted with palpitations. She describes a racing, irregular heartbeat that started the evening before admission and lasted several hours, along with fatigue. She denies chest pain, syncope, lightheadedness, and shortness of breath. On admission telemetry showed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 110 to 140, which converted spontaneously to sinus rhythm in the early morning of hospital day 1. Since then she has remained in sinus rhythm with rates in the 60s and 70s and had no further palpitations overnight.

Her history includes HTN and known paroxysmal atrial fibrillation diagnosed last year. On direct questioning she admitted that she has been taking her metoprolol succinate 50 mg only every other day for the past few months because of cost, and that she stopped apixaban 3 months ago because the copay was too high. She continues to take lisinopril 20 mg daily, which is a low-cost generic.

Vitals this morning are BP 126/74, HR 68, RR 16, temperature 98.2 F, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Heart is regular without murmur, lungs are clear, and there is no peripheral edema. Admission potassium was 3.4 and was replaced with potassium chloride 40 mEq by mouth, and this morning it is 4.0. Magnesium is 1.9. Troponin was negative twice, TSH is 1.9, hemoglobin is 13.1, and creatinine is 0.8. ECG this morning shows sinus rhythm. Echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 60%, mild left atrial enlargement, and no significant valve disease.

Impression is paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate, likely triggered by hypokalemia and by inconsistent beta-blocker use because of medication costs. Her stroke risk score is 2 from female sex and HTN, so anticoagulation is indicated.

Plan: Restart apixaban 5 mg twice daily. Change metoprolol succinate to the low-cost generic metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily. Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily. Case management and pharmacy have been asked to enroll her in a medication assistance program and to review a monthly cost estimate before discharge; if apixaban remains unaffordable, warfarin with INR monitoring is the alternative. We discussed that skipping doses can cause her atrial fibrillation to recur and raises her stroke risk. Continue telemetry, anticipate discharge tomorrow if she stays in sinus rhythm, repeat BMP in 1 week, and cardiology clinic follow-up in 2 weeks.
"""

Summarize the following clinical encounter note for a busy clinician.
Requirements:
- Write 3 to 6 sentences of plain prose (maximum 120 words), in the third person.
- Cover the patient's age/sex and reason for the visit, the key history and findings, the assessment, and the plan.
- Use only information stated in the note. Do not use headings or bullet points.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good afternoon. Before we start, I want you to know that we have a professional interpreter on the line with us, and I will pause after each sentence so she can interpret. Is that all right?
Patient: Yes, that is fine.
Doctor: Thank you. I see you are a 30-year-old female here for pelvic pain. Tell me about it.
Patient: The pain in my lower belly has been there for almost two years. It gets very bad before and during my period. Some days I cannot go to work.
Doctor: Is the pain there only with your period, or at other times too?
Patient: Mostly with the period, but now there are many days in the month when it hurts, a dull pain on the left side.
Doctor: Does it hurt with intercourse?
Patient: Yes, deep inside. It hurts so much that we avoid it.
Doctor: Any pain with bowel movements?
Patient: Yes, during my period it hurts a lot to have a bowel movement, and sometimes I feel bloated.
Doctor: Any pain when you urinate, or blood in the urine?
Patient: No pain when I urinate, and no blood in the urine.
Doctor: Any fever, vaginal discharge, or bleeding between periods?
Patient: No fever, no discharge, and no bleeding between periods. But my periods are very heavy, I change a pad every two hours the first two days.
Doctor: Have you lost weight without trying, or had vomiting?
Patient: No weight loss, no vomiting.
Doctor: What have you tried for the pain?
Patient: I took the birth control pill before, but my doctor stopped it because of my migraines with aura. For the pain I take naproxen, the small 220 pills, one or two when it is bad.
Doctor: Let me check the chart. I see naproxen 500 mg twice a day was prescribed at your last visit.
Patient: Oh, yes, you are right. I take the 500 mg one, twice a day, during my period. The small pills are old ones I had at home.
Doctor: Thank you for clarifying. What other health problems and medicines do you have?
Patient: Migraines with aura, and I take sumatriptan 50 mg when I get one. I have acid reflux, and I take omeprazole 20 mg every morning. I was told I have low iron, and I take ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day. And I have depression, and I take sertraline 50 mg every day.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No allergies.
Doctor: Good. Your vital signs today are blood pressure 118/74, heart rate 82, and temperature 98.2. Your urine pregnancy test today was negative. Your hemoglobin from last week was 10.9 g/dL and your ferritin was low. The transvaginal ultrasound last week showed a 3 cm left ovarian cyst with ground-glass echoes, which looks like an endometrioma, and your chlamydia and gonorrhea tests were negative. On exam, your abdomen is soft with mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant. On the pelvic exam you have deep tenderness behind the uterus and a tender left adnexa, with no mass that I can feel.
Patient: So what does that mean?
Doctor: Together, this is chronic pelvic pain with suspected endometriosis. Because you cannot take estrogen with migraines with aura, please do not restart the combined birth control pill. I am going to start norethindrone acetate 5 mg once daily, which is a progestin-only pill and is safe with migraine with aura. Keep taking naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food during your period, and keep the omeprazole to protect your stomach. Your mood has been low because of the pain, so I will increase sertraline from 50 mg to 100 mg every day. Continue ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day for the low iron. I am also referring you to pelvic floor physical therapy. If the pain is not better in three months, we will talk about laparoscopy to confirm the diagnosis and treat it. I want to see you back in eight weeks. Go to the emergency room for sudden severe pain, fainting, or fever.
Patient: Okay, thank you, Doctor.
"""

reference: A 30-year-old female seen with a professional interpreter reported almost two years of chronic pelvic pain, worse around her period, with deep pain during intercourse, painful bowel movements, and heavy periods, without urinary symptoms, fever, discharge, or weight loss. Her history includes migraines with aura, acid reflux, low iron, and depression, and her combined birth control pill was stopped for the migraines. Ultrasound showed a 3 cm left ovarian cyst consistent with an endometrioma, and hemoglobin was 10.9 g/dL. She was diagnosed with chronic pelvic pain with suspected endometriosis. Norethindrone acetate 5 mg once daily was started, sertraline was increased to 100 mg every day, and pelvic floor physical therapy and eight-week follow-up were arranged.

Denies dysuria, urgency, gross hematuria, flank pain, fever. No hx of stones. Postmenopausal, no hormone therapy. No regular meds. NKDA.

Vitals: BP 132/78, HR 72.
Exam: abd soft, NT; no CVA tenderness. Pelvic: atrophic vaginal mucosa; no prolapse.
PVR by bladder scan: 20 mL. UA today: neg. Prior urine cx: E. coli, pan-sensitive.

Impression: recurrent UTIs, likely contributed by postmenopausal vaginal atrophy. No retention, no sx today.

Plan:
- Start vaginal estradiol cream 0.5 g nightly x 2 wk, then twice weekly.
- Renal/bladder US.
- Urine cx before any abx for future sx.
- F/u 3 mo, sooner if another infection.

Doctor: Any fevers?

Clinical note:
"""
Nurse: Triage note for the 67-year-old male in bed four. Left flank pain that started about three hours ago, rated nine out of ten, and he vomited once in the waiting room. Blood pressure 158/94, heart rate 98, temp 98.6, oxygen sat 98% on room air.

Doctor: Hello, I'm the emergency doctor. Tell me what happened.

Patient: It came on out of nowhere. Sharp pain in my left side, and it shoots down toward my groin. I can't sit still, I keep pacing.

Doctor: Any fever or chills?

Patient: No fever, no chills.

Doctor: Any burning when you urinate, or blood in the urine?

Patient: No burning. The urine looked a little pink this morning, though.

Doctor: Have you ever had a kidney stone before?

Patient: Never.

Doctor: Have you traveled recently?

Patient: I flew back from Thailand three days ago, about a seventeen hour trip, and it was really hot there. I wasn't drinking much water.

Doctor: Did you have any diarrhea or a stomach bug while you were away?

Patient: No diarrhea, I was careful with what I ate.

Doctor: What medicines do you take?

Patient: Just amlodipine 5 mg once a day for my blood pressure. No allergies to medicines.

Doctor: Okay. On exam you look uncomfortable, you have tenderness over the left flank, and your belly is soft with no guarding. Your urine test shows blood but no sign of infection. The CT scan without contrast shows a 5 mm stone in the upper left ureter with mild hydronephrosis, which means some backup of urine into the kidney. Your creatinine is 1.2 and your white count is 9.8, so the kidney is working fine and there is no sign of infection. This is renal colic from a kidney stone. The nurse gave you ketorolac 15 mg IV and ondansetron 4 mg IV for the pain and nausea.

Patient: The pain is already down to a three.

Doctor: Good. I want to start tamsulosin 0.4 mg once daily to help the stone pass, and ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours with food for pain. Keep taking your amlodipine. Drink plenty of water and strain your urine to catch the stone. You need to see urology in about a week. Come straight back if you get a fever, uncontrolled pain, repeated vomiting, or if you can't pass urine.

Patient: Okay, thank you.
"""

Left flank tenderness was present, urinalysis showed blood without infection, and CT showed a 5 mm left ureteral stone with mild hydronephrosis, with creatinine 1.2 and white count 9.8. The diagnosis was renal colic from a kidney stone, and pain fell to three out of ten after IV ketorolac and ondansetron. The plan is tamsulosin and ibuprofen, continued amlodipine, fluids with urine straining, urology follow-up in a week, and return precautions.

Hospital medicine progress note, hospital day 2. A professional Spanish interpreter joined by video for the entire visit, and all history from the patient was obtained through the interpreter.

Her serum sodium on admission was 119 mEq/L. She received one 100 mL bolus of 3% saline in the emergency department, and her serum sodium rose to 124 mEq/L by this morning. Today she tells us through the interpreter that her headache and nausea are gone, but she still feels a little unsteady when she stands. She denies vomiting, seizures, chest pain, shortness of breath, and diarrhea. There were no events overnight.

Her history includes hypertension and hypothyroidism. Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once daily, started by her primary care physician six weeks ago, was stopped on admission. She continues amlodipine 5 mg once daily and levothyroxine 50 mcg once daily. A fluid restriction of 1 liter per day was started yesterday.

Mucous membranes are moist, there is no jugular venous distension, the lungs are clear, and there is no peripheral edema, consistent with euvolemia. Neurologic exam shows no focal deficit and a mildly unsteady gait.

Data: serum sodium 124 mEq/L this morning, up from 119 mEq/L on admission. Serum osmolality 258 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality 420 mOsm/kg. TSH 2.1 mIU/L, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and potassium 3.6 mEq/L. CT of the head showed no acute findings.

My impression is symptomatic hyponatremia, most likely caused by the thiazide diuretic, that is improving after hypertonic saline and fluid restriction. Hydrochlorothiazide will remain discontinued and will be listed as an adverse drug reaction in her chart. We will continue the fluid restriction, check serum sodium levels every six hours today, and limit the rise to no more than eight mEq/L in 24 hours. No further hypertonic saline is needed because her symptoms are improving. Amlodipine continues for blood pressure. Physical therapy will evaluate her gait. """

"""
38-year-old male, nephrology f/u on the ward, HD#2
admitted from ED w/ hyperkalemia, K 6.8 on outpt BMP
PMH: HTN, T2DM, CKD 3a (baseline Cr 1.5), obesity
Social: current smoker ~1 ppd x 15 yrs, no EtOH, no drugs

HPI
c/o generalized weakness x 3 d
palpitations last night, self-resolved
no syncope, no CP, no SOB
no N/V, no diarrhea, no abd pain
no decreased UOP, no dysuria, no hematuria
no leg swelling
pt very anxious, asking lots of Qs: "is my heart ok", "will I need dialysis", "can I still go to work", "is it the lisinopril"
Qs answered at bedside ~25 min, handout given

Meds per pt on admission:
lisinopril 20 mg daily
amlodipine 5 mg daily
metformin 1000 mg BID
atorvastatin 40 mg nightly
insulin glargine 20 units nightly
Clarified w/ pill bottles brought by brother: lisinopril is 40 mg daily, NOT 20 mg (PCP uptitrated 6 wks ago)
Initially denied NSAIDs, later admits ibuprofen 400 mg 3 times a week for back pain, last dose 2 d ago
no K supplements, no salt substitute

ED: calcium gluconate 1 g IV x1, regular insulin 10 units IV w/ D50 x1, albuterol neb 10 mg x1
ECG on admission: peaked T waves, no QRS widening
ECG today: NSR, T waves normal

Vitals today: BP 148/92, HR 82, RR 18, Temp 98.2 F, SpO2 98% RA, wt 104 kg
gen: anxious but NAD
CV: RRR, no m/r/g
lungs: CTAB
abd: soft, NT
ext: no edema
neuro: strength 5/5 throughout

Labs admission -> today:
K 6.8 -> 5.4
Cr 2.2 (baseline 1.5) -> 2.0
BUN 38 -> 30
Na 136, HCO3 20, glucose 212
eGFR 38
A1c 8.4
UA: 2+ protein, no blood
Renal US: normal size kidneys b/l, no hydronephrosis

Imp
hyperkalemia 2/2 ACE inhibitor (lisinopril 40 mg) + ibuprofen, in setting of AKI on CKD 3a
T2DM above goal, A1c 8.4
HTN, BP above goal today
current smoker

Mgmt
D/C lisinopril, avoid ACE inhibitors/ARBs until K and Cr stable
stop ibuprofen, avoid all NSAIDs, acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN for back pain
Lokelma 10 g TID x 48 h then reassess
start furosemide 40 mg PO daily
increase amlodipine from 5 to 10 mg daily for BP
hold metformin inpt (AKI), plan to resume at lower dose 500 mg BID at d/c if eGFR stable
continue atorvastatin and insulin glargine 20 units nightly
repeat BMP q6h x 2 then qAM
low K diet, dietitian to see pt, avoid salt substitutes
tobacco: counseled cessation ~5 min, pt receptive, start nicotine patch 21 mg daily, quitline info given
pt anxious: reassured K improving, no dialysis needed now, RN to update at bedside
dispo: d/c in 24-48 h if K <5.5 x 2 and Cr improving
f/u nephrology clinic 1 wk w/ BMP, PCP 2 wks
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good morning, and thanks for coming in. I have your chart here. You are an 81-year-old male, and your primary doctor sent you to talk about colon cancer screening. Is that right?

Patient: Yes, he said I'm overdue. I think my last colonoscopy was about five years ago.

Doctor: Let me look at the report. It says here your last colonoscopy was about ten years ago, and it was normal.

Patient: Ten? You know, you're right. My wife had hers five years ago and I mixed us up. Mine was ten years ago.

Doctor: No problem. Have you noticed any blood in your stool, black stools, a change in your bowel habits, or belly pain?

Patient: No blood, no black stools, my bowels are regular, and no belly pain.

Doctor: Any weight loss that you did not intend?

Patient: No, my weight has been steady.

Doctor: Any family history of colon cancer?

Patient: My father had it, in his seventies.

Doctor: Okay. Tell me about your health overall and your medicines.

Patient: I have A-fib, congestive heart failure, high blood pressure, and diabetes. I take Eliquis 5 mg twice a day, furosemide 40 mg every morning, which my cardiologist raised from 20 mg last month, metoprolol succinate 50 mg every day, metformin 500 mg twice a day, and a baby aspirin 81 mg every day. I also take ibuprofen 600 mg three times a day for my knees.

Doctor: Thank you. And how much alcohol do you drink in a day?

Patient: Oh, a couple of beers. Maybe two.

Doctor: I ask everyone this carefully, because it changes my advice. Is two a typical day?

Patient: Well... honestly it's closer to six beers a day. I didn't want to say. Not two, six.

Doctor: Thank you for being honest with me. Now your exam and results. Your blood pressure is 134/78 and your pulse is 70 and irregular. Your belly is soft and not tender, I can't feel an enlarged liver, and I don't see any yellowing of the eyes or swelling in your legs. Your labs from last week show a hemoglobin of 13.4, so you are not anemic. Your platelets are a little low at 142, your creatinine is 1.2, and your liver enzyme AST is a bit high at 58.

Patient: Is that bad?

Doctor: It tells me the alcohol is affecting your liver, and we will follow up on that. Now, about screening. You are 81, with heart failure and A-fib, you take a blood thinner, and you drink heavily. A colonoscopy needs a bowel prep that can dry you out while you are on a water pill, sedation carries more risk with your heart, and removing a polyp could cause bleeding on Eliquis. Your last colonoscopy was normal ten years ago, and the guidelines say that after 75 screening is an individual decision and after 85 we generally stop. A slow-growing polyp may never bother you in your lifetime. A safer choice is a stool test called a FIT. If it is positive, we would talk about a colonoscopy together with your cardiologist.

Patient: I'd rather do the stool test. I don't want that prep again.

Doctor: Good, I will give you a FIT kit to do at home. Second, ibuprofen and aspirin together with Eliquis raise your risk of a stomach bleed, and the alcohol adds to it. I want you to stop the ibuprofen and the baby aspirin. For your knees you can take Tylenol 500 mg two or three times a day, but no more than 2 grams a day because of your liver.

Patient: The aspirin was for my heart, though.

Doctor: Since you take Eliquis, the aspirin usually isn't needed, and I will send a note to your cardiologist to confirm. Third is the alcohol. Six beers a day can scar the liver and raises your risk of bleeding and falls. I am ordering a liver ultrasound, a FibroScan to check for scarring, and a repeat hepatic panel. I am starting thiamine 100 mg every day, and I am referring you to our addiction medicine clinic. Please don't stop drinking suddenly on your own, because withdrawal can be dangerous. Call us first and we will help you cut down safely.

Patient: I'll try. My wife keeps asking me to.

Doctor: Good. My impression is that you do not need a screening colonoscopy for now, you will do the FIT at home, and you have heavy alcohol use with probable alcohol-related liver injury. Let's meet again in three months, or sooner if you see blood in your stool.

Patient: Thank you, doctor.
"""

Labs showed hemoglobin 13.4, platelets 142, and AST 58. Given his age, comorbidities, anticoagulation, and drinking, the physician advised a home FIT test rather than colonoscopy, stopped ibuprofen and aspirin, started thiamine, and ordered a liver ultrasound, FibroScan, hepatic panel, and addiction medicine referral, with follow-up in three months.

Clinical note:
"""
Orthopedic surgery inpatient progress dictation. The patient is a 38-year-old male on the orthopedic ward, postoperative day 2, status post open reduction and internal fixation of a right distal radius fracture with a volar locking plate. He fell from a ladder while painting at home. He is right-hand dominant.

Overnight no acute events. Pain is 4 out of 10 at rest and 6 with movement. Yesterday he was switched from IV hydromorphone to oxycodone 5 mg by mouth every 4 hours as needed, correction, every 6 hours as needed, and the hydromorphone has been discontinued. He is also taking acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours and docusate 100 mg twice daily. He denies numbness, tingling, fever, chills, nausea, and chest pain. He reports constipation, with no bowel movement in 2 days. He is tolerating a regular diet and walking independently.

Social history. He lives alone in a second floor apartment and his family lives out of state. A friend can check on him about once a week. He cannot drive with the splint and he is worried about dressing, cooking, and bathing with his dominant hand out of use.

Vital signs: blood pressure 124/76, heart rate 70, respiratory rate 16, temperature 98.6 F, oxygen saturation 98 percent on room air. Examination of the right upper extremity shows a posterior splint that is clean, dry, and intact. The fingers are warm and pink with capillary refill under 2 seconds. Sensation is intact in the median, ulnar, and radial distributions. He can flex and extend all fingers. There is mild swelling of the hand and no drainage. Postoperative radiographs show anatomic alignment of the distal radius with the plate and screws in good position.

Assessment. Right distal radius fracture, postoperative day 2, doing well, pain controlled. Constipation related to opioid use. Limited social support at home, which delays safe discharge.

Plan. Continue oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed with the acetaminophen. Add senna 8.6 mg at bedtime for the constipation and continue docusate. Keep the arm elevated and the splint on, no weight bearing. Occupational therapy evaluation today for one-handed daily activities. Social work consult for home health visits, meal delivery, and transportation to the clinic. If he is safe with one-handed tasks and the home support is arranged, discharge tomorrow. Clinic follow-up in 2 weeks with repeat radiographs and suture removal, and referral to hand therapy.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
This is a dictation for a gastroenterology follow-up visit on a 60-year-old female with ulcerative colitis, last seen about eight months ago, who returns with a flare. She was diagnosed with extensive ulcerative colitis about ten years ago and had been well controlled on mesalamine. Over the last three weeks she has had five to six loose stools a day with visible blood on about half of them, along with urgency and lower abdominal cramping, and she is waking once or twice a night to have a bowel movement. She denies fever, vomiting, weight loss, joint pain, eye redness, and mouth sores, and she has not had any recent antibiotics or sick contacts.

She tells me she takes mesalamine delayed release 2.4 grams once daily, correction, she is actually taking only 1.2 grams once daily, one tablet, because she has been rationing her supply. The prescribed dose is 4.8 grams once daily. Her copay went up after her insurance changed, and the pharmacy told her the cost is now about 180 dollars a month, which she cannot afford. She works rotating shifts at a warehouse, alternating day weeks and night weeks, and with this irregular schedule she often forgets doses or skips them when she comes off a night shift. She has also been using over-the-counter loperamide 2 mg up to four times a day to control the diarrhea.

Other medical history includes hypertension, hypothyroidism, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and osteopenia. Her other medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, and omeprazole 20 mg daily, and she reports taking all of them. She has no known drug allergies.

Vitals today are blood pressure 126/78, heart rate 88, temperature 98.6 F, and weight 142 pounds, which is stable. On exam she looks well and mucous membranes are moist. The abdomen is soft with mild left lower quadrant tenderness, no distension, and no rebound or guarding, and bowel sounds are normal.

Labs this week show hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, MCV 78, ferritin 9 ng/mL, WBC 9.6, platelets 412, CRP 14 mg/L, and albumin 3.8. Fecal calprotectin is 640 micrograms per gram. Stool C diff PCR and stool culture are both negative.

My impression is a mild to moderate flare of extensive ulcerative colitis, caused by under-dosing of mesalamine because of cost and her irregular shift schedule, along with iron deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss. Plan is to increase mesalamine back to 4.8 grams once daily, taken as a single dose with food when she wakes up, regardless of which shift she is working. I will prescribe the generic as a 90-day supply and refer her to social work for pharmacy assistance programs. I am also starting budesonide MMX 9 mg once daily, taken when she first wakes up, for eight weeks. She should stop the loperamide. I am starting ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily for the iron deficiency. I am ordering a colonoscopy with biopsies in eight to twelve weeks after the flare settles to reassess disease extent and screen for dysplasia, and a repeat CBC and CRP in four weeks. She should call right away for more than eight stools a day, fever, heavy bleeding, or severe abdominal pain. Follow up in four weeks.
"""

"""
Doctor: Good morning. I have you down as a 72-year-old male here about rough spots on your scalp and face. Who came with you today?
Family member: I'm his daughter. I drive him to his appointments and set up his pill box, so I'll fill in what he forgets.
Patient: She remembers things better than I do.
Doctor: That helps. Tell me about the spots.
Patient: I've got scaly, rough patches on top of my head and on my forehead. They've been there about two years, but lately a few of them are crusty and sore when I comb my hair.
Family member: He worked outdoors as a landscaper for forty years and never wore a hat. One spot on his left temple bled last month after he scratched it.
Doctor: Has any spot grown quickly, or is there an open sore that won't heal?
Patient: The one on my temple looks bigger than it used to. Nothing is oozing now.
Doctor: Any itching?
Patient: Some itching, yes.
Doctor: Any fever, weight loss, or new lumps in your neck?
Patient: No fever, no weight loss, and I haven't felt any lumps.
Doctor: Have you ever had skin cancer, or tried any treatment on these spots?
Patient: A basal cell cancer was cut off my nose about ten years ago.
Family member: And he used fluorouracil cream last winter, but he stopped it after two weeks because his face got raw and red.
Patient: Yes, it burned too much, so I quit.
Doctor: Understood. Now please go through your medicines with me.
Patient: Lisinopril 20 mg every morning and amlodipine 5 mg once a day for my blood pressure, atorvastatin 40 mg at night, aspirin 81 mg daily, and metformin 500 mg twice a day for the sugar.
Family member: Dad, that's not right. The metformin was raised to 1000 mg twice a day in the spring. The 500 mg tablets are the old ones.
Patient: Oh, that's right. It's 1000 mg twice a day now.
Doctor: Good, so metformin 1000 mg twice a day. Your primary doctor sent recent labs for your diabetes, hypertension, and high cholesterol. Your A1c was 7.2, and creatinine was 1.3 with an eGFR of 54. Let me examine you now. Your blood pressure today is 138/80. There are multiple pink, rough, scaly papules across the scalp and forehead, about eight in total, each three to six millimeters. The lesion on the left temple is eight millimeters, thicker and crusted, without ulceration. I don't feel any enlarged lymph nodes in your neck, and there is no new pigmented lesion.
Doctor: This is actinic keratosis from many years of sun exposure. The thick spot on the left temple concerns me for an early squamous cell carcinoma, so I want a shave biopsy of that one today. The others I'll treat now with liquid nitrogen cryotherapy. It will sting and may blister.
Family member: Should he restart the cream?
Doctor: Not the fluorouracil, since it irritated him. Once the frozen areas heal, I'll start imiquimod 3.75% cream once daily at bedtime to the scalp and forehead for two weeks, then two weeks off, then repeat. Keep taking your other medicines, including the aspirin, as you are now. Use sunscreen SPF 50 every morning and a wide-brimmed hat. Come back in four weeks to review the biopsy and do a full skin check, and call us sooner if a spot bleeds, grows, or becomes painful.
Patient: Okay, we'll do that.
Family member: I'll write it all down.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Chief Complaint: Fall at home while on a blood thinner.

HPI: 86-year-old male brought in by EMS after a ground-level fall at home earlier this morning. He tripped on the edge of a rug while walking to the bathroom and landed on his left side, striking the left side of his head on the floor. There was no loss of consciousness, and he was able to sit up with help from his daughter, who found him within minutes. He takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation and took his morning dose about 2 hours before the fall. He currently has scalp soreness and left forearm pain. Past medical history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 3. Other home medications are metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily and lisinopril 10 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies.

ROS: Denies headache, vomiting, neck pain, chest pain, palpitations, dizziness before the fall, new weakness, numbness, or vision changes. No abdominal pain. No shortness of breath.

Physical Exam: Temp 36.8 C, HR 76 and irregularly irregular, BP 148/82, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, weight 58 kg. Alert and oriented, GCS 15. There is a left parietal scalp hematoma of about 3 cm that is tender, with no laceration and no step-off. Pupils are equal and reactive, cranial nerves are intact, strength is 5/5 and symmetric, and there is no pronator drift. Neck has no midline tenderness. Chest wall is nontender and lungs are clear. Heart is irregularly irregular without murmur. Abdomen is soft and nontender. The left forearm has a 4 cm abrasion with mild tenderness over the distal radius, no deformity, and intact sensation and perfusion. Pelvis is stable and both hips are nontender with full range of motion.

ED Course / Results: CT head without contrast showed no intracranial hemorrhage and no fracture, with a left parietal scalp hematoma. CT cervical spine showed no acute fracture. X-ray of the left forearm and wrist showed no fracture. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 78 and no acute ischemic changes. Labs: hemoglobin 12.9, creatinine 1.6, potassium 4.2, troponin negative. Because he is anticoagulated, a repeat CT head at 6 hours was obtained and was stable with no delayed bleed. The abrasion was cleaned and dressed. He was given acetaminophen 650 mg once for scalp soreness with good relief and then walked in the department with a steady gait.

Medical Decision Making: Mechanical fall without syncope in an elderly man on apixaban, with a scalp hematoma and a forearm abrasion. Imaging is negative for intracranial hemorrhage and fracture, and the stable 6 hour repeat CT supports safe discharge. He meets dose reduction criteria for apixaban given age over 80, weight 58 kg, and creatinine 1.6, so the dose will be reduced from 5 mg to 2.5 mg twice daily. Fall risk was discussed, and a home safety evaluation is recommended.

Disposition: Discharged home with his daughter. Hold apixaban tonight and resume tomorrow morning at 2.5 mg twice daily. Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain, and avoid NSAIDs. Continue metoprolol succinate and lisinopril. Return for headache, vomiting, confusion, drowsiness, or new weakness. Follow up with his primary care physician in 1 week, with home physical therapy and a home safety evaluation arranged.
"""

He takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation and took his morning dose about 2 hours before the fall. He currently has scalp soreness and left forearm pain. Past medical history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 3. Other home medications are metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily and lisinopril 10 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies.

ROS: Denies headache, vomiting, neck pain, chest pain, palpitations, dizziness before the fall, new weakness, numbness, or vision changes. No abdominal pain. No shortness of breath.

Physical Exam: Temp 36.8 C, HR 76 and irregularly irregular, BP 148/82, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, weight 58 kg. Alert and oriented, GCS 15. There is a left parietal scalp hematoma of about 3 cm that is tender, with no laceration and no step-off. Pupils are equal and reactive, cranial nerves are intact, strength is 5/5 and symmetric, and there is no pronator drift. Neck has no midline tenderness. Chest wall is nontender and lungs are clear. Heart is irregularly irregular without murmur. Abdomen is soft and nontender. The left forearm has a 4 cm abrasion with mild tenderness over the distal radius, no deformity, and intact sensation and perfusion. Pelvis is stable and both hips are nontender with full range of motion.

Clinical note:
"""
Telehealth video visit note, geriatrics. The patient is an 86-year-old male seen by secure video from his home, with his daughter beside him to help with the camera and read his medication bottles. He consented to the video format and confirmed his location.

The reason for the visit is follow-up of osteoporosis after a fragility fracture. Three months ago he developed sudden mid-back pain after bending to lift a laundry basket, and a lateral spine x-ray showed an L1 compression fracture. A DXA scan last month showed a T-score of -2.9 at the femoral neck. He has not yet started any bone-protective medication. His back pain is now 3 out of 10 at rest and 5 out of 10 after standing for a long time. He denies new back pain, numbness, leg weakness, or bowel or bladder changes. He has had no falls.

He returned 9 days ago from a 14-hour international flight to visit relatives overseas. During the trip he skipped some doses of his medicines and drank little water. Since returning he denies calf pain, leg swelling, chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, and diarrhea. He feels tired from jet lag but is otherwise well.

He is allergic to ibuprofen and other NSAIDs, which cause hives, so NSAIDs are avoided. His history includes hypertension, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease. His medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, calcium carbonate 500 mg twice daily with meals, and a vitamin D supplement. He first said he takes vitamin D 5000 units daily, but his daughter read the bottle on camera and corrected this to vitamin D3 1000 units daily. After the fracture, an urgent care physician prescribed tramadol 50 mg every 6 hours as needed. He took it for two weeks and then stopped on his own because of dizziness and constipation. For pain he now uses acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed.

Home measurements today were blood pressure 128/74, pulse 72, and temperature 98.2 F. His weight is stable at 71 kilograms according to his daughter. Labs drawn before the visit showed creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, eGFR 52, calcium 9.4 mg/dL, and 25-hydroxy vitamin D 24 ng/mL.

On video examination he appears comfortable and speaks in full sentences. There is mild thoracic kyphosis. He stood and walked a few steps with his walker, and his gait was slow but steady. He held both legs up to the camera and there was no visible swelling, redness, or asymmetry.

My assessment is osteoporosis with a recent L1 compression fragility fracture and high fracture risk, vitamin D insufficiency, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 52, which still allows an oral bisphosphonate. Suspicion for venous thromboembolism after the long flight is low because he has no symptoms and no leg findings.

For the plan, I am starting alendronate 70 mg once weekly, to be taken in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, and he must stay upright for 30 minutes afterward. He will continue calcium carbonate 500 mg twice daily with meals. I am increasing vitamin D3 from 1000 units to 2000 units daily. He will continue acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed, and tramadol remains discontinued. NSAIDs stay off his list. I ordered a basic metabolic panel and a repeat 25-hydroxy vitamin D level in three months. I placed a referral to physical therapy for balance and back strengthening, and we reviewed fall precautions. He and his daughter know to seek care promptly for calf pain, leg swelling, chest pain, or new severe back pain. Follow-up will be a video visit in six weeks.
"""

Patient: No back pain, no nausea, no vomiting.

Patient: No, I have not seen any.

"""

Infectious disease inpatient follow-up dictation. This is a 51-year-old male with HIV seen on the ward for routine HIV follow-up while he is hospitalized for left lower leg cellulitis, hospital day 3. A professional Spanish interpreter was used for the entire visit, and I confirmed with teach-back that the patient understood. He has been on bictegravir, emtricitabine, tenofovir alafenamide one tablet daily for four years and at first told me he has never missed a dose. Correction, after further questions he says he missed one dose last week when he was brought to the emergency department. He denies fever, chills, nausea, diarrhea, headache, night sweats, cough, and weight loss. He says the leg is less painful and the redness is shrinking. No new rashes and no oral thrush. On exam he is comfortable, no oral thrush, no lymphadenopathy, heart regular, lungs clear, abdomen soft. The left lower leg has erythema that has receded from the marked border, mild warmth, no fluctuance, and no drainage.

Data today: HIV viral load undetectable at less than 20 copies, CD4 count 540. Creatinine 0.9. Syphilis screen negative.

Assessment, HIV infection, virologically suppressed on antiretroviral therapy and immunologically stable. Left lower leg cellulitis improving on cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours.

Plan, continue bictegravir, emtricitabine, tenofovir alafenamide one tablet daily without changes. Switch cefazolin to oral cephalexin 500 mg four times daily to complete seven days total, with discharge expected tomorrow. Counseled on daily adherence using the interpreter, and a refill was provided. Offer the influenza vaccine before discharge. Repeat viral load and CD4 count in six months. Return to the HIV clinic in three months, and the clinic will schedule a professional interpreter for that visit.
"""
