She ran out of her controller inhaler about two weeks ago because the pharmacy is far from her home and she has no car and no reliable ride; her daughter works days and could not bring her in earlier. About ten days ago a clinic started propranolol 20 mg twice daily for hand tremor. She denies fever, chest pain, leg swelling, hemoptysis, and vomiting. She has had no prior intubations and one hospital admission for asthma three years ago.

Home medications (reviewed with the patient and her daughter by phone): fluticasone-salmeterol 250/50 one inhalation twice daily (ran out two weeks ago), albuterol HFA 2 puffs every 4 hours as needed, lisinopril 20 mg daily, propranolol 20 mg twice daily, and metformin. The patient first stated metformin 500 mg twice daily; correction, her daughter read the bottle over the phone and it is 1000 mg twice daily. No known drug allergies.

ROS: Positive for cough and rhinorrhea. Negative for fever, chest pain, orthopnea, abdominal pain, and dysuria.

Physical Exam: BP 156/92, HR 112, RR 28, temp 98.9 F, SpO2 89% on room air. Sitting upright, speaking in short phrases, using accessory muscles. Diffuse expiratory wheezes with prolonged expiratory phase and diminished air movement at both bases. Heart tachycardic and regular. No jugular venous distension, no leg edema. Peak flow 160 L/min (predicted about 380).

ED Course / Results: Received continuous albuterol-ipratropium nebulizers 2.5 mg/0.5 mg for three doses, methylprednisolone 125 mg IV once, magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 minutes, and oxygen 2 L by nasal cannula, with SpO2 improving to 95%. After treatment: HR 98, RR 20, wheezing much improved, peak flow 280 L/min, and SpO2 96% on room air. Chest x-ray showed hyperinflation with no infiltrate, effusion, or pneumothorax. ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ST changes. VBG pH 7.36, pCO2 42. WBC 12.4, glucose 238 mg/dL, potassium 3.4, bicarbonate 24 with a normal anion gap, creatinine 0.9, troponin negative.

Medical Decision Making: Moderate to severe acute asthma exacerbation, likely triggered by a viral upper respiratory infection, loss of controller therapy for two weeks, and the new non-selective beta-blocker propranolol. Considered pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, heart failure, and pneumothorax; the chest x-ray, ECG, normal troponin, and rapid response to bronchodilators make these unlikely. Hyperglycemia is from steroids on top of type 2 diabetes, with no evidence of DKA. Propranolol is discontinued because non-selective beta-blockers worsen bronchospasm; I will message her primary care physician about tremor management. She also needs a higher-dose controller, so fluticasone-salmeterol will be increased from 250/50 to 500/50 one inhalation twice daily.

Disposition: Observed for five hours with sustained improvement; discharge home. Prescriptions: prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days, fluticasone-salmeterol 500/50 one inhalation twice daily, and albuterol HFA as needed. Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily and metformin 1000 mg twice daily with extra home glucose checks while on prednisone. Because she has no car, the pharmacy filled the prescriptions here before she left (meds-to-beds) with a 30-day supply, and a social worker arranged a ride home with her daughter after work and a transportation voucher for the primary care visit in three days; the clinic will also offer a video visit. A nurse will call tomorrow to check on her breathing. Return precautions reviewed: worsening shortness of breath, inability to speak full sentences, blue lips, or no relief from albuterol.
"""

This is a follow-up visit for a 59-year-old male with stable exertional angina. He reports chest pressure when he walks briskly uphill or climbs two flights of stairs. The pressure lasts about three minutes and resolves with rest. The frequency is about twice a week and has not changed over the past three months. He denies pain at rest, syncope, palpitations, and orthopnea. He has used sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg as needed only once in the past month, with prompt relief.

His history includes hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Current medications are metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, and nitroglycerin 0.4 mg as needed. He reports taking all of them reliably.

On examination, blood pressure was 136/84, heart rate 62, respiratory rate 14, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Heart rhythm was regular with no murmurs. There was no JVD and no peripheral edema, and the lungs were clear. A resting ECG showed sinus rhythm at 62 beats per minute with no ST changes. A treadmill stress test last month reproduced his typical chest pressure at stage 3 with 1.5 mm of horizontal ST depression and no arrhythmia. His recent lipid panel showed an LDL of 92 mg/dL.

My impression is stable exertional angina with an abnormal stress test, hypertension that is above goal, and an LDL that is not at goal for his risk. I increased atorvastatin from 40 mg to 80 mg daily and started amlodipine 5 mg daily to improve both angina control and blood pressure. He will continue metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, and nitroglycerin as needed. I ordered coronary CT angiography to define his anatomy, and we will repeat the lipid panel in eight weeks. I reviewed warning signs, and he should go to the emergency department for chest pain at rest or lasting longer than fifteen minutes despite nitroglycerin. He will return in six weeks.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good afternoon. I see you are a 65-year-old female here at urgent care today because you want to be evaluated for ADHD. I am using a professional interpreter, so I will speak in short sentences and pause so everything gets translated. Is that okay?
Patient: Yes, that is fine. Thank you.
Doctor: Tell me what has been going on.
Patient: Since I was a girl I cannot focus. My mind wanders in conversations, I lose my keys and my glasses almost every day, and I leave projects half finished. When I came home from the hospital three weeks ago I saw how bad it is, because I forgot my pills many times.
Doctor: What were you in the hospital for?
Patient: My blood pressure was very high, 220 over something, and I had a terrible headache. They kept me four days.
Doctor: Did they scan your head?
Patient: Yes, a CT scan. They said it was normal.
Doctor: Good. Do you have trouble sitting still?
Patient: Inside I feel restless, but I can sit. I talk a lot and interrupt people, my daughter says.
Doctor: Did these problems start in school?
Patient: Yes. My teachers wrote that I daydream, and I could not finish tests on time.
Doctor: Have you felt sad or hopeless, or lost interest in things?
Patient: No, I am not depressed. I worry a little about money, but I am not sad.
Doctor: Any thoughts of harming yourself?
Patient: No, never.
Doctor: Any chest pain or palpitations?
Patient: No chest pain, no palpitations.
Doctor: Do you drink alcohol or use any drugs?
Patient: No alcohol, no drugs.
Doctor: How is your sleep?
Patient: About six hours. My husband says I snore a little.
Doctor: What medical conditions do you have?
Patient: I have diabetes, high blood pressure, an underactive thyroid, and high cholesterol.
Doctor: Let us go through your medicines. What did the hospital change?
Patient: They stopped the naproxen I took for my knees. They raised the amlodipine from 5 to 10 milligrams once a day. I also take lisinopril 20 milligrams every morning, metformin 500 milligrams twice a day, the thyroid pill levothyroxine 100 micrograms... wait, let me look at my list. The thyroid pill is 75 micrograms. And atorvastatin 40 milligrams at night.
Doctor: Okay, so levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily, not 100. Thank you for checking.
Patient: Yes, 75.
Doctor: Your hospital papers show a TSH of 2.1, an A1c of 7.2, creatinine 1.0, and an EKG with normal sinus rhythm. Today your blood pressure is 152 over 90 and your heart rate is 84. The ASRS screener you filled out in the waiting room was positive, five of six items.
Patient: What does that mean?
Doctor: It means your symptoms fit ADHD, but a screener cannot confirm it. On exam you are alert and pleasant, you asked me to repeat a few things, your speech is normal, there is no tremor, your heart is regular and your lungs are clear.
Doctor: My impression is long-standing inattention since childhood, which could be inattentive ADHD, but we cannot confirm that today. Your blood pressure is above goal, and stimulant medicines can raise blood pressure and heart rate, so I will not start one today. I will refer you to outpatient psychiatry for a full ADHD evaluation with cognitive testing. Please keep avoiding naproxen, check your blood pressure at home every morning, use a weekly pill organizer with phone alarms, and see your primary care doctor within one week about your blood pressure. Return here or go to the emergency room for a severe headache, chest pain, or confusion.
Patient: Yes, I understand. Thank you.
"""

This 72-year-old female returns for follow-up of polymyalgia rheumatica, diagnosed about four months ago and treated with a prednisone taper. She has trouble raising her arms to comb her hair and getting out of a low chair, and she also reports fatigue. She denies headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain with chewing, vision changes, fever, and weight loss, which makes giant cell arteritis unlikely. She has hypertension controlled on amlodipine 5 mg daily, and a bone density scan last year showed osteopenia.

- On sertraline x 8 wks. Pt states takes 100 mg daily. Bottle reviewed: sertraline 50 mg tab, 1 tab daily. Correction, pt takes 50 mg daily, not 100 mg.

Meds: sertraline 50 mg daily, metformin 500 mg BID, lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, diphenhydramine 50 mg qhs OTC. NKDA.

Vitals: BP 132/76, HR 70, wt 168 lb.
MSE: groomed, cooperative, psychomotor slowing, speech slow but clear, mood "down", affect constricted, thought process linear, no SI/HI, no AVH, oriented x3, insight fair, judgment fair.
PHQ-9: 14 today (was 19 at baseline 8 wks ago). MoCA 25/30.
Labs 1 wk ago: Na 136, K 4.4, Cr 1.3, eGFR 54, TSH 2.3, B12 520, A1c 7.1%.
ECG: NSR, QTc 430 ms.

Dx: MDD, recurrent, partial response to sertraline 50 mg (PHQ-9 19 -> 14), never titrated. Insomnia w/ OTC diphenhydramine use, anticholinergic burden in 74-year-old w/ BPH (Beers list).
- Increase sertraline from 50 mg to 100 mg daily (2 x 50 mg tabs every morning). Teach-back done w/ pt, then phone call w/ daughter to update pill organizer.
- D/c diphenhydramine today. Explained why: confusion, urinary retention, falls. Pt verbalized understanding.
- Start mirtazapine 7.5 mg qhs for sleep and appetite.
- Cont metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin, aspirin, tamsulosin, no change.
- Sertraline + aspirin: bleeding risk reviewed, report black stools. Repeat BMP at local lab near home in 2 wks (SIADH risk, age > 65).
- Discussed common side effects (GI upset, low sodium, falls). Pt repeated plan back in own words.
- Large-print med list given, pharmacy to blister-pack all meds, 90-day mail-order refills.
- Transport barrier: next visit by telephone/video in 4 wks, SW referral for medical transport benefit, labs at local lab.
- Crisis line number reviewed. RTC sooner if SI, worsening mood, falls, or black stools.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good morning, come on in. I see you are a 61-year-old male here about erectile dysfunction. What brings you in today?
Patient: Morning, Doctor. I have a lot of questions, if that's all right. I got back from a trip abroad about two weeks ago, and I've been worried sick. For about eight months I've had trouble getting and keeping an erection. Is that serious? Could it be my heart?
Doctor: Those are good questions, and we will go through them one at a time. First, the history. Do you still get morning erections?
Patient: Less than before. Maybe once a week. Is that a bad sign?
Doctor: It tells me there may be both physical and stress factors. Do you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or lightheadedness when you exert yourself?
Patient: No chest pain and no shortness of breath. I do feel a little lightheaded when I stand up fast, though. Is that related? Should I be worried about that?
Doctor: We will come back to that. Any burning with urination, discharge, or sores?
Patient: No burning, no discharge, no sores. But could I have caught something while traveling? I did have one encounter I regret.
Doctor: I hear you, and we will test you for peace of mind. What other health problems do you have, and what do you take?
Patient: I have high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, and an enlarged prostate. I take lisinopril 20 mg every morning, metformin 1000 mg twice a day, atorvastatin 20 mg at bedtime, and tamsulosin 0.8 mg at night. No, wait, tamsulosin is 0.4 mg, one capsule. I always mix that up.
Doctor: Okay, tamsulosin 0.4 mg at night. Do you use nitroglycerin or any heart medicine like a nitrate?
Patient: No, nothing like that. Is that important?
Doctor: Very important, and I will explain in a moment. Did you take anything else for the erections?
Patient: Yes, I bought some male enhancement pills at a market on the trip. I took one twice. I got a pounding headache and my face was flushed, and I got scared. Were those dangerous? What was in them?
Doctor: Those pills are not regulated, and some contain hidden sildenafil, so I do not want you taking them again. Let me share your numbers. Your BP today is 138/84, your pulse is 76, and your BMI is 29. Your ECG today shows a normal sinus rhythm with no signs of a prior heart attack. Your labs from last week show an A1c of 7.1%, LDL of 128 mg/dL, creatinine of 1.0, total testosterone of 410 ng/dL, and PSA of 1.8. On exam, your genital exam is normal, the testes are normal in size, and the prostate is smooth, mildly enlarged, and not tender. Your IIEF-5 score is 12, which is moderate erectile dysfunction.
Patient: So is it my heart? Is it my hormones? Is it all in my head?
Doctor: Your heart tracing is reassuring, and your testosterone is normal. I think this is erectile dysfunction from a mix of blood vessel risk factors, meaning diabetes, high blood pressure, and cholesterol, plus performance anxiety after the first episodes.
Patient: Will I need surgery? Is the medicine safe? Can I have a glass of wine with it?
Doctor: No surgery. I will start tadalafil 5 mg once daily, which also helps the prostate symptoms. One glass of wine is fine. Never take it with nitrates, and stand up slowly because it can lower your blood pressure, especially together with tamsulosin, so keep taking tamsulosin 0.4 mg at night. Stop the pills from the market. I am also increasing atorvastatin from 20 mg to 40 mg at bedtime because your LDL is high for someone with diabetes. I will order a urine chlamydia and gonorrhea test and HIV and syphilis tests, and I will give you a written summary because you have a lot of questions. I would also like to refer you to a counselor for the anxiety. Please see me in six weeks. Call us for an erection lasting more than four hours, chest pain, or a severe headache.
Patient: Okay. Thank you for explaining everything, Doctor.
"""

reference: A 61-year-old male, anxious and asking many questions, presented with eight months of erectile dysfunction after returning from international travel two weeks ago. He denied chest pain, shortness of breath, burning, discharge, and sores, but reported lightheadedness on standing and headache and flushing after unregulated enhancement pills bought abroad. He has high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, and an enlarged prostate; ECG, testosterone, and PSA were reassuring, with A1c 7.1% and LDL 128 mg/dL. The diagnosis was erectile dysfunction from vascular risk factors plus performance anxiety. Tadalafil 5 mg daily was started, the market pills were stopped, atorvastatin was increased to 40 mg, and STI testing, counseling referral, and six-week follow-up were arranged.

Visit modality: audio-only telephone visit, about 25 minutes. The patient is a 75-year-old male with a changing pigmented lesion on his upper back. History was obtained from the patient and from his daughter, who is his caregiver and stayed on the line for the whole call. Video was not possible because he has no smartphone and the home internet connection is unreliable.

Reason for visit: The daughter noticed a dark spot on his right upper back that has gotten bigger and darker. The patient cannot see his own back and had not noticed it. She first estimated that it had been changing for about 3 months, then corrected herself after checking the date stamp on an older photo on her phone and said it has really been closer to 6 months. She describes it as dark brown to black with an uneven edge and a lighter pink area along one side. The patient denies pain, itching, or bleeding from the spot. He denies any drainage or open sore. He denies fever, weight loss, and night sweats, and has not noticed new lumps in his neck or armpits. The daughter has not seen other new or changing spots when she helps him bathe, but she has not looked closely at his scalp or feet.

Skin history: A basal cell carcinoma of the left temple was removed with Mohs surgery about 4 years ago. He farmed outdoors for decades and had many sunburns as a young man. No personal history of melanoma. His brother had melanoma in his sixties.

Other conditions: atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a. No known drug allergies.

Medications, reviewed with the daughter reading from the bottles: Apixaban, which she first said was 2.5 mg twice daily; after reading the label she corrected this to 5 mg twice daily. Metformin 500 mg twice daily. Lisinopril 20 mg daily, increased from 10 mg by his PCP about 6 weeks ago. Atorvastatin 40 mg at bedtime. Metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. Aspirin 81 mg was stopped by cardiology when the apixaban was started, and the daughter confirmed he no longer takes it.

Data reviewed: Recent labs from his PCP show creatinine 1.3, eGFR 54, A1c 7.1%, and hemoglobin 13.2. Home readings this morning per the daughter were BP 138/78, pulse 72, and fingerstick glucose 128. The daughter uploaded two photos to the patient portal before the call, which I reviewed during the visit. They show a single lesion of about 9 mm with dark brown to black color, an irregular border, and a pink area along one edge. The photos are taken in room light without dermoscopy, so they cannot replace an in-person exam, and no total body skin exam was possible by phone.

Transportation: He does not drive. The daughter works full time and lives an hour away, and the clinic is about 40 miles from his home. He missed two earlier dermatology visits because no ride was available, and the daughter says that each trip means taking a full day off work.

Impression: Changing pigmented lesion of the right upper back with enlargement, color variation, and border irregularity, suspicious for melanoma until proven otherwise. The differential includes a dysplastic nevus and a pigmented basal cell carcinoma. This needs a biopsy and should not wait for a routine appointment.

Next steps, discussed with the patient and his daughter, who both agreed:
- In-person visit within 2 weeks for a full skin exam and same-day excisional biopsy, so that he needs only one trip. We will try to book it on the same day as his cardiology follow-up in the same building.
- Referral to clinic social work to arrange a medical transportation benefit or a volunteer driver. I will call the daughter back with the ride options.
- Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily; a small skin biopsy does not require holding it. Continue the other medications unchanged.
- Daughter to upload new photos with a ruler beside the lesion and to check his scalp and feet.
- Sun protection advice reviewed. Call sooner if the spot bleeds, forms a sore, or grows quickly.
- If pathology confirms melanoma, referral to dermatologic surgery for wide excision.
- Phone check in 1 week to confirm the ride and the appointment.
"""

Visit modality: audio-only telephone visit, about 25 minutes. The patient is a 75-year-old male with a changing pigmented lesion on his upper back. History was obtained from the patient and from his daughter, who is his caregiver and stayed on the line for the whole call. Video was not possible because he has no smartphone and the home internet connection is unreliable.

Reason for visit: The daughter noticed a dark spot on his right upper back that has gotten bigger and darker. The patient cannot see his own back and had not noticed it. She first estimated that it had been changing for about 3 months, then corrected herself after checking the date stamp on an older photo on her phone and said it has really been closer to 6 months. She describes it as dark brown to black with an uneven edge and a lighter pink area along one side. The patient denies pain, itching, or bleeding from the spot. He denies any drainage or open sore. He denies fever, weight loss, and night sweats, and has not noticed new lumps in his neck or armpits. The daughter has not seen other new or changing spots when she helps him bathe, but she has not looked closely at his scalp or feet.

Skin history: A basal cell carcinoma of the left temple was removed with Mohs surgery about 4 years ago. He farmed outdoors for decades and had many sunburns as a young man. No personal history of melanoma. His brother had melanoma in his sixties.

Other conditions: atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a. No known drug allergies.

Medications, reviewed with the daughter reading from the bottles: Apixaban, which she first said was 2.5 mg twice daily; after reading the label she corrected this to 5 mg twice daily. Metformin 500 mg twice daily. Lisinopril 20 mg daily, increased from 10 mg by his PCP about 6 weeks ago. Atorvastatin 40 mg at bedtime. Metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. Aspirin 81 mg was stopped by cardiology when the apixaban was started, and the daughter confirmed he no longer takes it.

Data reviewed: Recent labs from his PCP show creatinine 1.3, eGFR 54, A1c 7.1%, and hemoglobin 13.2. Home readings this morning per the daughter were BP 138/78, pulse 72, and fingerstick glucose 128. The daughter uploaded two photos to the patient portal before the call, which I reviewed during the visit. They show a single lesion of about 9 mm with dark brown to black color, an irregular border, and a pink area along one edge. The photos are taken in room light without dermoscopy, so they cannot replace an in-person exam, and no total body skin exam was possible by phone.

Transportation: He does not drive. The daughter works full time and lives an hour away, and the clinic is about 40 miles from his home. He missed two earlier dermatology visits because no ride was available, and the daughter says that each trip means taking a full day off work.

Impression: Changing pigmented lesion of the right upper back with enlargement, color variation, and border irregularity, suspicious for melanoma until proven otherwise. The differential includes a dysplastic nevus and a pigmented basal cell carcinoma. This needs a biopsy and should not wait for a routine appointment.

Next steps, discussed with the patient and his daughter, who both agreed:
- In-person visit within 2 weeks for a full skin exam and same-day excisional biopsy, so that he needs only one trip. We will try to book it on the same day as his cardiology follow-up in the same building.
- Referral to clinic social work to arrange a medical transportation benefit or a volunteer driver. I will call the daughter back with the ride options.
- Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily; a small skin biopsy does not require holding it. Continue the other medications unchanged.
- Daughter to upload new photos with a ruler beside the lesion and to check his scalp and feet.
- Sun protection advice reviewed. Call sooner if the spot bleeds, forms a sore, or grows quickly.
- If pathology confirms melanoma, referral to dermatologic surgery for wide excision.
- Phone check in 1 week to confirm the ride and the appointment.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Hi, come on in. So I hear this little guy has been really itchy. What's been going on?
Family member: Yes, he's had eczema since he was a baby, but this past week it's gotten so much worse. He scratches all night long and barely sleeps, and now some spots on his arms are oozing and crusty.
Doctor: Okay, so we have a 3-year-old male with known atopic dermatitis and a flare. Any fever?
Family member: No fever. No vomiting or diarrhea either, he's eating and drinking fine.
Doctor: Good. Any trouble breathing or wheezing?
Family member: No trouble breathing, no wheezing. He doesn't have asthma or any food allergies.
Doctor: Anything new at home, like soaps, pets, or foods?
Family member: We changed laundry detergent about two weeks ago. Nothing else new.
Doctor: And what have you been putting on his skin?
Family member: Hydrocortisone 1% cream, once or twice a day, plus a lotion after baths. It doesn't seem to help anymore.
Doctor: Alright, let's take a look. His temperature is 98.7, heart rate 104, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and he weighs about 15 kilos. On exam there are dry, red, scaly patches on both cheeks, the inner elbows, and behind the knees, with lots of scratch marks. On the right forearm and the chin there are honey-colored crusts. Lungs are clear and there are no swollen lymph nodes. I did a skin scraping from one scaly patch for a KOH prep, and it is negative for fungus, so this is not ringworm.
Family member: Okay, so what is it then?
Doctor: This is an atopic dermatitis flare with a secondary bacterial skin infection called impetigo on the forearm and chin. The hydrocortisone 1% is just too weak for his body. So I'm going to stop it on his body and start triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice a day to the red patches on the body, arms, and legs for up to two weeks, but not on the face. You can keep using the hydrocortisone 1% cream on his face. For the crusted spots I'm starting mupirocin 2% ointment, a thin layer three times a day for seven days.
Family member: Should we change anything with his baths?
Doctor: Short lukewarm baths, then put a thick moisturizer on within a few minutes, and go back to a fragrance-free detergent. Keep his nails trimmed short. I'd like him back with his pediatrician in one week, and come back sooner if he gets a fever, the redness spreads, or you see painful blisters.
Family member: Got it, thank you.
"""

reference: A 3-year-old male presented to urgent care with a week-long flare of his known atopic dermatitis with severe itching, poor sleep, and oozing, crusted spots on the arms. Examination showed dry, red, scaly patches with scratch marks and honey-colored crusts on the right forearm and chin, and a KOH prep from a scaly patch was negative for fungus. The diagnosis was an atopic dermatitis flare with secondary impetigo. Hydrocortisone 1% was stopped on the body but continued on the face, triamcinolone 0.1% ointment and mupirocin 2% ointment were started, and pediatrician follow-up in one week was advised.

SUBJECTIVE:
3-year-old male with known atopic dermatitis (eczema since infancy) and a flare over the past week. Very itchy, scratching all night with poor sleep, and some spots on the arms are oozing and crusty. Using hydrocortisone 1% cream once or twice a day plus a lotion after baths, which no longer helps.

OBJECTIVE:
Temperature 98.7, heart rate 104, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, weight about 15 kilos. KOH prep from a skin scraping negative for fungus.

ASSESSMENT:
Atopic dermatitis flare with a secondary bacterial skin infection (impetigo) on the forearm and chin; not ringworm.

3. Start mupirocin 2% ointment, thin layer three times a day for seven days to the crusted spots
4. Short lukewarm baths followed by a thick moisturizer, fragrance-free detergent, and short trimmed nails

Doctor: Any new pain in the calf, chest pain, or shortness of breath?
Patient: No pain in the calf, no chest pain, no trouble breathing.
Doctor: What blood thinner are you taking, and how are you taking it?
Patient: Apixaban 5 mg twice a day. But I work rotating shifts at a distribution center, some weeks nights and some weeks days, so the timing is all over the place. I miss a dose about once a week.
Doctor: I appreciate your honesty. Any bleeding, like nosebleeds, bleeding gums, black or bloody stools, or blood in the urine?
Patient: No nosebleeds, no bleeding gums, no black stools, and no blood in my urine. I just have a couple of small bruises.
Doctor: Any other pills, including over-the-counter ones?
Patient: Atorvastatin 20 mg at night, and ibuprofen 400 mg a couple of times a week for my knees.
Doctor: Okay, we need to talk about the ibuprofen. Your vitals today are BP 126/78, HR 74, SpO2 98% on room air, and weight 78 kg. Your left calf is slightly swollen compared with the right, soft, and not tender. The ultrasound of your leg veins today shows the clot in the left popliteal vein is mostly dissolved, with a small amount of residual nonocclusive thrombus. Your blood count is normal with hemoglobin 12.8 and platelets 245, and your creatinine is 0.9. Your mammogram and colonoscopy are up to date, and nothing suggests a hidden cancer.
Patient: So what happens now?
Doctor: This was an unprovoked DVT with no clear trigger, so the risk of it coming back is higher. After six months, I recommend staying on a blood thinner long term but at a lower dose, so I am reducing your apixaban from 5 mg twice a day to 2.5 mg twice a day. I am also stopping the ibuprofen, because with a blood thinner it raises your bleeding risk. You can use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for your knees instead.
Patient: My schedule is the hard part. What should I do with the shifts?

"""

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 2 for a 5-month-old female infant admitted with bronchiolitis due to RSV. Her mother reports that overnight she slept in short stretches because of nasal congestion and a wet cough, but had no pauses in breathing, no color change, and no vomiting. She took about 70 percent of her usual breast milk volume overnight, up from 50 percent yesterday, and had four wet diapers in the past 12 hours. She had a low-grade fever on admission but has had none since. She was born at term and is otherwise healthy and up to date on vaccines, and her mother denies diarrhea and rash.

Background from admission: four days of runny nose, cough, fast breathing, and poor feeding. In the ED, one albuterol 2.5 mg nebulizer treatment produced no improvement and was not continued, per guideline. RSV PCR from a nasal swab was positive, and a chest x-ray showed hyperinflation with peribronchial thickening and no focal consolidation. She received maintenance IV fluids overnight, which were stopped this morning because she is feeding better. Acetaminophen 80 mg every 6 hours as needed for fever is ordered, and she has needed it once.

Vitals this morning: temperature 99.1 F, heart rate 148, respiratory rate 52, and oxygen saturation 95% on 0.5 L per minute nasal cannula, improved from 91% on room air on admission. Weight is 6.4 kg. On exam she is alert and consolable, with mild subcostal retractions, scattered end-expiratory wheezes and fine crackles, no grunting, and no nasal flaring. Mucous membranes are moist and capillary refill is under 2 seconds.

Impression is bronchiolitis from RSV, improving, with mild hypoxemia now resolving and adequate hydration. Plan is to continue supportive care with nasal suctioning before feeds, wean oxygen as tolerated to keep saturations at or above 92 percent, and move to intermittent pulse oximetry. No steroids, antibiotics, or further bronchodilators. Continue feeding on demand and recheck hydration this afternoon. Discharge once she is off oxygen and feeding well, which I expect in one to two days, after discharge teaching about warning signs with her mother.
"""

This 45-year-old female is seen in cardiology clinic for resistant hypertension. The plan is to add spironolactone 25 mg daily to her current pill, recheck potassium and creatinine in one week, and refer her for an adrenal CT scan and an endocrinology evaluation. """

We discussed giving a high-calorie breakfast before the dose and a substantial snack after school, and serving dinner later in the evening. Doctor: Good afternoon. I see you're an 83-year-old female and your daughter is with you. What brings you to urgent care today?
Patient: My fibromyalgia has flared up. For ten days I've ached all over, my neck, shoulders, back, and hips, and I can't sleep at night.
Family member: She's been up most nights and she's exhausted. Her rheumatologist can't see her until next month, so we came here.
Doctor: I'm sorry to hear that. Any fever?
Patient: No fever.
Doctor: Any pain in your jaw when you chew, a new headache, tenderness of the scalp, or changes in your vision?
Patient: No jaw pain, no headache, and my vision is the same.
Doctor: Any swollen joints, a rash, or new weakness?
Patient: No swelling, no rash, and no weakness. I just hurt everywhere.
Doctor: Any falls?
Patient: I haven't fallen, but I feel dizzy in the morning after I take the muscle relaxer at night.
Doctor: Let's go over your medicines.

Patient: So is it something else?

Your blood pressure is acceptable. Here is the plan. I want you to stop the cyclobenzaprine because it can cause dizziness and falls at your age. I'm starting gabapentin 100 mg at bedtime to help with the pain and sleep. Keep taking duloxetine 30 mg every morning and amlodipine as before, and acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed, no more than four doses a day. Gentle walking and warm water exercise will help, and keep a regular bedtime routine. Please call your rheumatologist's office tomorrow and ask for an earlier visit within one to two weeks. Come back or go to the emergency department for fever, a new severe headache, vision changes, or a fall.
Family member: Thank you, doctor. We will do that.
"""

This is an emergency department dictation on a 59-year-old male with an acute asthma attack. Chief complaint is shortness of breath and wheezing for one day. History is from the patient and from his wife who is at the bedside because he can only speak in short phrases. He has had asthma for many years and says he caught a cold with a runny nose and cough four days ago, then the wheezing and chest tightness started yesterday and got steadily worse overnight until he could not lie flat. He used his albuterol inhaler about every hour through the night with only brief relief. He denies fever, chest pain, leg swelling, hemoptysis, and abdominal pain, and he has not been around anyone who is sick with the flu. Past medical history includes asthma, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, GERD, and obesity. His wife reads the medication list from her phone, fluticasone salmeterol 250/50 one inhalation twice daily, albuterol inhaler two puffs every four hours as needed, montelukast 10 mg nightly, lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, correction, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, she rechecked the bottle and it is 1000 twice daily, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. She also says he has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for the past week for knee pain, and the patient confirms that. He has never smoked and rarely drinks alcohol.

On arrival blood pressure 158/92, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 89% on room air, temperature 37.1 Celsius, and peak flow 180 liters per minute. On exam he is sitting upright in a tripod position and speaks in two to three word phrases, with accessory muscle use, diffuse expiratory wheezes, a prolonged expiratory phase, and decreased air movement at both bases. No stridor, no cyanosis, no peripheral edema, and the heart is tachycardic but regular without a murmur.

ED course, he received three back to back albuterol ipratropium nebulizers, methylprednisolone 125 mg IV once, and magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 minutes. After treatment his respiratory rate was 18, heart rate 92, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and peak flow 380 liters per minute. Labs show WBC 11.8, hemoglobin 14.6, platelets 245, glucose 248, potassium 3.4, and creatinine 1.0. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.36 and pCO2 42. Troponin was negative. Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation without infiltrate or pneumothorax, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes.

Medical decision making, this is a moderate to severe asthma exacerbation triggered by a viral upper respiratory infection and likely worsened by regular ibuprofen use. The hyperglycemia is from his diabetes and the stress of the illness, and the mild hypokalemia is from the albuterol. He was observed for four hours with no return of symptoms and was then safe for discharge. Plan is prednisone 40 mg daily for five days, and I am increasing his fluticasone salmeterol from 250/50 to 500/50, one inhalation twice daily. I am stopping the ibuprofen and he can use acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed for knee pain. He will continue albuterol, montelukast, lisinopril, metformin, and omeprazole as before and check his blood sugar twice a day while on prednisone. He will see his primary care doctor in two to three days and pulmonology in two weeks, and return right away for worsening breathing, trouble speaking, or blue lips. His wife understands the plan and agrees.

After albuterol ipratropium nebulizers, methylprednisolone, and magnesium sulfate, his saturation was 96% and peak flow improved from 180 to 380. The impression was a moderate to severe asthma exacerbation worsened by ibuprofen. He was discharged on prednisone, a higher fluticasone salmeterol dose, and no ibuprofen, with early follow-up.
note:
This is an emergency department dictation on a 59-year-old male with an acute asthma attack. Chief complaint is shortness of breath and wheezing for one day. History is from the patient and from his wife who is at the bedside because he can only speak in short phrases. He has had asthma for many years and says he caught a cold with a runny nose and cough four days ago, then the wheezing and chest tightness started yesterday and got steadily worse overnight until he could not lie flat. He used his albuterol inhaler about every hour through the night with only brief relief. He denies fever, chest pain, leg swelling, hemoptysis, and abdominal pain, and he has not been around anyone who is sick with the flu. Past medical history includes asthma, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, GERD, and obesity. His wife reads the medication list from her phone, fluticasone salmeterol 250/50 one inhalation twice daily, albuterol inhaler two puffs every four hours as needed, montelukast 10 mg nightly, lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, correction, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, she rechecked the bottle and it is 1000 twice daily, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. She also says he has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for the past week for knee pain, and the patient confirms that. He has never smoked and rarely drinks alcohol.

On arrival blood pressure 158/92, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 89% on room air, temperature 37.1 Celsius, and peak flow 180 liters per minute. On exam he is sitting upright in a tripod position and speaks in two to three word phrases, with accessory muscle use, diffuse expiratory wheezes, a prolonged expiratory phase, and decreased air movement at both bases. No stridor, no cyanosis, no peripheral edema, and the heart is tachycardic but regular without a murmur.

ED course, he received three back to back albuterol ipratropium nebulizers, methylprednisolone 125 mg IV once, and magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 minutes. After treatment his respiratory rate was 18, heart rate 92, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and peak flow 380 liters per minute. Labs show WBC 11.8, hemoglobin 14.6, platelets 245, glucose 248, potassium 3.4, and creatinine 1.0. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.36 and pCO2 42. Troponin was negative. Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation without infiltrate or pneumothorax, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes.

Medical decision making, this is a moderate to severe asthma exacerbation triggered by a viral upper respiratory infection and likely worsened by regular ibuprofen use. The hyperglycemia is from his diabetes and the stress of the illness, and the mild hypokalemia is from the albuterol. He was observed for four hours with no return of symptoms and was then safe for discharge. Plan is prednisone 40 mg daily for five days, and I am increasing his fluticasone salmeterol from 250/50 to 500/50, one inhalation twice daily. I am stopping the ibuprofen and he can use acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed for knee pain. He will continue albuterol, montelukast, lisinopril, metformin, and omeprazole as before and check his blood sugar twice a day while on prednisone. He will see his primary care doctor in two to three days and pulmonology in two weeks, and return right away for worsening breathing, trouble speaking, or blue lips. His wife understands the plan and agrees.

Clinical note:
"""
HD 2, hospitalist. 84-year-old female w/ LLE cellulitis, HTN, chronic venous stasis. Lives w/ daughter, ambulates w/ walker at baseline.
Admitted 2 days ago w/ red, warm, swollen L lower leg x 3 days.
NAE overnight. Afebrile. Leg pain improving, 5/10 -> 3/10. Eating well.
Denies fever, chills, purulent drainage, chest pain, SOB, calf pain.
Hx: no prior cellulitis, no DM, no PVD. Never smoker. Not on blood thinners.
Overnight RN: pain controlled, voiding well, slept okay, walked to bathroom w/ walker and 1 assist.

Meds: ceftriaxone 1 g IV q24h. Amlodipine 5 mg daily. Acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN. Lisinopril 10 mg daily on hold since admit (AKI). NKDA.

Vitals: Tmax 99.4 F, HR 82, BP 126/68, RR 16, SpO2 96% RA.
Exam: NAD, A&O. RRR, lungs CTA. L lower leg erythema, warmth, 1+ pitting edema; border marked on admit, receded ~2 cm from marked line. No bullae, no crepitus, no fluctuance, no purulence. DP pulses palpable. No foot ulcers.

Labs: WBC 14.2 -> 10.8. Cr 1.6 -> 1.2 (baseline 1.0). CRP 8.4. Blood cx x2 NGTD. LLE venous duplex neg for DVT.

A/P:
1. LLE cellulitis, improving on IV abx. Cont ceftriaxone 1 g IV q24h today. If continues to improve, switch to PO cephalexin 500 mg QID tomorrow, total 7 days. Elevate leg, compression once infection settles.
2. Mild AKI on admit, prerenal, improving w/ IV fluids. Hold lisinopril. BMP in AM.
3. HTN, BP controlled on amlodipine. Cont amlodipine 5 mg daily.
Acetaminophen PRN for pain. PT eval. Dispo home w/ daughter likely in 1-2 days.
"""

Telehealth note, video visit. The patient is a 62-year-old female seeking evaluation of gradual hearing loss. Her daughter, who lives with her, joined the video call and provided part of the history. Over about 2 years, the patient has noticed trouble following conversation in restaurants and when several people talk at once. Her daughter reports that she turns the television volume up and often asks people to repeat themselves. The loss seems about the same in both ears and has not changed suddenly. She denies ear pain, ear drainage, dizziness, and tinnitus. She has not had recent ear infections or head injury. Her only chronic condition is hypertension, and she takes lisinopril 10 mg once daily.

On video, her external ears looked normal, with no visible drainage. She had to ask me to repeat questions when I spoke at a normal volume with my face turned away, but understood me well when I faced the camera and spoke slowly. Otoscopy and a hearing test cannot be done by video.

Impression: gradual, probably bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, most consistent with presbycusis. Recommendations: in-person visit for otoscopy and audiometry, and a hearing aid evaluation if the audiometry confirms hearing loss. In the meantime, face her when speaking and reduce background noise. She should call sooner for sudden hearing loss, ear pain, or dizziness.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Hi, what brings you in today? I have you down as a 36-year-old female with back pain.
Patient: Yes. For about a week I've had low back pain that shoots down my right leg, from my buttock down the back of my thigh to my calf. It started after I lifted a heavy box while moving. My right foot has been tingling too.
Doctor: Any weakness in the leg, numbness in the groin or inner thighs, trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, or fever?
Patient: No weakness, no numbness in the groin, no trouble with my bladder or bowels, and no fever.
Doctor: Good. Do you have help at home?
Patient: Not really. I live alone and my family is far away, so it's been hard to shop for groceries or even get to the pharmacy.
Doctor: I understand. Let me examine you. Blood pressure is 118/70 and pulse is 72. You're tender over the right lower back muscles. The straight leg raise on the right reproduces the pain down your leg at about 40 degrees. Strength is normal in both legs, reflexes are normal, and sensation is slightly decreased on the outside of the right calf.
Doctor: This is a right lumbar radiculopathy, probably from a herniated disc, and there are no red flags like weakness or bladder problems. Most people improve within six weeks without surgery. I'm starting naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food for 10 days. Stay gently active and avoid heavy lifting. I'm referring you to physical therapy, and if you're not better in six weeks, we'll get an MRI. Since you live alone, I'm asking our social worker to call you tomorrow about grocery delivery and rides to therapy.
Patient: Thank you. That would really help. What if my leg gets weak?
Doctor: Come back or go to the emergency department right away for leg weakness, numbness in the groin, or loss of bladder or bowel control. Follow up with orthopedics in two weeks.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Hi, what brings you in today? I have you down as a 36-year-old female with back pain.
Patient: Yes. For about a week I've had low back pain that shoots down my right leg, from my buttock down the back of my thigh to my calf. It started after I lifted a heavy box while moving. My right foot has been tingling too.
Doctor: Any weakness in the leg, numbness in the groin or inner thighs, trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, or fever?
Patient: No weakness, no numbness in the groin, no trouble with my bladder or bowels, and no fever.
Doctor: Good. Do you have help at home?
Patient: Not really. I live alone and my family is far away, so it's been hard to shop for groceries or even get to the pharmacy.
Doctor: I understand. Let me examine you. Blood pressure is 118/70 and pulse is 72. You're tender over the right lower back muscles. The straight leg raise on the right reproduces the pain down your leg at about 40 degrees. Strength is normal in both legs, reflexes are normal, and sensation is slightly decreased on the outside of the right calf.
Doctor: This is a right lumbar radiculopathy, probably from a herniated disc, and there are no red flags like weakness or bladder problems. Most people improve within six weeks without surgery. I'm starting naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food for 10 days. Stay gently active and avoid heavy lifting. I'm referring you to physical therapy, and if you're not better in six weeks, we'll get an MRI. Since you live alone, I'm asking our social worker to call you tomorrow about grocery delivery and rides to therapy.
Patient: Thank you. That would really help. What if my leg gets weak?
Doctor: Come back or go to the emergency department right away for leg weakness, numbness in the groin, or loss of bladder or bowel control. Follow up with orthopedics in two weeks.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
79-year-old male, GI clinic, new pt referred by PCP for iron-deficiency anemia work-up.

CC: fatigue + DOE x 3 mo.
HPI: PCP labs 3 wk ago: Hgb 9.1, MCV 72, ferritin 7, TSAT 6%. Fatigue and DOE walking 1 block.
Denies melena, hematochezia, abd pain, dysphagia, early satiety, wt loss.
No change in bowel habits.
Last colonoscopy 9 yrs ago, normal per pt. No FH of colon CA.
PMH: HTN, HLD. No hx of GI bleed or ulcer. NKDA.
Meds: aspirin 81 mg daily (self-started for primary prevention, no CAD or stent), amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. Denies other NSAID use.
Social: never smoker, 1-2 beers/wk.

VS: BP 126/74, HR 82, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, Wt 76 kg (stable vs PCP).
Gen: NAD, mild conjunctival pallor.
CV: RRR. Lungs: CTAB.
Abd: soft, NT, ND, no masses, no HSM.
DRE: no mass, brown stool, guaiac neg.
Labs from PCP: B12 and folate nl, Cr 1.0.

Imp:
1. Iron-deficiency anemia, microcytic, r/o occult GI blood loss. Upper source (PUD, gastritis, celiac, malignancy) vs colonic source (neoplasm).
2. Daily aspirin w/o clear indication, may contribute.
3. HTN, HLD, stable.

Mgmt:
- Stop aspirin 81 mg (no CAD or stent, no indication).
- Start ferrous sulfate 325 mg every other day.
- EGD w/ biopsies + colonoscopy, schedule in 2 wk. Hold iron 5 d before colonoscopy.
- tTG-IgA and H. pylori stool antigen today.
- If EGD and colonoscopy neg, consider capsule endoscopy.
- Recheck CBC + ferritin in 4-6 wk.
- Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly.
- RTC after procedures. Return/ED for melena, hematochezia, syncope, chest pain.
"""

Outside labs showed Hgb 9.1, MCV 72 and ferritin 7, and exam showed mild conjunctival pallor with guaiac-negative brown stool on DRE. The impression was microcytic iron-deficiency anemia with possible occult GI blood loss, with daily aspirin as a possible contributor. Aspirin was stopped, ferrous sulfate was started, and EGD with biopsies, colonoscopy, tTG-IgA and H. pylori stool antigen were ordered.

"""
39-year-old female, hospital day 2, hospitalist progress note.
Admitted w/ AKI 2/2 dehydration after viral gastroenteritis.

Interval: vomiting + diarrhea x 3 d prior to admit, now resolved. Tolerating regular diet, drinking well. Took ibuprofen 400 mg q6h for cramps during the illness.
Denies hematuria, dysuria, flank pain. No fever. No chest pain.
No other home meds. NKDA.

VS: BP 112/70 (admit 94/58), HR 84 (admit 118), Temp 98.6 F, SpO2 99% RA.
Exam: NAD. Mucous membranes moist today (dry on admit). Abd soft, NT, ND. No edema. Cap refill brisk.

Labs: Cr 1.4 today (2.1 on admit, baseline 0.7). BUN 22 (38 on admit). K 3.8, Na 138, HCO3 22.
UA bland, no protein, no blood. FENa 0.6%.
Renal US: no hydronephrosis.

Dx: prerenal AKI from dehydration, improving. Viral gastroenteritis, resolved. Ibuprofen likely contributed.
Rx:
Normal saline 1 L bolus on admit, then 125 mL/hr, continue until PO intake adequate then stop.
STOP ibuprofen, avoid NSAIDs.
Repeat BMP in AM.
Strict I&O, daily weights.
D/c home tomorrow if Cr < 1.0 and eating.
F/u PCP w/ BMP in 1 wk.
"""

reference: A 39-year-old female was seen on hospital day 2 for acute kidney injury from dehydration after 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea, now resolved, with ibuprofen use during the illness. She denied hematuria, dysuria, flank pain, fever, and chest pain. Clinical note:
"""
Nurse: Okay, you're in room three. Your blood pressure is 118 over 76, pulse 82, temperature 98.2.
Doctor: Thank you, and welcome to urgent care. So I have you down as a 36-year-old female with pelvic pain that keeps coming back. Tell me what's been going on.
Patient: It's been about two years now. It's low in my belly, kind of on both sides, and it gets really bad right before and during my period. Today it's worse than usual, like a seven out of ten.
Doctor: Does it happen at other times of the month?
Patient: More and more, yeah. Some days it just aches all the time. And it hurts when I have sex, deep inside. It also hurts when I go to the bathroom during my period.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No, none.
Doctor: Any unusual discharge, burning when you urinate, or bleeding between periods?
Patient: No discharge, no burning, and no bleeding in between. My periods are heavy, but they come on time.
Doctor: Any nausea or vomiting?
Patient: No.
Doctor: What have you been taking for the pain?
Patient: Ibuprofen, 400 milligrams, maybe twice a day when it's bad. It only helps a little. I've been to the ER and to urgent care a few times, and they told me my tests were fine.
Doctor: Any surgeries, other health problems, or allergies to medicines?
Patient: No surgeries, nothing else, and no allergies.
Doctor: Have you seen a gynecologist?

Altogether, my working diagnosis is chronic pelvic pain, and I suspect endometriosis.
Patient: Is that serious?
Doctor: It's common and treatable, but we should confirm it. First, increase your ibuprofen to 600 milligrams every six hours with food for the next week. Second, I'm starting norethindrone acetate 5 milligrams once a day, taken continuously, and I'll write for a 90-day supply so you don't need a ride for refills. Third, I'm ordering a transvaginal ultrasound, and our social worker will give you a ride voucher for it. Your gynecology follow-up will be a video visit so you don't have to travel. Go to the emergency room for a fever, heavy bleeding, or severe pain that doesn't ease.
Patient: Okay, that works for me. Thank you.
"""

"""
Hospital day 2 for the 76-year-old female admitted with febrile neutropenia six days after cycle 3 of R-CHOP for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

Overnight events: Fever to 100.9 F at 2 AM with no rigors, and she remained hemodynamically stable. Her daughter, who is at the bedside and helps manage her medications at home, reports that the patient had chills and poor oral intake for two days before admission and that mouth soreness began three days ago. The patient confirms the mouth soreness and says swallowing is painful, but she denies cough, abdominal pain, diarrhea, burning with urination, and rash. Her daughter denies any sick contacts at home.

Current medications: cefepime 2 g IV every 12 hours (adjusted from every 8 hours on admission after her CrCl was estimated at 46 mL/min), filgrastim 300 mcg subcutaneously daily (started yesterday), nystatin suspension 5 mL swish and swallow four times daily (started today), and potassium chloride 40 mEq by mouth once this morning.

Vitals: Tmax 100.9 F, BP 108/64, HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air.
Labs: WBC 0.6 (0.9 yesterday), ANC 0.2, Hgb 9.4, platelets 88, K 3.2, creatinine 1.1. Blood cultures from admission show no growth at 24 hours. Chest x-ray on admission was clear and urinalysis was negative.

Exam: Tired-appearing but alert. Oral mucosa is erythematous with shallow ulcers on the buccal mucosa and white plaques on the tongue. Heart regular, lungs clear, abdomen soft and nontender, no perianal tenderness, no rash.

Febrile neutropenia: Continue cefepime 2 g IV every 12 hours with renal dosing. Continue filgrastim 300 mcg daily until the ANC recovers. Follow blood cultures to 5 days, neutropenic precautions, and daily CBC with differential.
Oral mucositis with thrush: Nystatin as above, salt and baking soda rinses, soft diet, and dietitian consult.
Hypokalemia: Potassium chloride 40 mEq by mouth once today and recheck potassium in the morning.
Disposition: Expect discharge when afebrile for 48 hours and the ANC is recovering. Oncology will hold cycle 4 until counts recover.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Nurse: Triage note for the doctor. This is a 33-year-old female with lung cancer on immunotherapy, here with cough and shortness of breath. Oxygen saturation is 92% on room air and temperature is 37.8 Celsius.
Doctor: Thank you. Hello, I'm sorry you are not feeling well. I see you are a 33-year-old female with stage four lung adenocarcinoma. What has been going on?
Patient: I've had a dry cough for about five days, and over the last two days I get winded just walking up the stairs. That is not normal for me.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: I felt warm last night and my thermometer said 99.9, but no shaking chills.
Doctor: Any chest pain, or coughing up blood?
Patient: No chest pain and no blood.
Doctor: Any leg pain or swelling?
Patient: No, my legs feel fine.
Doctor: I understand you recently traveled.
Patient: Yes, I got back eight days ago from a family wedding in Portugal. The flights were about ten hours each way.
Doctor: Any diarrhea, vomiting, or rash while you were away or since?
Patient: No diarrhea, no vomiting, and no rash. My cousin had a cold at the wedding, though.
Doctor: Okay. Tell me about your medicines.
Patient: I get pembrolizumab 200 mg by IV every three weeks, and my last infusion was ten days ago. I take levothyroxine 100 micrograms every morning for the underactive thyroid the immunotherapy caused. Wait, sorry, that is wrong. My endocrinologist lowered it to 75 micrograms four weeks ago, so it is 75.
Doctor: So levothyroxine 75 micrograms every morning, not 100. Is that right?
Patient: Yes, 75. I also have asthma, so I use albuterol, 2 puffs as needed, and I have needed it three or four times a day this week. I was on omeprazole 20 mg once a day for reflux, but I stopped it two weeks ago because my reflux got better. I have been taking ibuprofen 400 mg for headaches a few times this week, and acetaminophen 650 mg sometimes.
Doctor: Any drug allergies?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Thank you. Now your exam. Your heart rate is 108, respiratory rate 22, blood pressure 112/70, and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. You look tired but you are speaking in full sentences. I hear fine crackles at the bottom of both lungs with no wheezing. Your heart is fast but regular. Your calves are not swollen or tender, and both legs look the same. Your belly is soft and there is no rash.
Patient: What do the tests show?
Doctor: The chest x-ray shows hazy patchy opacities in both lower lungs, with no large effusion and no collapsed lung. The rapid COVID and flu tests are both negative. Your white blood cell count is 9.8, hemoglobin is 11.4, and creatinine is 0.7. The D-dimer is elevated at 1.9, which is nonspecific in someone with cancer. Your urine pregnancy test is negative. We gave you oxygen at 2 liters per minute and your saturation is up to 95%.
Patient: What do you think this is?
Doctor: The most likely explanation is pneumonitis, which is inflammation of the lungs caused by your immunotherapy. A lung infection and a blood clot in the lungs are also possible after your long flights, and your oxygen is low, so I cannot safely sort this out here. I am sending you by ambulance to the emergency department for a CT angiogram of the chest and further workup. I am calling the oncologist on call myself. Please do not receive your next pembrolizumab dose until oncology reviews you. I am not starting steroids here, because the emergency team and oncology will decide that after the CT. Stop the ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed instead. Leave the omeprazole off, keep taking levothyroxine 75 micrograms, and use albuterol 2 puffs every four hours as needed until you are seen.
Patient: Okay. I'm scared, but I understand.
Doctor: That is understandable. A nurse will stay with you until the ambulance arrives.
"""

Hospital day 2 for a 74-year-old female admitted with acute bacterial sinusitis. She presented with 11 days of right facial pain, thick green nasal drainage, and a fever that returned after initial improvement, and she was admitted because of severe headache and poor oral intake. She is very anxious this morning and had many questions. She asked whether the infection could spread to her brain or eyes, whether she will need surgery, whether she caught it from a visitor, and why she is not getting an MRI. I answered each question in turn and reviewed the CT result with her, and she said she felt calmer afterward. Her facial pressure and headache are better today and she is drinking well. She denies vision changes, double vision, neck stiffness, confusion, and swelling around the eyes. She denies chest pain and shortness of breath.

Her history includes hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Current medications are ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours since admission, amlodipine 5 mg daily, and acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for headache. Metformin 500 mg BID was held on admission. She has no known drug allergies.

Vitals this morning: T 99.0 F, HR 82, BP 134/78, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air. She appears anxious but is alert and oriented. She has right maxillary tenderness, purulent drainage in the right middle meatus, and boggy turbinates. There is no periorbital edema, extraocular movements are intact, and her neck is supple. Lungs are clear. Labs show WBC 12.4, down from 15.8 on admission, and creatinine 0.9. Fingerstick glucose has been 140 to 170. CT of the sinuses without contrast on admission showed an air-fluid level in the right maxillary sinus with mucosal thickening and no orbital or intracranial extension.

Impression is acute bacterial sinusitis, improving, with no complications on CT. Hypertension is controlled and type 2 diabetes is stable now that she is eating. Because she is tolerating a diet and improving, I am stopping IV ampicillin-sulbactam and starting amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg/125 mg PO BID to finish 10 days of total therapy. I am also restarting metformin 500 mg BID with meals. We will continue amlodipine, add saline nasal irrigation twice daily, and continue acetaminophen as needed. I will refer her to ENT if symptoms do not continue to improve. She can likely go home tomorrow if she remains stable, and I will see her in clinic in 1 week.
"""

"""
Hospital medicine progress note, hospital day 2, dictating on a 44-year-old female admitted with an upper gastrointestinal bleed. She presented two days ago with three days of black tarry stools and one episode of coffee ground emesis, along with lightheadedness on standing. She denies chest pain, denies shortness of breath at rest, denies abdominal distension, and denies any bright red blood per rectum. Past medical history includes a pulmonary embolism about eight months ago for which she takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily, hypertension on lisinopril 20 mg daily, type 2 diabetes on metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and chronic low back pain for which she had been taking ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for the past month. She is a current tobacco smoker at about one pack per day, correction, about half a pack per day, for twenty years. She denies alcohol use and has no known drug allergies.

On admission her hemoglobin was 7.4 compared with a baseline of 12.8 last year, and she received two units of packed red blood cells overnight with an appropriate rise. This morning her hemoglobin is 8.6, correction, 8.9. Platelets are 245, INR 1.3, creatinine 0.8, and BUN 28. Her last dose of apixaban was the evening before admission. She has been hemodynamically stable overnight with no further melena since admission. Vitals this morning are temperature 98.4 Fahrenheit, heart rate 88, blood pressure 118 over 72, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.

On examination she has conjunctival pallor and mild epigastric tenderness. Her rhythm is regular and the lungs are clear. She is in no acute distress. There is no guarding, no rebound, and no abdominal distension. Rectal exam in the emergency department showed melena.

Upper endoscopy yesterday afternoon showed a 1.5 cm gastric antral ulcer with a visible vessel, which was treated with epinephrine injection and two hemoclips, and biopsies were taken to test for H. pylori. She was started on pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus followed by an infusion at 8 mg per hour, which I am changing today to pantoprazole 40 mg IV twice daily.

Assessment and plan by problem. Number one, upper gastrointestinal bleed from an NSAID-associated gastric ulcer, status post endoscopic therapy and hemodynamically stable. I am continuing the PPI as above and permanently stopping ibuprofen and all other NSAIDs. We will follow the H. pylori pathology and treat if positive. I advanced her to a full liquid diet today and will repeat a CBC every 8 hours today. Number two, acute blood loss anemia, status post transfusion, goal hemoglobin above 7, and I will add iron studies. Number three, history of pulmonary embolism on apixaban, which has been held since admission. Given the high-risk bleed I will keep apixaban held and plan to restart in about 7 days if the hemoglobin stays stable, after confirming with GI and pharmacy, with no heparin bridging. Number four, hypertension, lisinopril is on hold while she is at risk of hypovolemia and her pressure is acceptable. Number five, type 2 diabetes, metformin is held in the hospital and I started insulin lispro correction scale with meals, hemoglobin A1c is 7.9%. Number six, tobacco use, I counseled her on cessation and started a nicotine patch 14 mg daily. Number seven, chronic low back pain, I started acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed and she will see her primary care clinician after discharge for non-NSAID options. Anticipate discharge in two days if hemoglobin remains stable.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Postpartum day 2 progress note for a 30-year-old female, gravida 2 para 2, who delivered a healthy term infant vaginally two days ago. Her labor was uncomplicated, but she sustained a second-degree perineal laceration that was repaired at delivery, and the estimated blood loss was 450 mL.

This morning she reports moderate perineal pain, about 4 out of 10, which is improving with medication. Her bleeding is lighter than yesterday. She is breastfeeding and says the baby is latching better since the lactation nurse visited. She feels tired and a little lightheaded when she stands up quickly. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, calf pain, and heavy vaginal bleeding. She has not had headaches or visual changes. She has not had a bowel movement since delivery and is worried about straining over her stitches.

She has no known drug allergies. For medications, she takes ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours as prescribed on the unit. She also uses over-the-counter supplements: a prenatal multivitamin daily, and fenugreek capsules that she started two days ago hoping to increase her milk supply. She took ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily during pregnancy for mild anemia but has not taken it since admission.

On examination she is tired-appearing but comfortable. Temperature is 98.4 F, heart rate 92, blood pressure 108/66, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The fundus is firm at the umbilicus and nontender. Lochia is moderate rubra without clots. The perineal repair is intact with mild edema and no hematoma or purulent drainage. Her breasts are soft. Her calves are soft and nontender without swelling. Lungs are clear and heart rhythm is regular. Hemoglobin this morning is 9.8 g/dL, down from 11.2 g/dL before delivery, and the platelet count is normal.

My impression is postpartum day 2 after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with a second-degree perineal laceration, mild postpartum anemia from blood loss, and a risk of constipation. Her lightheadedness is most consistent with the anemia and should improve with iron. We will continue ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours with food, and she may use ice packs and sitz baths for perineal comfort. I am starting docusate 100 mg twice daily to prevent constipation and restarting ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily. She should continue her prenatal multivitamin daily. I advised her to stop the fenugreek capsules and to review her milk supply concerns with the lactation nurse instead, because it can upset the stomach and its benefit is unproven. A repeat hemoglobin will be checked tomorrow morning, and she is expected to go home tomorrow with a postpartum clinic visit in two weeks.
"""

Reason for visit: follow-up of major depressive disorder and medication management for a 72-year-old male, the first psychiatry contact since a recent hospitalization.

History reported by the patient: He was hospitalized for five days about three weeks ago for a COPD exacerbation and was discharged on a prednisone taper, which he has finished, plus a new tiotropium inhaler. Since discharge his mood has been lower. He reports low energy, loss of interest in things he usually enjoys, early morning waking around 3 am, decreased appetite, and a 4 pound weight loss on his home scale. He feels discouraged about his health but denies suicidal thoughts, plan, or intent, denies hallucinations, and says there are no firearms in the home. He denies alcohol use since the hospitalization. His daughter calls him every day. PHQ-9 administered by phone today was 17, up from 12 at his last visit. He currently smokes about 10 cigarettes a day, up from 5 before the admission, and says he wants to quit.

Medications: when asked, he first said he takes sertraline 50 mg daily, then read the bottle aloud and corrected this to sertraline 100 mg once daily. Doctor: Hello, I'm seeing an 83-year-old female who fell at home this afternoon. Can you tell me what happened?

Doctor: Did you black out before or after you fell?
Patient: No, I remember the whole thing. I didn't pass out.
Doctor: Any neck pain, vomiting, confusion, or vision changes?
Patient: No neck pain, no vomiting, and I feel clear-headed. I just have a sore spot on my forehead.

Patient: Apixaban, 5 mg twice a day. I took this morning's dose.
Doctor: Any other medicines?
Patient: No, that's the only one.

Patient: Do I stop the blood thinner?

Your daughter should stay with you tonight, and come back right away if you get a worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, or unusual sleepiness. I'll also have physical therapy look at your home safety, please remove loose rugs, and see your primary care doctor in a week.
Patient: Okay, thank you.
"""

Orders and advice: Because he is still recovering from his hospitalization, in-office cryotherapy will be deferred. Start fluorouracil 5% cream, thin layer to the forehead and scalp twice daily for 3 weeks, and he was told to expect redness, crusting and irritation. Daily sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and a wide-brimmed hat. Continue current medications. In-person visit in 4 weeks for a total body skin exam, cryotherapy of persistent lesions, and biopsy of anything suspicious. Contact the clinic sooner for bleeding, ulceration, rapid growth, or return of fever. Follow up with his primary care clinician about the pneumonia.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
The patient is a 92-year-old male seen in geriatrics clinic for advance care planning and follow-up of his chronic conditions. He lives alone in his own home and has limited social support: a neighbor checks on him a few times a week and a son who lives in another state calls on weekends. He wants to remain at home for as long as possible.

His history includes heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, hypertension, and mild cognitive impairment. Over the past two weeks he has noticed more shortness of breath when walking to his mailbox and mild ankle swelling, and his home weight is up about 4 pounds. He denies chest pain, orthopnea, and dizziness. His medications are furosemide 20 mg daily, apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, and diphenhydramine 25 mg nightly, which he has taken for years to help him sleep.

Vitals today are BP 118/64, HR 70 and irregular, SpO2 95% on room air, and weight 168 pounds. He has mild bibasilar crackles and 1+ pitting edema of both ankles, with no jugular venous distension. His MoCA score today is 24 out of 30. He explained his conditions and the choices in his own words and showed good decision-making capacity. Labs from two weeks ago show creatinine 1.6 mg/dL with an eGFR of 38, hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, and potassium 4.3.

We spent 40 minutes on advance care planning. He understands that his heart and kidney disease are likely to progress. His goals are to stay in his home, avoid long hospital stays, and keep his independence. He would accept hospital admission for treatable problems such as pneumonia or fluid overload, but he does not want CPR or a breathing machine. He named his son as his health care proxy. We completed a POLST form today that documents DNR/DNI with selective treatment, and he signed it. Copies will go to his son and be kept on his refrigerator.

Impression is mild volume overload from heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, completed advance care planning, and a sedating anticholinergic that is not appropriate with his cognitive impairment. I increased furosemide from 20 mg to 40 mg daily and will recheck a basic metabolic panel in one week. I stopped diphenhydramine and reviewed sleep hygiene. He will continue apixaban and metoprolol succinate. I am referring him to home health nursing, social work, and palliative care for added support, and social work will help arrange a medical alert pendant and home meal delivery. He will weigh himself daily and call the clinic if his weight goes up more than 3 pounds in two days. Follow-up is in two weeks.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Telehealth video visit for urology follow-up. The patient joined by secure two-way video from her home, alone in a quiet room, and she is able to hear and see me without difficulty. This is a 70-year-old female with overactive bladder who also takes an anticoagulant. History is patient-reported and the examination is limited to what can be seen on video.

She has had urinary urgency and frequency for about a year, with urge incontinence two to three times a week and nocturia four times a night. She also reports dry mouth and constipation since starting oxybutynin several months ago. She first told me she takes oxybutynin 10 mg three times daily, then checked the bottle during the visit and corrected this to 5 mg twice daily. She denies dysuria, gross hematuria, fever, flank pain, or a feeling of incomplete emptying. She drinks about two liters of fluid a day and has tea in the evening.

Her past history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. Current medications are apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, furosemide 40 mg daily taken at 4 in the afternoon for ankle swelling that she says resolved months ago, and oxybutynin as above. She has no known drug allergies.

Home measurements this morning on her own cuff were blood pressure 128/76 and heart rate 66. On video she appears comfortable, speaks in full sentences, and has no respiratory distress. There is no visible swelling of the ankles when she raises her feet toward the camera. She is alert and follows instructions without difficulty.

Results reviewed: urinalysis from her primary care physician last week showed 5 to 10 red blood cells per high power field with negative nitrite and negative leukocyte esterase, and the urine culture showed no growth. Creatinine is 0.9 with an eGFR of 70, and HbA1c is 7.1%. A bladder scan at her last clinic visit showed a post-void residual of 40 mL.

Impression and plan. She has overactive bladder with urge incontinence and nocturia, with bothersome dry mouth and constipation on oxybutynin, which is also not an ideal drug at her age. She also has microscopic hematuria while on apixaban, which needs a full evaluation and should not be attributed to the anticoagulant alone. Stop oxybutynin. Start mirabegron 25 mg once daily. Mirabegron can raise blood pressure and can increase metoprolol levels, so she will check her blood pressure daily for two weeks and send the readings through the portal, and she will report a slow pulse or lightheadedness. Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily without interruption. Order a renal and bladder ultrasound and refer her for cystoscopy to evaluate the microscopic hematuria. Reduce furosemide from 40 mg to 20 mg daily and take it in the morning, since the ankle swelling has resolved and the afternoon dose worsens nocturia; her primary care physician will be notified. Complete a three-day bladder diary and limit tea after dinner. Refer to pelvic floor physical therapy. Follow-up video visit in four weeks. She should call right away or go to the emergency department for gross blood in the urine, fever, flank pain, or inability to urinate.
"""

Doctor: For how long?
Patient: Since I was twenty.
Doctor: Okay. The ER report says your CT of the head was normal, your glucose was 112, your sodium was 138, and the drug screen was negative. Now tell me what medicines you take.
Patient: Lisinopril 40 mg once a day. Actually, wait, let me look at the bottle. It says 10 mg. Sorry, 10 mg once a day. Doctor: Do you take all of those regularly?
Patient: Not really, doctor. The copay went up and I couldn't afford everything. I stopped the atorvastatin two months ago, I only use the tiotropium a few days a week, and I take the metformin once a day instead of twice.

"""

60-year-old male, urgent care visit, referred by employer health after positive TB screen.
IGRA positive on employer screening 1 wk ago. Asymptomatic.
Denies cough, fever, night sweats, wt loss, hemoptysis.
Born in a country w/ high TB burden. No known TB contact. No prior TB tx.
PMH: HTN. Meds: lisinopril 10 mg daily. NKDA. No liver dz, no alcohol use.
Vitals: BP 128/76, HR 70, T 98.2 F, SpO2 98% RA.
Exam: lungs CTA, no LAD, abd benign.
CXR today: clear, no infiltrate, no cavity.
Baseline LFTs: AST 26, ALT 30, normal. HIV test neg.
Imp: latent TB infection (LTBI), no evidence of active TB.
Rx:
- Start rifampin 600 mg daily x 4 months (4R regimen)
- Take on empty stomach. Counseled that urine, sweat and tears turn orange.
- Call for jaundice, dark urine, N/V, abd pain, fever, rash.
- No interaction w/ lisinopril. Cont lisinopril 10 mg daily.
- Monthly clinic checks for adherence and tolerance, LFTs if sx.
- F/u in 4 wks.
"""
