Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good afternoon. I see you are an 84-year-old female and you came in about a rash. Can you tell me about it?
Patient: Yes. I noticed a red patch on the back of my left thigh about a week ago, and it keeps getting bigger. It feels warm but it does not hurt or itch much.
Doctor: Have you traveled recently?
Patient: I got back about three weeks ago from two weeks in Sweden visiting my sister. We did a lot of walking in the woods near her house. I did not see a tick, but I am sure I got bitten.
Doctor: And I see in your records you were in the hospital after you got back.
Patient: Yes, four days for my heart failure. I had fluid in my lungs. They changed my water pill and sent me home about two weeks ago.
Doctor: Your history lists heart failure, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism, and chronic kidney disease. Do you remember the water pill dose?
Patient: Furosemide 80 milligrams once a day. Oh, no, wait, that is wrong, it is 40 milligrams once a day. It used to be 20.
Doctor: Good, so furosemide 40 milligrams once daily since the discharge. What else do you take?
Patient: Lisinopril 10 milligrams in the morning, levothyroxine 50 micrograms, metformin 500 milligrams twice a day, and ibuprofen 200 milligrams when my back hurts. The hospital told me to stop the ibuprofen, but I took a few anyway.
Doctor: Okay, we will come back to that. Any fever, chills, or headache?
Patient: I felt tired and achy and had chills for a few days last week, but no fever today and no headache.
Doctor: Any stiff neck, drooping of the face, joint swelling, chest pain, palpitations, or fainting?
Patient: None of those. No stiff neck, no droopy face, no swollen joints, no chest pain, no palpitations, and I have not fainted.
Doctor: Good. Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No, none.
Doctor: Your vitals today are temperature 99.0, blood pressure 118/68, heart rate 78 and regular, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. On the back of your left thigh there is an oval red rash about 12 centimeters across with central clearing. It is warm, not tender, with no blisters or drainage. I see no other skin lesions. Your heart is regular, your lungs are clear with no crackles, and there is trace ankle swelling, unchanged from discharge. Your ECG shows sinus rhythm at 76 per minute with a normal PR interval, so no sign of heart block. Labs today show a white blood cell count of 7.4, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, creatinine 1.1, eGFR 49, and normal liver tests. I sent a Lyme blood test, but it can be negative this early, so I am treating based on the rash.
Patient: So it is Lyme disease?
Doctor: Yes, this is early Lyme disease, erythema migrans, from a tick bite in Sweden. It has not spread to your heart or nerves. I am starting doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 10 days. Take it with food and a full glass of water, stay upright for 30 minutes afterward, and use sun protection because it makes the skin sensitive.
Patient: And the ibuprofen?
Doctor: Stop it completely. With your heart failure and kidneys, it can cause fluid retention and kidney damage. You can take acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for your back instead. Keep taking furosemide 40 mg once daily and the rest of your medications, and keep your heart failure follow-up.
Patient: What should I watch for?
Doctor: Come back or go to the emergency department for fever, severe headache, stiff neck, drooping of the face, palpitations, fainting, or if the rash spreads. I would like to recheck you in one week.
Patient: Thank you.
"""

84-year-old female with an enlarging red patch on the back of the left thigh for about a week, warm but not very painful or itchy. Doctor: Good morning. Please come in. I have you down as a 94-year-old female here with your daughter, and the concern is weight loss. Is that right?

Please come back in four weeks and we'll weigh you again.
Family member: That sounds good. Should we do any scans?
Doctor: Not right now. Given your goals, we'll hold off on invasive testing unless things change.
"""

Telehealth note, video visit. The patient is an 81-year-old female with chronic kidney disease stage 3b, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes, here for a scheduled nephrology follow-up. She joined from home using her tablet and could hear and speak clearly. She reports mild fatigue over the past month and knee pain from osteoarthritis that she has been treating with over-the-counter ibuprofen about twice a day. She denies shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, and decreased urine output. She has had no recent falls or poor oral intake.

Home measurements she took before the visit were blood pressure 132/76, heart rate 70, and weight 142 pounds, unchanged from her last visit. On video she appeared comfortable and spoke in full sentences, and no leg swelling was visible on camera.

Current medications are losartan 50 mg once daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, and acetaminophen 500 mg as needed. Labs drawn last week showed creatinine 1.5 and eGFR 36, which is stable compared with 3 months ago, potassium 4.9, hemoglobin 11.2, and a urine albumin-creatinine ratio of 180 mg/g.

Impression: chronic kidney disease stage 3b with moderately increased albuminuria, stable. Her eGFR is below the level where full-dose metformin is recommended, and ibuprofen is not safe for her kidneys. Her blood pressure is near goal.

Recommendations: reduce metformin to 500 mg twice daily. Stop ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for knee pain, not exceeding 3000 mg per day. Start dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily for kidney and cardiovascular protection, with instructions on hydration and sick-day rules. Continue losartan 50 mg once daily. Repeat a basic metabolic panel in 2 weeks after starting dapagliflozin, and repeat the urine albumin-creatinine ratio in 3 months. Follow-up video visit in 3 months, sooner if she develops vomiting, diarrhea, or poor oral intake.
"""

Infectious disease follow-up on hospital day 4 for a 49-year-old male admitted with left lower leg cellulitis, who is also being evaluated for latent tuberculosis infection after an interferon-gamma release assay returned positive during his admission workup. He was born in the Philippines and moved to the United States 22 years ago. When first asked, he said he had been treated for tuberculosis as a child. His sister explained the question in simpler words and pointed to the BCG scar on his arm, and he then clarified that he only received a vaccine and never took any tuberculosis medication, so he has had no prior treatment for latent tuberculosis.

He denies cough, hemoptysis, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, and fevers at home. He reports the left leg pain and redness are improving. He smokes about half a pack of cigarettes per day, correction, one pack per day according to his sister, and has done so for 25 years. He drinks one or two beers on weekends and denies heavy alcohol use. He has no known contact with anyone who has active tuberculosis. He has limited health literacy; he has trouble reading medication labels and relies on his sister to organize his pills.

Past history includes type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. Home medications are metformin 1000 mg twice daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. He received IV cefazolin for the first three days, and it was changed this morning to cephalexin 500 mg by mouth four times daily as the cellulitis responds.

Vitals this morning are blood pressure 152/92, heart rate 78, respiratory rate 16, temperature 98.3 F, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. He is comfortable and his lungs are clear. The left lower leg has decreasing erythema and mild tenderness without drainage or fluctuance.

A chest radiograph shows a small calcified granuloma in the right upper lobe without cavitation, infiltrate, or effusion. Three sputum samples were negative on AFB smear and the tuberculosis PCR was negative. HIV antigen/antibody was nonreactive, hepatitis B surface antigen was negative, and hepatitis C antibody was negative. AST was 28 and ALT 32. Hemoglobin A1c is 8.1 and creatinine 1.0.

Impression is latent tuberculosis infection with no evidence of active disease, left lower leg cellulitis that is improving, type 2 diabetes above goal, hypertension above goal, and current tobacco use.

Because rifampin would lower the levels of his atorvastatin and amlodipine and complicate his diabetes and blood pressure control, we chose isoniazid 300 mg once daily with pyridoxine 50 mg once daily for 9 months, starting today. I reviewed the plan in plain language using teach-back, and he was able to repeat that the pills prevent the sleeping germ from waking up, that he takes one white pill and one yellow pill each morning, and that he must call for yellow skin or dark urine. He was given a picture-based pill calendar, and the pharmacy will supply a weekly pill organizer. His sister agreed to call him each morning for the first month. We will increase amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg daily for his blood pressure and continue metformin and atorvastatin. Start a nicotine patch 21 mg daily and counseled on quitting for about five minutes; he is willing to try and a quitline referral was made. Liver function tests will be checked in 2 weeks and monthly while on isoniazid. He will follow up in the infectious disease clinic 2 weeks after discharge, and he should call for nausea, abdominal pain, or jaundice.

Clinical note:

Doctor: Good morning. So you're a 29-year-old female coming in for your routine prenatal visit, and by my count you're 28 weeks today. How have you been feeling?
Patient: Pretty good, honestly. I get tired in the afternoons, but I have a toddler at home, so I figured that's normal.
Doctor: That's very common. Any headaches, changes in your vision, or swelling in your face or hands?
Patient: No headaches and no vision changes. My ankles get a little puffy at night, but it's gone by morning.
Doctor: Okay. Any bleeding, leaking of fluid, or contractions?
Patient: No bleeding, no leaking, and no real contractions. Just some Braxton Hicks tightening now and then.
Doctor: And is the baby moving well?
Patient: Yes, every day, especially after dinner.
Doctor: Any burning when you urinate?
Patient: No.
Doctor: What are you taking right now?
Patient: Just my prenatal vitamin once a day.
Doctor: Good. Your blood pressure today is 112 over 68 and your weight is up about 18 pounds from before the pregnancy. Your urine dip shows no protein and no glucose. Let me measure your belly. Fundal height is 28 centimeters, which matches your dates, and the baby's heart rate by Doppler is 146 beats per minute.
Patient: That sounds good.
Doctor: Your one-hour glucose challenge test from last week came back at 118, which is normal, so no gestational diabetes. Your hemoglobin was 10.4, which is a little low, so you have mild anemia of pregnancy. Your blood type is O positive, so you won't need the Rh immune globulin shot.
Patient: Should I do something about the anemia?
Doctor: Yes, I'd like you to start ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily, and keep taking the prenatal vitamin. It can cause constipation, so drink plenty of water. Patient: Okay, I'll take it.
Doctor: To summarize, you're progressing normally at 28 weeks with mild anemia of pregnancy and some mild ankle swelling that is normal for this stage. Start the iron, Tdap today, repeat hemoglobin in four weeks, and I'll see you back in two weeks. Call us right away for headaches, vision changes, bleeding, leaking fluid, decreased movement, or regular contractions.
Patient: Will do, thank you.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Come on in. I see you are a 58-year-old male here for a follow-up of your right wrist fracture. Tell me what has been going on.
Patient: I fell off a ladder about three weeks ago and broke my wrist, the radius. They fixed it with a plate and I stayed in the hospital for two nights. The orthopedic clinic cannot see me until next week, and for the past few days my hand has been numb at night.
Doctor: So you had an ORIF, an open reduction and internal fixation, and you were discharged about three weeks ago. Where is the numbness?
Patient: My thumb, pointer finger, and middle finger. It wakes me up at night. And the wrist is more swollen than it was last week.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No fever, no chills.
Doctor: Any drainage or redness around the incision?
Patient: No drainage, no redness.
Doctor: Do your fingers ever turn blue or cold?
Patient: No, they stay pink.
Doctor: Any calf pain, chest pain, or trouble breathing since the surgery? We worry about blood clots after an operation.
Patient: No calf pain, no chest pain, and no trouble breathing.
Doctor: Good. You also have type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and reflux, correct?
Patient: Yes.
Doctor: Let us go over your medicines.
Patient: I take metformin 500 mg twice a day for my sugar, lisinopril 20 mg once a day for my pressure, atorvastatin 40 mg at night, and omeprazole 20 mg every morning. From the hospital I got oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed and acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours.
Doctor: Okay. How often are you using the oxycodone?
Patient: Only at night now, one or two a day. Oh wait, I looked at the metformin bottle this morning and it says 1000 mg twice a day, not 500. I misspoke.
Doctor: Good catch. So the metformin is 1000 mg twice a day, and we will keep it that way. Now, your vital signs today: blood pressure 136/84, pulse 80, temperature 98.3, and oxygen 98% on room air. I took the splint off. The incision is clean and dry, it is healing well, and there is no redness or drainage. The wrist is mildly swollen. You have decreased sensation in the thumb, index, and middle fingers, your Phalen test is positive, and your fingers are warm with a brisk capillary refill and a good radial pulse. The X-ray we took today shows the distal radius fracture with the plate and screws in good position, the alignment is maintained, and there is early callus. Your hospital labs at discharge showed an A1c of 7.4 percent and a creatinine of 1.0.
Patient: So is it healing okay?
Doctor: The bone is healing well. The numbness is most likely carpal tunnel syndrome from swelling after the fracture and surgery. I am calling the orthopedic on-call doctor to move your appointment up to within the next two days. In the meantime, I am stopping the oxycodone because you only need it at night, and I am increasing the acetaminophen to 1000 mg every 8 hours. Continue the other medicines the same. Please wear this removable wrist splint at night in a neutral position, keep your hand raised above your heart, and do your finger exercises. If the numbness becomes constant, your fingers turn pale or cold, or you get a fever or drainage from the incision, go to the emergency room.
Patient: Okay, I understand.
"""

Patient: I fell off a ladder about three weeks ago and broke my wrist, the radius. They fixed it with a plate and I stayed in the hospital for two nights. The orthopedic clinic cannot see me until next week, and for the past few days my hand has been numb at night.
Doctor: So you had an ORIF, an open reduction and internal fixation, and you were discharged about three weeks ago. Where is the numbness?
Patient: My thumb, pointer finger, and middle finger. It wakes me up at night. And the wrist is more swollen than it was last week.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No fever, no chills.
Doctor: Any drainage or redness around the incision?
Patient: No drainage, no redness.
Doctor: Do your fingers ever turn blue or cold?
Patient: No, they stay pink.
Doctor: Any calf pain, chest pain, or trouble breathing since the surgery? We worry about blood clots after an operation.
Patient: No calf pain, no chest pain, and no trouble breathing.
Doctor: Good. You also have type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and reflux, correct?
Patient: Yes.
Doctor: Let us go over your medicines.
Patient: I take metformin 500 mg twice a day for my sugar, lisinopril 20 mg once a day for my pressure, atorvastatin 40 mg at night, and omeprazole 20 mg every morning. From the hospital I got oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed and acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours.
Doctor: Okay. How often are you using the oxycodone?
Patient: Only at night now, one or two a day. Oh wait, I looked at the metformin bottle this morning and it says 1000 mg twice a day, not 500. I misspoke.
Doctor: Good catch. So the metformin is 1000 mg twice a day, and we will keep it that way. Now, your vital signs today: blood pressure 136/84, pulse 80, temperature 98.3, and oxygen 98% on room air. I took the splint off. The incision is clean and dry, it is healing well, and there is no redness or drainage. The wrist is mildly swollen. You have decreased sensation in the thumb, index, and middle fingers, your Phalen test is positive, and your fingers are warm with a brisk capillary refill and a good radial pulse. The X-ray we took today shows the distal radius fracture with the plate and screws in good position, the alignment is maintained, and there is early callus. Your hospital labs at discharge showed an A1c of 7.4 percent and a creatinine of 1.0.
Patient: So is it healing okay?
Doctor: The bone is healing well. The numbness is most likely carpal tunnel syndrome from swelling after the fracture and surgery. I am calling the orthopedic on-call doctor to move your appointment up to within the next two days. In the meantime, I am stopping the oxycodone because you only need it at night, and I am increasing the acetaminophen to 1000 mg every 8 hours. Continue the other medicines the same. Please wear this removable wrist splint at night in a neutral position, keep your hand raised above your heart, and do your finger exercises. If the numbness becomes constant, your fingers turn pale or cold, or you get a fever or drainage from the incision, go to the emergency room.
Patient: Okay, I understand.

Summarize the following clinical encounter note for a busy clinician.
Requirements:
- Write 3 to 6 sentences of plain prose (maximum 120 words), in the third person.
- Cover the patient's age/sex and reason for the visit, the key history and findings, the assessment, and the plan.

Clinical note:
"""
The patient is a 15-year-old male seen in the combined ear, nose, throat and eye clinic with his father for follow-up of chronic rhinosinusitis. He has had nasal congestion, thick yellow-green nasal drainage, postnasal drip, and a dull pressure sensation over both cheeks for more than 4 months, with worsening of the drainage over the past 10 days. He also reports itchy, watery eyes that are worse in the spring and a persistent cough at night that he attributes to the drainage. He denies fever, facial swelling, double vision, eye pain, and any change in his vision. There has been no nosebleed and no loss of smell. He has a history of allergic rhinitis and was started on loratadine 10 mg daily by his pediatrician last year, with limited benefit. He uses fluticasone nasal spray 2 sprays in each nostril daily but admits that he forgets doses about half of the time, and he does saline rinses only occasionally. He has no known drug allergies.

On examination, temperature is 36.9 C, heart rate 72, blood pressure 112/68, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye. Both eyes show mild conjunctival injection with a cobblestone appearance of the upper tarsal conjunctiva and clear watery discharge. The corneas are clear, the pupils are equal and reactive, and extraocular movements are full and painless. There is no periorbital edema or erythema. Anterior rhinoscopy shows pale, swollen inferior turbinates. Nasal endoscopy shows mucosal edema with mucopurulent secretions in the right middle meatus and no polyps or masses. There is mild tenderness over the maxillary sinuses, the oropharynx shows postnasal drainage without exudate, the ears are normal, and the neck has no adenopathy. A CT scan of the sinuses obtained last month showed bilateral maxillary and ethmoid mucosal thickening with partial opacification of the right maxillary sinus and no orbital involvement.

Impression is chronic rhinosinusitis with a purulent exacerbation, allergic rhinitis, and allergic conjunctivitis. We discussed that his symptoms are likely driven by untreated allergic inflammation plus inconsistent nasal steroid use. I recommended stopping loratadine and starting cetirizine 10 mg daily, continuing fluticasone nasal spray 2 sprays in each nostril daily with a routine tied to brushing his teeth, and starting olopatadine 0.2% ophthalmic solution one drop in each eye once daily. Because of the purulent secretions, I am starting amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg twice daily for 14 days. He will do saline sinus rinses twice daily. An allergy testing referral was placed, and we will repeat nasal endoscopy at the follow-up visit in 4 weeks. He should return sooner for fever, swelling around the eyes, vision changes, or severe headache. His father agreed with the plan.
"""

Examination showed conjunctival injection, pale swollen turbinates and mucopurulent secretions in the right middle meatus on nasal endoscopy, and CT showed bilateral maxillary and ethmoid mucosal thickening. The impression is chronic rhinosinusitis with a purulent exacerbation, allergic rhinitis and allergic conjunctivitis. Loratadine was stopped in favor of cetirizine, and fluticasone nasal spray, olopatadine eye drops, amoxicillin-clavulanate for 14 days and saline rinses were prescribed, with allergy testing referral and a 4-week follow-up.

Doctor: Hi, I understand you're here because the dressing on your PICC line came loose. Tell me what's been going on.
Patient: Yeah, the dressing got wet in the shower and started peeling off yesterday. The skin around it is red, but it doesn't hurt much.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No fever, no chills.
Doctor: And the leg with the osteomyelitis, how is it? Any new swelling or drainage?
Patient: About the same. A little sore when I walk, but no swelling and no drainage.
Doctor: Okay. You're on the ceftriaxone, 2 grams once a day, through the line, right?
Patient: Right. But honestly, I missed three doses last week. I've been drinking a lot, like six or seven beers a day, and I just forgot.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me, I'm not judging. That is heavy alcohol use, and it's getting in the way of your treatment. Any shakes or sweating when you go without a drink?
Patient: I get a bit shaky in the mornings, but no seizures.
Doctor: Let me look at the line. The site has mild redness about a centimeter around the insertion, no pus, and the line flushes easily. Your leg looks the same as last visit, no warmth and no drainage.
Patient: So is it infected?
Doctor: I think it's just irritation from the wet dressing, but we'll watch it. Here's the plan. I'll change the dressing now. Restart the ceftriaxone 2 grams once a day starting tonight, and don't double up for the missed doses. I'm also starting thiamine 100 mg once a day because of the drinking. I'll order an ESR and CRP today and let the infectious disease clinic know about the missed doses. I'd also like to refer you to an alcohol treatment program.
Patient: Okay, I can try that.
Doctor: Come back or go to the ER if you have fever, chills, spreading redness, or shaking and seizures.
"""

Leg is about the same with a little soreness when walking. Missed three doses last week and has been drinking six or seven beers a day; shaky in the mornings.

OBJECTIVE:
PICC site with mild redness about a centimeter around the insertion, no pus, and the line flushes easily. Leg looks the same as at the last visit with no warmth and no drainage.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good morning, welcome in. You're a 20-year-old male coming in for your annual physical and to catch up on vaccines, right?
Patient: Yeah, I'm a college student and my school wants my records updated.
Doctor: Great. How have you been feeling overall? Any new problems?
Patient: Pretty good. I get pimples on my face and back, and I've been on doxycycline 100 milligrams twice a day for acne for about four months. It's helped a lot.
Doctor: Good. Any stomach upset or sun problems with it?
Patient: No stomach upset and no sunburns beyond normal.
Doctor: And your asthma? I see mild intermittent asthma in your chart.
Patient: It's been fine. I use my albuterol inhaler, two puffs, only when I play basketball in the cold, maybe once or twice a month. No wheezing or cough lately, and no waking up at night.
Doctor: Any chest pain or fainting with exercise?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: How's your mood and sleep?
Patient: Fine, just a bit tired during finals.
Doctor: Do you smoke, vape, or drink?
Patient: No smoking or vaping. I have a couple of beers on weekends.
Doctor: Okay. Vitals today: blood pressure 118/72, heart rate 66, and your BMI is 23.8. Peak flow was 620 liters per minute, which is normal for you. Your PHQ-9 depression screen scored 1. Heart sounds normal, lungs clear with no wheezes, and your skin shows mild acne on the face and upper back with no cysts.
Patient: Sounds good. What about the vaccines?
Doctor: You had your childhood series, and Tdap at age eleven, so the next booster isn't due for several years. You had one HPV shot at age 14, so you need a second dose to finish the series. You also had your meningococcal ACWY shot at eleven but no booster, and since you live in the dorms, you should get the booster today. And it's flu season, so I recommend a flu shot too.
Patient: Fine, all three today.
Doctor: Great. For the acne, since four months of doxycycline has helped, I'd like to stop the doxycycline now to avoid long-term antibiotic use and switch you to adapalene 0.1% gel at night on the face and upper back, with sunscreen. Keep the albuterol as needed. I'll also order screening bloodwork for HIV and hepatitis C, which is recommended once for everyone your age. Come back in a year, or sooner if the acne flares.
Patient: Okay, thanks.
"""

Doctor: Good morning. I see you for celiac disease follow-up. You're a 52-year-old female, correct, and you've been on a gluten-free diet for about three years? I also see a history of deep vein thrombosis for which you take warfarin.
Patient: That's right. I'm really strict about the diet, but I still feel terrible a lot of the time.
Doctor: Tell me what's going on.
Patient: I'm bloated almost every day, and I have loose stools two or three times a day. And I'm tired all the time.
Doctor: Any belly pain?
Patient: No real pain, just the bloating.
Doctor: Any blood in your stool, black stools, vomiting, or fever? I ask because you're on a blood thinner.
Patient: No blood, no black stools, no vomiting, no fever.
Doctor: Any weight loss?
Patient: A few pounds over six months, maybe five.
Doctor: Tell me about the warfarin.
Patient: I take 7.5 mg every evening because of the clot I had in my leg.
Doctor: Let's check your pharmacy list. It says 5 mg.
Patient: Oh, you're right. It's 5 mg. The 7.5 was the dose when I first started.
Doctor: Good, so 5 mg every evening is what I'll record. What else do you take, including supplements?
Patient: Fish oil, 1000 mg twice a day. A multivitamin. Vitamin D, 1000 units a day. Turmeric capsules, 500 mg a day, for inflammation. And ginkgo biloba, 120 mg a day for memory. Iron too, ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day, since my blood count was low. And levothyroxine 75 mcg every morning for my thyroid.
Doctor: Do you know if those supplements are gluten-free?
Patient: I never checked the turmeric and the ginkgo. I bought them at a discount store.
Doctor: That's important, because hidden gluten in supplements can keep the intestine inflamed. Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: None.
Doctor: Any itchy blistering rash on your elbows or knees?
Patient: No rash.
Doctor: On exam, your blood pressure is 118/72 and your heart rate is 80. Your abdomen is mildly distended, soft, and not tender, with no enlarged liver or spleen, and I see no rash and no leg swelling.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: Your labs show a tTG IgA of 48, and normal is under 4, so it is still high after three years. Your hemoglobin is 10.9, your TSH is 2.4, vitamin D is low at 18, and ferritin is low at 9. Your INR is 3.4, which is above your goal of 2 to 3.

Seventh, you need an EGD with duodenal biopsies and a colonoscopy for the iron deficiency anemia, and the anticoagulation clinic and I will plan your warfarin around them once your INR is back under 3. We will repeat the tTG IgA in three months.
Patient: That sounds good. I'll throw out the turmeric and ginkgo today.
Doctor: Go to the emergency room if you see black stools or any bleeding that won't stop.
"""

Doctor: Good morning. I see you for celiac disease follow-up. You're a 52-year-old female, correct, and you've been on a gluten-free diet for about three years? I also see a history of deep vein thrombosis for which you take warfarin.
Patient: That's right. I'm really strict about the diet, but I still feel terrible a lot of the time.
Doctor: Tell me what's going on.
Patient: I'm bloated almost every day, and I have loose stools two or three times a day. And I'm tired all the time.
Doctor: Any belly pain?
Patient: No real pain, just the bloating.
Doctor: Any blood in your stool, black stools, vomiting, or fever? I ask because you're on a blood thinner.
Patient: No blood, no black stools, no vomiting, no fever.
Doctor: Any weight loss?
Patient: A few pounds over six months, maybe five.
Doctor: Tell me about the warfarin.
Patient: I take 7.5 mg every evening because of the clot I had in my leg.
Doctor: Let's check your pharmacy list. It says 5 mg.
Patient: Oh, you're right. It's 5 mg. The 7.5 was the dose when I first started.
Doctor: Good, so 5 mg every evening is what I'll record. What else do you take, including supplements?
Patient: Fish oil, 1000 mg twice a day. A multivitamin. Vitamin D, 1000 units a day. Turmeric capsules, 500 mg a day, for inflammation. And ginkgo biloba, 120 mg a day for memory. Iron too, ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day, since my blood count was low. And levothyroxine 75 mcg every morning for my thyroid.
Doctor: Do you know if those supplements are gluten-free?
Patient: I never checked the turmeric and the ginkgo. I bought them at a discount store.
Doctor: That's important, because hidden gluten in supplements can keep the intestine inflamed. Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: None.
Doctor: Any itchy blistering rash on your elbows or knees?
Patient: No rash.
Doctor: On exam, your blood pressure is 118/72 and your heart rate is 80. Your abdomen is mildly distended, soft, and not tender, with no enlarged liver or spleen, and I see no rash and no leg swelling.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: Your labs show a tTG IgA of 48, and normal is under 4, so it is still high after three years. Your hemoglobin is 10.9, your TSH is 2.4, vitamin D is low at 18, and ferritin is low at 9. Your INR is 3.4, which is above your goal of 2 to 3.
Patient: Is that bad?
Doctor: It raises your bleeding risk. Diarrhea and poor absorption of vitamin K, plus fish oil, turmeric, and ginkgo, can all push the INR up. My impression is celiac disease with persistent symptoms and an elevated tTG IgA, most likely from ongoing hidden gluten exposure, along with iron deficiency anemia, vitamin D deficiency, and a supratherapeutic INR.
Doctor: Here is the plan. First, stop the turmeric capsules and the ginkgo biloba, because they add bleeding risk with warfarin and may contain gluten. Second, only continue the fish oil and multivitamin if they are labeled gluten-free. Third, increase vitamin D from 1000 units to 2000 units a day. Fourth, keep the warfarin at 5 mg every evening and get an INR recheck in one week with the anticoagulation clinic. Fifth, I'm referring you to a celiac dietitian to review every food, supplement, and medicine label. Sixth, take the ferrous sulfate at least four hours apart from the levothyroxine. Seventh, you need an EGD with duodenal biopsies and a colonoscopy for the iron deficiency anemia, and the anticoagulation clinic and I will plan your warfarin around them once your INR is back under 3. We will repeat the tTG IgA in three months.
Patient: That sounds good. I'll throw out the turmeric and ginkgo today.
Doctor: Go to the emergency room if you see black stools or any bleeding that won't stop.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good morning. I see you are a 71-year-old male here to review your blood sugar and weight. Your primary care doctor sent you because your A1c has been creeping up. How have you been feeling?
Patient: Pretty good, doc. I am a little tired in the afternoons, and I have gained some weight around the belly over the last two years.
Doctor: Any increased thirst or urinating more than usual?
Patient: No, nothing like that. No blurry vision either.
Doctor: What about numbness or tingling in your feet, or chest pain with walking?
Patient: No numbness in my feet and no chest pain. I walk the dog most days.
Doctor: Good. Tell me about your medicines.
Patient: I take atorvastatin 20 mg once a day, amlodipine 5 mg once a day, and a baby aspirin 81 mg each morning.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: Yes, lisinopril. I got swelling of my lips and tongue about five years ago, and they told me it was angioedema. I was told never to take it again.
Doctor: Thank you. I will keep that on your chart as an allergy to lisinopril with angioedema, so no ACE inhibitors for you.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: Let me go through your numbers. Today your blood pressure is 138/84, heart rate 72, weight 228 pounds, and BMI 33. Your waist measures 112 centimeters. Your heart sounds regular, the lungs are clear, and your feet have normal sensation on the monofilament test with good pulses. The labs from last week show hemoglobin A1c 6.2 percent, fasting glucose 112, triglycerides 210, HDL 36, LDL 84, and creatinine 1.0 with an eGFR of 78.
Patient: So am I diabetic?
Doctor: Not yet. You have prediabetes, and together with the belly fat, high triglycerides, low HDL, and elevated blood pressure, this is metabolic syndrome. It raises the risk of diabetes and heart disease, but it is very treatable.
Patient: What should I do?
Doctor: The most important step is lifestyle. I would like you to aim for 150 minutes of walking a week, cut back on sugary drinks and refined carbohydrates, and see our dietitian. I am also starting metformin 500 mg once a day with dinner, and we will increase it slowly if your stomach tolerates it. Your kidney function is fine for it. I am increasing amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg daily because your pressure is above goal, and I will send a note to your primary care doctor. Please keep taking the atorvastatin and the aspirin. Do not take any ACE inhibitor. We will repeat the A1c and a lipid panel in three months.
Patient: Sounds fair. Should I check my sugar at home?
Doctor: Not needed right now. Come back in three months.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Visit modality: synchronous video visit through a secure platform. The patient was at home with her husband present, her location was confirmed, and verbal consent for telehealth was obtained. Examination was limited to what could be seen on camera.

Reason for visit: three-week post-operative follow-up after right total hip arthroplasty for severe osteoarthritis.

Interval history: The patient is a 63-year-old female who underwent right total hip arthroplasty through a posterior approach and went home on post-operative day 2 with a walker. She reports hip pain of 3/10 at rest and 5/10 with walking, improving each week. She has mild ankle swelling by evening that improves with elevation. She denies fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, calf pain, wound drainage, bleeding, and black stools. She walks around the house with the walker, does her home exercises daily, and started outpatient PT last week.

Allergy: documented NSAID allergy. Ibuprofen and naproxen caused hives and lip swelling in the past, so all NSAIDs, including aspirin, are avoided. Because of this allergy, VTE prophylaxis after surgery was prescribed with apixaban rather than aspirin.

Past medical history: T2DM, HTN, and hypothyroidism.

Medication review: metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and levothyroxine 88 mcg daily, all unchanged. Post-operative medications are acetaminophen 1,000 mg every 8 hours scheduled, oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed, docusate 100 mg twice daily, and apixaban. She first said she takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily. I asked her to hold the bottle up to the camera, and the label reads 2.5 mg. Correction: apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily. She stopped taking oxycodone five days ago because her pain is controlled.

Home measurements: BP 132/78 and pulse 74 on her home cuff, temperature 98.2 F by home thermometer, fasting fingerstick glucose 110 to 130 this week.

Data reviewed: hemoglobin 11.2 and creatinine 0.9 at the 2-week visit, and HbA1c 6.9% before surgery. AP pelvis X-ray at the 2-week visit showed well-positioned components without fracture or dislocation.

Video exam: She appears comfortable, speaks in full sentences, and is in no distress. The incision, shown on camera, is clean and dry with well-approximated edges and no erythema or drainage. No visible calf asymmetry. She stood from a chair and walked across the room with the walker with a steady gait, and she performed a straight leg raise on the operative side.

Impression: Uncomplicated recovery three weeks after right total hip arthroplasty. T2DM, HTN, and hypothyroidism are stable. The NSAID allergy has been respected in the analgesic and VTE prophylaxis plan.

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 3 progress note for an 85-year-old male admitted with an acute gout flare of the right ankle. He presented with two days of severe right ankle pain, swelling, and warmth and could not bear weight. Arthrocentesis of the right ankle on admission returned cloudy fluid with a white cell count of 28,000, needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals, a negative Gram stain, and cultures with no growth to date. He has a history of gout, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, and hypertension. Before admission he took allopurinol 100 mg daily and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, and he had been taking colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily for 2 days, which caused loose stools and did not help.

Overnight he was afebrile and slept fairly well. This morning he reports that his ankle pain has improved from 8 out of 10 to 4 out of 10 since starting prednisone. He denies fever, chills, chest pain, and pain in any other joint. The loose stools have resolved since colchicine was stopped.

Vitals this morning are temperature 36.9 C, heart rate 76, blood pressure 148/84, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. The right ankle remains swollen and warm with mild erythema and tenderness over the lateral malleolus, and range of motion is limited, but he can bear partial weight with a walker. The other joints are without swelling. His heart is regular, lungs are clear, and there is no edema of the legs.

Uric acid was 9.6 mg/dL on admission. Creatinine is 1.7 mg/dL with an eGFR of 38, unchanged from admission, the white blood cell count has fallen from 13.2 to 11.4, and C-reactive protein has fallen from 62 to 34 mg/L. The right ankle x-ray showed soft tissue swelling without fracture or erosions.

My assessment is an acute gout flare of the right ankle that is improving on prednisone. His chronic kidney disease limits the use of colchicine and anti-inflammatory drugs, and the hydrochlorothiazide likely contributed to the flare. His blood pressure is above goal.

For the plan, continue prednisone 30 mg once daily and taper over 10 days after discharge. Colchicine remains stopped. Stop hydrochlorothiazide and start amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure. Continue allopurinol 100 mg daily and recheck a uric acid level in four weeks with the goal of titrating the dose. Avoid NSAIDs. Ice and elevate the ankle, and ask physical therapy to evaluate him for a walker before discharge. Discharge is anticipated in one to two days if his pain keeps improving, with rheumatology follow-up in four weeks.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Visit modality: Audio-only telephone visit. The patient was at home and gave verbal consent to a phone visit. No video was available, so no visual examination could be performed.

Reason for visit: Recurrent tonsillitis. This is a 26-year-old female with another sore throat for 4 days. She is currently about 14 weeks pregnant.

History: She reports 4 days of sore throat, pain with swallowing, and fever. She also reports tender swollen glands in her neck and a hoarse voice. This is her fourth episode of tonsillitis in the past 12 months, and each earlier episode was treated with antibiotics. Her partner looked at her throat with a flashlight and saw white patches on both tonsils. She denies difficulty breathing, drooling, trouble opening her mouth, a muffled voice, neck stiffness, rash, cough, vaginal bleeding, and abdominal cramping. She had a rapid strep test at our lab yesterday morning, which was positive, and a CBC showed WBC 13.2.

Past medical history: asthma, hypothyroidism, and GERD. She has no known drug allergies. She first told me she takes levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, but after reading the bottle she corrected this, and the dose is 75 mcg daily. She also uses albuterol as needed for asthma, famotidine 20 mg twice daily for GERD, a prenatal vitamin daily, and over-the-counter ibuprofen as needed for throat pain. Her TSH last week was 4.6 mIU/L.

Patient-reported measurements: Temperature 101.3 F this morning on her home thermometer. Home cuff blood pressure 112/70 and heart rate 96. SpO2 98% on a home finger pulse oximeter.

Observations by phone: She speaks in full sentences with a mildly hoarse voice. I could not hear stridor or a muffled voice.

Impression: Acute streptococcal tonsillitis with recurrent tonsillitis in a patient who is 14 weeks pregnant. Hypothyroidism with a TSH above the target for pregnancy.

Recommendations: Start penicillin V potassium 500 mg twice daily for 10 days, which is compatible with pregnancy. Take acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for throat pain and fever. Stop the ibuprofen, because NSAIDs should be avoided in pregnancy. I also advised against tetracycline and fluoroquinolone antibiotics in pregnancy. Increase levothyroxine from 75 mcg to 88 mcg daily, with a repeat TSH in 4 weeks. Continue albuterol as needed, famotidine 20 mg twice daily, and the prenatal vitamin daily. Use warm salt-water gargles and drink plenty of fluids. I will notify her obstetrician about the infection and the thyroid dose change. Given four episodes in a year, I am referring her to ENT to discuss tonsillectomy after delivery. She should go to the emergency department for difficulty breathing, drooling, inability to swallow fluids, or trouble opening her mouth. I will call her in 3 days to check on her response to the antibiotic.
"""

Doctor: Good morning. You're a 43-year-old female here for a follow-up on the left wrist fracture from two weeks ago, correct?

Doctor: How is the pain?
Patient: Better. About a three out of ten most of the time. It throbs at night when my hand hangs down.
Doctor: Any numbness or tingling in your fingers?
Patient: No numbness, no tingling.
Doctor: Any increasing swelling, or fingers turning pale or blue?
Patient: The bruising is yellow now and spreads down into my hand, but my fingers are pink and warm. The swelling is no worse.
Doctor: That bruising is expected, especially since you're on a blood thinner. Remind me what you take?
Patient: Apixaban 5 mg twice a day for the clot in my lung I had last year. And I've been taking ibuprofen 400 mg for the wrist pain, about twice a day.
Doctor: Any nosebleeds, bleeding gums, or blood in your urine or stool?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Good. Ibuprofen together with apixaban raises your bleeding risk, so I want you to stop the ibuprofen. Use acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed instead, and please don't stop the apixaban, because you still need it for your pulmonary embolism.
Patient: Okay. Should I take anything for bone healing?

Patient: So I don't need surgery?

We'll repeat the X-ray in two weeks, and after the cast comes off I'll send you to hand therapy. Keep the cast dry, and call us right away for increasing swelling, numbness, cold or blue fingers, severe pain, or any unusual bleeding.
Patient: Will do. Thank you.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Chief Complaint: Shortness of breath and wheezing.

HPI: 19-year-old male with asthma since childhood who presents with one day of worsening shortness of breath, wheezing, chest tightness, and a dry cough. This followed two days of nasal congestion and sore throat. He used his albuterol inhaler about every hour overnight with only brief relief and came in because he could not finish a sentence. He also reports a racing heart. He first told the triage nurse that he takes his controller inhaler, fluticasone-salmeterol, twice a day, but on further questioning he admitted he ran out about three months ago and has used only albuterol since then. He has had two ED visits for asthma in the past year, with no ICU stays and no intubations. He denies fever, chest pain, leg swelling, hemoptysis, vomiting, and abdominal pain.

Past Medical History: asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema.

Medications: albuterol HFA 2 puffs every 4 hours as needed, fluticasone-salmeterol 100/50 mcg one inhalation twice daily (not taking), montelukast 10 mg nightly, cetirizine 10 mg daily. Over-the-counter supplements: a pre-workout powder containing caffeine and other stimulants, one scoop daily for two months, and creatine 5 g daily. No known drug allergies.

Social History: College student who lives with roommates. He first said he drinks a few beers a day, then corrected himself and said it is about 4 beers most nights and 10 to 12 on weekend nights, with his last drink about 14 hours ago. He denies tobacco, vaping, and other drug use.

ROS: Constitutional: no fever or chills. Cardiovascular: no chest pain or leg swelling. GI: no vomiting. Neurologic: no confusion. All other systems negative except as in the HPI.

Physical Exam: Vitals on arrival: temperature 37.4 C, heart rate 118, blood pressure 134/78, respiratory rate 28, oxygen saturation 91% on room air, peak expiratory flow 220 L/min, about 40% of predicted. General: moderate respiratory distress, speaking in 3 to 4 word sentences. Lungs: diffuse bilateral expiratory wheezes with a prolonged expiratory phase and decreased air movement at the bases; no stridor. CV: tachycardic, regular rhythm, no murmur. Neck: trachea midline. Skin: dry eczematous patches in both antecubital fossae, no cyanosis. Neuro: alert and oriented, mild fine tremor of both hands, no asterixis.

ED Course and Results: Oxygen 2 L by nasal cannula was started. He received three back-to-back ipratropium-albuterol nebulizers, methylprednisolone 125 mg IV once, and magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 minutes. After treatment heart rate was 98, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and peak expiratory flow 340 L/min, about 62% of predicted. Labs: venous blood gas pH 7.38 and pCO2 41; WBC 11.8, hemoglobin 15.2 g/dL; sodium 139, potassium 3.4, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, glucose 112 mg/dL; serum ethanol level undetectable. ECG showed sinus tachycardia at 116 with normal intervals. Chest x-ray showed hyperinflated lungs without pneumothorax or consolidation. CIWA score was 2 with no signs of alcohol withdrawal.

Medical Decision Making: 19-year-old male with a moderate to severe acute asthma exacerbation, most likely triggered by a viral upper respiratory infection and several months without controller therapy. The stimulant pre-workout supplement and repeated albuterol likely contribute to his racing heart and tremor. Pneumothorax and pneumonia are not supported by the chest x-ray, and pulmonary embolism is unlikely given no leg swelling and no pleuritic pain. He has heavy alcohol use, but the ethanol level is undetectable and he has no withdrawal signs.

Disposition: After four hours of observation he is speaking full sentences, oxygen saturation is 96% on room air, and peak expiratory flow is 400 L/min, about 73% of predicted. He is discharged home. Prescribed prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days. Fluticasone-salmeterol is restarted at a higher strength, increased from 100/50 mcg to 250/50 mcg, one inhalation twice daily, and he should rinse his mouth afterward. Continue albuterol HFA 2 to 4 puffs every 4 hours as needed with a spacer, montelukast 10 mg nightly, and cetirizine 10 mg daily. Doctor: Hello, I understand you came in because of a spell at work today. I have you as a 58-year-old male. Tell me what happened.
Patient: Out of nowhere my heart started pounding, my chest got tight, I got sweaty and shaky, and I felt like I was going to die. It lasted maybe fifteen minutes. This is the fourth time in three weeks.
Doctor: Have you had chest pain at rest or with exertion, any fainting, or any trouble breathing between these spells?
Patient: No chest pain between them, no fainting, and no trouble breathing.
Doctor: Any alcohol, drugs, or a lot of caffeine lately?
Patient: No drugs. I hardly drink. Just one coffee in the morning.
Doctor: Any history of heart problems or thyroid problems?
Patient: No, nothing. I had a heart check years ago and it was normal.
Doctor: Okay. Your heart rate is 84, your blood pressure is 126 over 78, and your oxygen level is 98 percent. Your heart sounds regular, your lungs are clear, and your ECG today is normal. I'd like to start sertraline 25 mg once a day for a week, then go up to 50 mg once a day, and refer you for cognitive behavioral therapy. Slow breathing can help when a spell starts, and try to keep the coffee to one cup. Come back in two weeks, and go to the ER if you get chest pain that does not go away or you faint.
Patient: Will the medicine make me sleepy?
Doctor: Some people feel a bit queasy the first week, but it usually settles.
Patient: Okay, I will try it.

Clinical note:
"""
Family medicine office dictation for a 52-year-old male with hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension, here to follow up on his cholesterol and discuss statin therapy. A professional medical interpreter was used by video for the whole visit. He reports mild fatigue lately and no other complaints. He denies chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, and leg pain with walking.

The main issue today is cost. He tells me the copays for his prescriptions add up every month, so he has been taking his atorvastatin only every other day, and he stopped ezetimibe 10 mg daily about three months ago to make his pills last. He first told me he takes atorvastatin 20 mg, but after reviewing the bottle with the interpreter, correction, it is atorvastatin 40 mg tablets, one tablet on the days that he takes it. He is also worried about statins because friends told him they damage the muscles and liver. He denies muscle aches, muscle weakness, dark urine, and abdominal pain when he does take the medication. His other medications are metformin 500 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies.

Vitals today are blood pressure 136/84, heart rate 76, and weight 205 pounds with a BMI of 31. On exam there are no xanthomas, his heart is regular in rate and rhythm, lungs are clear, abdomen is obese and soft, and there is no leg edema with normal pedal pulses. Labs today show LDL 168, total cholesterol 242, HDL 38, triglycerides 210, hemoglobin A1c 7.8%, creatinine 0.9, and AST and ALT within normal limits. Ezetimibe stays stopped for now and we will reconsider it if the repeat LDL is still above goal. Metformin is increased from 500 mg twice daily to 1000 mg twice daily. Lisinopril 20 mg daily and amlodipine 5 mg daily continue unchanged. I am referring him to the clinic pharmacist and social worker for help with medication costs, and I will switch his prescriptions to 90 day supplies at a discount generic program. Repeat a fasting lipid panel and ALT in eight weeks, and see him back in three months with an A1c. Dietary counseling was given, and he should call us sooner for muscle pain or dark urine.
"""

HD#2 geriatrics consult f/u. 84-year-old female admitted w/ unintentional wt loss and frailty.

Health literacy: pt cannot read small print on pill bottles, unsure what each pill is for, has been taking amlodipine twice a day instead of once. Daughter fills pillbox but not every wk. Teach-back used today w/ simple words and pictures, pt could not repeat plan first time, got it after 2nd try.

Home meds as clarified by daughter w/ bottles:
amlodipine 5 mg daily (pt was taking BID by mistake)
alendronate 70 mg weekly
omeprazole 20 mg daily
vitamin D3 1000 IU daily
acetaminophen 500 mg PRN knee pain

A/P:

- Start mirtazapine 7.5 mg qHS for appetite and mood
- Stop omeprazole (no clear indication now, GERD sx quiet, may blunt appetite)
- Amlodipine stays 5 mg ONCE daily, new pillbox filled by RN, pictogram med list w/ large print
- Dietitian: high-calorie high-protein diet, oral nutrition supplement BID between meals
- Dental referral for denture fit
- Continue alendronate, vitamin D3; acetaminophen PRN
- PT/OT for strength and mobility, walker
- SW for meals on wheels and home health RN for weekly pillbox check
- Teach-back with daughter present before d/c, wt check in 2 wk at PCP

Summarize the following clinical encounter note for a busy clinician.
Requirements:
- Write 3 to 6 sentences of plain prose (maximum 120 words), in the third person.
- Cover the patient's age/sex and reason for the visit, the key history and findings, the assessment, and the plan.

Clinical note:
"""
The patient is a 44-year-old male seen in the family medicine clinic for 12 days of nasal congestion and facial pain. He is accompanied by his sister, who helps manage his medications and provided part of the history because of his memory difficulties after a traumatic brain injury several years ago. They report that he had a typical cold at the start, began to improve around day 5, and then worsened again over the last 4 days with thick yellow nasal drainage, pressure and pain over the right cheek and upper teeth, a fever of 38.2 Celsius at home, and a headache that is worse when he bends forward. The patient himself says the headache is moderate and the pain is mostly on the right side. His sister has been giving him pseudoephedrine 60 mg every 6 hours and oxymetazoline nasal spray for the past 6 days. He and his sister both deny vision changes, swelling around the eyes, stiff neck, confusion beyond his baseline, shortness of breath, and chest pain.

Past medical history includes T2DM, HTN, hyperlipidemia, and a traumatic brain injury (TBI) with mild memory impairment. His sister initially stated that he takes lisinopril 10 mg daily, but after checking the bottles she brought with her, she clarified that the dose is lisinopril 20 mg daily. Other regular medications are metformin 500 mg BID, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and amlodipine 5 mg daily. He also takes several over-the-counter supplements: vitamin D3 2000 units daily and fish oil 1000 mg daily, and for this illness he has been taking echinacea capsules and zinc lozenges. He has a sulfa antibiotic allergy that causes a rash. He does not smoke and drinks alcohol rarely.

On examination, temperature is 38.0 Celsius, heart rate 96, blood pressure 158/94, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is alert and at his baseline orientation. There is tenderness to percussion over the right maxillary sinus, purulent drainage in the right nasal passage with swollen turbinates, and mild erythema of the posterior pharynx with postnasal drainage. The tympanic membranes are normal, there is no periorbital edema, the neck is supple, the lungs are clear, and the heart is regular. POC testing showed a hemoglobin A1c of 8.2%, and clinic labs show glucose 182, creatinine 0.9, eGFR 96, and potassium 4.1.

Impression is acute bacterial sinusitis, since symptoms have persisted beyond 10 days with a double worsening pattern and fever. His blood pressure is elevated, most likely from the pseudoephedrine, and his diabetes is above goal. We explained to the patient and his sister that decongestants raise blood pressure and can worsen blood sugar. Plan is to stop the pseudoephedrine and the oxymetazoline spray immediately. Start amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg/125 mg BID for 7 days with food, which is safe with his documented sulfa allergy. Start fluticasone nasal spray 2 sprays in each nostril once daily and saline nasal irrigation twice daily. Increase metformin from 500 mg BID to 1000 mg BID with meals, and continue lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and amlodipine 5 mg daily. He may continue vitamin D3 and fish oil but should stop the echinacea, which has no proven benefit. Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours PRN for pain. Recheck blood pressure and review his home glucose log in 1 week, and call sooner if there is no improvement in 3 days. If symptoms worsen, we will consider a CT of the sinuses. His sister will use a weekly pill organizer and keep an updated medication list. Return precautions were reviewed, including severe headache, vision changes, eye swelling, or confusion, and both the patient and his sister verbalized understanding.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Nurse: The patient is a 58-year-old female here for a skin check, mostly about rough spots on her scalp and forearms. Blood pressure 132/78, pulse 70.

Doctor: Hello, nice to meet you. Tell me about the rough spots.

Patient: They're scaly, kind of sandpaper-like, on the tops of my forearms and a few on my scalp. They've been there maybe a year and seem to be getting more numerous.

Doctor: Do they hurt, itch, or bleed?

Patient: They sting a bit when I'm in the sun, but no itching and no bleeding.

Doctor: Any sore that won't heal, or a spot that has grown quickly?

Patient: No, nothing like that. No new moles either.

Doctor: Tell me about your sun exposure.

Patient: I garden every weekend and I've always burned easily. I use sunscreen sometimes, honestly not every time.

Doctor: Any personal history of skin cancer?

Patient: No.

Doctor: What medicines do you take?

Patient: Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once a day and atorvastatin 20 mg at night.

Doctor: Okay. Last visit I did a shave biopsy of the thick spot on your left temple. That came back as a hypertrophic actinic keratosis with no sign of squamous cell carcinoma, so that is good news.

Patient: What a relief.

Doctor: On exam today you have about a dozen rough, erythematous scaly patches on both forearms and six on the scalp, and the left temple biopsy site is healed. None are ulcerated or tender, and I see no suspicious pigmented lesions on your face, arms, or back. This confirms actinic keratoses from long-term sun damage.

Patient: Can we get rid of them?

Doctor: Yes. Today I'll freeze the scalp spots with liquid nitrogen, which will sting for a moment and then crust over for a week or two. Your skin will get red, raw, and crusty, which means it is working. Use acetaminophen if it is sore, and avoid sun on the treated skin. Please wear SPF 50 sunscreen every day and a wide-brimmed hat when gardening. Hydrochlorothiazide can make your skin more sensitive to the sun, so I'll let your primary doctor know. Patient: Okay, that makes sense.
"""

Doctor: Good morning. I'm using a professional interpreter on the video line so we can speak in your language. You're an 84-year-old male here for your routine HIV follow-up, and we're seeing you in urgent care today because the clinic had no openings. Is that right?
Patient: Yes, doctor. I have been well. I take my HIV pill every day.
Doctor: Do you ever miss a dose?
Patient: Maybe one time in the last three months, when I was traveling to see my son.
Doctor: Which pill do you take?
Patient: Biktarvy, one tablet once a day, in the morning.
Doctor: Any fever, night sweats, or weight loss?
Patient: No fever, no night sweats, and my weight is the same.
Doctor: Any diarrhea or nausea with the medicine?
Patient: No diarrhea, no nausea.
Doctor: Any cough, shortness of breath, or chest pain?
Patient: No, nothing like that. Sometimes I get a headache in the evening, and my neighbor said my blood pressure is high.
Doctor: Let me check. Your blood pressure today is 158/90, and it was 154/88 at your last two visits. Heart rate is 72 and temperature is 98.2. Your heart and lungs sound normal. I don't see any swelling in your legs, mouth sores, or rashes, and your lymph nodes are not enlarged.
Patient: What about my blood tests?
Doctor: Your labs from last week show an HIV viral load that is undetectable, and your CD4 count is 540. Your creatinine is 1.0, and your cholesterol is acceptable on the atorvastatin. Are you still taking atorvastatin 20 mg at bedtime?
Patient: Yes, every night.
Doctor: Any other medicines, vitamins, or antacids?
Patient: Only calcium tablets sometimes, for my stomach.
Doctor: Calcium can lower how much of the HIV medicine your body absorbs, so please don't take the calcium tablets within two hours of your Biktarvy.
Patient: Okay, I will take them in the evening.
Doctor: My impression is that your HIV is well controlled on Biktarvy, but your high blood pressure is not controlled. I'm starting amlodipine 5 mg once a day. Come back in 4 weeks to recheck your blood pressure, and go to the emergency room for a severe headache, chest pain, or vision changes.
Patient: I understand. Thank you for the interpreter.
"""

Inpatient ophthalmology follow-up dictation on the hospital ward. This is a 50-year-old male with primary open-angle glaucoma whom I am seeing at the bedside during his admission for right lower lobe community-acquired pneumonia, hospital day 3. I was asked to see him because his home eye drops were not on his medication reconciliation.

He reports that he stopped both of his glaucoma drops about 2 months ago because of cost. They were latanoprost 0.005 percent at bedtime and a brand-name combination of dorzolamide-timolol twice daily, with a copay of about 90 dollars a month. He first said he stopped only the combination drop, correction, he stopped both drops around the same time. He denies eye pain, blurred vision, halos around lights, headache, and nausea. He reports narrowing of his peripheral vision on the left, which he has noticed over the past few months. His right eye, correction, his left eye, is the worse one.

Past medical history is type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Current inpatient medications are ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, and his home lisinopril 10 mg daily. Temperature is 99.1 F, blood pressure 136/82, heart rate 80, respiratory rate 18, and SpO2 96% on room air. WBC is 11.4, down from 15.2 on admission. His last visual field 4 months ago showed a superior arcuate defect in the left eye.

Impression is primary open-angle glaucoma in both eyes, worse on the left, with elevated pressures due to cost-related nonadherence, community-acquired pneumonia that is improving, and type 2 diabetes.

For the treatment, restart latanoprost 0.005 percent, one drop in both eyes at bedtime, using the low-cost generic. Discontinue the brand-name dorzolamide-timolol combination for now because of the cost. Continue the pneumonia treatment per the primary team. I have asked social work and pharmacy to review medication assistance programs and a 90-day generic supply before discharge. I taught him how to instill the drops. He will follow up in the glaucoma clinic in 2 weeks for a pressure recheck and a repeat visual field, and I will consider laser trabeculoplasty if the pressures stay high.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
The patient is a 55-year-old female seen in the infectious disease clinic for fever that began three days ago, nine days after she returned from a three-week trip to West Africa. She reports shaking chills that come in waves, a frontal headache, muscle aches, and poor appetite. She did not take malaria prophylaxis. She has had two episodes of vomiting but denies diarrhea, cough, rash, confusion, and dark urine. She has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg every six hours for the fever. She drinks about six beers most evenings, with her last drink the night before this visit, which is heavy alcohol use. She also takes omeprazole 20 mg daily for reflux and has no known drug allergies.

On examination, temperature was 101.8 F, BP 118/72, HR 102, RR 18, and SpO2 98% on room air. She is tired but alert and oriented. The spleen tip is palpable, the abdomen is otherwise soft and nontender, and there is no rash. Lungs are clear and there is no neck stiffness.

Rapid malaria antigen testing was positive for Plasmodium falciparum, and the thick and thin smears showed a parasitemia of about 1%. CBC showed hemoglobin 12.4 and platelets 96, and the white count was 5.2. AST was 92 and ALT 58. Creatinine was 0.9 and glucose was 104. She has no features of severe malaria, with a normal mental status, no respiratory distress, and normal creatinine.

Impression: Uncomplicated falciparum malaria after travel to an endemic region, with thrombocytopenia and mildly elevated liver enzymes. Her heavy alcohol use raises concern for withdrawal and nutritional deficiency.

Recommendations: Start atovaquone-proguanil 250 mg/100 mg, 4 tablets once daily for 3 days, taken with food. Stop ibuprofen because of the low platelets and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed, not exceeding 2 g a day given her alcohol use and liver enzymes. Start thiamine 100 mg daily and folic acid 1 mg daily. She was counseled to cut down and stop alcohol and to seek care right away for confusion, tremor, hallucinations, or seizure. Repeat smear, CBC, and LFTs in 48 hours and again at day 7, and return to clinic in 3 days. She should go to the ED for persistent vomiting, since she may not keep the doses down.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
The patient is a 55-year-old female seen in the infectious disease clinic for fever that began three days ago, nine days after she returned from a three-week trip to West Africa. She reports shaking chills that come in waves, a frontal headache, muscle aches, and poor appetite. She did not take malaria prophylaxis. She has had two episodes of vomiting but denies diarrhea, cough, rash, confusion, and dark urine. She has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg every six hours for the fever. She drinks about six beers most evenings, with her last drink the night before this visit, which is heavy alcohol use. She also takes omeprazole 20 mg daily for reflux and has no known drug allergies.

On examination, temperature was 101.8 F, BP 118/72, HR 102, RR 18, and SpO2 98% on room air. She is tired but alert and oriented. The spleen tip is palpable, the abdomen is otherwise soft and nontender, and there is no rash. Lungs are clear and there is no neck stiffness.

Rapid malaria antigen testing was positive for Plasmodium falciparum, and the thick and thin smears showed a parasitemia of about 1%. CBC showed hemoglobin 12.4 and platelets 96, and the white count was 5.2. AST was 92 and ALT 58. Creatinine was 0.9 and glucose was 104. She has no features of severe malaria, with a normal mental status, no respiratory distress, and normal creatinine.

Impression: Uncomplicated falciparum malaria after travel to an endemic region, with thrombocytopenia and mildly elevated liver enzymes. Her heavy alcohol use raises concern for withdrawal and nutritional deficiency.

Recommendations: Start atovaquone-proguanil 250 mg/100 mg, 4 tablets once daily for 3 days, taken with food. Stop ibuprofen because of the low platelets and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed, not exceeding 2 g a day given her alcohol use and liver enzymes. Start thiamine 100 mg daily and folic acid 1 mg daily. She was counseled to cut down and stop alcohol and to seek care right away for confusion, tremor, hallucinations, or seizure. Repeat smear, CBC, and LFTs in 48 hours and again at day 7, and return to clinic in 3 days. She should go to the ED for persistent vomiting, since she may not keep the doses down.
"""

- azithromycin 250 mg PO daily (day 3 of 5, after 500 mg on day 1)

- tiotropium 18 mcg inhaled daily
- lisinopril 10 mg PO daily
- nicotine patch 21 mg/24 h, started HD2

3. HTN - cont lisinopril, BP at goal

86-year-old female, urgent care visit. Known nephrotic syndrome (membranous nephropathy on renal bx), f/b nephro.
c/o worsening leg swelling x1 wk, foamy urine, ~8 lb wt gain. Also fatigue.
Denies CP, SOB at rest, orthopnea, fever, dysuria, gross hematuria.
Social: works irregular shifts (overnight and early AM) at family bakery, schedule changes wk to wk. Admits missing midday furosemide dose ~3x/wk, hard to time meds around sleep.
PMH: nephrotic syndrome, HTN, hyperlipidemia.
Sleeps in 4-5 hr blocks during the day after overnight shifts. Denies NSAID use. Daughter helps w/ pillbox on weekends only. Not checking BP at home.
Meds: furosemide 40 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. NKDA.
Vitals: BP 148/84, HR 82, RR 16, SpO2 96% RA, Temp 98.2 F, wt 158 lb (150 lb at last nephro visit).
Exam: NAD, mild periorbital edema.
Lungs CTA bilat.
No crackles.
JVP not elevated.
2+ pitting edema bilat LE to knees.
Abd soft, NT, no ascites.
Results: UA dip protein 4+, nitrite neg. BMP: Na 138, K 4.4, Cr 1.3 (baseline 1.2), eGFR 39. Serum albumin 2.4.
A/P:
Nephrotic syndrome w/ vol overload, edema worse d/t missed diuretic doses. Cr near baseline.
HTN above goal today, likely from fluid retention.
Hyperlipidemia, stable on statin.
Increase furosemide to 40 mg BID: 1st dose on waking, 2nd ~6 hrs later, set phone alarms to match shift schedule.
Continue lisinopril 10 mg daily, no change today given Cr.
Continue atorvastatin 20 mg nightly.
Low salt diet, restrict to 2 g/day, elevate legs. Avoid NSAIDs.
Daily wts, call if gain >3 lb in 2 days.
Repeat BMP in 1 wk.
Nephro appt within 1 wk, scheduled around work shifts.
ED if SOB, CP, or decreased urine output.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Nephrology clinic dictation for a 51-year-old male referred for high potassium while on lisinopril. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease. I used plain language and teach-back today because he has difficulty reading and understanding medical forms, and his daughter, who reads his labels for him, came along. Primary care labs two weeks ago showed a potassium of 5.9 on lisinopril 20 mg daily, and a repeat today on a non-hemolyzed sample shows potassium 6.1, correction, 5.9, so it is confirmed. He feels fairly well and has mild fatigue, but he denies muscle weakness, denies palpitations, denies nausea, and denies decreased urine output. When I asked about diet, he said his doctor told him to cut back on salt, so for the past two months he has been using a salt substitute on all of his food. The daughter brought the container and it is made with potassium chloride. He also drinks a large glass of orange juice every day. He denies taking ibuprofen or other pain pills and denies potassium supplements.

Current medications are lisinopril 20 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, and metformin 500 mg twice daily.

Vitals today are blood pressure 142/86, heart rate 78, and weight 214 pounds. On exam he is comfortable. The lungs are clear and the heart rhythm is regular. There is no edema. ECG today shows normal sinus rhythm with no peaked T waves and a normal QRS. Labs today show creatinine 1.5, which is near his baseline of 1.4, eGFR 55, bicarbonate 22, and glucose 148. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein.

My impression is hyperkalemia, mild to moderate, most likely from lisinopril combined with a potassium-based salt substitute and daily juice on top of stage 3a chronic kidney disease. Hypertension is above goal today and diabetes is stable.

Plan is first to stop the salt substitute, which is the most important change, and the daughter will remove it from the kitchen. Reduce lisinopril from 20 mg to 10 mg daily. Increase amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg daily to cover his blood pressure. Continue metformin at the current dose. I gave him a picture-based handout on high potassium foods and drinks, asked him to switch the orange juice to apple juice, and I am referring him to a dietitian. He repeated the main steps back to me correctly. Repeat basic metabolic panel in one week at a lab close to his home. Return to nephrology clinic in 4 weeks, sooner if he has weakness or palpitations.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
The patient is a 70-year-old male seen in the ophthalmology clinic for follow-up of primary open-angle glaucoma in both eyes, diagnosed four years ago. He has been using latanoprost 0.005% one drop in each eye at bedtime and reports good adherence, missing perhaps one dose a month. He denies eye pain, denies redness, denies halos around lights, and denies sudden vision loss. He has noticed no new difficulty with peripheral vision. He does report mild dryness and an occasional burning sensation in both eyes, which he treats with artificial tears as needed. His medical history includes hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia, and he takes lisinopril 10 mg daily and tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies and no history of asthma, COPD, or slow heart rate.

On examination, best corrected visual acuity is 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. Pupils are equal and reactive with no afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressure by applanation is 19 mmHg in the right eye and 22 mmHg in the left eye, compared with 17 and 19 mmHg at the last visit. Slit lamp exam shows clear corneas, deep and quiet anterior chambers, and mild nuclear sclerosis in both lenses. Gonioscopy shows open angles in both eyes. Dilated fundus exam shows a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.7 in the right eye and 0.8 in the left eye, with inferior thinning of the neuroretinal rim in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography shows retinal nerve fiber layer thinning in the left eye, slightly worse than on the previous scan. Visual field testing is stable in the right eye and shows slight progression of an early superior arcuate defect in the left eye. His blood pressure is 132/78 and his heart rate is 64 today.

My impression is primary open-angle glaucoma in both eyes, with mild progression in the left eye on visual field and OCT and intraocular pressure above his target of less than 18 mmHg. He also has mild nuclear sclerosis that is not visually significant today and mild dry eye.

Because of the progression and the pressure above target, I am adding dorzolamide-timolol 2%/0.5% one drop in both eyes twice daily to his current regimen. He will continue latanoprost 0.005% one drop in each eye at bedtime and artificial tears as needed. I counseled him on pressing on the inner corner of the eye after each drop and on possible side effects, including fatigue and a slow pulse, and I will recheck his heart rate at the next visit. I noted that he takes tamsulosin, so the surgeon should be told about the risk of floppy iris syndrome when he eventually needs cataract surgery. He should return in six weeks for a repeat pressure check, and I will repeat the visual field test and optical coherence tomography in four months. He should call sooner for eye pain, redness, or sudden changes in vision.
"""

"""
The patient is a 70-year-old male seen in the ophthalmology clinic for follow-up of primary open-angle glaucoma in both eyes, diagnosed four years ago. He has been using latanoprost 0.005% one drop in each eye at bedtime and reports good adherence, missing perhaps one dose a month. He denies eye pain, denies redness, denies halos around lights, and denies sudden vision loss. He has noticed no new difficulty with peripheral vision. He does report mild dryness and an occasional burning sensation in both eyes, which he treats with artificial tears as needed. His medical history includes hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia, and he takes lisinopril 10 mg daily and tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies and no history of asthma, COPD, or slow heart rate.

On examination, best corrected visual acuity is 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. Pupils are equal and reactive with no afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressure by applanation is 19 mmHg in the right eye and 22 mmHg in the left eye, compared with 17 and 19 mmHg at the last visit. Optical coherence tomography shows retinal nerve fiber layer thinning in the left eye, slightly worse than on the previous scan.
