Clinical note:
"""
Geriatrics telehealth note.

Visit modality: real-time video visit through a secure platform. The patient was at home with her daughter present on camera at the patient's request. Location and identity were confirmed verbally and she consented to the video format.

Reason for visit: advance care planning and follow-up of multiple chronic conditions after recent international travel.

History (patient-reported): This is a 66-year-old female with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes, stage 3b chronic kidney disease, hypertension, knee osteoarthritis, and hyperlipidemia. She returned 9 days ago from a two-week family trip abroad that included two long flights and she ate much saltier food than usual. Since returning she reports ankle swelling, a 5 pound weight gain, and mild shortness of breath climbing one flight of stairs. She denies chest pain, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fever, diarrhea, cough, and calf pain. Before the trip she had two episodes of low home blood sugar, the lowest reading 58, with sweating and shakiness.

Medications were reviewed by holding the bottles up to the camera: carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, losartan 50 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg once daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, glipizide 5 mg daily, and ibuprofen 400 mg as needed for knee pain, about four days a week. She first reported taking metformin 1000 mg twice daily, but after reading the bottle on camera she corrected this to 500 mg twice daily.

Home measurements: blood pressure 132/78 and heart rate 72 on her home cuff, SpO2 96% on a finger oximeter, temperature 98.4 F, weight 169 pounds today versus her usual 164 pounds, and fasting glucose readings 112 to 140 this week.

Visual exam by video: she looks comfortable and speaks in full sentences. There is no increased work of breathing and no cyanosis. She has 1+ ankle edema bilaterally. She is alert and oriented with appropriate mood.

Recent data: labs last month showed creatinine 1.6, eGFR 38, potassium 4.6, and A1c 7.4. An echocardiogram 6 months ago showed LVEF 35%.

Advance care planning: we spent about 30 minutes on goals of care. She wants to stay independent at home and would not want to live long term in a nursing facility. She named her daughter as her health care surrogate and has no written advance directive on file. After we discussed the expected course of heart failure and kidney disease, she stated she would accept hospitalization and short-term treatments, including a trial of BiPAP, but she would not want CPR or prolonged mechanical ventilation if there were little chance of recovery. Her daughter agreed and asked what to expect.

Impression: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction with mild volume overload after travel and a high-sodium diet. Recent hypoglycemia on glipizide with A1c 7.4. Stage 3b chronic kidney disease. Hypertension acceptable at home. Ibuprofen is unsafe with her heart failure and kidney disease. Advance care planning completed with a documented surrogate and treatment preferences.

Recommendations: increase furosemide to 40 mg twice daily for 3 days, then return to 40 mg once daily if weight returns to about 164 pounds. Stop glipizide. Continue metformin 500 mg twice daily. Stop ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for knee pain. Follow a 2 gram sodium diet and weigh daily, calling for a gain of 3 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week. BMP in 1 week. Cardiology visit within 2 weeks. Advance directive forms will be mailed naming her daughter as surrogate, and a POLST form documenting no CPR will be completed at an in-person geriatrics visit in 4 weeks. A nurse will call in 1 week to review daily weights.
"""

Doctor: Good afternoon. I have you down as a 68-year-old male here because of a blood test result. Tell me what happened.
Patient: My regular doctor called me two days ago. She said my PSA came back high, 6.8, and that last time it was 3.9. She said I should get it looked at, and I didn't want to wait, so I came here.
Doctor: That makes sense. When was the last one done?
Patient: About two years ago, at my yearly physical.
Doctor: Any trouble passing urine?
Patient: I get up twice a night to pee, sometimes three times, and the stream is weak. It's been that way for a year or so.
Doctor: Any burning when you urinate, or any blood in the urine?
Patient: No burning, no blood.
Doctor: Fever or chills? Any pain in your back, hips, or bones?
Patient: No fever. No bone pain either. My back is fine.
Doctor: Any weight loss that you haven't been trying for?
Patient: No, my weight has been steady.
Doctor: What medications do you take?
Patient: Lisinopril 20 mg once a day for blood pressure, and atorvastatin 20 mg at night. I also take saw palmetto, 160 mg twice a day, because my neighbor told me it helps the prostate.

Patient: So is it cancer?

Here is the plan. I'm going to start tamsulosin 0.4 mg once a day at bedtime for the urinary symptoms. I want you to stop the saw palmetto, since it won't help and it can muddy things. Keep taking the lisinopril and the atorvastatin. We'll repeat the PSA in six weeks, and no bike riding or ejaculation for two days before the draw. I'm also referring you to urology for an MRI of the prostate. If you get a fever, can't pass urine, or see blood, come back right away.
Patient: Okay, that sounds good. Thank you.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Cardiology progress dictation, hospital day 2, on a 54-year-old male admitted for evaluation of palpitations. He came in two days ago after several weeks of episodes where his heart feels like it is racing and fluttering, lasting about ten to twenty minutes and mostly happening in the evening after coffee. He denies chest pain, denies syncope, denies shortness of breath, and denies any lightheadedness during the episodes. He is very anxious about all of this and has asked me many questions this morning, including whether this could be a heart attack, whether he will need a pacemaker, and whether he can keep drinking coffee, and I answered each of them at the bedside. Past history includes hypertension and generalized anxiety disorder, and at home he takes lisinopril 10 mg daily and sertraline 50 mg daily, with no known drug allergies. On telemetry overnight he had two short runs of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, the longest about four minutes with a rate up to 128, and otherwise sinus rhythm. Vitals this morning are blood pressure 146 over 88, heart rate 82, respiratory rate 16, temperature 36.9 Celsius, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. On exam he is anxious but comfortable, the rhythm is regular at the moment with no murmurs, the lungs are clear, there is no leg edema, and the thyroid is not enlarged. Troponin was negative twice, potassium 4.2, magnesium 2.0, TSH 1.8, and hemoglobin 14.6. The ECG on admission showed normal sinus rhythm without ST changes, and the echocardiogram this morning shows an ejection fraction of 60 percent, normal chamber sizes, and no significant valve disease. My impression is new paroxysmal atrial fibrillation with a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 1 for hypertension, plus hypertension above goal and anxiety that is likely contributing to his symptoms. Plan is to start metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily for rate control, correction, make that 50 mg daily, to increase lisinopril from 10 mg to 20 mg daily, to continue sertraline, to stop caffeine, and to place a 14 day ambulatory event monitor at discharge. We discussed anticoagulation, and given the score of 1 we will review it in clinic rather than start it now. He will follow up with cardiology in two weeks. I spent extra time reassuring him and he says he feels better.
"""

Dermatology inpatient progress note, hospital day 2, for a 20-year-old female admitted with a severe flare of atopic dermatitis. She has a history of mild asthma. She denies fever, denies pain or oozing from the lesions, and has used no new skin products other than a sunscreen she bought during the trip. Impression: severe flare of atopic dermatitis, improving on inpatient treatment, without signs of secondary infection. Her mild asthma is stable.

Plan: continue triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily to the body, avoiding the face, under wet wrap therapy. Continue cetirizine 10 mg at bedtime for itching. Use bland emollients liberally and stop the new sunscreen. Expect discharge tomorrow if the itching continues to improve, with dermatology clinic follow-up in 2 weeks.
"""

Dictation for a dermatology clinic visit. This is an 85-year-old male with hypertension who presents for evaluation of facial redness that he has had for several years. He reports persistent redness over the cheeks and nose, with small red bumps that come and go, and flushing that is worse with hot drinks, red wine, and sun exposure. He denies eye irritation, denies itching, and denies any new skin care products or any new medicines.

On exam there is diffuse erythema over the central face with scattered inflammatory papules and a few pustules on the cheeks and chin, plus visible telangiectasias over both cheeks. There are no comedones, there is no thickening of the nose skin, and the eyelids and conjunctivae look normal.

Impression is papulopustular rosacea, with the worsening likely related to the topical steroid. For the plan, I will have him stop the hydrocortisone cream today and start metronidazole 0.75% gel twice daily to the whole face. I counseled him on trigger avoidance, gentle cleansing, and a daily broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30. Return to clinic in eight weeks to check the response.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Hello, I'm the emergency physician. I have you down as a 61-year-old male, and I can see your lips are swollen. When did this start?
Patient: About an hour ago. We had shrimp pasta for dinner, and within half an hour my lips started tingling and swelling. Then my tongue felt thick and I got hives on my chest and arms. They're very itchy. A little later my throat started getting tight, so my wife drove me here.
Doctor: Any trouble breathing, wheezing, vomiting, or dizziness?
Patient: I can breathe okay, no trouble breathing, no wheezing, no vomiting. No dizziness and I haven't passed out.
Doctor: Have you eaten shrimp before without problems?
Patient: Yes, many times. This has never happened to me.
Doctor: Do you have any medical conditions, and what medicines do you take?
Patient: I have atrial fibrillation. I take apixaban 5 mg twice a day as a blood thinner. No known drug allergies and no new medicines lately.
Doctor: Thank you. Your blood pressure is 142/88, pulse 104, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. You have swelling of the lips and tongue and hives on the chest and arms. Your voice is clear with no stridor, and your lungs are clear without wheezing.
Doctor: This is an allergic reaction with angioedema, most likely from the shrimp. Because your throat feels tight, I'm treating it urgently. I'm giving epinephrine 0.3 mg into your thigh muscle right now, plus diphenhydramine 50 mg and methylprednisolone 125 mg through the IV. Because you take apixaban, I'll hold firm pressure on the injection site for five minutes to limit bruising. I'm also getting an ECG, since epinephrine can speed up the heart, and I'll send a tryptase level and a basic metabolic panel.
Patient: Is it going to get worse? Will I be okay?
Doctor: Most people respond well. We'll watch you here for at least six hours.
Doctor: It's been about two hours and the swelling is going down. The ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 98 with no ischemic changes, and your creatinine is 1.1. After six hours of observation your throat is no longer tight and the hives are fading, so you can go home. Keep taking apixaban 5 mg twice a day as you do now. I'm prescribing prednisone 40 mg once a day for three days, and an epinephrine auto-injector to use in your thigh if the symptoms return, and then call emergency services. Avoid shrimp and other shellfish, and I'm referring you to an allergist. Come back right away for trouble breathing, throat tightness, or swelling that returns.
Patient: Thank you, doctor. That makes me feel better.
"""

Doctor: Good morning. A professional interpreter is here with us, so please speak in short sentences and pause so the interpreter can translate. I see you are a 65-year-old male here about chest discomfort when you walk. Tell me about it.
Patient: Yes. For about three months, when I climb stairs or walk fast uphill, I feel pressure in the middle of my chest. It goes away if I stop and rest for about three minutes.
Doctor: Does the pressure spread to your arm, neck, or jaw? Do you get shortness of breath with it?
Patient: No, it stays in the middle. I don't have shortness of breath.
Doctor: Do you ever have pain at rest, or wake up at night with pain? Any fainting?
Patient: No pain at rest, no pain at night, and no fainting.
Doctor: Do you have other health problems, and what medicines do you take?
Patient: I have high blood pressure. I take amlodipine 5 mg every morning, and nothing else.
Doctor: Thank you. Your blood pressure today is 136/82 and your heart rate is 72. Your heart sounds regular with no murmur, your lungs are clear, and there is no leg swelling. The ECG we did when you arrived shows a normal rhythm with no acute changes.
Patient: So what is wrong with my heart?
Doctor: What you describe is stable exertional angina, which means the heart muscle is not getting enough blood flow when you exert yourself, most likely from narrowed heart arteries. Here is the plan. I will increase your amlodipine to 10 mg once daily. I am also prescribing nitroglycerin 0.4 mg tablets to put under your tongue if the pressure comes, and you can take one every 5 minutes, up to three tablets. If the pain is not better after the first tablet, call emergency services. I am also ordering an exercise stress test and blood tests for cholesterol, and I want to see you back in four weeks. The interpreter will go over the written instructions with you in your language.
Patient: Yes, I understand. Thank you, doctor.
"""

He denied shortness of breath, pain at rest, pain at night, and fainting. Examination was unremarkable and the ECG showed a normal rhythm with no acute changes. The impression was stable exertional angina. Amlodipine was increased to 10 mg once daily, nitroglycerin 0.4 mg tablets under the tongue were prescribed, and an exercise stress test and cholesterol blood tests were ordered with return in four weeks.

Clinical note:
"""
Dictating a pediatric specialty clinic visit for a 5-year-old female who is here with her mother for right ear pain and fever. History of present illness, the mother says the ear pain started 2 days ago, correction, 3 days ago, right after a cold that had been going on for about a week with a runny nose and a cough. She has been tugging at her right ear, woke up crying twice last night, and had a fever up to 38.6 Celsius at home that came down partly with ibuprofen. She also had a mild sore throat yesterday. She is eating a little less but is drinking fluids well and is passing urine normally. She denies vomiting, diarrhea, neck stiffness, or drainage from the ear, and the mother has noticed no change in her hearing and no rash.

Past medical history includes mild persistent asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, and three ear infections in the last 6 months. The last infection was treated with amoxicillin about 2 months ago, which she tolerated well. She has no known drug allergies. Current medications per the mother are fluticasone HFA 44 mcg 2 puffs twice daily, albuterol HFA 2 puffs every 4 to 6 hours as needed, cetirizine 2.5 mg once daily, hydrocortisone 1% cream twice daily to the eczema patches as needed, and diphenhydramine at bedtime that the mother started over the counter last week for the congestion. She had no wheezing episodes this month and has needed albuterol only twice. Immunizations are up to date including the pneumococcal conjugate series, but she has not had the flu shot this season. She attends kindergarten and a classmate had a similar illness. No smokers at home.

Vitals today, temperature 38.4 Celsius, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and weight 20 kilograms, correction, 18 kilograms on the clinic scale. On examination she is tired appearing but consolable and well hydrated. Right tympanic membrane is bulging, erythematous, and opaque with decreased mobility on pneumatic otoscopy, and the landmarks are obscured. Left tympanic membrane is pearly with good landmarks and normal mobility. No mastoid tenderness or swelling and no postauricular erythema. Nose has pale boggy turbinates with clear rhinorrhea. Throat is mildly erythematous without exudate, neck is supple with shallow bilateral anterior cervical nodes, lungs are clear to auscultation with no wheeze, heart is regular without murmur. Skin shows dry patches in both antecubital fossae. Tympanometry showed a flat type B tracing on the right and a normal type A tracing on the left. A rapid strep antigen test done in clinic was negative.

Impression is acute otitis media of the right ear, which is her fourth episode in 6 months and meets criteria for recurrent otitis media. Her asthma is well controlled, her allergic rhinitis is not well controlled and is likely contributing, and the atopic dermatitis is stable. Plan, start amoxicillin 900 mg twice daily for 7 days, correction, 800 mg twice daily for 7 days, which is about 90 milligrams per kilogram per day based on the corrected weight. Use ibuprofen 180 mg every 6 hours as needed for ear pain or fever. Increase the cetirizine from 2.5 mg to 5 mg once daily. Stop the diphenhydramine at bedtime because it thickens secretions and can disturb sleep. Continue the fluticasone, albuterol, and hydrocortisone 1% cream as prescribed. Refer to pediatric otolaryngology to discuss tympanostomy tubes given the recurrent episodes. Recheck in 2 weeks with repeat tympanometry, and arrange an audiology evaluation if the right-sided effusion persists. We recommend the influenza vaccine once she has been afebrile for a few days. Return precautions reviewed with the mother, return sooner if fever persists beyond 48 hours, if there is ear drainage, swelling behind the ear, severe pain, or if she is not drinking well. The mother verbalized understanding. End of dictation.
"""

reference: A 5-year-old female with mild persistent asthma, allergic rhinitis and atopic dermatitis presented with her mother for 3 days of right ear pain and fever after a week-long cold, with three prior ear infections in the last 6 months. Examination showed a bulging, erythematous, opaque right tympanic membrane with decreased mobility, a flat tracing on tympanometry, and a negative rapid strep test. The impression is acute otitis media of the right ear, her fourth episode in 6 months. Amoxicillin 800 mg twice daily for 7 days and ibuprofen were prescribed, cetirizine was increased to 5 mg daily, and diphenhydramine was stopped. Referral to otolaryngology and a 2-week recheck were arranged.

"""
A 65-year-old male is seen in the family medicine clinic with 10 days of nasal congestion and facial pressure. He first thought it was a cold and felt a little better around day 5, but then he got worse again with thick yellow-green nasal drainage, pain over both cheeks, and pain in his upper teeth. He also has a mild headache and a cough that is worse when he lies down. He denies fever, chills, vision changes, double vision, facial swelling, and neck stiffness.

He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. When I asked him to tell me about his medicines, he could not read the names on the bottles and described a white pill and a small pink pill that he takes in the morning. He admits he sometimes skips them when he feels well. His daughter fills his pillbox on Sundays. From the pharmacy list that I reviewed with him, he takes lisinopril 20 mg daily and metformin 500 mg twice daily. He has no known drug allergies. Because of his limited health literacy, I used plain language and short sentences throughout the visit.

Vitals today: BP 138/82, HR 78, temperature 98.6 F, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air. His fingerstick glucose was 156. His A1c was 7.4% at the last visit 2 months ago. On exam he has boggy nasal turbinates with thick yellow nasal drainage. Maxillary sinus tenderness is present bilaterally. The throat is mildly red without exudate, the tympanic membranes are normal, and the lungs are clear. There is no periorbital swelling.

My impression is acute bacterial sinusitis, since his symptoms have lasted more than 10 days and worsened after initial improvement. His hypertension and type 2 diabetes are reasonably controlled. I am starting amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg/125 mg twice daily with food for 7 days, saline nasal rinses twice daily, and fluticasone nasal spray 2 sprays in each nostril once daily. He may take acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain. I advised him to avoid pseudoephedrine decongestants because of his blood pressure. He will continue lisinopril and metformin. I asked him to repeat the instructions back to me, gave him a one-page medication schedule with pictures and large print, and our nurse will call him in 3 days to check on him. He should return sooner for vision changes, facial swelling, severe headache, or fever, and we will see him again in 2 weeks.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Rheumatology inpatient follow up dictation, hospital day 2, on a 75-year-old female admitted with an acute gout flare of the right first metatarsophalangeal joint. She flew home from overseas six days ago after a fourteen hour flight, ate rich meals and drank more wine than usual during the trip, and two days after arriving developed severe right big toe pain to the point that she could not bear weight and came to the emergency department. She denies fever, denies chills, denies any trauma to the foot, and denies calf pain or leg swelling, which mattered to check given the long flight. She has chronic kidney disease stage 3, hypertension, and one previous milder gout attack in the same toe years ago. Home medications on admission were hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily and amlodipine 5 mg daily. Vitals this morning are temperature 98.9 Fahrenheit, heart rate 84, blood pressure 142 over 82, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. On exam the right first MTP joint is warm, red, swollen and exquisitely tender with limited motion, the left foot is normal, and both calves are soft and nontender without asymmetry. Arthrocentesis yesterday showed needle shaped negatively birefringent crystals consistent with monosodium urate, synovial white count 18,000, and the gram stain and culture are negative so far. Serum uric acid was 9.4, creatinine 1.5 with an eGFR of 35, and the blood white count was 11.6. Impression is an acute gout flare, crystal proven, precipitated by travel, dietary indiscretion, dehydration and hydrochlorothiazide use, in the setting of chronic kidney disease stage 3. Because of her kidney function NSAIDs are avoided and colchicine is not preferred. She was started yesterday on prednisone 40 mg daily, correction, prednisone 30 mg daily for five days, with her pain improving from nine out of ten to four out of ten. Plan is to continue prednisone 30 mg daily, stop the hydrochlorothiazide and start losartan 25 mg daily instead for blood pressure and its mild uric acid lowering effect, continue amlodipine 5 mg daily, encourage oral hydration, and elevate the foot with ice. I will plan to start allopurinol 50 mg daily at rheumatology clinic follow up in two weeks once the flare has resolved, with a uric acid recheck after. Anticipate discharge tomorrow if the pain continues to improve and she is walking safely.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
84-year-old female seen in geriatrics clinic for advance care planning and follow-up of her chronic conditions, which include heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, and osteoarthritis of both knees. She came with her daughter. She no longer drives and depends on her daughter, who works full-time, for rides. The clinic is about 40 minutes from her home, and she missed her last two visits because no ride was available. Her daughter is worried that follow-up will keep slipping.

She feels stable overall. She has knee pain that is worse with walking and takes over-the-counter naproxen 220 mg twice daily for it. She denies chest pain, orthopnea, leg swelling, lightheadedness when she stands, and falls in the past year. She also denies low mood. She takes furosemide 20 mg daily and lisinopril 5 mg daily.

Vitals: BP 128/70, HR 68, SpO2 96% on room air, weight 61 kg, unchanged from the last visit. On exam both knees have crepitus with mild bony enlargement. The lungs are clear, and there is no jugular venous distension, peripheral edema, or knee effusion. Labs from 2 weeks ago showed creatinine 1.3 with eGFR 38 and potassium 4.4.

We spent most of the visit on advance care planning. She understands her heart and kidney conditions and has decision-making capacity. She wants to stay in her own home as long as possible. She would not want CPR or a breathing machine if her heart stopped, but she would accept hospital treatment for reversible problems. She named her daughter as her health care surrogate, and her daughter agreed. We completed a health care surrogate designation and a POLST form with a DNR/DNI order today, and copies were given to both of them and scanned into the chart.

Impression: advance care planning completed, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction compensated, stage 3 chronic kidney disease stable, and knee osteoarthritis. I am stopping naproxen because of her kidney disease and heart failure and starting acetaminophen 650 mg three times daily. We will continue furosemide 20 mg daily and lisinopril 5 mg daily. Because of her transportation barriers, I placed a referral to social work for paratransit enrollment and ride assistance, and I arranged home health nursing visits. A BMP will be drawn at a lab near her home in 2 weeks. Her next visit in 3 months will be by video, and she will call sooner for weight gain, swelling, or shortness of breath.
"""

"""
Doctor: Good to see you again. I have you down as a 26-year-old female here for follow-up of bipolar I disorder. How have the last few weeks been?
Patient: Honestly rough. I work rotating shifts at a distribution center, and last month they moved me to nights. My schedule changes every week, so my sleep has been all over the place.
Doctor: How much are you sleeping?
Patient: Maybe four hours some days, then ten hours on my days off. About a week ago I had three days where I felt really wired, with racing thoughts, talking fast, and spending too much. It settled after I finally slept.
Doctor: Any thoughts of hurting yourself or ending your life?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Any voices or seeing things that are not there?
Patient: No hallucinations.
Doctor: How about side effects from the lithium, like shaking, diarrhea, vomiting, or being very thirsty?
Patient: A little hand shaking, but no diarrhea, no vomiting, and I am not extra thirsty.
Doctor: Tell me how you take the lithium.
Patient: Lithium 600 mg in the morning and 600 mg at night. With the shift changes I sometimes take the night dose really late or skip it. Probably twice a week.
Doctor: Any other medicines or supplements?
Patient: Just ibuprofen 400 mg now and then for headaches, maybe three times a week. I have an IUD for birth control.
Doctor: Thank you. Your blood pressure today is 114/70 and your heart rate is 80. I see a fine tremor in both outstretched hands. Your speech is a normal rate, your mood is up and down by your report, your thoughts are organized, and you do not seem to be responding to anything unseen. Your labs from this week show a lithium level of 0.5 mEq/L, creatinine 0.8, and TSH 2.1. The lithium level is on the low side, which fits with the missed doses.
Patient: Is the wired stretch the bipolar coming back?
Doctor: My impression is bipolar I disorder with a brief hypomanic episode triggered by sleep disruption from your rotating shifts, and a low lithium level from missed doses. Here is the plan. Keep lithium 600 mg twice daily, but tie the doses to your main sleep period, one when you wake up and one twelve hours later, and set phone alarms. Start melatonin 3 mg thirty minutes before your main sleep period. Stop the ibuprofen, because it can raise your lithium level, and use acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for headaches instead. We will repeat the lithium level in two weeks, drawn twelve hours after your last dose, and I would like you to keep a sleep log. I will write a letter asking your employer for a more consistent schedule. Let us meet again in four weeks, and call sooner if you stop sleeping, feel wired again, or have any thoughts of hurting yourself.
Patient: Okay, that makes sense.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Hi there, come on in. I hear he's got a barky cough. Tell me what's been going on.
Family member: Yes, it started with a runny nose two days ago, and then tonight he woke up with this awful barking cough and a noisy sound when he breathes in. It really scared me.
Doctor: I'm sure it did. So this is a 5-year-old male with a barky cough since last night. Has he had a fever?
Family member: He felt warm, I think around 100, so I gave him children's acetaminophen about two hours ago.
Doctor: Okay. Any drooling or trouble swallowing?
Family member: No drooling, and he's been drinking fine.
Doctor: Any chance he swallowed or choked on something, like a small toy or food?
Family member: No, nothing like that. No vomiting either, and no rash.
Doctor: Has he had croup before, or any asthma?
Family member: Never croup, and no asthma. His shots are up to date and he has no medicine allergies.
Doctor: Good. Did you give him any cough syrup?
Family member: Yes, a dose of an over-the-counter cough syrup last night, but it didn't do anything.
Doctor: Okay, let's check him. His temperature is 100.4, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, and he weighs 18 kilos. He's sitting comfortably in your lap. He has that barking cough, and when he gets upset I hear some inspiratory stridor, but at rest there is no stridor and no retractions. His throat is mildly red, ears are clear, and the lungs have good air movement with no wheezing. I also did a rapid flu and COVID swab and both are negative.
Family member: So what is it?
Doctor: This is croup, a viral infection that swells the area just below the vocal cords. Because he has stridor when he's upset, I'm going to give him dexamethasone 10 mg by mouth right now, one single dose, which helps the swelling. We'll watch him here for about an hour. Stop the cough syrup, it doesn't help croup. For fever or discomfort you can give acetaminophen 270 mg every 6 hours as needed.
Family member: Is it okay to go home after that?
Doctor: If he stays comfortable with no stridor at rest during the observation, yes. Keep him calm, and a steamy bathroom or cool night air can help if he gets noisy. Call his pediatrician tomorrow for a recheck, and come back right away or call 911 if you hear stridor at rest, he's drooling, he's working hard to breathe, or his lips look blue.
Family member: Okay, thank you.
"""

A rapid flu and COVID swab was negative. The diagnosis was croup, and he received a single oral dose of dexamethasone with observation in clinic, was told to stop cough syrup, and was given acetaminophen as needed with return precautions and pediatrician follow-up.

Doctor: Good afternoon. You're a 37-year-old female here for your COPD follow-up, correct?
Patient: Yes. I'm doing okay, but I've had more breathlessness lately going up stairs.
Doctor: How often are you needing your rescue inhaler?
Patient: About four times a week now. It used to be once or twice.
Doctor: And your daily inhaler, remind me what you take.
Patient: The umeclidinium-vilanterol, one puff every morning, and albuterol when I need it. I haven't missed any doses.
Doctor: Good. Have you had any flare-ups since I saw you last?
Patient: One, about four months ago. I got a steroid burst and an antibiotic from urgent care, and it settled in a week.
Doctor: Any coughing up blood, chest pain, or fever now?

Doctor: Any swelling in your ankles or waking up at night short of breath?

Doctor: You quit smoking about three years ago, right?

Doctor: Wonderful. And remind me, your alpha-1 antitrypsin level was low when we tested years ago?
Patient: Yes, that's why I got COPD so young.

Stop the umeclidinium-vilanterol and start fluticasone-umeclidinium-vilanterol, 100/62.5/25 micrograms, one inhalation every morning. Keep albuterol, two puffs as needed. Patient: Okay, that makes sense. Thank you.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Dermatology inpatient consultation dictation. Requested by the hospitalist service for evaluation of a changing pigmented lesion. The patient is a 53-year-old female on hospital day 3 for cellulitis of the right lower leg. At the skin check on admission, the nurse noticed a dark mole on her left upper back, and the patient says her husband has told her it has been getting bigger and darker over about six months. She says it has been itchy and bled once after she scratched it. She denies pain from the lesion, new moles elsewhere, and unintentional weight loss. She has fair skin, burns easily, and had several blistering sunburns as a teenager. No prior skin cancer. She works as a night-shift nurse on a rotating schedule and sleeps during the day, so she has trouble attending morning appointments and has not had a full skin exam in many years.

Past history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hypothyroidism. Current inpatient medications are cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours, lisinopril 10 mg daily, which was reduced from 20 mg by the primary team because her blood pressures were soft on admission, levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and insulin sliding scale. Her home metformin 1000 mg twice daily is on hold while she is in the hospital, and vancomycin was stopped on hospital day 2 after the MRSA nasal swab was negative. No known drug allergies.

Vitals today are blood pressure 122/74, heart rate 76, and temperature 98.2 F. Labs show white blood cell count 9.8, down from 13.4 on admission, creatinine 0.9, and hemoglobin A1c 7.4%. On exam, there is a pigmented lesion on the left upper back measuring 7 mm in greatest diameter, correction, 9 mm on repeat measurement with a ruler. It is asymmetric with an irregular, notched border and variegated color with shades of brown, black, and a focal area of blue-gray. The center is slightly raised with a small crusted erosion. There is no ulceration and no active bleeding. Dermoscopy shows an atypical network, irregular streaks, and a blue-white veil. There is no lymphadenopathy in the axillae, neck, or groin. The rest of the full skin exam shows about twenty benign-appearing nevi and no other atypical lesions. The erythema of the right lower leg is receding.

My impression is a changing pigmented lesion on the left upper back, 9 mm, with asymmetry, border irregularity, color variegation, diameter over 6 mm, and evolution, suspicious for melanoma versus a severely dysplastic nevus. The cellulitis is improving.

Procedure and recommendations. I explained the concern to the patient and obtained verbal consent. I performed a bedside excisional biopsy today using an elliptical excision with 2 mm margins under 3 mL of 1% lidocaine with epinephrine, closed with nylon sutures, well tolerated, with minimal bleeding. Send to dermatopathology with a request for Breslow thickness if melanoma is confirmed. Keep the site dry for 48 hours. Sutures will be removed in 14 days in the dermatology clinic, and because of her night shifts we will schedule a late-afternoon appointment and call her with the pathology result at a time she chooses. If melanoma is confirmed, she will need wide local excision and a discussion of sentinel lymph node biopsy with surgical oncology. Full skin exams every six months afterward, with daily sunscreen and sun protection counseling. Continue antibiotics and diabetes management per the primary team.
"""

Dermatology inpatient consultation dictation. Requested by the hospitalist service for evaluation of a changing pigmented lesion. The patient is a 53-year-old female on hospital day 3 for cellulitis of the right lower leg. At the skin check on admission, the nurse noticed a dark mole on her left upper back, and the patient says her husband has told her it has been getting bigger and darker over about six months. She says it has been itchy and bled once after she scratched it. She denies pain from the lesion, new moles elsewhere, and unintentional weight loss. She has fair skin, burns easily, and had several blistering sunburns as a teenager. No prior skin cancer. She works as a night-shift nurse on a rotating schedule and sleeps during the day, so she has trouble attending morning appointments and has not had a full skin exam in many years.

Past history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hypothyroidism. Current inpatient medications are cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours, lisinopril 10 mg daily, which was reduced from 20 mg by the primary team because her blood pressures were soft on admission, levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and insulin sliding scale. Her home metformin 1000 mg twice daily is on hold while she is in the hospital, and vancomycin was stopped on hospital day 2 after the MRSA nasal swab was negative. No known drug allergies.

Vitals today are blood pressure 122/74, heart rate 76, and temperature 98.2 F. Labs show white blood cell count 9.8, down from 13.4 on admission, creatinine 0.9, and hemoglobin A1c 7.4%. On exam, there is a pigmented lesion on the left upper back measuring 7 mm in greatest diameter, correction, 9 mm on repeat measurement with a ruler. It is asymmetric with an irregular, notched border and variegated color with shades of brown, black, and a focal area of blue-gray. The center is slightly raised with a small crusted erosion. There is no ulceration and no active bleeding. Dermoscopy shows an atypical network, irregular streaks, and a blue-white veil. There is no lymphadenopathy in the axillae, neck, or groin. The rest of the full skin exam shows about twenty benign-appearing nevi and no other atypical lesions. The erythema of the right lower leg is receding.

My impression is a changing pigmented lesion on the left upper back, 9 mm, with asymmetry, border irregularity, color variegation, diameter over 6 mm, and evolution, suspicious for melanoma versus a severely dysplastic nevus. The cellulitis is improving.

Procedure and recommendations. I explained the concern to the patient and obtained verbal consent. I performed a bedside excisional biopsy today using an elliptical excision with 2 mm margins under 3 mL of 1% lidocaine with epinephrine, closed with nylon sutures, well tolerated, with minimal bleeding. Send to dermatopathology with a request for Breslow thickness if melanoma is confirmed. Keep the site dry for 48 hours. Sutures will be removed in 14 days in the dermatology clinic, and because of her night shifts we will schedule a late-afternoon appointment and call her with the pathology result at a time she chooses. If melanoma is confirmed, she will need wide local excision and a discussion of sentinel lymph node biopsy with surgical oncology. Full skin exams every six months afterward, with daily sunscreen and sun protection counseling. Continue antibiotics and diabetes management per the primary team.

"""
Doctor: Hello. I'm using a professional medical interpreter by video for the whole visit so we understand each other well. Please speak normally and the interpreter will translate. I have you down as a 43-year-old female with swelling of the lips and tongue. When did it start?
Patient: This morning when I woke up, about three hours ago. My lips felt big and then my tongue felt thick.
Doctor: Any trouble breathing or swallowing?
Patient: My voice sounds funny and it is a little hard to swallow, but I can breathe okay.
Doctor: Any hives, itching, vomiting, belly pain, or chest pain?
Patient: No hives, no itching, no vomiting, no belly pain, and no chest pain.
Doctor: Have you had swelling like this before?
Patient: A few weeks ago my lip swelled a little and went away by itself, so I didn't come in.
Doctor: Any new foods, soaps, insect bites, or new medicines?
Patient: Nothing new.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Tell me every medicine you take, and how you really take them.
Patient: For blood pressure I take lisinopril, 10 milligrams every morning, and a water pill, hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 milligrams every morning. For sugar I have metformin 500 milligrams twice a day, but I only take it once a day because I can't afford to refill it so often. And I stopped atorvastatin two months ago because it costs too much.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me, that helps. Do you have the lisinopril bottle with you?
Patient: Yes, in my bag. The interpreter can read the label. Oh, it says 20 milligrams, not 10. Sorry, I was wrong, it is 20 milligrams once a day.
Doctor: Thank you for checking. So the lisinopril dose is 20 milligrams once a day. There are no hives on your skin. I looked in with a flexible scope and found mild swelling at the base of the tongue, but the airway is open. Your glucose is 248, potassium 4.2, and creatinine 0.9, and your A1c last month was 9.2.
Patient: Is it from food? Is it dangerous?
Doctor: It is most likely angioedema caused by the lisinopril, which is a known side effect of that class of blood pressure medicines, the ACE inhibitors. It can happen even after taking them for a long time, and it is dangerous because the tongue and throat can keep swelling, so we will treat it now and watch you closely. I'm giving epinephrine 0.3 milligrams into the muscle, methylprednisolone 125 milligrams IV, diphenhydramine 50 milligrams IV, and famotidine 20 milligrams IV.
Patient: What about my medicines?
Doctor: Stop the lisinopril for good, and never take another ACE inhibitor. Because your blood pressure is high without it, I'm increasing the hydrochlorothiazide from 12.5 to 25 milligrams every morning until your primary doctor picks a replacement. Your high blood pressure, diabetes, and high cholesterol all need steady treatment, so I want you to restart atorvastatin 40 milligrams once a day and take the metformin twice a day as prescribed. Our social worker will come see you about discount pharmacy programs so cost does not stop you from taking them. I want to watch you in the emergency department for at least six hours. If the swelling is clearly going down, you can go home, and if it is not, we will admit you to the hospital for airway monitoring. See your primary doctor in two to three days. Come back right away for trouble breathing, trouble swallowing, or a change in your voice.
Patient: Okay, I understand. Thank you.
"""

Because she takes an anticoagulant, I asked about bleeding, and she denies black stools, blood in the urine, nosebleeds, and easy bruising. Her caffeine intake is one cup of tea in the morning.

Current medications are apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 25 mg once daily, and levothyroxine 75 mcg once daily. Clinical note:
"""
ED nephrology eval. 63-year-old male w/ CKD stage 3b (baseline Cr 1.9, eGFR ~38), sent in by PCP after outpatient labs showed high K.

HPI:
C/o generalized weakness x 2 d.
Intermittent palpitations since yesterday.
Leg cramps x 3 wks.
Denies chest pain. Denies SOB. Denies syncope. Denies N/V. Denies diarrhea.
Eating and drinking normally, urine output unchanged per pt.

OTC use (did not tell PCP):
Started OTC potassium supplement ~3 wks ago for leg cramps, 1 tab daily.
Uses salt substitute on all food.
Turmeric capsules daily.
Ibuprofen 600 mg TID x 2 wks for knee OA.

PMH: CKD 3b, HTN, knee OA.
NKDA.

Home meds:
Lisinopril 40 mg daily
Amlodipine 10 mg daily
Atorvastatin 40 mg nightly
Sodium bicarbonate 650 mg BID

Vitals: BP 158/92, HR 58, RR 18, SpO2 97% RA, Temp 36.8 C.

Exam:
Gen: NAD, mildly fatigued.
CV: bradycardic, regular, no m/r/g.
Lungs: CTAB.
Abd: soft, NT.
Ext: no edema.
Neuro: strength 5-/5 symmetric, no focal deficit.

Results:
K 6.4, repeat K 6.2 non-hemolyzed.
Cr 2.6 (baseline 1.9), BUN 48, eGFR 26, HCO3 19, Na 137.
UA: trace protein, no blood.
ECG: peaked T waves, QRS 96 ms, no AV block, rate 56.
Renal US: no hydronephrosis.

ED course:
Calcium gluconate 1 g IV given.
Regular insulin 10 units IV w/ D50 1 amp.
Albuterol 10 mg neb.
Lokelma 10 g PO x1.
Repeat K 5.4 at 4 h, ECG T waves improved.

Impression:
Hyperkalemia 2/2 OTC potassium supplement + salt substitute + ACEi in setting of AKI on CKD 3b.
AKI on CKD 3b, Cr 2.6 from baseline 1.9, likely NSAID + ACEi, no obstruction on renal US.
HTN, BP elevated today.

Plan:
Stop potassium supplement, salt substitute, turmeric, and ibuprofen. Counseled to avoid all OTC supplements and NSAIDs w/o asking nephrology.
Acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN for knee pain.
Hold lisinopril until K and Cr improve.
Continue amlodipine 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, sodium bicarbonate 650 mg BID.
Lokelma 10 g daily x 3 d.
Low K diet teaching.
Admit to tele obs, repeat BMP q4h x 2 then q AM, nephrology will follow.
Outpt nephrology f/u 1 wk after d/c w/ BMP.
"""

K was 6.4 and Cr 2.6 from a baseline of 1.9, and the ECG showed peaked T waves that improved after calcium gluconate, insulin with D50, albuterol and Lokelma. Lithium not restarted for now.

Lorazepam short-term only, max 2 doses/day.

Revisit lithium in 2nd trimester w/ perinatal psych + OB. If restarted, check level q4 wks and more often near delivery.

"""

78-year-old female seen in the geriatrics clinic for unintentional weight loss and declining strength. She lives alone and reports that over the past six months her appetite has dropped and she now eats mostly one full meal a day, with tea and toast otherwise. She denies dysphagia, denies nausea, denies abdominal pain, denies diarrhea, and denies night sweats. Mood is described as okay and her PHQ-2 score is 1. Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good afternoon. Before we start, I'm using a professional interpreter on the line today, so please speak naturally and pause so she can interpret. Is that okay?
Patient: Yes, that's fine.
Doctor: I have a 35-year-old female here for recurrent urinary tract infections. Tell me what has been happening.
Patient: In the last year I have had four infections. Burning when I pass urine, and I feel like I have to go all the time. Each time the doctor gave me antibiotics and it got better, but it comes back in a few weeks.
Doctor: Do you notice a pattern, for example after intercourse?
Patient: Yes, most of the time within a day after being with my husband.
Doctor: Do you have burning, blood in the urine, fever, or back pain right now?
Patient: No fever and no back pain. No blood. The last infection was three weeks ago and I finished the pills.
Doctor: What antibiotic was it?
Patient: Nitrofurantoin, 100 mg twice a day for five days.
Doctor: And what else do you take?
Patient: Cranberry pills, 500 mg once a day. And phenazopyridine, the orange pill, when it burns, 200 mg three times a day for two days.
Doctor: Any kidney stones, diabetes, or trouble emptying your bladder?
Patient: No stones, no diabetes.
Doctor: How much water do you drink, and do you urinate after intercourse?
Patient: Maybe three glasses a day. And no, I usually don't urinate right after.
Doctor: Thank you. Your temperature today is 36.7, blood pressure 118/72, and heart rate 76. Your kidney area is not tender and your lower belly is not tender. The urine dipstick today is negative for nitrite, leukocytes, and blood. The bladder scan shows you are emptying well, with only 20 mL left behind. Your urine culture from last month grew E. coli that was sensitive to nitrofurantoin.
Patient: So it's not an infection today?
Doctor: Correct, nothing active today. My impression is recurrent urinary tract infections that follow intercourse, with no sign of a structural problem so far. Here is the plan. I'm starting nitrofurantoin 100 mg as a single dose within two hours after intercourse to prevent infections. Keep taking the cranberry. Use the phenazopyridine only if you have burning, and no more than two days. Drink about two liters of water a day and empty your bladder within thirty minutes after intercourse. We will send a urine culture each time you have symptoms before starting an antibiotic. I'd also like a renal ultrasound to be thorough, and I'll see you back in three months.
Patient: Okay, thank you.
"""

Nephrology dictation, hospital day 2, on a 35-year-old female with end stage renal disease from IgA nephropathy on in-center hemodialysis three times a week through a left forearm arteriovenous fistula, admitted with volume overload and shortness of breath. The patient works rotating night shifts as a hotel housekeeper and her schedule changes week to week, which is why she keeps missing her morning chair time. Over the last five days she has had progressive shortness of breath, orthopnea that has her sleeping in a recliner, leg swelling, and a weight gain of about five kilograms above her dry weight of 62 kilograms. She has had a mild dry cough. She denies chest pain, fever, palpitations, nausea, and vomiting, and she makes about a cup of urine a day. Her sister says she has been drinking a lot of fluids and eating canned soup on her late nights, and she was also taking naproxen 220 mg twice daily over the counter for headaches.

Past history includes hypertension, anemia of chronic kidney disease, and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Home medications are amlodipine 10 mg daily, carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, sevelamer carbonate 800 mg three times daily with meals, calcitriol 0.25 mcg daily, furosemide 80 mg twice daily, and epoetin alfa 10,000 units three times weekly at dialysis. She has no known drug allergies.

On admission blood pressure was 168/98, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 24, and oxygen saturation 90% on room air, with a weight of 67.1 kilograms. This morning after dialysis last night her blood pressure is 148/86, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, and weight 63.8 kilograms. On exam the jugular venous pressure is elevated, there are bibasilar crackles, and there is 2 plus pitting edema of both legs. The fistula has a palpable thrill and an audible bruit. There is no pericardial rub.

Admission labs showed potassium 5.8, BUN 78, creatinine 9.6, hemoglobin 8.9, and phosphorus 6.4. The chest x-ray showed pulmonary vascular congestion with small bilateral pleural effusions. The ECG showed no peaked T waves or conduction changes. She had urgent hemodialysis last night with ultrafiltration of 3.5 liters over four hours, and her potassium came down to 4.2.

Impression is volume overload from missed and shortened hemodialysis sessions in a patient with end stage renal disease, with mild hyperkalemia, now improving, and uncontrolled hypertension from volume excess and recent NSAID use.

Plan is hemodialysis again today with an ultrafiltration goal of three liters, and I will lower her target dry weight from 62 to 61 kilograms. Fluid restriction of one liter a day, two gram sodium and low potassium diet, and a renal dietitian visit. Stop naproxen and avoid all NSAIDs. Social work and the dialysis unit will try to move her to a late evening chair time that fits her shift schedule, and I explained this to her and her sister in plain language. Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Welcome back. This is your three-month visit, and I see in the chart that you're a 31-year-old female living with HIV, on your current treatment for about two years. How have you been?
Patient: Honestly, a little anxious. I read online that HIV pills can damage your kidneys and liver, and I keep worrying about it. Is that going to happen to me? And what if the virus becomes resistant? Also, I've had some headaches. Is that from the medicine?
Doctor: Those are good questions and I'll go through each one. First, are you still taking Biktarvy, one tablet once daily?
Patient: Yes, every morning with breakfast. I haven't missed a single dose.
Doctor: Wonderful. Your labs from last week look excellent. Your viral load is undetectable, less than 20 copies, your CD4 count is 640, creatinine is 0.8, eGFR is 105, and your liver tests are normal. So your kidneys and liver are fine and the virus is well controlled.
Patient: So the pills aren't hurting me? What about resistance if I miss one?
Doctor: An occasional missed dose is unlikely to cause trouble with this regimen, but taking it every day is the best protection. About the headaches, how often do you get them?
Patient: Maybe twice a week, mild, usually in the afternoon. And I've had trouble sleeping because I keep worrying. No fever, no night sweats, no weight loss, no diarrhea, and no rash.
Doctor: Thank you. Your blood pressure today is 118/72, heart rate 80, and temperature 98.4. Your lymph nodes feel normal, your mouth is clear with no thrush, and your lungs are clear.
Patient: One more thing. My partner and I want to have a baby next year. Is that possible? Could I pass HIV to the baby, or to my partner?
Doctor: Yes, it is possible. With an undetectable viral load there is essentially no risk of sexual transmission to your partner, and the risk to the baby is very low if you keep taking treatment. Since you're planning a pregnancy, I'd like you to start folic acid 0.4 mg daily now. We can keep your current regimen.
Patient: Okay. Do I need any tests?
Doctor: It's been three years since your last Pap smear, so we'll do a Pap smear today, send urine testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia, and give you your flu shot.
Patient: And the anxious feelings?
Doctor: Anxiety is very understandable, and your headaches are probably related to stress and poor sleep rather than the medicine. Try limiting caffeine in the afternoon, and I'll refer you to our clinic counselor. If it persists we can talk about medication. Continue Biktarvy one tablet once daily, and come back in three months for a repeat viral load, or sooner if you have any concerns.
Patient: Thank you, that helps a lot.
"""

The patient is a 79-year-old male seen in the endocrinology clinic for follow-up of Graves disease with hyperthyroidism, diagnosed about two months ago. He has had no chest pain, and no eye pain or double vision.

Vitals today are BP 128/76, HR 78, and weight 172 pounds, up 3 pounds since the last visit. On exam he has a very mild fine tremor of the outstretched hands. The thyroid is diffusely enlarged and smooth without discrete nodules. There is no proptosis or lid lag, and his reflexes are normal.

Impression is Graves disease with hyperthyroidism, responding well to methimazole. Because the free T4 has normalized, I will continue methimazole at the same dose of 10 mg daily and recheck free T4 and TSH in six weeks. Rheumatology progress note, hospital day 3. The patient is a 46-year-old male with systemic lupus erythematosus who was admitted three days ago with a flare causing inflammatory polyarthritis of the hands and knees, fatigue, and new foamy urine with ankle swelling. There were no events overnight. His joint pain and morning stiffness are improving. He denies fever, chest pain, new rash, oral ulcers, and headache.

Current inpatient medications are methylprednisolone 500 mg IV daily, with today being the third and final dose, hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily continued from home, and lisinopril 10 mg daily, which was started on admission for blood pressure and proteinuria.

My assessment is a systemic lupus erythematosus flare with inflammatory polyarthritis and probable lupus nephritis, responding to pulse steroids. His hypertension is above goal.

- testes nontender, no swelling, no hernia

- ceftriaxone 2 g IV + metronidazole 500 mg IV started

- admit to surgery
- NPO, cont IV fluids
- STOP ibuprofen, avoid NSAIDs periop
- STOP pre-workout and creatine until recovered; hold fish oil and vitamin D3 while inpatient
- hold omeprazole and escitalopram while NPO, resume post-op
- albuterol PRN available
- BMP in AM to recheck Cr
- pt verbalized understanding, agrees w/ plan

Chief Complaint: Left forearm laceration.

He was hospitalized three weeks ago for acute appendicitis and underwent a laparoscopic appendectomy, was discharged on hospital day 2, and has had no complications since. Home medication is acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for residual soreness. No known drug allergies.

ROS: Negative for fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, chest pain, and shortness of breath.

Full active range of motion of the wrist and all fingers with 5/5 strength. Sensation intact in the median, ulnar, and radial distributions. Radial pulse 2+, capillary refill under 2 seconds. Abdomen: laparoscopic port sites are healing well, clean and nontender, no erythema or drainage.

ED Course / Results: X-ray of the left forearm shows no fracture and no radiopaque foreign body. Wound irrigation with 500 mL of normal saline was performed. Local anesthesia was achieved with 5 mL of 1% lidocaine. The laceration was closed with six simple interrupted 4-0 nylon sutures with good approximation and hemostasis. Tdap 0.5 mL IM was given.

Medical Decision Making: 34-year-old male with a simple forearm laceration without tendon, nerve, or vascular injury and no foreign body on imaging. His recent hospitalization and appendectomy do not change wound management, and the port sites show no sign of infection. Antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated for this clean wound. Tdap was given because his last tetanus booster was more than 10 years ago.

Disposition: Discharged home in stable condition. Increase acetaminophen to 1000 mg every 6 hours as needed and start ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 hours as needed with food. Keep the wound clean and dry for 24 hours, then wash gently. Suture removal in 10 to 14 days with primary care. Return for redness, drainage, fever, numbness, or loss of finger movement. Keep the scheduled postoperative appointment.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good morning. You're a 59-year-old female with breast cancer, ten days out from cycle 2 of docetaxel and cyclophosphamide, here for your nadir blood count check. How are you feeling?
Patient: Tired, mostly. I've been wiped out since last weekend. And my mouth felt a little sore, but it's not terrible.
Doctor: Any fever, chills, sore throat, or cough?
Patient: No fever, I check it twice a day, and it was 98.2 this morning. No chills, no sore throat, no cough.
Doctor: Any burning when you pee, diarrhea, or redness at your port?
Patient: No, none of those. And no bone pain either.
Doctor: Which medicines are you taking right now?
Patient: Ondansetron 8 mg when I feel nauseated, which hasn't been much. That's all besides the chemo.
Doctor: Good. Your temperature today is 98.2, blood pressure 118/70, heart rate 84, and oxygen saturation 98 percent. Your mouth looks fine with no ulcers, the lungs are clear, and the port site is clean and dry. Your labs came back this morning. The white count is 1.8, your absolute neutrophil count is 700, hemoglobin is 10.9, and platelets are 148.
Patient: Is that bad?
Doctor: It's low, but it is the expected nadir. This is neutropenia from the chemotherapy. Because you have no fever, it is not febrile neutropenia, so you don't need to go to the hospital today and we won't change your chemo right now.
Patient: Will my next chemo be delayed?
Doctor: We'll decide based on your count on the day. If the neutrophil count is under 1000, we may delay by a week. To prevent this next time, starting with cycle 3 you'll get pegfilgrastim 6 mg as an injection 24 hours after chemo. Take loratadine 10 mg daily for 5 days starting the day of the injection to prevent bone pain. We'll repeat a CBC in 1 week and again before cycle 3.
Patient: What should I watch for?
Doctor: Check your temperature twice a day, and call us right away for 100.4 or higher, chills, sore throat, or burning with urination. Don't take acetaminophen before checking your temperature. Wash your hands often, avoid sick contacts, and skip raw or undercooked foods. If you get a fever, go straight to the emergency department.
Patient: Okay, I understand.
"""

"""
Pulmonary medicine follow-up dictation on hospital day 3 for a 69-year-old female with COPD who was admitted with an acute exacerbation and is being seen to set up her maintenance regimen before discharge. She is a former smoker with about 40 pack-years who quit 5 years ago. She tells me she was prescribed Trelegy Ellipta, one inhalation daily, but she stopped using it about two months ago because it costs too much on her fixed income, and for the month before that she was stretching it by using it every other day. Since then she has used only her albuterol inhaler, up to six times a day, and she ran out of it 4 days before admission. She came in with 3 days of worsening dyspnea, increased cough, and more sputum that was yellow. Today she says her breathing is better and she is coughing less. She denies fever, chest pain, leg swelling, and hemoptysis. Her only other medication is amlodipine 5 mg daily for hypertension. She has no known drug allergies.

Current inpatient treatment is prednisone 40 mg daily, day 3 of 5, doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, day 3 of 5, albuterol nebulizer as needed, and 2 liters of oxygen by nasal cannula, which we are weaning. Vitals this morning: temperature 36.9 Celsius, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 20, blood pressure 130/78, and oxygen saturation 93% on 2 liters. On exam she is sitting upright and speaking in full sentences, with a prolonged expiratory phase and scattered end-expiratory wheezes, no accessory muscle use, no crackles, and no leg edema. Labs show a white blood cell count of 11.4, which is expected on steroids, eosinophils 320, and bicarbonate 29. The chest x-ray shows hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms and no infiltrate. Her most recent outpatient spirometry showed an FEV1 of 42 percent of predicted, correction, 38 percent of predicted.

Doctor: Hello, I have you down as an 85-year-old male who cut his arm. What happened?
Patient: I was opening boxes at work with a box cutter and it slipped. I work nights as a security guard at a warehouse, and my shifts change all the time, some nights, some weekends.
Doctor: Let me see. Does it hurt, and is it still bleeding?
Patient: It's my left forearm. There's some pain, but the bleeding stopped after I pressed a towel on it.
Doctor: Any numbness or tingling in your fingers? Can you make a fist?
Patient: No numbness, no tingling, and I can move all my fingers.
Doctor: Do you take any blood thinners or other medicines?
Patient: No blood thinners. I have high blood pressure, and I take amlodipine 5 mg a day.
Doctor: When was your last tetanus shot?
Patient: I don't remember. Maybe fifteen years ago.
Doctor: Okay. Your blood pressure is 138/80 and your pulse is 76. This is a laceration that needs stitches. I'll wash it out, numb it, and close it with stitches. Because your last tetanus shot was over ten years ago, I'll give you a tetanus booster too. Since your work schedule is irregular, I'll use stitches that dissolve so you don't need a separate visit to take them out. For pain you can take acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours if needed. Keep the dressing dry for two days.
Patient: Can I go back to work tomorrow night?
Doctor: Light duty with no heavy lifting for one week. Have your own doctor look at the wound any day that fits your shift, and come back sooner if it gets red, swollen, or starts draining, or if you get a fever.
Patient: That works. Thank you.
"""

Dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency x 2 d.
Mild suprapubic pressure since yesterday.

No hx of recurrent UTI, last UTI > 5 yrs ago per pt.
D/c'd from hospital ~3 wks ago after admission for CAP, tx'd w/ IV ceftriaxone then PO azithromycin. No foley during stay. No cough or SOB now.
d/c summary: CXR w/ improving RLL infiltrate.

Social:
Lives alone, limited social support. No family nearby, neighbor checks in occasionally.
Drove self here, no one to pick up Rx for her.
Worried about managing alone if sx worsen.

PMH: HTN, hypothyroidism, HLD, GERD, migraine.
NKDA.

Lisinopril 20 mg daily (increased from 10 mg at d/c).
Levothyroxine 100 mcg daily - CORRECTION: pt checked the bottle, it reads 88 mcg daily.
Atorvastatin 20 mg nightly.
Omeprazole 20 mg daily.
Sumatriptan 50 mg PRN migraine.
HCTZ 25 mg daily was STOPPED in hospital (Na 129 on admit per d/c summary), not taking.

Vitals: Temp 37.1 C, HR 84, BP 138/82, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA.

Exam:
Gen: NAD, ambulatory.
Lungs: CTAB.
Abd: soft, mild suprapubic tenderness, no rebound or guarding.
Back: no CVA tenderness.

Results:
POC UA: LE 2+, nitrite pos, trace blood, protein neg.
Urine hCG neg.
Urine cx sent.
Na 138, Cr 0.8, eGFR 92 on d/c labs.

Impression:
Acute uncomplicated UTI (cystitis), afebrile, hemodynamically stable. No flank pain or CVA tenderness to suggest pyelo.
CAP resolved, no resp sx.
HTN, BP mildly elevated today, lisinopril recently increased.

Tx/Dispo:
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg PO BID x 5 d. Avoid FQ given recent abx exposure. Avoid TMP-SMX w/ lisinopril (hyperK risk).
Phenazopyridine 200 mg TID x 2 d for dysuria.
Push PO fluids.
Urine cx pending, will call pt w/ results. Confirmed best phone # on file.
Written instructions given, teach-back done, pt verbalized understanding.

SW/care coordination referral placed for home support resources.
Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily, levothyroxine 88 mcg daily, atorvastatin, omeprazole, sumatriptan PRN. Do NOT restart HCTZ.
F/u PCP in 1 wk for BP recheck and BMP (lisinopril increased, recent hyponatremia).
ED precautions: fever, flank pain, vomiting, unable to keep fluids down.
"""

He reports nasal congestion, thick yellow-green drainage down the back of his throat, pressure over both cheeks and between the eyes, and a reduced sense of smell for more than three months, worse over the last three weeks. He has been using oxymetazoline nasal spray twice a day for the past three weeks and says it helps for only a few hours before the stuffiness returns. He also has fluticasone nasal spray, 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, but uses it only about half the time. He has not been doing saline rinses. He denies fever, denies facial swelling, denies eye pain or redness, denies double vision or any change in his vision, and denies nosebleeds. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril 10 mg once daily. He has no known drug allergies.

He has a home blood pressure cuff, and his blood pressure today is 134/80 with a pulse of 72. A CT of the sinuses done last month showed mucosal thickening in both maxillary and ethmoid sinuses with no polyps and no bony erosion. No physical exam or nasal endoscopy was possible by phone. He spoke in full sentences throughout the call and sounded congested, without cough or hoarseness.

Impression is chronic rhinosinusitis with an acute flare of purulent drainage, and probable rebound congestion from prolonged use of oxymetazoline. His hypertension appears controlled on his current treatment.

I am stopping the oxymetazoline today, because use beyond three days can make congestion worse. I am starting doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days, to be taken with food and a full glass of water, with sun protection. He should use the fluticasone nasal spray, 2 sprays in each nostril once daily, every day, and start saline rinses with distilled water twice daily. He will continue lisinopril. He should seek urgent care for swelling around the eyes, vision changes, severe headache, or high fever. I am scheduling an in-person visit in three weeks for nasal endoscopy, and we will discuss referral for sinus surgery if symptoms persist.

Clinical note:
"""
Hematology/Oncology consult note

Reason for consult: Chemotherapy-induced neutropenia with fever, evaluation of management and growth factor support. Requesting service: general medicine, hospital ward.

History of present illness: The patient is a 37-year-old male with stage III diffuse large B-cell lymphoma receiving R-CHOP, who presented to the emergency department last night with fever and chills. At home he measured a temperature of 101.9 F. He also reports mild mouth soreness. He denies cough, shortness of breath, dysuria, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. On intake he told the team that he received his last chemotherapy two weeks ago, correction, the oncology infusion record shows cycle 2 day 1 was nine days ago. Pegfilgrastim was not given after cycle 2 because it was not authorized in time. Blood cultures were drawn and he was started on cefepime on arrival.

Pertinent history: Hypertension, obesity, and GERD. He has a right chest implanted port placed before chemotherapy. He currently smokes about one pack of cigarettes per day for 15 years and drinks alcohol rarely. He takes several over-the-counter supplements started after his diagnosis: echinacea, turmeric capsules, and St. John's wort for mood. He first told us he had stopped the St. John's wort before chemotherapy, but on further questioning he clarified that he took it daily until admission.

Medications before admission: lisinopril 20 mg once daily, omeprazole 20 mg once daily, acyclovir 400 mg twice daily for prophylaxis, and ondansetron 8 mg every 8 hours as needed for nausea. No known drug allergies.

Examination: Tmax 101.9 F, blood pressure 108/64, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Ill-appearing but nontoxic. Mild oral mucositis on the buccal mucosa without thrush. The port site is without erythema, tenderness, or drainage. Lungs are clear and the heart is tachycardic and regular. The abdomen is soft and nontender. No rash.

Data review: WBC 0.6 with an absolute neutrophil count of 180, hemoglobin 9.8, platelets 88, creatinine 1.0. Chest x-ray shows no infiltrate. Urinalysis is negative. Blood cultures from the port and a peripheral vein have no growth at 18 hours.

Impression: One, chemotherapy-induced neutropenia with fever, high risk, source not yet identified, at the expected nadir after cycle 2 of R-CHOP without growth factor support. Two, anemia and thrombocytopenia from chemotherapy without bleeding. Three, supplement use with a drug interaction concern, since St. John's wort induces CYP3A4 and can lower chemotherapy levels. Four, tobacco use. Five, hypertension with borderline blood pressure in the setting of infection.

Recommendations: Continue cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours and add vancomycin only for instability, port-site infection, or gram-positive cultures. Start filgrastim 480 mcg subcutaneously once daily until the neutrophil count has recovered. Continue acyclovir 400 mg twice daily and ondansetron 8 mg every 8 hours as needed. Hold lisinopril while his blood pressure is low-normal and he is infected. Stop St. John's wort, echinacea, and turmeric capsules now, and no supplements during chemotherapy without oncology review. Start a nicotine patch 21 mg daily and counsel on tobacco cessation. Neutropenic precautions and a daily CBC with differential, with platelet transfusion if below 10 or bleeding, and red cells if hemoglobin falls below 7. For future cycles, give pegfilgrastim 6 mg with each cycle and review chemotherapy dosing with his primary oncologist. We will follow daily.
"""

reference: A 37-year-old male with stage III diffuse large B-cell lymphoma on R-CHOP was admitted with chemotherapy-induced neutropenia with fever, nine days after cycle 2, with WBC 0.6 and an absolute neutrophil count of 180. Pegfilgrastim was not given after cycle 2, and he had been taking St. John's wort, echinacea, and turmeric capsules and smokes a pack a day. Blood cultures showed no growth at 18 hours. The consultant recommended continuing cefepime, starting filgrastim, holding lisinopril, stopping all supplements, starting a nicotine patch, and giving pegfilgrastim with future cycles.

Doctor: Good afternoon. So you're a 75-year-old male, and I understand you hit your head falling off a ladder about six weeks ago. Tell me how you've been since then.
Patient: Well, doc, the headaches just won't go away. They're mostly across my forehead, and they come on most afternoons. I also get dizzy when I stand up too fast, and I can't concentrate on my crossword like I used to.
Doctor: Did you pass out when you fell?
Patient: No, I don't think so. I remember the whole thing. I was a little foggy for an hour or so, though.
Doctor: And the CT scan of your head in the emergency room?
Patient: They said it was normal, no bleeding.
Doctor: Right, I have that report here, and it showed no bleed and no fracture. Any vomiting, double vision, numbness, or weakness since then?
Patient: No vomiting, no double vision, and no numbness or weakness. Bright lights bother me a bit, and I'm sleeping badly, waking up at three in the morning.
Doctor: What medicines and supplements are you taking?
Patient: Amlodipine 5 mg every morning for blood pressure, and a baby aspirin, 81 mg daily. And I take ginkgo biloba 120 mg twice a day for my memory, plus fish oil, 1000 mg once daily.

Avoid ladders, driving when dizzy, and alcohol until you're better, and increase your activity gradually.
Patient: Okay, I'll stop the ginkgo tonight.
Doctor: Good. Let's see you back in six weeks, sooner if the headaches worsen, you vomit repeatedly, or you notice weakness or confusion.
"""

"""
Dictating an inpatient urology consultation requested by the cardiology service. The patient is a 46-year-old male on hospital day 3 after a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent to the left anterior descending artery, correction, to the right coronary artery. The reason for consultation is erectile dysfunction and a question about whether he can resume sildenafil.

He reports about eighteen months of gradually worsening difficulty achieving and maintaining erections, along with fewer morning erections, and his libido remains good. Before this admission he took sildenafil 50 mg as needed with good effect. He denies penile curvature or pain, testicular pain, hematuria, dysuria, urinary hesitancy, and chest pain at this time. He denies depressed mood. He is not on any nitrate and has not needed nitroglycerin since admission. Past medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and prediabetes. He quit smoking five years ago. Current medications are aspirin 81 mg once daily, clopidogrel 75 mg once daily, atorvastatin 80 mg once daily, and metoprolol succinate 50 mg once daily.

Vitals, blood pressure 118/70, heart rate 62, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is comfortable and in no distress. Genitourinary exam shows a normal circumcised phallus without plaques, both testes descended with normal size and consistency, and no masses.

Labs this admission, total testosterone 412 ng/dL, hemoglobin A1c 6.0%, LDL cholesterol 118 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL.

My impression is erectile dysfunction, most likely vasculogenic and related to his atherosclerotic disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and prediabetes, with a normal testosterone level. A beta blocker contribution is possible but unlikely to be a major factor, and his benefit from metoprolol outweighs this concern. Recommendations are to hold sildenafil 50 mg while he is hospitalized and until his cardiologist clears him after discharge. He must never take sildenafil with any nitrate, including sublingual nitroglycerin, and should tell all providers about his sildenafil use. There are no other medication changes from a urology standpoint. Continue risk factor management and cardiac rehabilitation per cardiology. I will see him in the urology clinic in six weeks to reassess and discuss options, including resuming a PDE5 inhibitor if cleared, or alternatives such as a vacuum erection device. Thank you for this consultation. End of dictation.
"""

Dictating an inpatient urology consultation requested by the cardiology service. Clinical note:
"""
Telephone visit (audio only), orthopedics hand clinic.
Patient is a 71-year-old female, at home. Identity confirmed with two identifiers and she consented to a phone visit. No video, so no visual exam was possible; findings below are patient-reported.

Reason for visit: right hand numbness and tingling, carpal tunnel syndrome follow-up.

History: Six months of numbness and tingling in the right thumb, index, and middle fingers that wakes her two to three times a night. Shaking the hand relieves it. It is worse when she holds her phone or drives. She drops cups and has trouble with buttons. She denies neck pain, pain radiating from the shoulder or elbow, tingling in the left hand, and fever. She has had no recent injury. Her arm does not feel weak overall. The hand feels clumsy.

She works as a home health aide with rotating day and overnight shifts, so her sleep times change week to week and she often forgets or cannot use her night splint when her sleep is in the daytime.

Nerve conduction study ordered by her primary doctor two months ago showed moderate right median neuropathy at the wrist and a normal left side. Past history: hypertension and hypothyroidism, TSH normal last month. Medications: amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, and over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg two or three times a day for hand pain. No known drug allergies.

Home measurements: blood pressure 132/78 and pulse 70 on her home cuff.

Guided self-exam by phone: holding her wrists flexed for 60 seconds brought on tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers within 30 seconds. Tapping over the wrist at home also reproduced the tingling. She reports she can make a full fist and touch her thumb to each fingertip. Speech was clear and she was comfortable on the call.

Impression: right carpal tunnel syndrome, moderate by nerve conduction study, with night symptoms and mild loss of hand function. Blood pressure is acceptable on home readings.

Management: Stop the ibuprofen because of her age and blood pressure. Start acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed, maximum 3000 mg a day. Wear a neutral wrist splint whenever she sleeps, whether that is day or night, and during repetitive tasks. Schedule an in-person visit within 2 weeks, on a day off from work, for a corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel. If symptoms return or weakness develops, I will refer her for surgical carpal tunnel release. Take breaks from repetitive wrist flexion at work. Continue amlodipine and levothyroxine. Call sooner for constant numbness or loss of grip strength.
"""
