Clinical note:
"""
79-year-old male seen in the gastroenterology clinic for heartburn that has not responded to treatment over the past 6 months. He describes a burning feeling behind the breastbone and a sour taste in his mouth almost every day, worse after dinner and when lying flat, with frequent night waking. He denies trouble swallowing, food sticking, vomiting, black stools, blood in his stool, and weight loss. He has been taking omeprazole 20 mg once daily, but when asked to show how he takes it, he swallows it with dinner rather than before a meal, and he sometimes skips it when he forgets. He also chews calcium carbonate tablets several times a day for relief and takes ibuprofen as needed for knee pain, which he calls his arthritis pills. He has limited health literacy and says he has trouble reading the labels on his bottles; his daughter fills a pill box for him on Sundays. His other history is hypertension, treated with amlodipine 5 mg once daily.

Today his blood pressure is 136/78, heart rate 74, and weight 182 lb, which is stable. He is comfortable, and the abdomen is soft and nontender without masses. Hemoglobin last week was 13.6, which is normal. I used plain language and teach-back throughout the visit and drew a simple picture schedule; at the end he could say back that the stomach pill goes before breakfast.

My impression is refractory GERD, likely worsened by incorrect timing of omeprazole and regular ibuprofen use. He has no alarm features, but given his age and persistent symptoms I recommend an EGD. I am increasing omeprazole to 40 mg once daily, taken 30 minutes before breakfast. He will stop ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for knee pain, no more than 4 doses a day. Continue amlodipine 5 mg once daily, and use calcium carbonate only as needed. Raise the head of the bed and avoid eating within 3 hours of bedtime. A large-print picture medication chart was given to him and his daughter. The EGD will be scheduled in 4 weeks, with follow-up in 8 weeks.
"""

79-year-old male seen in the gastroenterology clinic for heartburn that has not responded to treatment over the past 6 months. He describes a burning feeling behind the breastbone and a sour taste in his mouth almost every day, worse after dinner and when lying flat, with frequent night waking. He denies trouble swallowing, food sticking, vomiting, black stools, blood in his stool, and weight loss. He has been taking omeprazole 20 mg once daily, but when asked to show how he takes it, he swallows it with dinner rather than before a meal, and he sometimes skips it when he forgets. He also chews calcium carbonate tablets several times a day for relief and takes ibuprofen as needed for knee pain, which he calls his arthritis pills. He has limited health literacy and says he has trouble reading the labels on his bottles; his daughter fills a pill box for him on Sundays. His other history is hypertension, treated with amlodipine 5 mg once daily.

Today his blood pressure is 136/78, heart rate 74, and weight 182 lb, which is stable. He is comfortable, and the abdomen is soft and nontender without masses. Hemoglobin last week was 13.6, which is normal. I used plain language and teach-back throughout the visit and drew a simple picture schedule; at the end he could say back that the stomach pill goes before breakfast.

My impression is refractory GERD, likely worsened by incorrect timing of omeprazole and regular ibuprofen use. He has no alarm features, but given his age and persistent symptoms I recommend an EGD. I am increasing omeprazole to 40 mg once daily, taken 30 minutes before breakfast. He will stop ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for knee pain, no more than 4 doses a day. Continue amlodipine 5 mg once daily, and use calcium carbonate only as needed. Raise the head of the bed and avoid eating within 3 hours of bedtime. A large-print picture medication chart was given to him and his daughter. The EGD will be scheduled in 4 weeks, with follow-up in 8 weeks.
"""

"""
Inpatient endocrinology note. The patient is a 19-year-old male seen on the surgical ward on hospital day 2 after a laparoscopic appendectomy. The primary team asked us to see him because his admission labs showed an HbA1c of 5.9% and a fasting glucose of 112. He has no prior diagnosis of diabetes. He denies excessive thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision, and unintentional weight loss. He reports gaining about 25 pounds over the last two years, drinks two to three sugar-sweetened sodas daily, and gets little exercise. He takes no regular medications. Plan is lifestyle counseling with referral to a dietitian, stopping sugar-sweetened sodas, and building up to 150 minutes of moderate exercise weekly once cleared by surgery. """

Clinical note:
"""
ICU progress note, hospital day 2. The patient is a 40-year-old female admitted with acute kidney injury from dehydration after four days of vomiting and poor oral intake from presumed viral gastroenteritis. She has no chronic medical conditions and takes no medications at home. She was hypotensive on arrival and was admitted to the ICU for close monitoring.

Overnight events: none. She slept well and her vomiting has stopped. She tolerated sips of clear liquids and says she feels less thirsty and less lightheaded than yesterday. She denies abdominal pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, and confusion.

Current treatment: lactated Ringer's infusion at 125 mL per hour and ondansetron 4 mg IV every 8 hours as needed for nausea, of which she needed one dose overnight. Urine output over the last 24 hours was 1.1 L.

Vitals this morning: temperature 37.0 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 112/68, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Weight is 64 kg.

Exam: mucous membranes are moist, there is no jugular venous distension, the lungs are clear, the abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there is no leg edema.

Lab trend: creatinine 2.4 mg/dL on admission, 1.9 mg/dL yesterday, and 1.5 mg/dL this morning, with a baseline of 0.8 mg/dL. BUN has fallen from 42 to 24. Potassium is 3.6 and sodium is 138. Urinalysis was bland. Renal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis.

Impression: acute kidney injury due to dehydration, prerenal in type, improving with fluids. Going forward, I will reduce lactated Ringer's to 75 mL per hour, repeat a basic metabolic panel this afternoon and tomorrow morning, avoid NSAIDs and other nephrotoxins, advance her diet as tolerated, and stop ondansetron if she has no further nausea. If creatinine continues to fall, she can transfer out of the ICU to the floor tomorrow.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good to see you again. I have you down as a 58-year-old male, about three weeks out from the hospital stay for the bone infection in your left foot. How are you feeling?
Patient: Better, I think. The foot is less sore. I'm still getting the IV antibiotic through the line in my arm.
Doctor: Right, the PICC line. Remind me what you're getting and how often.
Patient: Cefazolin, two grams, three times a day. The home nurse showed me how to hook it up.
Doctor: Good. Any fevers or chills?
Patient: No fevers, no chills.
Doctor: Any redness, swelling, or pain around the PICC site?
Patient: No, the arm looks fine.
Doctor: How about the foot wound? Any pus or bad smell?
Patient: A little clear drainage on the dressing in the morning, but no pus and no smell.
Doctor: Any diarrhea, rash, or nausea from the antibiotic?
Patient: No diarrhea, no rash. A little nausea sometimes, mostly in the evening.
Doctor: Okay. Let's go through your other medicines. Last time you were taking insulin glargine at night. What dose?
Patient: Thirty units. Actually, no, sorry, twenty units. The thirty was what I took before the hospital stay. They lowered it to twenty when I was in there.
Doctor: Good, so twenty units at night is correct. And your sugars at home?
Patient: Mornings are 150 to 180 or so. Sometimes 200 after dinner.
Doctor: That's higher than I'd like with a bone infection. And metformin?
Patient: Metformin 1000 milligrams twice a day, same as before.
Doctor: Still taking lisinopril 10 milligrams and the baby aspirin, 81 milligrams?
Patient: Yes, both every morning. I stopped the oxycodone, I haven't needed it for a week. And I quit the ibuprofen like you told me when I left the hospital.
Doctor: Now, any over-the-counter supplements or herbal products? I know you were taking a few.
Patient: Yes. I take turmeric capsules, 500 milligrams twice a day, for my joint aches. Fish oil, one capsule daily. And a zinc and vitamin C supplement that a friend recommended.
Doctor: Okay, I'll come back to that. Your labs from this morning: the white count is 7.2, creatinine is 1.3, up from 1.1 last week, and your liver enzymes are a little high, AST 58 and ALT 71. Your ESR has come down from 62 to 38, and the CRP from 4.1 to 1.8.
Patient: So the infection is getting better?
Doctor: The inflammation markers say yes. Let me look at you. Your blood pressure is 136 over 82, pulse 78, temperature 98.4. The PICC site is clean and dry, with no redness and no swelling. The wound on the bottom of your left foot has pink granulation tissue, about two centimeters, a little clear drainage, no pus, and no redness spreading beyond the edge. It is not tender when I press over the bone.
Doctor: To summarize, you have osteomyelitis of the left second metatarsal from MSSA, which showed on the MRI and the bone biopsy in the hospital, and it is improving on IV cefazolin. Continue cefazolin 2 grams IV every 8 hours through the PICC to finish six weeks total, so about three more weeks. Stop the turmeric today, and stop the zinc and vitamin C supplement too. We will check a CBC, ESR, CRP, and liver tests every week, and repeat the liver tests in one week to make sure they come down. Please see podiatry in two weeks and wear the offloading shoe, and come back to see me in two weeks. Call us for fever, spreading redness, or any problem with the PICC line.
Patient: Okay. I'll throw the turmeric out tonight.
"""

"""
Hospital day 3, postoperative day 2 progress note for a 46-year-old female who underwent a total laparoscopic hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for symptomatic uterine fibroids with heavy menstrual bleeding. The oophorectomy was performed for risk reduction because she is a BRCA1 mutation carrier.

Since surgery she has had marked hot flashes, about 8 to 10 a day, and drenching night sweats that wake her three times a night. She rates her distress from these symptoms as 7 out of 10. Her incisional pain is controlled and she is walking in the hallway, tolerating a regular diet, and passing flatus. She denies chest pain, calf pain or leg swelling, shortness of breath, fever, and heavy vaginal bleeding. She has no personal history of breast cancer or blood clots, and she does not smoke.

Current medications are acetaminophen 1000 mg every 6 hours and enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily. She received ketorolac 15 mg IV every 6 hours for the first 48 hours, which was stopped this morning, and we started ibuprofen 600 mg by mouth every 6 hours as needed instead.

Vitals this morning are temperature 98.6 F, heart rate 84, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Hemoglobin is 11.2 compared with 12.6 before surgery, and white count is 9.1. On exam she is comfortable, the lungs are clear, the abdomen is soft with appropriate incisional tenderness, the laparoscopic port sites are clean and dry, and the calves are soft and nontender.

Impression is expected recovery after hysterectomy with oophorectomy, complicated by surgical menopause with severe vasomotor symptoms. Because she has no breast cancer, no clotting history, and no uterus, estrogen-only therapy is appropriate until the usual age of natural menopause, and I discussed the benefits and risks with her. I am starting a transdermal estradiol patch 0.05 mg per 24 hours, changed twice weekly. Continue acetaminophen and enoxaparin, with ibuprofen as needed for pain. Advised layered clothing and avoiding hot triggers. Pathology is pending, and a baseline bone density scan will be arranged as an outpatient. Plan for discharge tomorrow if pain remains controlled, with a postoperative clinic visit in two weeks.
"""

Medications confirmed with her daughter reading the bottles: furosemide 20 mg daily, apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily, and diphenhydramine 25 mg at bedtime, which she uses for sleep.

Advance care planning: We spent about 25 minutes discussing her goals. She wants to stay in her own home, avoid long hospital stays and machines, and would accept hospital treatment for reversible problems such as infection. She has mild asthma that is controlled with albuterol as needed and no other chronic conditions. She denies hemoptysis, leg swelling, vomiting, diarrhea, and recent travel, and she does not smoke. She has no known drug allergies.

Overnight she had one temperature of 38.4 C that came down after acetaminophen 650 mg, and she has been afebrile since early morning. She is receiving ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours and azithromycin 500 mg IV every 24 hours, both started in the emergency department, and she used albuterol once overnight. Because the pneumococcal antigen is positive and she is improving, I will stop azithromycin today and continue ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours for one more day. If she remains afebrile and her oxygen saturation stays above 92% on room air tomorrow, she will switch to oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily to complete 7 days of antibiotics in total. Continue albuterol as needed, acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed, incentive spirometry, and walking in the hallway. We will follow the blood cultures to final. She will see her primary care doctor within one week after discharge and does not need a repeat chest x-ray unless her symptoms persist.
"""

"""
The patient is a 77-year-old female seen in cardiology clinic for follow-up of high LDL cholesterol and statin intolerance, about three weeks after a hospitalization for a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent to the left anterior descending artery. The myalgias resolved within a week after she stopped atorvastatin. She has no chest pain, no shortness of breath, no palpitations, no lightheadedness, and no bleeding or dark stools while on dual antiplatelet therapy.

Impression is high LDL cholesterol with documented statin intolerance in a patient with a recent non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, and her LDL is well above the goal of less than 55 to 70 mg/dL. """

"""
Cardiology clinic visit for a 67-year-old female with peripheral artery disease who comes in for ongoing leg pain with walking. For about six months she has had cramping pain in both calves, worse on the right, that begins after she walks about two blocks and goes away within a few minutes of standing still. She denies pain at rest, denies foot ulcers or sores that are slow to heal, denies chest pain, and denies palpitations. She has hypertension and hyperlipidemia, and she takes amlodipine 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. She has no known drug allergies. She currently smokes about half a pack of cigarettes per day and has done so for roughly 40 years, and she says she has tried to quit twice without success.

Vitals today are blood pressure 142/84 and heart rate 76. On exam the right dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are barely palpable and the left pulses are diminished, both feet are cool to the touch, and there are no ulcers, no gangrene, and capillary refill is under three seconds. Her ankle-brachial index today is 0.62 on the right and 0.78 on the left. Her LDL cholesterol last month was 128, and her hemoglobin A1c was 5.6 percent.

My impression is symptomatic peripheral artery disease with intermittent claudication, made worse by ongoing tobacco use and an LDL above goal. Plan is to start aspirin 81 mg daily, to increase atorvastatin from 20 mg to 80 mg daily, to begin a supervised exercise program with walking to near-maximal pain three times per week, and to order an arterial duplex ultrasound of both legs. We spent several minutes on smoking cessation, and since she is ready to try again I am starting a nicotine patch 14 mg daily and referring her to the state quitline. I explained that smoking is the most important modifiable factor for limb loss and heart attack. She should wear well-fitting shoes and check her feet every day. She will return in six weeks with a repeat lipid panel.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Family medicine inpatient follow-up on hospital day 3 for a positive depression screen. The patient is a 22-year-old female admitted three days ago with an acute pulmonary embolism found on CT pulmonary angiography, and she is being treated with apixaban. The nursing admission screen was positive, and today her PHQ-9 score is 14, which is moderate. She describes about two months of low mood, loss of interest in activities, poor sleep, low energy, and trouble concentrating that began after she lost her job. She denies suicidal thoughts, thoughts of self-harm, hallucinations, and periods of unusually high energy. She also denies alcohol, tobacco, and drug use, and she has no history of seizures or an eating disorder. About six weeks ago she started taking over-the-counter St. John's wort on her own for her mood. She was also taking a combined oral contraceptive pill, which was stopped on admission because of the clot. She has no known drug allergies.

Current medications are apixaban 10 mg twice daily, which will step down to 5 mg twice daily after 7 days of treatment, and acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed for pleuritic chest pain, which she has needed twice a day.

Vitals today: blood pressure 118/70, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 18, temperature 36.9 C, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. She appears tired but cooperative, with a flat affect, normal speech, a linear thought process, and good orientation. Lungs are clear. Labs show hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, and TSH 1.8. A urine pregnancy test was negative on admission. CT pulmonary angiography showed bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli.

My assessment is a moderate depressive episode, likely major depressive disorder, single episode, in the setting of an acute pulmonary embolism on apixaban. St. John's wort is a strong inducer of the enzymes that clear apixaban and could lower its levels, so it must be stopped. I am choosing bupropion over an SSRI to avoid added bleeding risk with apixaban.

The plan is to stop St. John's wort today and counsel her to check with us before using any herbal supplement. Start bupropion XL 150 mg every morning. Continue apixaban 10 mg twice daily, then 5 mg twice daily as scheduled. Inpatient behavioral health consult for a psychotherapy referral. Repeat PHQ-9 in 4 weeks. Follow up with family medicine one week after discharge and with the anticoagulation clinic. Discuss non-estrogen contraception with gynecology before discharge. Return right away for any suicidal thoughts.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Pulm f/u, HD#4. 59-year-old female, current smoker, admitted w/ AECOPD.
Reason: incidental RUL nodule on CTA chest (done on adm to r/o PE).

Interval:
Wheeze and cough improving, off O2 since yesterday.
c/o mild DOE walking in hallway, cough w/ white sputum.
Denies hemoptysis, wt loss, night sweats, CP, bone pain, HA.
Slept ok overnight, appetite good, eating full trays.
Smoking hx: 1 ppd x 35 yrs per pt. Correction: daughter says 1.5 ppd and pt agrees, "more like a pack and a half." So 1.5 ppd x 35 yrs = 52 pack-yrs.
Has not smoked since adm, asks for help quitting.
FH: mother w/ lung ca.
No asbestos or radon exposure known. Works as a retail cashier.

PMH: COPD, HTN, T2DM, HLD, hypothyroidism.
No prior chest CT for comparison.

Meds:
Prednisone 40 mg daily, today = day 5, last dose then stop.
Azithromycin 500 mg daily, 3-day course done, DC'd.
DuoNeb q4h -> q6h PRN.
Start tiotropium 18 mcg daily.
Start nicotine patch 21 mg/24 h daily.
Metformin 1000 mg BID held since contrast, resume today.
Lisinopril 10 mg daily, continue.
Levothyroxine 88 mcg daily, continue.
Atorvastatin 20 -> 40 mg nightly (LDL 142).

Vitals: BP 138/82, HR 88, RR 20, SpO2 94% RA, temp 36.9 C.
Exam: scattered exp wheeze, prolonged exp phase, no crackles. No clubbing, no LAD, no hepatomegaly. Alert, NAD at rest.

Data:
CTA chest: no PE. Spiculated RUL nodule. Prelim read 8 mm; CORRECTION final radiology read 11 mm. Mild centrilobular emphysema. No mediastinal LAD, no effusion.
WBC 11.2 (15.6 on adm), Hgb 12.9, Plt 301, Na 138, K 4.1, Cr 0.8, LDL 142, A1c 7.4%, TSH 1.9.

Imp:
1. 11 mm spiculated RUL nodule, incidental. High risk for malignancy: current smoker, 52 pack-yrs, upper lobe, spiculated, FH lung ca.
2. AECOPD, improving, near baseline.
3. Tobacco use disorder, motivated to quit.
Recs:
PET/CT outpt in ~4 wks, after AECOPD resolved (avoid false +).
PFTs outpt to assess surgical candidacy.
Pulm clinic 2 wks after PET to decide nav bronch vs CT-guided bx vs thoracic surg referral.
Pt and daughter told about nodule and need for f/u, both verbalize understanding.
Nicotine patch started, quit line referral given.
Finish prednisone today. Start tiotropium. Space out nebs.
D/c tomorrow if SpO2 stays >= 92% RA w/ ambulation.
Resume metformin today. Continue lisinopril, levothyroxine.
Discussed w/ primary team.
"""

The final radiology read showed an 11 mm spiculated nodule, and she smokes 1.5 packs per day for 35 years. The impression is a high-risk incidental nodule with improving AECOPD. Plan is outpatient PET/CT in about 4 weeks, PFTs, pulmonary clinic follow-up, a nicotine patch, and tiotropium.

"""
Telehealth note, telephone visit (audio only), patient at home. The patient is a 56-year-old female with known Crohn's disease affecting the terminal ileum and colon who called with a 2-week history of worsening symptoms. She reports 6 to 8 loose stools per day, up from her baseline of 1 to 2, with crampy lower abdominal pain, urgency, and nighttime awakenings to use the toilet. She has had weight loss of about 5 pounds, from 153 to 148 pounds on her home scale. She also reports tiring easily. She denies blood in the stool, vomiting, fever, mouth sores, and new joint pain.

She was prescribed adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks. She admits she skipped her last two doses because the copay increased after her insurance plan changed and she could not afford it. She has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg a few times a day for the cramping.

Her home temperature this morning was 98.9 F. No physical examination was possible by telephone. Her voice sounded tired but she spoke in full sentences. Labs drawn last week at her local lab were reviewed: CRP 28 mg/L, hemoglobin 11.4, albumin 3.4, and fecal calprotectin 640 mcg/g.

Impression: Crohn's disease flare, precipitated by interruption of adalimumab because of cost, with mild anemia. Recommendations: order stool testing for Clostridioides difficile today, and she will drop off the sample at her local lab. Start prednisone 40 mg once daily once that test is negative, then taper by 5 mg each week, with calcium and vitamin D while on steroids. Stop ibuprofen because NSAIDs can worsen Crohn's disease, and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for cramping. Resume adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks. Our office will submit a prior authorization and a copay assistance application today and refer her to the clinic social worker for help with insurance costs, and the specialty pharmacy will deliver to her home. Repeat the CRP and CBC in 2 weeks, with a nurse call in 1 week to check on symptoms. She should go to the emergency department for fever, vomiting, severe abdominal pain, or blood in the stool.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Cardiology clinic follow-up for a 55-year-old female seen three weeks after an acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery. Her history includes paroxysmal atrial fibrillation diagnosed two years ago, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia, and she has taken an anticoagulant for the atrial fibrillation since the diagnosis. She has no known drug allergies.

Since discharge she has felt well. She walks 20 minutes daily without chest pain, and she denies shortness of breath, palpitations, lightheadedness, and syncope. She has noticed easy bruising on both forearms, but she denies black stools, blood in the urine, nosebleeds, and gum bleeding.

On medication review she first told me she takes apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily. When she read the label on her bottle, she corrected this to apixaban 5 mg twice daily, which is the dose her primary care physician prescribed and is appropriate for her age, weight, and kidney function. The other medications she brought in are clopidogrel 75 mg daily and aspirin 81 mg daily, both started at discharge, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly and metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily, also started at discharge, and her long-standing lisinopril 10 mg daily and metformin 1000 mg twice daily.

Because lisinopril and atorvastatin are not safe in pregnancy, I reviewed her reproductive status. She is postmenopausal, with her last menstrual period about 14 months ago, and the urine pregnancy test done in the hospital was negative. Pregnancy is therefore not a concern for her current or planned prescribing, and she does not need contraception.

Blood pressure today was 126/74 with a heart rate of 64 and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Weight is 82 kg. Jugular venous pressure is normal, rhythm is regular without murmur, lungs are clear, and there is no leg edema. The right radial access site is well healed, and she has a few small ecchymoses on both forearms. ECG today shows sinus rhythm at 62 with anterior T-wave inversions and no new changes. The inpatient echocardiogram showed an LVEF of 45% with anterior hypokinesis. Labs from this week show LDL cholesterol 96 mg/dL, hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, potassium 4.3, and hemoglobin A1c 7.4%.

My impression is that she is recovering well from an anterior STEMI with stent placement, with mildly reduced LVEF and an LDL still above goal. Her bleeding risk is elevated on triple antithrombotic therapy, which accounts for the bruising. Her blood pressure and diabetes are acceptable.

I stopped the aspirin today and will continue clopidogrel 75 mg daily together with apixaban 5 mg twice daily; clopidogrel will continue for 12 months from the stent, after which apixaban alone will be used. I increased atorvastatin from 40 mg to 80 mg nightly and increased metoprolol succinate from 25 mg to 50 mg daily. I started pantoprazole 40 mg daily for stomach protection while she is on two antithrombotic drugs. Lisinopril and metformin are unchanged. She is referred to cardiac rehabilitation. I ordered a repeat lipid panel in six weeks, and if LDL remains above 55 mg/dL I will add ezetimibe. A repeat echocardiogram is planned in three months to reassess LVEF. She will call or go to the emergency department for chest pain, fainting, or any significant bleeding. Follow-up in clinic in four weeks.
"""

Interval history: Over the last two months he reports a weaker urinary stream, hesitancy at the start of voiding, and a sense of incomplete emptying. His primary care physician started oxybutynin 5 mg BID about a month ago for the urgency, and since then the hesitancy has gotten worse and he has dry mouth and constipation. He denies dizziness when he stands up. His symptom score (IPSS) completed during the call was 19, with a bother score of 4.

Past history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension (HTN), type 2 diabetes (T2DM), and hyperlipidemia. He read his pill bottles to me on camera. He first said his apixaban was 2.5 mg BID, and then he turned the bottle and corrected himself: the label reads 5 mg BID, which is the dose he has been taking without missed doses. His other medications are tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg BID, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. He has no known drug allergies.

Home measurements this morning with his own cuff and scale were BP 134/80, HR 68, weight 92 kg, and fingerstick glucose 118 mg/dL. On video he looks comfortable and in no distress, speaks in full sentences, and walks steadily when asked to cross the room. An abdominal, genital, and rectal exam cannot be done by video, so suprapubic fullness and prostate size were not assessed today.

Results reviewed from last week: PSA 2.9 ng/mL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, eGFR 78, A1c 6.9%, and a urinalysis negative for blood, nitrite, and leukocyte esterase. Impression: BPH with worsening LUTS, with oxybutynin likely contributing to the hesitancy. He is on apixaban for atrial fibrillation, so bleeding risk and any future procedure have to account for that.

Plan discussed with the patient using teach-back. Stop oxybutynin today. Increase tamsulosin from 0.4 mg to 0.8 mg daily, and check his BP sitting and standing at home for the first week and call if he feels lightheaded. He was advised to go to the ED for gross hematuria, inability to void, or fever. Follow-up by video in six weeks.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good morning. I have you down as a 53-year-old male here for follow-up of your psoriatic arthritis. How have things been since we last met?
Patient: Not great. The joint pain in my hands is back, and my right second toe has been swollen and sore for about six weeks. Mornings are the worst, I have stiffness for almost an hour.
Doctor: Any back pain, or pain in your heels?
Patient: My right heel hurts when I first get out of bed, but no back pain.
Doctor: Any red or painful eyes, or blurry vision?
Patient: No, my eyes are fine.
Doctor: How about fever, diarrhea, or belly pain?
Patient: No fever, no diarrhea, and no belly pain.
Doctor: And the skin?
Patient: I still get scaly patches on both elbows and my scalp, but they are not any worse.
Doctor: Tell me about your medicines.
Patient: I take methotrexate 15 mg once a week and folic acid 1 mg every day. I also take naproxen 500 mg twice a day for the joint pain, which is most days now. For my blood pressure I take amlodipine 5 mg daily.
Doctor: Any alcohol with the methotrexate?
Patient: Just one beer on weekends.
Doctor: Okay. Your vitals today are blood pressure 134 over 84, heart rate 76, and temperature 36.8 Celsius. On exam your right second toe is swollen and sausage-like, three finger joints in your right hand are tender and swollen, you have tenderness where the right Achilles tendon attaches, there is nail pitting, and you have scaly plaques on both elbows. Your knees and shoulders look fine. Your labs from last week show an ESR of 32 and a CRP of 18 mg/L, while your ALT and creatinine were normal. The hand X-rays show no erosions.
Patient: So what does that mean?
Doctor: You have active psoriatic arthritis with dactylitis and enthesitis despite the methotrexate, plus plaque psoriasis and well-controlled hypertension. I would like to add adalimumab 40 mg injected under the skin every other week. Before the first dose we need a TB test and hepatitis screening, so I am ordering a QuantiFERON and hepatitis B and C blood tests today. Continue methotrexate 15 mg weekly and folic acid. Once the injections are working, we can cut the naproxen down. Come back in 12 weeks, and call us right away if you get a fever or any infection.
Patient: Can I give the injection myself?
Doctor: Yes, our nurse will teach you. Please wait for the TB result before the first injection.
Patient: Sounds good, thank you.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 3 endocrinology progress note for a 71-year-old female with long-standing type 1 diabetes on an insulin pump, admitted after a severe hypoglycemic episode. She works rotating night shifts at a part-time warehouse job, so her meal timing and sleep vary widely from week to week. Three days ago a coworker found her sweaty, shaky and confused during a night shift, and the paramedics measured a fingerstick glucose of 38 mg/dL. She improved after intravenous dextrose and was admitted for monitoring and pump adjustment. She reports about four symptomatic lows each week over the past two months, mostly in the early morning after her shift, and she often does not feel them until she is quite low. Overnight in the hospital she had one asymptomatic low of 62 mg/dL on her continuous glucose monitor and treated it with juice. She denies chest pain, palpitations, seizure activity, or focal weakness, and she denies any head strike or fall.

Her history includes hypertension, hypothyroidism, hyperlipidemia, stage 3a chronic kidney disease, and diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Home medications are insulin lispro by continuous subcutaneous infusion, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. She also uses several over-the-counter supplements. She first told me she takes chromium picolinate 200 mcg twice daily, but after reading the bottle label she corrected this to 500 mcg once daily. She also takes cinnamon capsules every day, dose unknown, and alpha-lipoic acid 600 mg daily. She has no known drug allergies.

Vitals this morning are temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 74, blood pressure 138/76, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She is alert, oriented and comfortable. Mucous membranes are moist, heart sounds are regular without a murmur, lungs are clear, and the abdomen is soft and non-tender. The pump infusion site on the left abdomen is clean without redness. Monofilament sensation is reduced over both feet, unchanged from her baseline.

Data review: arrival glucose was 38 mg/dL and HbA1c is 6.4%. Creatinine is 1.3 with an eGFR of 44, potassium 4.4, and TSH 2.1. C-peptide is undetectable, in keeping with her known type 1 diabetes. CT of the head without contrast in the emergency department showed no acute findings. The continuous glucose monitor download shows 18% of readings below 70 mg/dL, concentrated between 4 and 9 in the morning, with the lowest values after correction boluses taken near the end of her shift.

Assessment is recurrent severe hypoglycemia with impaired awareness of hypoglycemia in a patient with type 1 diabetes on an insulin pump. This is likely multifactorial: overly aggressive basal and correction settings that do not fit her shifting schedule, reduced insulin clearance from her declining kidney function, and the glucose-lowering effect of her supplements. An HbA1c of 6.4% is lower than appropriate for her age and hypoglycemia history, so I am setting an individualized goal of 7.5 to 8%.

Today I will reduce the overnight basal rate from 0.85 to 0.65 units per hour and relax the correction factor. With her diabetes educator I will set up two pump profiles, one for work nights and one for days off. Stop chromium picolinate, cinnamon capsules and alpha-lipoic acid. Start glucagon 3 mg nasal powder as needed for severe hypoglycemia, and her daughter will be taught to use it. Continue levothyroxine, lisinopril and atorvastatin unchanged. Set the continuous glucose monitor low alert at 80 mg/dL. Dietitian visit before discharge, repeat basic metabolic panel in the morning, and endocrine clinic follow-up in two weeks. Anticipate discharge tomorrow if there are no further lows.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Hi, come on in and have a seat. I see you're a 51-year-old female and this is your first time at our urgent care. What brings you in today?
Patient: My leg. Whenever I walk about a block, my right calf starts cramping and burning so badly that I have to stop. It goes away after a few minutes of rest, and then it starts again when I walk.
Doctor: How long has that been going on?
Patient: About three weeks. But I was in the hospital until a little over two weeks ago, so I wasn't walking much before that.
Doctor: I see in your discharge papers that you were admitted for a heart attack. Tell me what happened.
Patient: I had a heart attack and they put a stent in one of the arteries in my heart. I stayed five days.
Doctor: Do you have any rest pain, like leg pain when you're lying down or at night?
Patient: No, only when I walk. Nothing at rest.
Doctor: Any sores or wounds on your feet?
Patient: No sores. My right foot feels colder than the left, though.
Doctor: Any chest pain or shortness of breath since you went home?
Patient: No chest pain and no shortness of breath.
Doctor: Any bleeding or black stools? You're on two blood thinners.
Patient: No bleeding and no black stools.
Doctor: Let's go through your medications. Tell me what you take.
Patient: Aspirin 81 mg every day, clopidogrel 150 mg once a day, atorvastatin 80 mg at night, metoprolol succinate 25 mg once a day, lisinopril 5 mg once a day, and metformin 1000 mg twice a day for my diabetes. Oh, and I take ibuprofen 400 mg three or four times a day for the leg pain.
Doctor: Can you read me the clopidogrel and metoprolol bottles? I want to be sure of those doses.
Patient: Okay, hold on. I'm sorry, the clopidogrel says 75 mg, not 150. And the metoprolol succinate says 50 mg, not 25.
Doctor: Thank you, that matches your hospital records. So clopidogrel 75 mg and metoprolol succinate 50 mg, both once a day. Do you smoke?
Patient: I smoked a pack a day for about 25 years, but I quit the day I got to the hospital.
Doctor: That is the most important thing you can do for your legs, so well done. Who is at home to help you?
Patient: Nobody, I live alone. My sister lives in another state. A neighbor drove me today but I can't count on her, and I missed my cardiology follow-up last week because I had no ride.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me, we'll work on that. Let me examine you. Your blood pressure is 148/86, your heart rate is 68, and your oxygen saturation is 98 percent. Your heart is regular and your lungs are clear. The right foot is cool with mild pallor, and the capillary refill is slow at four seconds. I can't feel the pulses in the right foot, and they are faint on the left. Your calves are soft with no swelling and no tenderness, and there are no ulcers on either foot. We did an ankle-brachial index here, and it is 0.62 on the right and 0.81 on the left, which confirms reduced blood flow, worse on the right. From your hospital labs, your hemoglobin was 12.1, creatinine 0.9, hemoglobin A1c 7.8 percent, and LDL 88.
Doctor: So here is my impression. You have peripheral artery disease, which means the arteries to your legs are narrowed, and it is causing intermittent claudication in your right calf. There are no signs of critical limb ischemia, since you have no rest pain and no wounds. This is on top of your recent heart attack and stent, your type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol.
Doctor: Here is the plan. First, keep taking aspirin 81 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg every day and don't miss doses because of the stent, and continue atorvastatin 80 mg at night. Second, stop the ibuprofen, because with two blood thinners it raises your bleeding risk and it is hard on your kidneys. Third, your blood pressure is above goal, so I'm increasing the lisinopril from 5 mg to 10 mg once a day, and we will check a basic metabolic panel in two weeks. Fourth, I'm ordering an arterial duplex ultrasound of both legs and referring you to vascular surgery. Fifth, walk until the calf pain is moderate, rest, and repeat, for 30 minutes at least three times a week, and I'll refer you to cardiac rehab, which includes supervised exercise. Sixth, check your feet every day and wear shoes at all times. Because you live alone, I'm also asking our social worker to set up transportation for your appointments and a home health nurse to help with your pill organizer.
Patient: Okay, I'm a little overwhelmed, but I'll try. What if my leg gets worse?
Doctor: Go to the emergency room right away if you get pain in the leg at rest, if the foot turns cold, pale, or blue, if you get a sore that won't heal, or if you have chest pain. We'll also give you a written list of your medications with the changes.
Patient: Thank you, doctor.
"""

- void after intercourse, keep hydrated, goal 2 L water/day

Clinical note:
"""
The patient is a 36-year-old female on hospital day 2 for an upper gastrointestinal bleed from a duodenal ulcer. She presented with two days of black, tarry stools and lightheadedness after several weeks of taking ibuprofen 600 mg two to three times a day for tension headaches. She works rotating night and day shifts at a distribution center, sleeps at irregular times, and often skips meals, which she believes made her headaches worse. She denies vomiting blood, denies chest pain, denies abdominal pain at the moment, and denies alcohol use. She has no known drug allergies.

Overnight she had no further black stools and no change in her condition. Her admission hemoglobin was 7.2 g/dL and she received one unit of packed red blood cells, after which it rose to 8.4 g/dL this morning. Vital signs today were blood pressure 112/68, heart rate 86, respiratory rate 16, temperature 36.9 C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. BUN was 28, creatinine 0.7, platelets 280, and INR 1.0. On exam she is pale but comfortable, the abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness and no rebound, and there is no active bleeding. EGD on the day of admission found an 8 mm duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel that was treated with epinephrine injection and two hemoclips, and gastric biopsies were sent for Helicobacter pylori.

Impression is an upper gastrointestinal bleed from an NSAID-associated duodenal ulcer, status post endoscopic hemostasis, with acute blood loss anemia that is stable. Pantoprazole 40 mg IV twice daily will continue for 72 hours and then be changed to 40 mg orally twice daily. Ibuprofen is stopped permanently, and she will use acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for headaches instead. We will advance her diet to soft foods today and recheck her hemoglobin every 8 hours. I will follow the H. pylori biopsy result and treat if it is positive. Because she works varying shifts, I asked pharmacy and nursing to write her medication schedule around her waking hours rather than clock times and to give her a printed copy. She should return to the hospital for black stools or fainting. Discharge is likely in one to two days if her hemoglobin is stable.
"""

"""

Clinical note:
"""
This 35-year-old male was referred to gastroenterology for iron-deficiency anemia found on routine blood work by his primary care doctor. He has limited health literacy, so I used plain language, asked him to repeat the plan back to me in his own words, and gave him a picture-based instruction sheet. He told me he cannot read the lab results on the patient portal.

He says he has felt tired for about six months and gets dizzy when he stands up fast. He craves ice and chews a cup of it every day. He denies black or tarry stools, blood in the stool, belly pain, vomiting blood, weight loss, trouble swallowing, and changes in his bowel habits. He eats meat a few times a week. He has had back pain from his warehouse job for a year and takes ibuprofen 600 mg about three times a day for it. He drinks alcohol rarely and does not smoke. He has no known family history of colon cancer or celiac disease.

Vitals today are BP 118/72 and HR 84, with a BMI of 24. He has mild conjunctival pallor. The abdomen is soft and non-tender with no masses or enlarged liver or spleen. A rectal exam showed brown stool that was negative for blood.

Labs from last month show a hemoglobin of 10.4 g/dL, an MCV of 72, a ferritin of 8 ng/mL, and normal kidney function.

My impression is iron-deficiency anemia in an adult male, which is concerning for slow blood loss from the gut. His frequent ibuprofen use may be causing stomach or duodenal ulcers or gastritis, and celiac disease is also possible, so he needs a full evaluation of both the upper and lower gut.

Plan: stop the ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for back pain instead. Start pantoprazole 40 mg daily before breakfast. Start ferrous sulfate 325 mg once every other day, taken with orange juice and not with milk or tea. Schedule an upper endoscopy with small bowel biopsies and a colonoscopy. The nurse reviewed the bowel prep with him using a pictorial sheet, and a nurse navigator will call him to go over it again. Order tTG-IgA, total IgA, and an H. pylori stool antigen. Repeat the CBC and ferritin in 8 weeks. He should go to the emergency room for black stools, vomiting blood, or fainting, and he correctly repeated these warning signs back to me.
"""

Hospital day 3 for a 91-year-old female admitted with right lower-extremity cellulitis. She lives alone and has limited social support, with one neighbor who checks on her occasionally, and she waited several days before calling for help because she did not want to be a burden. Her history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. On admission she gave her apixaban dose as 5 mg twice daily, but her neighbor brought in the pill bottles, and the pharmacy label and the pharmacy record both confirm that the correct dose is 2.5 mg twice daily, which is appropriate for her age and kidney function, so the 2.5 mg dose was ordered. She has no known drug allergies.

Her home medications are apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, linagliptin 5 mg daily, and furosemide 40 mg daily, and she takes acetaminophen as needed for joint pain. Vancomycin was started in the emergency department for possible MRSA, but there was no purulence, the nasal MRSA PCR was negative, and blood cultures show no growth at 48 hours, so I discontinued vancomycin yesterday and changed to cefazolin 1 gram IV every 8 hours. Furosemide was held on admission because of mild volume depletion and was resumed today at a lower dose of 20 mg daily.

Vitals this morning are temperature 37.0 Celsius, HR 76 and irregular, BP 134/70, RR 18, and SpO2 96% on room air. The left leg is normal. White blood cell count was 14.2 on admission and 9.8 today, creatinine is 1.6 and near her baseline of 1.5, potassium is 4.3, and CRP has fallen from 86 to 40. A venous duplex of the right leg showed no deep vein thrombosis.

My impression is that the cellulitis is responding well to cefazolin. Her atrial fibrillation is rate controlled, her heart failure looks compensated, and her chronic kidney disease is at baseline. Plan is to continue cefazolin 1 gram IV every 8 hours for one more day and then switch to oral cephalexin 500 mg four times daily to finish a 7 day course, to elevate the leg and keep marking the border of the redness, to continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, amlodipine, and linagliptin, and to use acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain. Because she lives alone with limited social support and now has reduced mobility, I have asked social work and case management to assess her for short-term skilled nursing facility rehab versus home with home health nursing, and to arrange meal delivery, a medical alert device, and pharmacy blister packs to prevent further dosing confusion. Clinical note:
"""
Gastroenterology clinic dictation. This is a 74-year-old male seen in follow-up for persistently elevated liver enzymes in the setting of known fatty liver disease. He was referred by his primary care physician after routine labs about three months ago showed elevated transaminases, and a repeat panel last month was still abnormal. His history includes type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, and osteoarthritis of both knees. He is a current smoker, about ten cigarettes a day for many years, and he says he drinks one beer on weekend days, correction, he says two beers on weekend days, so roughly four beers a week. He denies abdominal pain, jaundice, itching, abdominal swelling, black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, confusion, fever, and unintentional weight loss. He does report some fatigue and says he has gained about ten pounds over the past year.

Medications as he reports them are metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, correction, lisinopril 20 mg daily, I just looked at the pill bottle he brought, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, amlodipine 5 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily, and naproxen 220 mg as needed for his knee pain, which he takes most days. No known drug allergies.

On exam today blood pressure 138/78, heart rate 76, temperature 98.2 F, weight 224 pounds, BMI 33. He is comfortable and in no distress. No scleral icterus, no jaundice, no spider angiomata, no palmar erythema. Abdomen is obese, soft, nontender, nondistended, no palpable hepatosplenomegaly, no ascites, no shifting dullness. No asterixis. No peripheral edema.

Data review. Labs from last month show ALT 87, correction, ALT 78, AST 52, alkaline phosphatase 98, total bilirubin 0.8, albumin 4.1, platelets 205, INR 1.0, creatinine 1.1, and hemoglobin A1c 7.6 percent. LDL cholesterol 118. Hepatitis B surface antigen negative, hepatitis C antibody negative, ANA negative, ferritin and iron saturation within normal limits. FIB-4 calculates to 2.1, which is indeterminate. Abdominal ultrasound from last month showed diffusely increased hepatic echogenicity consistent with hepatic steatosis, normal liver contour, no focal lesion, no ascites, and a normal spleen size. FibroScan today showed a liver stiffness of 9.8 kPa with CAP 312, consistent with significant steatosis and possible stage 2 fibrosis.

Impression. Number one, elevated liver enzymes due to metabolic dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease, with possible stage 2 fibrosis, in the setting of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and ongoing moderate alcohol use which may be contributing. Number two, current tobacco use. Number three, chronic naproxen use, which I am not comfortable with given his liver and his kidney function.

Plan. I am stopping the naproxen today and he can use acetaminophen up to 2 grams per day for the knee pain. I am increasing the atorvastatin from 20 mg to 40 mg nightly, which is safe in fatty liver and will help the LDL. Continue metformin, lisinopril, amlodipine, and aspirin as they are. I advised him to cut alcohol out completely. Start nicotine patch 14 mg daily and I offered a referral to the tobacco quitting program, which he accepted. Referral to the dietitian for a weight loss program, with a goal of losing 7 to 10 percent of his body weight, and 150 minutes of walking a week. I will message his primary care physician about adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist for diabetes and weight. Repeat hepatic function panel in 3 months, repeat FibroScan in 12 months, and hepatitis A and B vaccination status to be checked. Return to clinic in 3 months. End of dictation.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Nurse: This is an 85-year-old female here with right flank pain that started about two hours ago. She was in the hospital about three weeks ago. Vitals are BP 154/82, heart rate 96, temp 98.6, and 97% on room air.

Doctor: Hello, I'm the emergency doctor. Tell me what's going on.

Patient: Oh, it's the worst pain. Right here in my back, going down toward my groin. It comes in waves and I can't get comfortable.

Doctor: When did it start?

Patient: About two hours ago, I was just sitting watching TV. I threw up once too.

Doctor: Any fever or chills?

Patient: No fever, no chills.

Doctor: Any burning when you pee?

Patient: No burning. But my urine looked pinkish this morning.

Doctor: Have you ever had a kidney stone before?

Patient: Never.

Doctor: You were in the hospital recently. What was that for?

Patient: Pneumonia, three weeks ago. I was there five days and they sent me home on antibiotics, which I finished. Since I got home I've been taking ibuprofen for my knees, 400 milligrams two or three times a day.

Doctor: Okay, that's good to know. Any belly pain, diarrhea, chest pain, or trouble breathing?

Patient: No belly pain, no diarrhea. No chest pain, no trouble breathing. The cough is almost gone.

Doctor: What other medicines do you take?

Patient: Amlodipine 5 milligrams every morning. That's all, besides the ibuprofen.

Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?

Patient: No, none.

Doctor: Okay. Let me examine you. Your belly is soft and not tender, but you're quite tender when I tap on your right back over the kidney. Heart sounds regular, lungs clear, and your legs aren't swollen.

Doctor: Your results are back. Your urine test shows a lot of blood but no sign of infection. Your white count is 9.8, and your creatinine, which is your kidney function, is 1.3. That is a little higher than the 1.0 you had when you left the hospital. The CT scan shows a 5 millimeter stone in the right ureter, the tube from the kidney to the bladder, with mild hydronephrosis, which means some swelling of the kidney behind the stone.

Patient: Oh no. What do we do?

Doctor: This is renal colic from a kidney stone. Many stones this size pass on their own. We gave you acetaminophen 1000 milligrams through the IV and ondansetron 4 milligrams for the nausea, and I see your pain is better now. Because of your age and your kidney numbers, I want you to stop the ibuprofen. It can hurt the kidneys. For pain at home, take acetaminophen 650 milligrams every 6 hours as needed, and I'm giving you a small supply of oxycodone 2.5 milligrams every 6 hours as needed for severe pain only, 8 tablets. It can make you sleepy and constipated, so be careful when you stand up. Drink plenty of fluids and strain your urine. See urology in about one week, and have your kidney function rechecked with your regular doctor in a few days. Come back right away for fever, uncontrolled pain, vomiting you can't stop, or if you can't pee.

Patient: Okay, I understand.
"""

Nephrology progress note, hospital day 3. This 36-year-old female is 8 months status post deceased-donor kidney transplant for IgA nephropathy and was admitted with acute kidney injury after 4 days of vomiting and diarrhea from presumed viral gastroenteritis. Her last scheduled lab draw was missed because she lives about 90 minutes from the transplant center and has no reliable transportation. She depends on her sister for rides, and this has led to several missed monitoring visits.

Today she feels much better. The diarrhea stopped yesterday and she is tolerating oral intake. She denies fever, dysuria, decreased urine output, pain over the graft, shortness of breath, and leg swelling.

Because of her transportation barriers, the transplant coordinator will arrange lab draws at an outpatient lab near her home with results sent to our team, social work will provide ride vouchers, and a telehealth visit is set for 1 week after discharge. Doctor: How have things been since then?
Patient: The pain is still there, mostly in my right side and back, and it comes in waves. I strain my urine like they told me, but no stone has come out.
Family member: He's my son and he lives with me. Since this morning he's been throwing up, and he hasn't kept much water down for two days. I also saw pink urine in the toilet.
Doctor: Any fever, chills, or burning when you urinate?
Patient: No fever, no chills, and no burning.
Doctor: How are you taking the medicines?
Patient: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg every evening, and ibuprofen 600 mg about three times a day for the pain.

Patient: Is that bad?

Keep taking the tamsulosin every evening and drink at least three liters of fluid a day.

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 3 for a 68-year-old female admitted with symptomatic hyponatremia. She presented two days before admission with confusion, nausea, headache, and unsteady walking. She works rotating night shifts at a distribution warehouse with an irregular sleep and meal schedule, and she reports drinking large amounts of water and tea to stay awake on shifts and often skipping meals when her shift changes. Her primary care physician started hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily three weeks ago for HTN, and she also takes sertraline 50 mg daily for depression. She denies vomiting, diarrhea, seizure, chest pain, and shortness of breath.

No acute events overnight. Her serum sodium was 118 on arrival, 123 after two 100 mL boluses of 3% saline in the emergency department, and 126 this morning, so the correction has stayed well under the eight-point daily limit. Her mentation has cleared, and the headache and nausea have resolved.

Vitals today: BP 138/82, HR 76, RR 16, temp 98.1 F, SpO2 97% on room air. Weight is 71 kg, unchanged from admission. She is alert and oriented, mucous membranes are moist, there is no peripheral edema, jugular venous pressure is normal, and the lungs are clear. She appears euvolemic.

Labs this morning show serum osmolality 258, urine osmolality 412, TSH 2.1, morning cortisol normal, potassium 3.3, creatinine 0.7, glucose 96, and an inappropriately elevated urine sodium.

My impression is symptomatic hypotonic hyponatremia, most likely thiazide-induced, with possible contribution from sertraline and high free water intake. She also has mild hypokalemia, and her HTN needs a new regimen.

Hydrochlorothiazide is discontinued permanently and will be listed as an adverse reaction. Continue sertraline 50 mg daily with close monitoring for now. Fluid restriction to 1.2 liters per day. Start amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure. Give potassium chloride 20 mEq by mouth twice today. Repeat BMP every 8 hours today, then daily. Because of her night-shift schedule, we will tie her medications to a consistent anchor time relative to when she wakes rather than clock time, supply a weekly pillbox, and ask pharmacy for a written schedule. She will get a printed fluid target for work shifts, and a repeat sodium check is planned three days after discharge at a lab draw time that fits her days off. Anticipate discharge tomorrow if sodium continues to rise and she stays asymptomatic.
"""

Doctor: Good morning. I see you're a 70-year-old female here to talk about your cholesterol results and whether you should start a statin. How are you feeling today?
Patient: A little nervous, honestly. I've been reading online about those cholesterol pills, and I read they can destroy your muscles and your memory and your liver. Is that true? My neighbor had to stop hers.
Doctor: Those are very reasonable questions, and I'll go through each one. First, do you have any muscle pain, weakness, chest pain, or shortness of breath right now?
Patient: No muscle pain, no chest pain, and I'm not short of breath. My knees ache from arthritis, but that's all. Oh, and I forget where I put my glasses sometimes. Is that the memory thing already?
Doctor: No, that's very common and not caused by anything you're taking. Any yellow skin, dark urine, or belly pain?
Patient: No, nothing like that. Can I ask one more thing? What if I start it and feel worse?
Doctor: Then you stop it and call us. Let's go through your medicines. What are you taking?
Patient: Metformin 500 mg twice a day. No, wait, 1000 mg twice a day, the doctor raised it last year. Lisinopril 10 mg every morning, omeprazole 20 mg every day for reflux, and ibuprofen 400 mg most days for my knees.
Doctor: Anything else, like acetaminophen or supplements? Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: Acetaminophen 500 mg once in a while. No allergies.
Doctor: And how much alcohol do you drink in a typical week?
Patient: Oh, a glass of wine with dinner. Well, if I'm honest, three or four glasses of wine every evening. Is that bad for the cholesterol?
Doctor: That counts as heavy drinking for a woman, and it matters for your liver, blood pressure, and triglycerides. We'll come back to that. Any family history of heart disease?
Patient: My father had a heart attack at 62. I worry about that all the time.
Doctor: I understand. Your blood pressure today is 148/86, pulse 78, and weight 74 kilograms. Your heart and lungs sound normal, and there is no swelling in your legs. Your knees are mildly stiff and tender but not swollen. Your labs from last week show total cholesterol 262, LDL 168, HDL 48, triglycerides 230, AST 36 and ALT 30, which are both normal, so your liver is fine for now. Your A1c is 7.3 and creatinine is 0.9.
Patient: So what does all this mean? Am I going to have a heart attack?
Doctor: You have high cholesterol, type 2 diabetes, hypertension that is above goal, and osteoarthritis in your knees. With your age and your father's history, your risk of a heart attack or stroke over ten years is about 24 percent, which is high. A statin lowers that risk by about a third. Serious muscle or liver problems are rare, and good studies have not shown that statins cause memory loss.
Patient: Alright. What will we do?
Doctor: Here is the plan. I will start atorvastatin 20 mg every night. I will increase your lisinopril from 10 mg to 20 mg daily for your blood pressure. I want you to stop the ibuprofen because it raises blood pressure and can hurt your kidneys, and use acetaminophen 500 mg up to three times a day for your knees instead. Cut back the wine to no more than one glass a day with a couple of alcohol-free days each week, and I can connect you with a counselor. I'll order a repeat lipid panel and liver tests in 8 weeks, a kidney panel and potassium two weeks after the lisinopril change, and a nurse will call you in 2 weeks to ask about muscle aches. Come back in 8 weeks. Call us right away if you have severe muscle pain, dark urine, or yellow skin.
Patient: Okay, I feel better. Thank you for explaining everything.
"""

"""
Telehealth visit conducted as an audio-only telephone call, with a professional Vietnamese medical interpreter on the line throughout. The patient is at home with his daughter present, and verbal consent for the telephone visit was obtained. This is a 94-year-old male seen for follow-up of mild cognitive impairment and poor sleep.

History: The daughter reports that over the past year he has been forgetting appointments and repeating questions, and he sometimes misplaces his keys and glasses. He still dresses, bathes, and feeds himself independently, while she manages his pills and finances. She denies falls, hallucinations, getting lost outside, or new confusion. The patient himself denies low mood, headaches, and weakness on one side. He takes diphenhydramine 25 mg nightly from the pharmacy shelf to help him sleep and says he feels groggy in the mornings. He has not driven for several years.

Past medical history: hypertension, hyperlipidemia, hearing loss. Current medications are amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, aspirin 81 mg daily, and diphenhydramine as above. No known drug allergies.

Home measurements: The daughter checked his blood pressure with a home cuff just before the call and it was 128/72 with a pulse of 64.

Limited exam by phone: Speech is fluent and appropriate through the interpreter, he follows multi-step questions, and he was oriented to person, place, and the month but not the exact day. He recalled 2 of 3 words at five minutes. No visual exam was possible.

Data reviewed: CT head six months ago showed mild age-related atrophy and chronic small vessel changes without mass or infarct. B12 was 540 and TSH was 2.1 on the last labs.

Impression: Mild cognitive impairment, stable, with likely contribution from nightly anticholinergic use and hearing loss. Hypertension appears controlled based on the home reading.

Next steps: Stop diphenhydramine today. Start melatonin 3 mg at bedtime. Continue amlodipine, atorvastatin, and aspirin at current doses. Refer for a hearing evaluation. Repeat in-person cognitive testing with MoCA in 3 months. The daughter will keep using the pill organizer and supervise medications. Sleep hygiene was reviewed through the interpreter, and the patient and daughter verbalized understanding. Call sooner for sudden confusion, falls, or new hallucinations. Follow up in person in 3 months.
"""

"""
Hospital day 2 for this 73-year-old female admitted with acute kidney injury from dehydration after four days of vomiting and watery diarrhea, presumed viral gastroenteritis. Her creatinine was 2.4 on admission, up from a baseline of 0.9. Overnight she had no fever and tolerated clear liquids. She has had two loose stools and no vomiting since admission. She denies abdominal pain, blood in the stool, dysuria, flank pain, and chest pain. She reports feeling less dizzy when she stands.

Her home lisinopril 20 mg daily for hypertension and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily have been held since admission because of the kidney injury and volume depletion. She is receiving lactated Ringer's at 100 mL/h, potassium chloride 20 mEq by mouth twice today for low potassium, and ondansetron 4 mg IV as needed for nausea, of which she needed one dose overnight.

Urinalysis was bland with a specific gravity of 1.030 and no blood or protein, and FeNa was 0.6%, consistent with prerenal azotemia. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis.

Assessment is prerenal acute kidney injury from dehydration due to viral gastroenteritis, improving, with hypokalemia that is also improving. Her hypertension is controlled off her medications for now. We will continue lactated Ringer's at 100 mL/h until she is drinking well, advance her diet as tolerated, and recheck creatinine and potassium this afternoon and tomorrow morning. Lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide stay on hold until her creatinine returns to baseline and she is eating normally. She should avoid NSAIDs. If she continues to improve, she can go home in 24 to 48 hours with a basic metabolic panel in one week with her primary care doctor.
"""

The patient is a 73-year-old male on hospital day 2 for acute urinary retention due to benign prostatic hyperplasia. A professional medical interpreter was used for the entire visit. He denies fever, denies dysuria, denies visible blood in the urine, and denies flank pain. He has hypertension, treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies.

Doctor: Good. Come back in three weeks with repeat blood work.

Clinical note:
"""
Seen in the infectious disease clinic for a painful blistering rash. This 82-year-old male developed burning pain over the right side of his lower chest and back five days ago, and a rash of clustered blisters appeared three days ago, wrapping around the right side of his trunk toward the front. The pain is a constant burning, rated 7 out of 10, with sharp stabbing episodes, and even his shirt touching the skin is painful, which wakes him at night. He remembers having chickenpox as a child and has never received the recombinant zoster vaccine. He denies fever, headache, eye pain, vision changes, facial rash, and new weakness. He has not been on steroids or any immunosuppressive medication.

Past history includes HTN treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily and chronic kidney disease stage 3 with a baseline creatinine around 1.5. He has no known drug allergies. He lives with his wife. He tried over-the-counter acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours with little relief.

On exam today, temperature 98.2 F, heart rate 72, blood pressure 146/84, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. He is comfortable at rest but winces when the rash is touched. There are grouped vesicles on erythematous bases in a band along the right T8 dermatome from the mid back around to the upper abdomen, stopping at the midline, with some early crusting and no pus, spreading redness, or necrosis. There are no lesions on the face, scalp, or tip of the nose, and the eyes are clear. Neurologic exam is non-focal and strength is normal.

Labs from today show creatinine 1.5 with an eGFR of 43, hemoglobin 13.8, and WBC 7.2.

Impression: Herpes zoster of the right T8 dermatome, uncomplicated, within 72 hours of rash onset, in an 82-year-old with CKD stage 3 and mildly elevated blood pressure from pain.

Management: Start valacyclovir for 7 days. The usual dose is 1000 mg three times daily, but because his eGFR is 43 I reduced it to 1000 mg every 12 hours. Continue acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed. Start gabapentin 100 mg at bedtime for nerve pain, with titration at follow-up and dosing adjusted for his kidney function. Add lidocaine 5% patches to the painful skin for 12 hours on and 12 hours off. Avoid NSAIDs because of his CKD. Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily and recheck blood pressure at follow-up. Keep the rash clean, dry, and covered, and avoid contact with infants and with anyone who is immunocompromised or has never had chickenpox until the lesions crust. I will give the recombinant zoster vaccine after he recovers, in about two to three months. He should call right away for eye pain, new facial rash, fever, or spreading redness, and we will see him back in one week to assess pain and the risk of postherpetic neuralgia.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Pulmonology inpatient progress dictation, hospital day 3, on a 73-year-old female with interstitial lung disease admitted with acute on chronic hypoxemic respiratory failure. A professional interpreter was used for the entire visit by video, and everything below was confirmed with the patient through the interpreter. She has known fibrotic interstitial lung disease diagnosed about four years ago with a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern on high resolution CT, along with hypertension, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and recurrent urinary tract infections. She was admitted three days ago after a week of worsening shortness of breath and dry cough. She denies fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, and leg swelling. She has a documented allergy to sulfa drugs which causes a diffuse rash, so trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole is not an option for her.

Home medications were reviewed through the interpreter using her pill bottles. She takes prednisone 20 mg daily, correction, prednisone 10 mg daily, the bottle clearly says 10 mg, plus mycophenolate 500 mg twice daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily. She also takes nitrofurantoin 100 mg nightly to prevent urinary infections, which she has used for about two years.

On admission she was hypoxemic with oxygen saturation 86% on room air, improving to 93% on 4 liters nasal cannula. CT angiogram was negative for pulmonary embolism. High resolution CT showed her known basilar fibrosis with new bilateral ground glass opacities, consistent with an acute exacerbation. She received ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily for 2 days, which was stopped yesterday after the procalcitonin returned low and the blood cultures and respiratory viral panel were negative. She was started on methylprednisolone 60 mg IV every 12 hours on admission in place of her home prednisone. Today she says her breathing is slightly better.

Vitals today are temperature 37.0 Celsius, heart rate 92, blood pressure 98 over 60, respiratory rate 22, and oxygen saturation 93% on 3 liters, weaned from 4 liters. Labs show white count 13.1, creatinine 0.8, potassium 4.2, and glucose 168 on steroids. On exam she is comfortable at rest and speaking in short sentences, with bibasilar velcro crackles and digital clubbing. There is no wheezing. There is no peripheral edema.

Impression is acute exacerbation of fibrotic interstitial lung disease, slowly improving on high dose steroids. Her blood pressure runs low, so I am reducing amlodipine from 5 mg to 2.5 mg daily. I am stopping the nitrofurantoin because of the risk of pulmonary toxicity, and urology and her primary doctor will arrange another way to prevent urinary infections that avoids sulfa drugs. Because she is on high dose steroids and has a sulfa allergy, I am starting atovaquone 1500 mg daily for pneumocystis prophylaxis instead of trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole. Plan is to continue methylprednisolone 60 mg IV every 12 hours for now, continue mycophenolate 500 mg twice daily and omeprazole 20 mg daily, wean oxygen to keep saturation at or above 90%, start physical therapy, and repeat the metabolic panel and chest x-ray tomorrow. Discharge teaching will be done with a professional interpreter, and we will discuss goals of care and antifibrotic therapy with her at the next visit.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Nurse: Rooming a 13-year-old male with his mother, wheezing and trouble breathing. Triage vitals: temperature 98.9, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Peak flow is 210, which is about 55 percent of his predicted value.
Doctor: Thanks. Hi there, I hear you've been having a hard time breathing. Tell me what's going on.
Patient: I keep coughing and wheezing, especially at night, and my chest feels tight. I can't run at all, and even the stairs at school make me out of breath.
Family member: It started about three days ago after a cold. He's been using his rescue inhaler every three or four hours, and last night he used it like six times.
Doctor: Does the rescue inhaler help?
Patient: A little, for maybe an hour.
Doctor: Any fever, vomiting, chest pain, or swelling of the lips?
Family member: No fever, no vomiting, and he says no chest pain or swelling of the lips.
Doctor: What does he take every day for his asthma?
Family member: He's supposed to take Flovent, the 44 microgram one, two puffs twice a day. Actually, wait, let me look at the box. It says 110 micrograms, two puffs twice a day. Sorry, that's the right one.
Doctor: And is he actually taking it?
Family member: Honestly, no. It ran out about two months ago. The refill was almost 90 dollars with our new insurance plan and we just couldn't afford it right now. We've only been using the albuterol because it's cheaper.
Doctor: I really appreciate you telling me that. It's very common, and it's probably a big reason he's flaring up. Is he still on the montelukast?
Family member: No, he stopped that last spring because it gave him bad dreams.
Doctor: Okay. Anything else?
Family member: Cetirizine 10 mg once a day for his runny nose in the spring, and a cream for the eczema on his elbows when it flares.
Doctor: Okay, so the cetirizine is for his allergic rhinitis, and he has eczema too. Any allergies to medications?
Family member: No drug allergies.
Doctor: Alright. Let me listen to your chest. He is working a bit hard to breathe, using his neck muscles a little. I hear diffuse expiratory wheezes with decreased air movement at both bases, no stridor. His throat is clear, and I see dry patches on both elbows. Heart is fast but regular. We also got a chest X-ray, and it shows some hyperinflation but no pneumonia.
Doctor: This is an asthma exacerbation, moderate, triggered by a cold and made worse because he has been without his controller medicine for two months. We'll give him an albuterol-ipratropium nebulizer treatment, three back to back over the next hour, plus a dose of oral prednisone.
Nurse: He finished the third nebulizer. Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air and peak flow is 330, about 85 percent of predicted.
Doctor: Good, he sounds much better and the wheezing is mild now. Here is the plan for home. Prednisone 40 mg once a day for five days. Albuterol, two puffs with the spacer every four hours for the next two days, instead of just as needed, then back to as needed. Restart fluticasone 110 micrograms, two puffs twice a day with the spacer, and rinse his mouth afterward. I'll send the generic and our social worker will help with a patient assistance program and a 90-day supply so the cost doesn't get in the way again. Let's officially stop the montelukast, and continue the cetirizine 10 mg daily and the eczema cream as before. I'm also giving you a written asthma action plan.
Family member: That helps a lot, thank you.
Doctor: See his pediatrician in two to three days. Go to the ER if he can't speak a full sentence, his lips look blue, or he needs albuterol more often than every four hours.
Family member: Understood.
"""

reference: A 13-year-old male with asthma, allergic rhinitis and eczema came to urgent care with three days of wheezing, cough and chest tightness after a cold, and he had been without his controller inhaler for two months because of cost. His heart rate was 112, respiratory rate 26 and oxygen saturation 93%, with diffuse expiratory wheezes, and a chest X-ray showed hyperinflation without pneumonia. After three nebulizer treatments his oxygen saturation was 97% and peak flow rose from 55 to 85 percent of predicted. The diagnosis is a moderate asthma exacerbation. He went home on prednisone 40 mg once a day for five days, scheduled albuterol and restarted fluticasone 110 micrograms, with montelukast stopped and social work help with cost.

Patient: Okay, thank you.
"""
