Clinical note:
"""
This is a pulmonology clinic follow-up visit for a 55-year-old female with pulmonary sarcoidosis, stage II on chest imaging, diagnosed about three years ago by endobronchial ultrasound lymph node biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas. She also has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. Since her last visit she reports a persistent dry cough, exertional shortness of breath after one flight of stairs, and fatigue. She denies fever, night sweats, hemoptysis, chest pain, and eye redness or eye pain. She lives alone, has limited social support with no family nearby, and admits she has trouble keeping track of her pills and has missed some doses.

When asked about her prednisone she first told me she takes 10 mg daily, but after we reviewed the pill bottle she brought she is actually taking 20 mg daily, which is the dose prescribed at her last visit, so 20 mg daily is her correct current dose. She also takes metformin 500 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, and omeprazole 20 mg daily. On direct questioning she also buys over-the-counter supplements on her own, namely calcium carbonate 1200 mg daily, vitamin D3 5000 units daily, and echinacea capsules daily, which she started to protect her bones and boost her immunity while on steroids.

Vital signs today were blood pressure 134/82, heart rate 78, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air at rest. During a six-minute walk test she covered 380 meters and her saturation fell to 90%. She is comfortable and speaks in full sentences. Her lungs are clear to auscultation without wheeze or crackles. There is no erythema nodosum or other skin lesion. Her eyes show no conjunctival injection. Pulmonary function testing today showed FVC 74% of predicted, down from 80% a year ago, and DLCO 58% of predicted, down from 64%. Chest CT from last month shows stable bilateral perihilar lymphadenopathy and perilymphatic nodules without new fibrosis. Laboratory results today include serum calcium 10.9 mg/dL, which is mildly elevated, creatinine 0.9, and hemoglobin A1c 7.4%.

My impression is pulmonary sarcoidosis with a modest decline in lung function despite prednisone 20 mg daily, so she needs a steroid-sparing agent. Her mild hypercalcemia is most likely related to her calcium and vitamin D supplements in the setting of sarcoidosis, since granulomas increase production of active vitamin D. Her diabetes is above goal with an A1c of 7.4% on steroids, and her hypertension and reflux are stable.

I asked her to stop the calcium carbonate, vitamin D3, and echinacea today and explained why supplements can be harmful in sarcoidosis. I am starting methotrexate 10 mg once weekly with folic acid 1 mg daily after baseline CBC, liver tests, and hepatitis serologies, and I reviewed that methotrexate is taken once a week only and never daily. Prednisone stays at 20 mg daily for now. Metformin is increased from 500 mg twice daily to 1000 mg twice daily for her A1c. Lisinopril and omeprazole continue unchanged. Because she lives alone, I referred her to social work and asked the pharmacy to prepare weekly blister packs, and a nurse will call her in two weeks to check on medication use. We will repeat the serum calcium with a 24-hour urine calcium in two weeks and repeat pulmonary function tests in three months, and she should have an annual eye exam. She was told to call us for worsening breathlessness, fever, or chest pain, and she will return to clinic in six weeks.
"""

Doctor: Hello, what brings you in today?
Patient: My acne has gotten a lot worse over the last month, mostly along my jawline and chin. It's the worst it's been since college.

Patient: Tretinoin cream, 0.025 percent, at bedtime, and spironolactone 50 mg once a day, which my last doctor started about six months ago. And a benzoyl peroxide wash, 4 percent, in the shower.
Doctor: Was that working?
Patient: It was working until about a month ago. Now I have new painful bumps on my chin and jaw. No scarring that I can see, and no cysts that drain.
Doctor: Any fever, joint pain, or rash anywhere else on your body?
Patient: No fever, no joint pain, and no rash anywhere else.
Doctor: Is there any chance you could be pregnant? When was your last period?
Patient: Actually, it's been about eight weeks. I've been nauseous in the mornings and my breasts are tender. I hadn't thought of it with all the acne.
Doctor: Okay, that matters a lot for which medicines we can use. Are you on birth control?
Patient: No, we weren't using anything.
Doctor: Any allergies to medications?
Patient: None.
Doctor: Let's do a urine pregnancy test right now.
Patient: Okay.
Doctor: The urine pregnancy test is positive, so you're pregnant.
Patient: Oh wow. We were hoping for this, just not this quickly. Is my acne medicine safe?
Doctor: Not all of it. Let me examine you. Your blood pressure is 108 over 66 and your heart rate is 76. On your face I see about 15 inflammatory papules and a few pustules along the jawline and chin, with a few comedones on the forehead. No nodules, no cysts, and no scarring.
Doctor: So this is acne vulgaris, moderate, and it is probably worsened by pregnancy hormones. Because you're pregnant, I'm stopping the spironolactone and the tretinoin cream today, since neither is recommended in pregnancy. We'll start azelaic acid 15 percent gel twice a day, which is considered safe. You can continue the benzoyl peroxide wash once daily. Please avoid oral isotretinoin and doxycycline for the rest of your pregnancy. I'd also like you to start a prenatal vitamin once daily and call your obstetrician this week to book your first prenatal visit.
Patient: Okay. How long until my skin improves?
Doctor: Probably six to eight weeks. We'll see you back in eight weeks to check how it's responding.
"""

44-year-old female, pulm clinic, f/u ILD.
HPI: ILD dx 3 mo ago, likely hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Keeps 2 parrots at home x 6 yr. Prednisone started 6 wk ago at 40 mg daily, now on 20 mg daily. Cough better, DOE improved to walking 2 blocks (was 1 block). Denies fever, hemoptysis, joint pain, rash. No wheeze. NKDA.

Exam: bibasilar fine crackles, no clubbing, no edema
PFTs today: FVC 72% pred (was 64%), DLCO 58% (was 49%)
HRCT 3 mo ago: patchy ground-glass + mosaic attenuation, no honeycombing
Imp: ILD, likely hypersensitivity pneumonitis, improving on steroids
Plan:
- cont prednisone 20 mg daily x 4 wk, then taper to 10 mg daily
- cont TMP-SMX DS 1 tab MWF while on prednisone
- remove birds from home, avoid exposure
- repeat PFTs + HRCT in 3 mo
- f/u 6 wk, sooner if SOB worsens
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Developmental-behavioral pediatrics clinic follow-up for ADHD medication management. The patient is a 14-year-old female accompanied by her mother, seen for a four-week recheck. She has combined-presentation attention deficit hyperactivity disorder diagnosed at age 9, with comorbid generalized anxiety disorder, mild persistent asthma, and allergic rhinitis.

Interval history: Her mother reports that the methylphenidate extended-release 36 mg tablet taken each morning helps in the morning but wears off by early afternoon, when the patient has trouble paying attention in her last two classes and becomes irritable. The patient works irregular shifts at her family's restaurant, mostly weekend lunches and some weekday evenings, so her wake-up and meal times change from day to day. On late-start days she has sometimes taken the tablet at noon, and then she lies awake until after midnight. She also reports reduced appetite at lunch and trouble falling asleep. At the last visit guanfacine extended-release 1 mg at bedtime was added for evening symptoms; she stopped it two weeks ago, correction, three weeks ago, because it made her dizzy and sleepy at school. She denies chest pain, fainting, tics, and thoughts of self-harm. She does describe her heart racing at times when she feels anxious.

The patient was anxious throughout the visit and asked many questions, including whether the medicine will stunt her growth, whether she could become addicted, whether it is safe with her inhaler, why her heart races, and whether she will need it forever. I answered each question in turn and she appeared reassured. Her other medications are as follows. Her mother first said sertraline 25 mg daily, then read the pharmacy label and corrected this to sertraline 50 mg once daily. She also uses albuterol HFA 2 puffs as needed, fluticasone HFA 44 mcg 2 puffs twice daily, cetirizine 10 mg daily, and melatonin 3 mg at bedtime. No known drug allergies.

Blood pressure is 106/64, heart rate 88, height 160 cm, and weight 52.4 kg, which is 1.2 kg lower than at the last visit, with a BMI of 20.5. She is anxious but cooperative, with no tics, a regular heart rhythm without murmur, and clear lungs without wheezing. An ECG obtained today because of her racing-heart question shows normal sinus rhythm with normal intervals. Labs from her primary care physician last month showed hemoglobin 12.6, TSH 1.8, and ferritin 24 ng/mL.

Impression is ADHD with end-of-day wearing off and rebound irritability, made harder by variable timing from her work schedule. Generalized anxiety disorder is stable on sertraline, her asthma is well controlled, and her allergic rhinitis is quiet. Plan is to increase methylphenidate extended-release from 36 mg to 54 mg every morning, taken within one hour of waking, and on days she wakes after 10 am she should skip the tablet rather than take it at noon. Guanfacine stays discontinued. Continue sertraline 50 mg daily, albuterol, fluticasone, cetirizine, and melatonin unchanged. I reviewed the state prescription monitoring database and reassured her about growth, which we will track at each visit, and about the low misuse risk when taken as prescribed. She is referred for cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety. We wrote out a dosing schedule for her shift days and a letter for school accommodations, with a calorie-rich breakfast and after-school snack to help weight. Recheck blood pressure, heart rate, and weight in four weeks.
"""

"""
Nephrology consultation requested by the hospitalist team for heavy proteinuria and leg swelling in a 60-year-old female.

HPI: The patient reports four weeks of progressive swelling of both legs, puffy eyelids in the morning, foamy urine, and a weight gain of about 5 kg. She denies gross hematuria, flank pain, fever, rash, and joint pain. She has had type 2 diabetes mellitus for ten years and takes metformin 500 mg BID. She takes no other medications and no over-the-counter pain relievers.

Exam: BP 142/86, HR 80, and she is afebrile. There is periorbital edema and 2+ pitting edema to the knees bilaterally. Lungs are clear, there is no JVD, and there is no rash.

Data: Urine protein to creatinine ratio is 7.2 g/g, and urinalysis shows 4+ protein, no blood, and oval fat bodies. Serum albumin is 1.9 g/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and total cholesterol 310 mg/dL. A1c is 7.1%. Renal ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys with no hydronephrosis.

Impression: Nephrotic syndrome with preserved kidney function. The cause is not yet clear and needs a tissue diagnosis. Diabetic kidney disease is less likely given the rapid onset over weeks.

Recommendations: Ultrasound-guided renal biopsy once coagulation studies are back. Send ANA, complement C3 and C4, hepatitis B and C serologies, HIV, PLA2R antibody, and serum protein electrophoresis. Start furosemide 40 mg IV twice daily for the edema, with daily weights and a 2 g sodium diet. Continue metformin 500 mg BID while kidney function stays normal. We will follow along with you.
"""

- amlodipine 5 mg daily

- atorvastatin 40 mg nightly
- HCTZ 12.5 mg daily STOPPED 2 wk ago by PCP for K 3.2

- vitamin D3 2000 units daily
- licorice root tea 2-3 cups/day x 1 yr
NKDA.

This 33-year-old male with a 15-year history of type 1 diabetes is seen in the combined eye and ear, nose, and throat clinic for his annual diabetic retinopathy screening and for a second concern of chronic nasal congestion. He reports no change in vision, no floaters, no flashes of light, and no eye pain. For the past several months he has had persistent nasal stuffiness, clear post-nasal drip, and frequent sneezing, worse in spring, which he has been treating with oxymetazoline nasal spray nearly every night. He denies sinus pressure, facial pain, nosebleeds, ear pain, and hearing loss.

His medications are insulin glargine 24 units at bedtime and insulin lispro with meals. He has had no hypoglycemic episodes. His most recent hemoglobin A1c, drawn two weeks ago, was 8.1%. Blood pressure today is 124/78 with a heart rate of 70.

On examination, uncorrected distance visual acuity is 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye, with intraocular pressures of 15 and 16 mmHg. Pupils are equal and reactive. After dilation with tropicamide 1%, the dilated fundus examination shows scattered microaneurysms and a few dot hemorrhages in both eyes, with no neovascularization and no vitreous hemorrhage. Optical coherence tomography of the macula shows no macular edema, with a central subfield thickness of 260 microns in each eye. Anterior rhinoscopy shows pale, boggy inferior turbinates with clear rhinorrhea, no polyps, and a midline septum. Ears and oropharynx are normal.

Assessment is mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy without macular edema in both eyes, and allergic rhinitis with rhinitis medicamentosa from overuse of oxymetazoline. He should stop oxymetazoline and start fluticasone nasal spray 50 mcg, two sprays in each nostril once daily. Saline rinses were also recommended. Glycemic control with his primary diabetes team was reinforced, with a goal A1c below 7%. We will repeat the dilated eye exam with macular OCT in 12 months, and he will return to the ENT clinic in 6 weeks to review his nasal symptoms.
"""

Chief Complaint: Right flank pain with nausea

HPI: The patient is an 18-year-old female with type 1 diabetes, asthma, and depression who presents with 6 hours of severe, colicky right flank pain radiating to the groin, with nausea and two episodes of vomiting. The pain started suddenly this morning, comes in waves, and is 9 out of 10 at its worst. She also notes burning with urination and urinary urgency since last night. She denies fever, chills, abdominal trauma, and gross blood in her urine. She was discharged from the hospital 3 weeks ago after an admission for diabetic ketoacidosis that followed a weekend of heavy drinking. She has not had a kidney stone before.

Medications and history: Home medications are insulin glargine at bedtime, insulin lispro with meals per sliding scale, and albuterol as needed. The patient first reported taking glargine 20 units nightly. Correction: after we reviewed her discharge paperwork, she confirmed that her dose was increased to 24 units nightly at discharge and she has been taking 24 units, not 20 units. At discharge naproxen 500 mg twice daily, which she had been taking for cramps, was stopped because it was no longer needed, and she says she has not taken it since. She also told us she stopped taking her sertraline 50 mg daily on her own 2 weeks ago because she felt it was not helping her depression. She has no known drug allergies.

Social history: She drinks about 8 to 10 drinks on weekend nights and had 3 drinks two nights ago. She denies other drug use and does not smoke. She denies any alcohol today and has no tremor, sweating, or anxiety.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good to see you again. You're a 45-year-old male here for your routine HIV follow-up, and I see you just got back from a trip. How was it?
Patient: It was great, thanks. I was in Kenya for three weeks visiting friends, and I got back about two weeks ago.
Doctor: Wonderful. Did you take your Biktarvy every day while you were away?
Patient: Yes, one tablet every morning. I only took it late once, about six hours late, because of the flight.
Doctor: That's fine. Did you take anything for malaria?
Patient: Yes, atovaquone-proguanil, one tablet daily. I started it two days before I left and finished it a week after I got home.
Doctor: Good. Any fever, chills, or sweats since you got back?
Patient: No fever, no chills, no night sweats.
Doctor: Any diarrhea or stomach trouble on the trip?
Patient: Yes, around the second week I had bad watery diarrhea for two days. I took azithromycin 500 mg once a day for three days that I got from a pharmacy there, and it cleared up. I also chewed Tums, two or three a day, for heartburn.
Doctor: Okay. The Tums matter, because calcium can bind to the Biktarvy and lower how much you absorb. We'll talk about that in a minute. Any cough, rash, weight loss, or yellow eyes?
Patient: No, none of those.
Doctor: Let me go over your other medicines. I have lisinopril 10 mg daily for blood pressure, atorvastatin for your high cholesterol, and omeprazole for reflux. Is that right?
Patient: Yes. The atorvastatin is 40 milligrams every evening.
Doctor: Our list says 20 milligrams. Can you check?
Patient: Hold on, let me look at the photo of the bottle on my phone. Oh, you're right, it's 20 milligrams every evening. I was thinking of my old dose.
Doctor: Thanks for checking. And the omeprazole?
Patient: 20 mg every morning, but honestly I haven't had heartburn in months except on the trip.
Doctor: Good to know. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or headaches?
Patient: No chest pain, no shortness of breath, just the occasional mild headache.
Doctor: Alright, here are your results from last week. Your viral load is undetectable, less than 20 copies per mL, your CD4 count is 612, creatinine 1.0, ALT 28, LDL 98, and A1c 5.6 percent. All of that looks great. Today your blood pressure is 146 over 88, and on the repeat it's 144 over 86. Heart rate is 74, temperature 36.7 Celsius, and weight is stable at 82 kilograms. I don't see any thrush, your lymph nodes are not enlarged, your lungs are clear, your abdomen is soft, and there's no rash.
Patient: So what does it all mean?
Doctor: Your HIV remains well controlled on Biktarvy. The diarrhea sounds like traveler's diarrhea that resolved with azithromycin, and since you have no fever and finished your malaria prophylaxis, I don't need any malaria testing. Your hypertension was above goal on both readings today, so I'm going to increase your lisinopril from 10 mg to 20 mg once a day and recheck your kidney function and potassium in two weeks. Keep taking atorvastatin 20 milligrams. Your reflux has settled, so let's stop the omeprazole. If you need an antacid like Tums again, take it with your Biktarvy only when you eat, or take the Biktarvy at least two hours before it. We'll do your routine sexually transmitted infection screening today with a syphilis blood test and urine tests, and give you your flu shot. Please keep a blood pressure log at home.
Patient: Sounds good.
Doctor: I'll see you in three months with repeat labs. Come in sooner if you get a fever or any new symptoms.
"""

reference: A 45-year-old male with HIV on Biktarvy presented for routine follow-up two weeks after a three-week trip to Kenya, during which he had two days of traveler's diarrhea treated with azithromycin. He completed malaria prophylaxis with atovaquone-proguanil and denies fever, chills, night sweats, cough, rash, weight loss, and chest pain. His viral load is undetectable with a CD4 count of 612, and his blood pressure was 146/88 and 144/86. HIV is well controlled, the diarrhea resolved, and his hypertension is above goal. Lisinopril was increased from 10 mg to 20 mg, omeprazole was stopped, atorvastatin 20 mg continues, and Biktarvy and antacid timing, STI screening, a flu shot, and a follow-up visit in three months were arranged.

Visit modality: synchronous video visit on the patient's smartphone. The patient was at home, identity was confirmed verbally, and she consented to telehealth.

Reason for visit: infectious disease follow-up to start treatment for latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI).

History: The patient is a 70-year-old female who works rotating night and day shifts at a warehouse, so her sleep and meal times change from week to week. A workplace screening interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) was positive 2 weeks ago. Her chest x-ray was normal, with no infiltrates or cavitation. Impression: Latent tuberculosis infection with no symptoms or imaging findings of active TB. Hypertension stable on current therapy. Sleep disruption related to shift work.

Treatment: Start rifampin 600 mg once daily for 4 months. I chose rifampin over isoniazid because the course is shorter and a single daily dose can be tied to the time she wakes up, whatever shift she is on. She should take it on an empty stomach, an hour before or two hours after food. I counseled her that rifampin turns urine, sweat, and tears orange, that it can stain soft contact lenses, and that she should call us right away and hold the dose for nausea, vomiting, dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, or right upper abdominal pain. Rifampin does not interact with lisinopril, but she should check with us or her pharmacist before starting any new medicine. For adherence she will set two phone alarms labeled for day and night shifts, use a weekly pill organizer, and have the pharmacy mail a 30-day supply. Repeat AST and ALT before her next visit. Continue lisinopril 10 mg daily. Telehealth follow-up in 4 weeks, then monthly. She repeated the plan back accurately.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good to see you. You're an 84-year-old male here for your routine HIV follow-up. How have you been since last time?
Patient: Not too bad. A bit tired, but I'm old, so that's expected.
Doctor: Any fevers, night sweats, weight loss, cough, or diarrhea?
Patient: No fevers, no night sweats, and my weight is steady. No cough, no diarrhea.
Doctor: How is your sleep?
Patient: I wake up a lot at night. No falls, though.
Doctor: Tell me about your medicines. Are you taking your HIV pills every day?
Patient: Yes, Biktarvy, one tablet once a day with breakfast. I haven't missed any that I can think of. Maybe two this month, when I had a rough night.
Doctor: And your other medications?
Patient: Amlodipine 5 mg a day for my blood pressure. That's all.
Doctor: Let's talk about drinking. How much alcohol do you have in a typical day?
Patient: A few beers. Maybe six, sometimes eight, in the evening. It got worse after my wife passed.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me. That is heavy alcohol use, and it matters for your liver and your sleep, and it can lead to missed pills. Any shakes in the morning or seizures when you skip a drink?
Patient: My hands shake a little in the morning until I have my first beer. No seizures.
Doctor: Any vomiting blood, black stools, or belly pain?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Your blood pressure today is 136/78, so your hypertension is reasonably controlled, and your heart rate is 74. Your weight is stable. You are alert, there is a mild fine tremor of both hands, your abdomen is soft and nontender, and I don't feel an enlarged liver. Your labs from last week show your HIV viral load is undetectable and your CD4 count is 540. ALT is 58 and AST is 72, which are mildly elevated. Hemoglobin is 12.8 and creatinine is 1.1.
Doctor: The good news is that your HIV is well controlled. The liver tests are probably from the alcohol. I want you to cut down gradually rather than stopping suddenly, because stopping all at once can be dangerous at your level of drinking. Starting today, I'm adding thiamine 100 mg once a day and folic acid 1 mg once a day. Continue Biktarvy one tablet daily and amlodipine as you are taking them. I'll refer you to our addiction counselor, and we can talk about a medicine to reduce cravings next visit after we recheck your liver tests. We'll repeat the liver tests and viral load in three months.
Patient: Okay, I'll try.
Doctor: Come back in three months, or sooner if you have more shaking, confusion, or black stools.
"""

Summarize the following clinical encounter note for a busy clinician.
Requirements:
- Write 3 to 6 sentences of plain prose (maximum 120 words), in the third person.
- Cover the patient's age/sex and reason for the visit, the key history and findings, the assessment, and the plan.
- Use only information stated in the note. Do not use headings or bullet points.

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 3 dermatology progress note for a 66-year-old female with moderate plaque psoriasis on a biologic who was admitted with cellulitis of the right lower leg. Her psoriasis has been followed for about 12 years and has been controlled on secukinumab 300 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks, with her last dose 2 weeks before admission. Her other history includes type 2 diabetes.

There were no events overnight. She says the right leg is less painful and less red than on admission. Over the past week the plaques on her elbows, knees, and scalp have become more scaly and itchy, which she attributes to the stress of being in the hospital. She denies fever, chills, joint pain, new pustules, diarrhea, and mouth sores. She has no known drug allergies.

Her current medications are cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours and metformin 500 mg twice daily. Her secukinumab has been on hold since admission because of the active infection.

Vital signs this morning were temperature 99.1 F, heart rate 82, blood pressure 132/76, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On examination, the redness on the right shin has receded about 2 cm from the marked border, with mild warmth and trace tenderness and no fluctuance or purulent drainage. Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale are present on both elbows, both knees, and the scalp, covering about 8% of her body surface area. There are no pustules and no swollen joints. White blood cell count is 9.4, down from 13.2 on admission. Blood cultures from admission show no growth at 48 hours. Her QuantiFERON test before starting the biologic was negative according to her chart. Glucose this morning was 148 mg/dL.

My impression is right lower leg cellulitis that is improving on intravenous antibiotics, and moderate plaque psoriasis with a mild flare while secukinumab is on hold. Her diabetes is stable. I will continue cefazolin today and, if she stays afebrile, switch to oral cephalexin 500 mg four times daily tomorrow to complete a 7-day course. Secukinumab will remain on hold until the cellulitis has resolved, and then she may resume it at her next scheduled dose. I am starting clobetasol 0.05% ointment twice daily to the plaques on her elbows and knees for 2 weeks, avoiding the right leg, the face, and skin folds, along with a thick emollient after bathing. Metformin continues unchanged. She will follow up in the dermatology clinic in 4 weeks.
"""

Her plaques on the elbows, knees, and scalp have become more scaly and itchy, and she denies fever, joint pain, new pustules, and diarrhea. The cellulitis is improving, her white blood cell count fell from 13.2 to 9.4, and plaques cover about 8% of her body surface area. The assessment was improving cellulitis and a mild psoriasis flare while the biologic is held. Plan is to switch to oral cephalexin tomorrow, keep secukinumab on hold, start clobetasol ointment, and arrange clinic follow-up in 4 weeks.

Requirements:
- Write 3 to 6 sentences of plain prose (maximum 120 words), in the third person.
- Cover the patient's age/sex and reason for the visit, the key history and findings, the assessment, and the plan.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good morning. What brings the baby in today?
Family member: She has had a fever for three days. It goes up to 102 at night, and she is just really fussy and not eating as well.
Doctor: I'm sorry to hear that. Just to confirm, this is your 7-month-old female infant, correct?
Family member: Yes, she turned seven months last week.
Doctor: Any cough or runny nose?
Family member: She has a little runny nose and a mild cough since the fever started.
Doctor: Any vomiting or diarrhea?
Family member: No vomiting and no diarrhea. She still has about five wet diapers a day.
Doctor: Any rash, or any trouble breathing?
Family member: No rash. She's not breathing fast or anything. And no seizures, she hasn't had any shaking.
Doctor: Good. What have you been giving her for the fever?
Family member: The infant acetaminophen liquid, 3.75 mL every six hours.
Doctor: That works out to about 120 mg, which is right for her weight. Is she up to date on her vaccines?
Family member: Yes, she got all of her shots at the six-month visit. Her big brother had a cold last week, though.
Doctor: Okay, that helps. Today in the office her temperature is 38.4 Celsius, heart rate 150, respiratory rate 36, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and she weighs 8 kilograms. She is alert and fussy but consolable, and her fontanelle is soft and flat. She has some clear nasal drainage. Her right eardrum is red and bulging, the left ear looks normal, her throat is clear, her lungs are clear with no wheezing, her belly is soft, and I don't see any rash. The rapid flu swab and RSV swab we did in the room were both negative.
Family member: So what is it?
Doctor: She has a right acute otitis media, or AOM, along with a viral URI, which is a cold. Here is the plan. I'm starting amoxicillin 360 mg by mouth twice a day for 10 days. Keep giving the acetaminophen 120 mg every 6 hours as needed, and since she is over six months you can also add ibuprofen 40 mg every 8 hours as needed for fever or fussiness. Use saline drops with gentle suction for her nose, and keep offering breast milk or formula often.
Family member: When should we come back?
Doctor: Come back in 48 to 72 hours if the fever is still there. Go to the emergency department if she is breathing hard, has fewer than four wet diapers a day, is hard to wake up, or if the fever goes above 104.
Family member: Okay, that makes sense. Thank you.
"""

reference: A 7-month-old female infant was brought in by a family member with three days of fever up to 102, fussiness, reduced feeding, a runny nose and mild cough, with no vomiting, diarrhea, rash or seizures. Temperature was 38.4 Celsius and the exam showed a red, bulging right eardrum with clear lungs, and rapid flu and RSV swabs were negative. The assessment was right acute otitis media with a viral URI. Amoxicillin 360 mg twice a day for 10 days was started, acetaminophen was continued and ibuprofen 40 mg as needed was added, with a recheck in 48 to 72 hours if the fever persists.

"""
Doctor: Welcome back. I have you down as a 33-year-old male here to follow up on the small spot we found in your right lung. I see you missed the visit in the spring. What happened?
Patient: Yeah, sorry about that. My car died and I don't have another way to get here. The bus takes almost two hours each way, and my cousin who drives me works days.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me, that matters, and we will come back to it. How have you been feeling?
Patient: Pretty good. I get a dry cough sometimes at night, mostly when my allergies are bad, and my nose gets stuffy.
Doctor: Any coughing up blood, chest pain, or shortness of breath?
Patient: No blood, no chest pain, and I'm not short of breath, even on the stairs.
Doctor: Any weight loss, night sweats, or fevers?
Patient: No. My weight is the same, and no sweats or fevers.
Doctor: Do you smoke?
Patient: I smoked about a pack a week in my twenties, but I quit four years ago.
Doctor: Okay. And remind me how the spot was found?
Patient: I fell off a ladder and they did a CT of my chest at the emergency room.
Doctor: Right. That first scan showed a 6 millimeter solid nodule in the right upper lobe. You had the repeat CT chest last week, and I have the result. The nodule is still 6 millimeters, unchanged from seven months ago, with smooth edges. There are no new nodules, no enlarged lymph nodes, and no emphysema. That is reassuring.
Patient: So it's not cancer?
Doctor: A nodule that stays the same size is very unlikely to be cancer, and with your age and light smoking history your risk is low. We still need one more CT in about twelve months to be safe. What medicines are you taking?
Patient: Cetirizine, 10 milligrams once a day, for my allergies. And lisinopril, 10 milligrams once a day, for blood pressure.
Doctor: Okay. Today your blood pressure is 128 over 78, pulse 72, and your oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Your lungs are clear with no wheezing, your heart sounds regular, and I don't feel any enlarged lymph nodes in your neck.
Doctor: So my impression is a stable 6 millimeter solid nodule in the right upper lobe, seasonal allergic rhinitis causing your night cough, and hypertension that is well controlled. Here is the plan. We will repeat the CT chest in 12 months. Continue cetirizine 10 mg once a day and lisinopril 10 mg once a day. I will start fluticasone nasal spray, two sprays in each nostril once a day, for the stuffy nose and cough. Since getting here is hard, I will book the CT and the clinic visit on the same day, and our social worker will help you apply for the medical transportation voucher through your insurance. If your car or ride falls through, call us to reschedule or switch to a video visit instead of skipping.
Patient: That helps a lot. Thank you.
"""

"""
Doctor: Hi there. I understand we have a 6-year-old female here with ear pain. Can you tell me what's been going on?
Family member: She woke up crying two nights ago holding her right ear, and yesterday she had a fever and was really fussy. She keeps pulling at it.
Doctor: Did you check her temperature at home?
Family member: Yes, it was 101 yesterday evening. I gave her ibuprofen and that helped for a few hours.
Doctor: Any vomiting, diarrhea, rash, or stiff neck?
Family member: No vomiting, diarrhea, rash, or stiff neck. She's been drinking okay but she's not eating much.
Doctor: Any drainage coming out of the ear, or trouble hearing?
Family member: No drainage. She says sounds are muffled on that side.
Doctor: Any sore throat or cold symptoms?
Family member: A little sore throat yesterday. She's had a runny nose and a stuffy nose for about a week. She also has seasonal allergies and takes cetirizine 5 mg every morning.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Family member: No, none.
Doctor: Okay. Her vitals today are temperature 38.4 Celsius, heart rate 104, respiratory rate 22, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. She weighs 20 kilograms. Let me look in her ears. The left eardrum looks normal. The right eardrum is red and bulging with pus behind it, and it doesn't move when I puff air at it. Tympanometry on the right is flat, which fits with fluid. Her throat is mildly red with no exudate, her neck is supple, and her lungs are clear. I also did a rapid strep swab, and it was negative.
Family member: So is it an ear infection?
Doctor: Yes, this is an acute otitis media of the right ear. Because she has a fever and significant pain, I'm starting amoxicillin 900 mg by mouth twice a day for 10 days. Keep giving ibuprofen 200 mg every six hours as needed for pain or fever, and continue the cetirizine. She should improve within 48 to 72 hours. Call us if she's not better by then, or if she gets worse ear pain, swelling behind the ear, or a high fever. We'll recheck her ears in about two weeks to make sure the fluid has cleared.
Family member: Okay. Can she go to school?
Doctor: Once she's been fever-free for 24 hours, yes.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good morning. I have your referral here for widespread pain. You're a 63-year-old male, correct? Tell me what's been going on.
Patient: Yeah. For about two years now I hurt all over. My neck, shoulders, back, hips, even my hands feel sore. I wake up exhausted no matter how long I sleep, and my brain feels foggy. I forget words in the middle of sentences.
Doctor: Does anything make it better or worse?
Patient: Cold weather and stress make it worse. A hot shower helps a little.
Doctor: Any swelling or redness in your joints, morning stiffness that lasts more than an hour, rashes, or dry eyes?
Patient: No swelling that I can see, the stiffness wears off in about twenty minutes, no rashes, and my eyes are fine.
Doctor: Any fever, weight loss, or weakness in your arms or legs?
Patient: No fever, I've actually put on a few pounds, and no weakness. My muscles just ache.
Doctor: What medicines are you taking right now?
Patient: Lisinopril 20 mg every morning for blood pressure, metformin 500 mg twice a day for my sugar, omeprazole 20 mg every morning for reflux, and duloxetine 60 mg once a day that my primary care doctor started four months ago. And ibuprofen, I take 800 mg three times a day for the pain.
Doctor: Eight hundred, three times a day, is a lot for over the counter. Can you check the bottle?
Patient: Hold on, sorry, correction. It's the 200 mg tablets. I take two at a time, so 400 mg, about twice a day.
Doctor: Okay, that's 400 mg twice a day, thank you. And how much do you drink?
Patient: A couple of beers a night, I'd say.
Doctor: I want to be sure about this because it matters for your medicines and your liver.
Patient: Honestly, it's closer to six beers a night, and more on weekends. It helps me fall asleep.
Doctor: Thanks for being honest. Do you snore?
Patient: My wife says I snore loudly and stop breathing sometimes, but I've never had a sleep study.
Doctor: Alright. Your blood pressure today is 138 over 84, pulse 78, weight 94 kilograms. On exam you have tenderness over many soft-tissue points at the neck, shoulders, chest wall, and hips, but there is no joint swelling, your strength is normal, and your range of motion is full. Your labs from last week: ESR 12, CRP 2, TSH 2.1, CK 110, hemoglobin 14.2, vitamin D 22, A1c 6.8, AST 58 and ALT 41. The ANA, rheumatoid factor, and anti-CCP are all negative. X-rays of your hands and neck showed only mild arthritis changes.
Patient: So what is it?
Doctor: This is fibromyalgia, in a man who also has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and reflux. Nothing here points to rheumatoid arthritis or lupus. The AST being higher than the ALT, along with the heavy drinking, makes me think alcohol is affecting your liver, and your drinking is heavy enough that I would call it alcohol use disorder. Heavy drinking also worsens sleep quality and pain.
Doctor: Here's the plan. First, stop the ibuprofen. NSAIDs are a bad idea with your blood pressure, kidneys, and drinking, and they don't help fibromyalgia. Second, duloxetine is not a good fit with heavy alcohol use and a high AST, so lower it to 30 mg daily for one week, then stop. Third, start gabapentin 100 mg at bedtime and we'll increase it slowly, but you can't drink with it because it adds to the drowsiness. Fourth, acetaminophen 500 mg up to twice a day if needed, never more than 2 grams a day. Fifth, vitamin D3 2,000 units daily. I'm referring you to physical therapy for a graded exercise program, to cognitive behavioral therapy, to addiction medicine for the drinking, and for a sleep study. We'll repeat liver tests in six weeks, and I'll see you back in eight weeks.
Patient: Okay, I'll give it a go.
"""

Doctor: Good morning. I have your referral here for widespread pain. You're a 63-year-old male, correct? Tell me what's been going on.
Patient: Yeah. For about two years now I hurt all over. My neck, shoulders, back, hips, even my hands feel sore. I wake up exhausted no matter how long I sleep, and my brain feels foggy. I forget words in the middle of sentences.
Doctor: Does anything make it better or worse?
Patient: Cold weather and stress make it worse. A hot shower helps a little.
Doctor: Any swelling or redness in your joints, morning stiffness that lasts more than an hour, rashes, or dry eyes?
Patient: No swelling that I can see, the stiffness wears off in about twenty minutes, no rashes, and my eyes are fine.
Doctor: Any fever, weight loss, or weakness in your arms or legs?
Patient: No fever, I've actually put on a few pounds, and no weakness. My muscles just ache.
Doctor: What medicines are you taking right now?
Patient: Lisinopril 20 mg every morning for blood pressure, metformin 500 mg twice a day for my sugar, omeprazole 20 mg every morning for reflux, and duloxetine 60 mg once a day that my primary care doctor started four months ago. And ibuprofen, I take 800 mg three times a day for the pain.
Doctor: Eight hundred, three times a day, is a lot for over the counter. Can you check the bottle?
Patient: Hold on, sorry, correction. It's the 200 mg tablets. I take two at a time, so 400 mg, about twice a day.
Doctor: Okay, that's 400 mg twice a day, thank you. And how much do you drink?
Patient: A couple of beers a night, I'd say.
Doctor: I want to be sure about this because it matters for your medicines and your liver.
Patient: Honestly, it's closer to six beers a night, and more on weekends. It helps me fall asleep.
Doctor: Thanks for being honest. Do you snore?
Patient: My wife says I snore loudly and stop breathing sometimes, but I've never had a sleep study.
Doctor: Alright. Your blood pressure today is 138 over 84, pulse 78, weight 94 kilograms. On exam you have tenderness over many soft-tissue points at the neck, shoulders, chest wall, and hips, but there is no joint swelling, your strength is normal, and your range of motion is full. X-rays of your hands and neck showed only mild arthritis changes.
Patient: So what is it?
Doctor: This is fibromyalgia, in a man who also has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and reflux. Nothing here points to rheumatoid arthritis or lupus. Heavy drinking also worsens sleep quality and pain.

We will repeat a basic metabolic panel and recheck your standing blood pressure with your primary doctor in two weeks. Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good morning. So you're a 79-year-old female and you were sent over because a nodule was found on your thyroid. Tell me how you found out.
Patient: My regular doctor ordered an ultrasound of my neck to look at the artery in my neck, the carotid. They said they saw a little lump in my thyroid by accident. I've been worried sick about cancer ever since.
Doctor: I understand. That is a common worry, but most thyroid nodules turn out to be benign. Let me ask you some questions. Have you noticed a lump in your neck yourself?
Patient: No, I can't feel anything.
Doctor: Any pain in the neck, trouble swallowing, or hoarseness?
Patient: No pain, no trouble swallowing, and my voice is the same.
Doctor: Any shortness of breath when you lie flat?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Any palpitations, shakiness, heat intolerance, or weight loss?
Patient: None of those. My weight is steady, actually.
Doctor: Have you ever had radiation to your head or neck, or does anyone in the family have thyroid cancer?
Patient: No radiation, and no one with thyroid cancer.
Doctor: What medicines do you take?
Patient: Amlodipine 5 mg every morning for my blood pressure, alendronate 70 mg once a week for my bones, and biotin 5000 mcg a day for my hair and nails.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Your vitals are blood pressure 138/74 and heart rate 70. On exam, the right side of your thyroid has a firm nodule about 1.5 to 2 centimeters that moves with swallowing. The left lobe feels normal. There are no enlarged lymph nodes in your neck, and there's no tenderness. Your ultrasound report shows a 1.6 centimeter solid, hypoechoic nodule in the right lobe with smooth margins and no calcifications, which is a TI-RADS 4 category, meaning moderately suspicious. Your TSH last month was 1.4, which is normal, so the gland is neither overactive nor underactive.
Patient: Is it cancer?
Doctor: We don't know yet. The risk is lowish but not zero, and the only way to tell is a needle biopsy. So the working problem is a solitary right thyroid nodule with normal thyroid function. I recommend an ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration. It's a quick office procedure with a numbing shot and a very small needle. Given your health, you're a good candidate, and the result will tell us whether we simply watch it or discuss surgery. One more thing: the biotin can interfere with thyroid blood tests, so please stop it now and stay off it for at least 3 days before we repeat the TSH and free T4.
Patient: I'll stop it.
Doctor: Continue the amlodipine for your hypertension and the alendronate for your osteoporosis. We'll schedule the biopsy within two weeks and I'll see you after the result.
Patient: Thank you, Doctor.
"""

Visit modality: Telephone visit (audio only). The patient is at home, consented to a phone visit, and his identity was confirmed verbally. No video was available, so no visual exam was performed.

Reason for visit: Follow-up of benign prostatic hyperplasia with lower urinary tract symptoms in a 79-year-old male.

Patient-reported history: He works rotating night shifts as a security guard and sleeps during the day, so his sleep schedule changes from week to week. He reports a weak urinary stream, hesitancy, a feeling of incomplete emptying, and urgency. He wakes three to four times to urinate during his main sleep period. He denies burning with urination, blood in the urine, fever, flank pain, and any episode of being unable to urinate. He has hypertension and takes lisinopril 10 mg daily. He takes tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily but at inconsistent times because of his changing shifts, and he sometimes misses it when his schedule shifts. He also takes diphenhydramine 25 mg before his main sleep period most days to help him sleep in the daytime.

Home measurements: BP 136/78 and HR 72 on his home cuff this morning.

Data reviewed: The AUA symptom score completed by phone today is 19, in the severe range. His PSA was 3.8 ng/mL three months ago. Prostate volume was 55 mL by ultrasound last year. A bladder scan at his last visit showed a post-void residual of 90 mL. Creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and the urinalysis was negative last month.

Impression: Benign prostatic hyperplasia with moderate to severe lower urinary tract symptoms and an enlarged prostate, inadequately controlled on tamsulosin alone, with inconsistent dosing timing because of shift work. Nighttime diphenhydramine is an anticholinergic that can worsen retention and is not recommended in older adults. There are no symptoms of infection or acute retention.

Recommendations:
1. Continue tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, but take it 30 minutes after the first meal after waking up each day, whatever shift he is on. He will set a phone alarm as a reminder.
2. Start finasteride 5 mg daily for the enlarged prostate. I explained it takes three to six months to work, may cause sexual side effects, and lowers the PSA by about half, so his baseline PSA of 3.8 is documented today.
3. Stop diphenhydramine. Use blackout curtains and a consistent wind-down routine for daytime sleep.
4. Limit fluids and caffeine in the three to four hours before his main sleep period, timed to his schedule rather than the clock.
5. Continue lisinopril 10 mg daily.
6. In-person visit in three months with a digital rectal exam, a repeat post-void residual by bladder scan, a urinalysis, and a repeat PSA.
7. Call for inability to urinate, fever, blood in the urine, or flank pain.
"""

Doctor: Great. How long has the acne been going on?

Family member: It's painful for him, too. Some of the bumps on his cheeks are big and red.
Doctor: Do those bumps hurt?
Patient: The big ones do, yeah. I have a few marks left on my cheeks too.
Doctor: What have you tried so far?
Patient: A salicylic acid face wash from the store, but it made my face dry and red, so I stopped it two weeks ago. I use a benzoyl peroxide wash every day. And the adapalene gel from my pediatrician.
Family member: He puts the adapalene on every night, I make sure.

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 2 progress note for an 83-year-old male admitted yesterday after a syncopal episode. Yesterday afternoon, while standing up from a chair after lunch, he felt lightheaded, his vision grayed out, and he lost consciousness for less than a minute according to a witness. He fell but did not seem to strike his head, and he was alert within a minute. He denies chest pain, palpitations, and shortness of breath before the event. There was no seizure activity, no tongue biting, and no incontinence. He admits to a poor appetite and low fluid intake for several days. Past history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. Home medications are apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 100 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies.

Overnight there were no events. Telemetry shows atrial fibrillation with controlled rates between 58 and 88 and no pauses longer than 2 seconds or ventricular tachycardia. Troponin was negative twice. CT head on admission showed no hemorrhage. Echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 55% with mild aortic sclerosis and no stenosis. Today temperature is 36.8 Celsius, heart rate 70, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Orthostatic blood pressures were 138/80 supine and 104/62 after 3 minutes standing, with lightheadedness on standing. On exam he is alert and his mucous membranes are dry. The rhythm is irregularly irregular with a soft systolic murmur, the lungs are clear, there is no scalp hematoma or bruising, and the neurologic exam is nonfocal. Hemoglobin is 12.9 and stable, creatinine is 1.3 up from a baseline of 1.0, sodium 138 and potassium 4.2.

My impression is that the syncope is most consistent with orthostatic hypotension from volume depletion, compounded by his antihypertensives and tamsulosin. Arrhythmic or structural causes are less likely given the telemetry and echocardiogram. His atrial fibrillation is rate controlled. He remains on apixaban with no bleeding and a negative head CT.

For today, give a 500 mL bolus of normal saline, then encourage oral fluids. Stop lisinopril. Decrease metoprolol succinate from 100 mg to 50 mg daily. Continue tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, taken at bedtime, with slow position changes. Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily; no dose reduction is needed at this time. Fall precautions and a physical therapy evaluation. Repeat orthostatic blood pressures and a basic metabolic panel tomorrow morning. Anticipate discharge tomorrow if the orthostatics improve, with primary care and cardiology follow-up in 1 to 2 weeks.
"""

"""
Cardiology clinic new patient visit, dictating. This is a 54-year-old male referred by his primary care physician for evaluation of palpitations. He had mild lightheadedness with two of the episodes. He denies chest pain, denies syncope, denies shortness of breath, and denies leg swelling. He drinks about three cups of coffee a day and two beers on the weekend. There is no history of thyroid disease and no family history of sudden cardiac death. I am starting metoprolol succinate 25 mg once daily for both the palpitations and the blood pressure, and he will continue amlodipine 5 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg. I advised cutting caffeine to one cup daily and limiting alcohol. He should call or go to the emergency department for fainting or chest pain. Return to clinic in four weeks to review the monitor and echo results.
"""

Ambient scribe transcript. Gynecology specialty clinic follow-up visit for a 40-year-old female with chronic pelvic pain.

Patient: That would help a lot. Thank you.
"""

No overnight events. His cough is improving and he is no longer short of breath at rest. He reports morning stiffness in both hands lasting about 90 minutes and swelling of both wrists, worse since admission. He denies fever now, chest pain, hemoptysis, rash, mouth sores, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

For medication reconciliation, the admission list says methotrexate 15 mg once weekly, correction, 20 mg once weekly according to the bottle his neighbor brought in, taken with folic acid 1 mg daily. His other home medications are prednisone 5 mg daily, hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, a tiotropium inhaler once daily, and naproxen 500 mg twice daily from his primary care physician. In the hospital he is receiving ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, day three of five, and I ordered a nicotine patch 21 mg every 24 hours.

Vitals this morning temperature 99.1 F, heart rate 88, blood pressure 138/80, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 94% on room air. On exam both wrists are swollen and warm with tenderness, and he has six swollen and eight tender joints in the hands and wrists, with a rheumatoid nodule over the left olecranon. Crackles are present at the right base. There is no rash and no oral ulcers.

My impression is first, a rheumatoid arthritis flare of moderate activity in the setting of pneumonia. Second, community-acquired pneumonia, improving on antibiotics. Plan is as follows. I am holding methotrexate until the pneumonia has resolved and creatinine is back to baseline, then restarting at a lower dose of 15 mg once weekly. Continue folic acid 1 mg daily and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily. I am increasing prednisone from 5 mg to 10 mg daily for the flare and will taper back to 5 mg after discharge. I am stopping naproxen permanently because of his kidney function, the methotrexate interaction, and the steroid. Continue the nicotine patch 21 mg every 24 hours, and he was counseled on quitting.

Because transportation is a barrier, he lives about 60 miles from the clinic, has no car, and depends on a neighbor for rides, I asked social work to arrange transportation vouchers. Clinical note:
"""
This is a dictation for an inpatient eye evaluation on hospital day 3. The patient is a 64-year-old male admitted three days ago with community-acquired pneumonia, who also has type 2 diabetes, and who developed redness and yellow discharge in the left eye yesterday morning, correction, it was the right eye, and today the left eye has become red and watery as well. He woke up this morning with both eyelids crusted shut and says the eyes feel gritty. He denies eye pain, sensitivity to light, blurred vision, or any change in his vision, and he does not wear contact lenses. He also denies sore throat, ear pain, and nasal congestion. He has a cough from the pneumonia that is slowly improving. Home medications include metformin 1000 mg twice a day, which has been held since admission, and several over-the-counter supplements, namely ginkgo biloba 120 mg twice a day, fish oil 1000 mg daily, and biotin 5000 mcg daily. For the past two days he has also been using an over-the-counter naphazoline redness relief drop several times a day, which he brought from home. In the hospital he is receiving ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg daily for the pneumonia. He has no known drug allergies. Vital signs today are temperature 99.0, heart rate 80, blood pressure 136/80, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. White count this morning is 11.4, down from 14.2 on admission, and glucose is 148. On exam visual acuity is 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left with his glasses, pupils are equal and reactive, and extraocular movements are full. There is diffuse conjunctival injection in both eyes, worse on the right, with mucopurulent discharge and crusting along the lid margins. The corneas are clear, fluorescein staining shows no ulcer or abrasion, the anterior chamber is quiet, and there is no preauricular lymphadenopathy. The oropharynx is clear and the ear canals and tympanic membranes look normal. My impression is acute bacterial conjunctivitis, worse in the right eye than the left, in a patient with community-acquired pneumonia and type 2 diabetes. For the plan, start moxifloxacin 0.5 percent ophthalmic solution one drop in both eyes three times daily for seven days. Stop the naphazoline drops because they can worsen redness. Hold the ginkgo biloba while he is in the hospital because of bleeding risk, and hold the biotin because it can interfere with some lab assays. Use warm compresses, strict hand hygiene, contact precautions, and no sharing of towels. A conjunctival culture is not needed now but will be sent if there is no improvement in 48 hours. Continue the ceftriaxone and azithromycin per the primary team. Ophthalmology clinic follow-up in one week, and he should call right away for eye pain, light sensitivity, or loss of vision.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good afternoon, come on in. I have you down as an 88-year-old female here about your bladder infections, and I see your daughter came with you.
Patient: Yes, she drove me. I've got another one of those infections.
Family member: Mom got back from visiting family overseas ten days ago. She got an infection over there and was treated, but the burning came back after we got home.
Doctor: Welcome back. Tell me what you've been feeling.
Patient: It burns when I pee, I have to go all the time, and my lower belly aches. My urine looks dark and cloudy. I felt warm one night too.
Doctor: Any blood in the urine, back pain, vomiting, or new confusion?
Patient: No blood, no back pain, no vomiting. I'm just tired.
Family member: She's been sharp as ever, no confusion.
Doctor: Good. Tell me about the trip.
Patient: Fourteen hours on the plane each way. I didn't drink much because I didn't want to use the bathroom on the plane, and where we stayed the bathroom was far from my room, so I held it a lot.
Doctor: That can set off an infection. What treatment did you get over there?
Patient: A clinic gave me ciprofloxacin. I took it for three days and stopped when I felt better.
Family member: Mom, it was five days, you finished the whole box. It was 500 milligrams twice a day for five days.
Patient: Oh, that's right, five days.
Doctor: Okay, so ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice a day for five days, and the symptoms came back about three days after you finished. Your primary doctor sent a urine culture last week, and the result is back. It grew ESBL E. coli, which is resistant to ciprofloxacin and to many of the usual oral antibiotics, but it is still sensitive to fosfomycin.
Patient: Is that bad?
Doctor: It's treatable. Let me go over your history first. You have atrial fibrillation, high blood pressure, stage 3 kidney disease, and arthritis, right?
Patient: Yes, that's right.
Doctor: And your medicines?
Patient: The apixaban for my heart rhythm, 2.5 mg twice a day. Amlodipine 5 mg every morning. Acetaminophen when my knees hurt. The oxybutynin for my bladder, 5 mg twice a day. And the estrogen cream, twice a week.
Doctor: That's estradiol vaginal cream, 0.5 g twice a week, correct?
Patient: Yes.
Doctor: Let me examine you. Temperature is 99.4, blood pressure 138/74, heart rate 78, and oxygen level 97% on room air. Your lower belly is mildly tender right above the pubic bone, and there's no tenderness over the kidneys in your back. Lungs are clear, and your heart rhythm is irregular, which is your known atrial fibrillation. We did a bladder scan, and after you urinated you still had 180 mL left in the bladder, which is more than we'd like. Your kidney labs show creatinine 1.4 and an eGFR of 36, and the kidney and bladder ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis and no stones.
Patient: What does it mean that I'm not emptying?
Doctor: The oxybutynin can make the bladder muscle lazy and trap urine, which feeds infections, especially at your age. So you have a urinary tract infection with ESBL E. coli, and your bladder isn't emptying completely. I want to stop the oxybutynin.
Patient: But then I'll leak.
Doctor: We'll watch for that, and if you need something else, we have options that don't cause retention. Here's the plan. For the infection, you'll take a 3 g dose of fosfomycin by mouth tonight and another in three days, which is safe at your kidney function. Stop the oxybutynin. Increase the estradiol cream to 0.5 g every night for two weeks, then back to twice a week, which helps keep the tissue healthy and lowers infection risk. Drink more fluids, about six glasses a day, and try to empty your bladder every three hours while awake, sitting all the way back and waiting a moment before you stand up. I'll also put a note in your chart about the resistant bacteria so future antibiotics are chosen with that in mind. I want a repeat bladder scan and a visit in 4 weeks, and if the infections continue, we'll look inside the bladder with a cystoscopy.
Family member: Should she still take the apixaban?
Doctor: Yes, keep taking apixaban 2.5 mg twice a day. Fosfomycin doesn't interact with it, and nothing changes there.
Patient: Okay, so no more oxybutynin, the cream every night for two weeks, and the antibiotic tonight.
Doctor: Exactly right. Please come back sooner or go to the emergency room if you get a high fever, shaking chills, vomiting, can't pass urine, or become confused.
"""

The impression was a urinary tract infection with an ESBL-producing organism and incomplete bladder emptying. Oxybutynin was stopped, fosfomycin 3 g was prescribed tonight and in three days, and estradiol vaginal cream was increased to nightly for two weeks. Apixaban is unchanged, with a repeat bladder scan and visit in 4 weeks and cystoscopy if infections continue.

Doctor: Good afternoon, come on in. I have you down as an 88-year-old female here about your bladder infections, and I see your daughter came with you.
Patient: Yes, she drove me. I've got another one of those infections.
Family member: Mom got back from visiting family overseas ten days ago. She got an infection over there and was treated, but the burning came back after we got home.
Doctor: Welcome back. Tell me what you've been feeling.
Patient: It burns when I pee, I have to go all the time, and my lower belly aches. My urine looks dark and cloudy. I felt warm one night too.
Doctor: Any blood in the urine, back pain, vomiting, or new confusion?
Patient: No blood, no back pain, no vomiting. I'm just tired.
Family member: She's been sharp as ever, no confusion.
Doctor: Good. Tell me about the trip.
Patient: Fourteen hours on the plane each way. I didn't drink much because I didn't want to use the bathroom on the plane, and where we stayed the bathroom was far from my room, so I held it a lot.
Doctor: That can set off an infection. What treatment did you get over there?
Patient: A clinic gave me ciprofloxacin. I took it for three days and stopped when I felt better.
Family member: Mom, it was five days, you finished the whole box. It was 500 milligrams twice a day for five days.
Patient: Oh, that's right, five days.
Doctor: Okay, so ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice a day for five days, and the symptoms came back about three days after you finished. Your primary doctor sent a urine culture last week, and the result is back. It grew ESBL E. coli, which is resistant to ciprofloxacin and to many of the usual oral antibiotics, but it is still sensitive to fosfomycin.
Patient: Is that bad?
Doctor: It's treatable. Let me go over your history first. You have atrial fibrillation, high blood pressure, stage 3 kidney disease, and arthritis, right?
Patient: Yes, that's right.
Doctor: And your medicines?
Patient: The apixaban for my heart rhythm, 2.5 mg twice a day. Amlodipine 5 mg every morning. Acetaminophen when my knees hurt. The oxybutynin for my bladder, 5 mg twice a day. And the estrogen cream, twice a week.
Doctor: That's estradiol vaginal cream, 0.5 g twice a week, correct?
Patient: Yes.
Doctor: Let me examine you. Temperature is 99.4, blood pressure 138/74, heart rate 78, and oxygen level 97% on room air. Your lower belly is mildly tender right above the pubic bone, and there's no tenderness over the kidneys in your back. Lungs are clear, and your heart rhythm is irregular, which is your known atrial fibrillation. We did a bladder scan, and after you urinated you still had 180 mL left in the bladder, which is more than we'd like. Your kidney labs show creatinine 1.4 and an eGFR of 36, and the kidney and bladder ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis and no stones.
Patient: What does it mean that I'm not emptying?
Doctor: The oxybutynin can make the bladder muscle lazy and trap urine, which feeds infections, especially at your age. So you have a urinary tract infection with ESBL E. coli, and your bladder isn't emptying completely. I want to stop the oxybutynin.
Patient: But then I'll leak.
Doctor: We'll watch for that, and if you need something else, we have options that don't cause retention. Here's the plan. For the infection, you'll take a 3 g dose of fosfomycin by mouth tonight and another in three days, which is safe at your kidney function. Stop the oxybutynin. Increase the estradiol cream to 0.5 g every night for two weeks, then back to twice a week, which helps keep the tissue healthy and lowers infection risk. Drink more fluids, about six glasses a day, and try to empty your bladder every three hours while awake, sitting all the way back and waiting a moment before you stand up. I'll also put a note in your chart about the resistant bacteria so future antibiotics are chosen with that in mind. I want a repeat bladder scan and a visit in 4 weeks, and if the infections continue, we'll look inside the bladder with a cystoscopy.
Family member: Should she still take the apixaban?
Doctor: Yes, keep taking apixaban 2.5 mg twice a day. Fosfomycin doesn't interact with it, and nothing changes there.
Patient: Okay, so no more oxybutynin, the cream every night for two weeks, and the antibiotic tonight.
Doctor: Exactly right. Please come back sooner or go to the emergency room if you get a high fever, shaking chills, vomiting, can't pass urine, or become confused.

SUBJECTIVE:
88-year-old female with a recurrent bladder infection, accompanied by her daughter. She returned from overseas ten days ago, where she was treated for an infection with ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice a day for five days, and the burning came back after she got home. She reports burning with urination, urgency, lower abdominal aching, dark cloudy urine, feeling warm one night, and tiredness. She denies blood in the urine, back pain, vomiting, and new confusion. During the trip she drank little and held her urine on 14-hour flights. History of atrial fibrillation, high blood pressure, stage 3 kidney disease, and arthritis. Medications: apixaban 2.5 mg twice a day, amlodipine 5 mg every morning, acetaminophen when her knees hurt, oxybutynin 5 mg twice a day, and estradiol vaginal cream 0.5 g twice a week.

OBJECTIVE:
Temperature 99.4, blood pressure 138/74, heart rate 78, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Lower abdomen mildly tender above the pubic bone, no tenderness over the kidneys; lungs clear; irregular heart rhythm consistent with known atrial fibrillation. Bladder scan post-void residual 180 mL. Creatinine 1.4, eGFR 36. Kidney and bladder ultrasound: no hydronephrosis, no stones. Urine culture from her primary doctor last week: ESBL E. coli resistant to ciprofloxacin and many oral antibiotics, sensitive to fosfomycin.

ASSESSMENT:
Urinary tract infection with ESBL E. coli after international travel. Incomplete bladder emptying, likely worsened by oxybutynin. Atrial fibrillation, high blood pressure, stage 3 kidney disease, and arthritis.

PLAN:
1. Fosfomycin 3 g by mouth tonight and another dose in three days.
2. Stop oxybutynin; options that do not cause retention are available if needed.
3. Increase estradiol vaginal cream to 0.5 g every night for two weeks, then back to twice a week.
4. Drink more fluids, about six glasses a day, and empty the bladder every three hours while awake.
5. Continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice a day unchanged.
6. Add a chart note about the resistant bacteria so future antibiotics are chosen accordingly.
7. Repeat bladder scan and return visit in 4 weeks; cystoscopy if infections continue.
8. Return sooner or go to the emergency room for high fever, shaking chills, vomiting, inability to pass urine, or confusion.

Clinical note:
"""
Nurse: This is a 17-year-old female here for facial redness and bumps. Vitals: BP 108/64, heart rate 72, temp 98.2.

Doctor: Hi there. What's been going on with your face?

Patient: My cheeks and nose have been red for like four months. They get really hot and flushed, especially after I eat spicy food or when I'm out in the sun. And I've got these little bumps.

Doctor: Any burning or stinging?

Patient: Yeah, it stings when I put moisturizer on.

Doctor: Any blackheads?

Patient: No, not really. My friends have acne but mine doesn't look like that.

Doctor: Any eye problems, like dryness or a gritty feeling?

Patient: No, my eyes are fine.

Doctor: Any joint pain, rashes on other parts of your body, or fever?

Patient: No, nothing like that.

Doctor: What have you tried so far?

Patient: A hydrocortisone cream from the pharmacy, 1 percent, about twice a day for two weeks. It helped for a day and then it looked worse.

Doctor: Okay. Are you taking any vitamins or supplements?

Patient: I take niacin, 500 milligrams every day, because I read it's good for energy and hair. And biotin gummies, 5000 micrograms daily.

Doctor: That's helpful. Any medical conditions or allergies?

Patient: No. No allergies.

Doctor: Alright. On exam, there's redness over the cheeks, nose, and chin, with a few small red bumps and a couple of pustules. I can see fine visible blood vessels on the cheeks. No blackheads. Your eyelids look normal. I also did a quick skin scraping from the cheek and looked at it under the microscope with a KOH prep, and it was negative for fungus and no mites were seen.

Patient: So what is it?

Doctor: This looks like rosacea. The flushing is probably being made worse by the niacin, and steroid creams can make rosacea worse too. So I'd like you to stop the hydrocortisone cream and stop the niacin. I'd also stop the biotin, since it can cause breakouts. For treatment, start metronidazole 0.75 percent gel once a day on the whole face after washing, use a gentle moisturizer, and a mineral sunscreen with SPF 30 every morning. Try to avoid triggers like spicy food, hot drinks, and a lot of sun. It takes six to eight weeks to see improvement, so be patient.

Patient: Is it going to go away?

Doctor: It's a chronic condition, but we can control it well. Follow up with a dermatologist in six weeks, and if it's not better we can add other treatments. Come back sooner if your eyes become red or painful, or the redness spreads.

Patient: Okay, thank you.
"""

reference: A 17-year-old female presented to urgent care with four months of facial redness, flushing triggered by spicy food and sun, small bumps, and stinging with moisturizer. She denies blackheads, eye problems, joint pain, rashes elsewhere, and fever, and she had tried hydrocortisone cream, which made it look worse. She also takes over-the-counter niacin and biotin. Exam showed redness with papules, pustules, and visible blood vessels, and a KOH prep was negative for fungus with no mites seen. Clinical note:
"""
The patient is a 25-year-old female seen in the dermatology clinic for a flare of atopic dermatitis that began about six weeks ago. She is visibly anxious and asked many questions throughout the visit, including whether the condition is contagious, whether topical steroids will thin her skin permanently, whether diet is causing it, and whether she will need injections for the rest of her life. I answered each question in turn, and she said she felt more reassured by the end of the visit.

She has had eczema since childhood. The current flare involves itchy, dry, red patches in the folds of both elbows, behind the knees, and on the sides of her neck, with itch that wakes her from sleep several nights a week. She denies fever, denies oozing or crusting, and denies new soaps, detergents, or pets. She has seasonal allergic rhinitis and takes cetirizine 10 mg once daily. She has been applying over-the-counter hydrocortisone 1% cream once or twice a day with little benefit, and she moisturizes only occasionally. She has no known drug allergies.

Her office blood pressure is 110/68 and heart rate is 74. Exam shows lichenified erythematous plaques in both antecubital fossae and both popliteal fossae, with excoriations and mild scale on the sides of the neck, and dry skin on the forearms. There is no weeping, no honey-colored crusting, and no punctate erosions. A skin swab sent by her primary care doctor last week grew only normal skin flora.

My impression is a moderate flare of atopic dermatitis without signs of secondary infection, along with stable seasonal allergic rhinitis. I explained that her swab result means she does not need an antibiotic.

I am stopping the hydrocortisone 1% cream because it is too weak for these plaques. I am starting triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily to the elbows and knees for up to two weeks, and hydrocortisone 2.5% ointment twice daily to the neck for up to one week. She will continue cetirizine 10 mg daily and apply a fragrance-free petrolatum-based moisturizer twice daily and after bathing. I reviewed safe steroid use, short lukewarm showers, and avoiding wool and fragranced products, and I gave her written instructions so she can review the answers at home. If control is inadequate, we will discuss a biologic treatment option. Follow-up in four weeks.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Chief Complaint: Sudden severe headache.

HPI: 40-year-old female with hypertension, migraine, and current tobacco use who presents with a sudden severe headache that began about two hours ago while she was carrying groceries up a flight of stairs. She describes it as the worst headache of her life, reaching maximum intensity within seconds, located at the back of her head and radiating into the neck. She has had nausea with one episode of vomiting and mild neck stiffness. She first told the triage nurse she took sumatriptan 100 mg at home with no relief; on further questioning she clarified that she took one 50 mg tablet, not 100 mg. She says this is different from her usual migraines, which are one-sided and throbbing. She denies head trauma, fever, vision loss, double vision, weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, seizure, and loss of consciousness.

She lives alone, has no family nearby, and has few people she can call. She has not taken amlodipine 10 mg daily or lisinopril 20 mg daily for about one month because she could not afford the refills. She smokes about ten cigarettes a day and drinks alcohol rarely.

ROS: Positive for nausea. Negative for chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, dysuria, and rash.

Physical Exam: Vitals BP 188/104, HR 96, RR 18, temp 98.6 F, SpO2 98% on room air. Uncomfortable, lying still in a dark room. Mild neck stiffness with flexion, no Kernig or Brudzinski sign. Pupils equal and reactive, fundi without papilledema, cranial nerves II through XII intact, strength 5/5 in all extremities, sensation intact, finger-to-nose normal, gait steady. Heart regular without murmur. Lungs clear.

ED Course / Results: CT head without contrast about three hours after onset showed no hemorrhage, mass, or hydrocephalus. CT angiography of the head and neck showed no aneurysm, dissection, or vessel narrowing. Labs: WBC 8.9, hemoglobin 13.4, platelets 262, sodium 139, potassium 3.9, creatinine 0.8, glucose 102, INR 1.0, troponin negative, urine pregnancy test negative. ECG showed normal sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy. She received acetaminophen 1000 mg by mouth, metoclopramide 10 mg IV, and labetalol 10 mg IV once; BP improved to 164/92 and her headache improved from 9 out of 10 to 4 out of 10.

Medical Decision Making: Thunderclap headache, with subarachnoid hemorrhage the leading concern. A non-contrast CT within six hours of onset and a normal CT angiogram effectively exclude subarachnoid hemorrhage, and I discussed the option of lumbar puncture with the patient, who preferred not to have one. I also considered cervical artery dissection and aneurysm (negative on CTA), meningitis (afebrile, low suspicion), venous sinus thrombosis, and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, which can follow triptan use; for this reason sumatriptan is discontinued until she is evaluated by neurology. Hypertensive emergency is unlikely with no papilledema, normal creatinine, and negative troponin, but her BP is elevated because she has been off her antihypertensives. Final impression is thunderclap headache with negative CT and CTA, likely a migraine variant aggravated by uncontrolled hypertension, with medication non-adherence due to cost.

Disposition: Because she lives alone, I offered observation; she stayed in the ED observation unit for six more hours with repeat neurologic checks, her headache settled to 2 out of 10, and BP was 148/88 at discharge. Restart lisinopril 20 mg daily, and restart amlodipine at a reduced dose of 5 mg daily rather than 10 mg since she has been off it for a month. Sumatriptan is discontinued. Social work arranged enrollment in a medication assistance program, a $4 generic list for her refills, a sliding-scale community clinic, and a taxi voucher home. A nurse will phone her within 24 hours since no one will be with her tonight. Follow up with primary care in 3 days for a BP check and neurology within 2 weeks. Strict return precautions given: call 911 for a new severe headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, weakness, trouble speaking, or seizure. Counseled to stop smoking.
"""

"""
Telehealth video visit with an 88-year-old male with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis who reports new symptoms over the past five days. He joined from home by video with his daughter helping with the tablet. He has numbness and weakness of the left leg that began about five days ago and is slowly getting worse. His left foot drags when he walks and he had one near fall in the bathroom, with no injury. He denies fever, denies burning with urination, denies new cough, and denies blurred vision. He has not noticed any new problems with his arms or his speech. A urinalysis at his primary care office last week was normal, according to him and his daughter.

He stopped his dimethyl fumarate 240 mg twice daily about three months ago because the copay became more than he can afford, and he did not tell our clinic. He also takes amlodipine 5 mg daily for hypertension. He has no known drug allergies.

Home measurements today are blood pressure 134/78, pulse 70, and temperature 98.1 on his home thermometer. On the video exam he is alert, his speech is clear and fluent, and his face moves symmetrically. He holds both arms out without drift. When he stands with his walker, he lifts the left leg noticeably less than the right, and a left foot drop is visible when he takes a few steps.

My impression is a multiple sclerosis relapse involving the left leg, likely related to being off disease modifying therapy for three months. By history and the recent urinalysis there are no signs of infection. His hypertension has been stable. We also have medication non-adherence because of cost.

Plan is to start prednisone 60 mg daily for five days, taken in the morning with food, and to have him check his blood pressure each day while on it. I am ordering an MRI of the brain and cervical spine with and without contrast within the next week. I am referring him to social work and our pharmacy assistance program to arrange copay help, and he will restart dimethyl fumarate 240 mg twice daily once that is in place. Home physical therapy for leg strengthening and fall precautions were discussed. He will have a follow-up video visit in two weeks. He should go to the emergency department for fever, vision loss, inability to walk, or new weakness in an arm.
"""
