Clinical note:
"""
Oncology clinic follow-up for a 78-year-old female with stage I, estrogen receptor positive, HER2 negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast, status post lumpectomy and radiation, who is 18 months into a planned five years of adjuvant endocrine therapy with anastrozole. Other conditions include hypertension, type 2 diabetes, stage 3a chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism, and osteoporosis. She has no known drug allergies. This is her first visit since a four-day hospital stay about three weeks ago after a fall at home, which caused a left distal radius fracture that was repaired surgically. Her adult daughter came with her and helped with the history.

The patient has limited health literacy and told us she has trouble reading labels, so I used plain language, short sentences, and teach-back throughout. When asked how she takes her medicines, she first said she takes anastrozole 2 mg every morning because she takes "two little pills." Her daughter had brought every pill bottle in a bag, and when we read the labels together the anastrozole is 1 mg, one tablet once daily, and the second pill she meant is her levothyroxine. She also first said metformin 1000 mg twice a day, but the bottle reads metformin 500 mg twice daily. The corrected regimen is anastrozole 1 mg once daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily. She was sent home from the hospital on ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for wrist pain and has taken it nearly every day since.

She reports mild joint aches in her hands and knees that are worse in the morning, occasional hot flashes, and wrist pain that is slowly improving. She denies a new breast lump, nipple discharge, bone pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, cough, fever, black stools, and stomach pain.

On examination, blood pressure is 148/86, heart rate 78, temperature 36.8 C, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Weight is 68 kg. The right breast lumpectomy scar is well healed with no mass, and the left breast has no mass. There is no axillary lymphadenopathy on either side. The left wrist incision is clean and dry without redness or drainage, and she has full finger motion. Lungs are clear and the heart rhythm is regular. The abdomen is soft and non-tender.

Labs drawn today show creatinine 1.2 mg/dL with eGFR 49, hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, calcium 9.3 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1c 7.4%, TSH 2.1, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 19 ng/mL. A bone density scan done during the hospital stay showed a lumbar spine T-score of -2.9. Her last screening mammogram of the left breast, done about four months ago, was negative.

Impression: stage I breast cancer on adjuvant anastrozole with no clinical sign of recurrence and mild joint aches and hot flashes from the aromatase inhibitor; osteoporosis with a fragility fracture; regular ibuprofen use in the setting of stage 3a chronic kidney disease and hypertension, which is unsafe; blood pressure above goal; and medication confusion related to limited health literacy.

Plan: continue anastrozole 1 mg once daily and encourage walking and stretching for the joint aches. Stop ibuprofen today and use acetaminophen 500 mg every six hours as needed for wrist pain. Start alendronate 70 mg once weekly after a dental check, with teaching to take it with a full glass of water and stay upright for 30 minutes, and start vitamin D3 1000 units daily. Increase amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg daily, and her daughter will check blood pressure at home and bring the log. Continue metformin 500 mg twice daily and levothyroxine 75 mcg daily. Repeat a basic metabolic panel in two weeks to recheck kidney function off ibuprofen. The clinic pharmacist will prepare a pill organizer with her daughter and a one-page picture medication list, and the nurse will call in one week to check understanding. Orthopedic follow-up continues as scheduled. A social worker will see her today about transportation and home support. Return to clinic in three months, sooner for new breast changes, bone pain, or black stools.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 3 for this 39-year-old female admitted with left-sided renal colic, during which a CT of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast incidentally showed a 3.1 cm right adrenal mass along with a 4 mm left ureteral stone. Endocrinology is following for the adrenal incidentaloma work-up. The mass measures 8 Hounsfield units, is homogeneous with smooth margins, and has no calcification, which favors a benign lipid-rich adenoma.

Her flank pain is much better today and she is tolerating oral intake. On targeted review she denies headaches, palpitations, sweating spells, easy bruising, and muscle weakness. She has hypertension diagnosed four years ago, treated with lisinopril 10 mg daily, and she says her home readings have been running high. She also uses over-the-counter supplements: biotin 10 mg daily for hair thinning and a licorice root extract capsule every morning for digestion. She has no history of cancer.

Vitals this morning are temperature 36.9 Celsius, BP 148/92, HR 78, RR 16, and SpO2 98% on room air. She is comfortable, with no moon facies, no abdominal striae, and no muscle weakness on rising from a chair. Mild left costovertebral angle tenderness remains.

The work-up so far shows normal plasma free metanephrines, which makes pheochromocytoma unlikely. A 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test gave a cortisol of 1.2 mcg/dL, which excludes autonomous cortisol secretion. Potassium is 3.4 mmol/L and creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. An aldosterone to renin ratio was drawn but is unreliable, because she is taking lisinopril and licorice root, and biotin can also interfere with the immunoassays used for these hormones.

Impression is a right adrenal incidentaloma that is most likely a benign non-functioning adenoma pending aldosterone testing, hypertension with mild hypokalemia that may be partly related to licorice root, and a left ureteral stone with renal colic that is improving.

Recommendations: stop the licorice root extract and hold the biotin for at least 72 hours before repeat labs. Change lisinopril to amlodipine 5 mg daily now so that renin and aldosterone can be interpreted later. Repeat the aldosterone to renin ratio and potassium as an outpatient in two weeks. No further imaging is needed for the mass given its low attenuation and size under 4 cm. Continue ibuprofen 600 mg every 6 hours as needed for stone pain, and urology will follow the stone. She will follow up in endocrinology clinic in four weeks and was counseled to bring every supplement to each visit.
"""

The impression is a likely benign non-functioning adenoma with hypertension and mild hypokalemia. Hospital day 3 for this 39-year-old female admitted with left-sided renal colic, during which a CT of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast incidentally showed a 3.1 cm right adrenal mass along with a 4 mm left ureteral stone. Endocrinology is following for the adrenal incidentaloma work-up. Her flank pain is much better today and she is tolerating oral intake. On targeted review she denies headaches, palpitations, sweating spells, easy bruising, and muscle weakness. Hospital day two progress dictation, orthopedics, on a 23-year-old male, correction, he is postoperative day one from open reduction and internal fixation of a right distal radius fracture with a volar locking plate. He fell from a skateboard two days ago and landed on his outstretched right hand. This morning he reports his wrist pain is about four out of ten and well controlled. He denies numbness, denies tingling in the fingers, denies fever, and denies chest pain or nausea. He has no other medical problems. Vitals are temperature 98.6 F, heart rate 72, blood pressure 124/76, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Postoperative x-rays of the wrist show anatomic alignment of the distal radius with the plate and screws in good position. Impression is a closed right distal radius fracture, status post ORIF, doing well. Plan is discharge home today in the volar splint with elevation and active finger range of motion. Continue acetaminophen 650 milligrams every six hours scheduled and oxycodone 5 milligrams every six hours as needed for breakthrough pain, with a three-day supply. Follow up in orthopedic clinic in two weeks for a wound check, suture removal, and repeat x-rays. Return sooner for increasing pain, numbness, or fever.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 2 for this 16-year-old female admitted with nine days of heavy vaginal bleeding and symptomatic anemia. She was hospitalized three weeks ago for similar bleeding and was discharged on norethindrone acetate, which she stopped after five days because of nausea. Overnight she had two further episodes of heavy flow, soaking about one pad every two hours at the worst, but over the past 12 hours the flow has slowed to about one pad every four hours. She reports lightheadedness when standing and fatigue. She denies abdominal pain, fever, syncope, chest pain, and easy bruising. She says she has never been sexually active. Menarche was at age 12 with irregular cycles since, and there is no family history of bleeding disorders.

Current medications are norethindrone acetate 5 mg three times daily, restarted on admission, ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily, and ondansetron 4 mg IV as needed for nausea. She received one unit of packed red blood cells yesterday for a hemoglobin of 7.4.

Vital signs this morning: temperature 98.6 F, blood pressure 108/64 sitting, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. She is pale but alert and conversational, mucous membranes are moist, and her heart is regular without a murmur. The abdomen is soft and nontender without masses. Pelvic examination was deferred. Hemoglobin is 8.6 this morning, platelets 312, INR 1.1, ferritin 6, TSH 1.8, and urine hCG is negative. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal-appearing uterus and ovaries without a mass. A von Willebrand panel was sent and is pending.

My impression is acute abnormal uterine bleeding, most consistent with anovulatory bleeding, with iron deficiency anemia; a bleeding disorder has not yet been excluded.

Plan: continue norethindrone acetate 5 mg three times daily until the bleeding stops, then decrease to 5 mg once daily. Change ondansetron to the oral route, 4 mg as needed, and take medications with food to limit nausea. Continue ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily. Repeat hemoglobin tomorrow morning. Follow up the von Willebrand panel and consult hematology. Plan discharge once bleeding is minimal and hemoglobin is stable, with adolescent gynecology follow-up in one week.
"""

The impression was acute abnormal uterine bleeding, most consistent with anovulatory bleeding, with iron deficiency anemia, and a bleeding disorder is not yet excluded. Clinical note:
"""
This 43-year-old female is seen in cardiology clinic for peripheral artery disease with claudication. Over the last eight months she has developed cramping pain in the left calf after walking about one block, which goes away within a few minutes of standing still, and the right calf has now started to cramp at about two blocks. She denies pain at rest, foot ulcers, color change in the toes, chest pain, and shortness of breath. She smokes about one pack per day and has a 25 pack-year history. She also has type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidemia. Her medications are metformin 1000 mg twice daily and pravastatin 20 mg daily, and she is not taking an antiplatelet drug. She has no history of heart failure and had a tubal ligation several years ago.

She lives alone in a third-floor apartment without an elevator, has no family nearby, and does not own a car, so she depends on the bus to reach appointments and the pharmacy. She says that no one is available to help with rides or to check her feet, and she has missed two prior clinic visits because she could not get transportation.

Today her BP is 142/86 and her HR is 82, with a BMI of 31. Femoral pulses are 2+ bilaterally, but the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent on the left and faint on the right. The left foot is cooler than the right with mild hair loss, capillary refill is 3 seconds, and there are no ulcers or gangrene. The ankle-brachial index is 0.62 on the left and 0.78 on the right. Her LDL is 138 mg/dL, her hemoglobin A1c is 7.8%, and her creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL.

My impression is symptomatic peripheral artery disease with lifestyle-limiting claudication, driven by active smoking, an LDL above goal, and diabetes.

Plan: start aspirin 81 mg daily. Stop pravastatin and start atorvastatin 80 mg daily. Start cilostazol 100 mg twice daily, 30 minutes before breakfast and dinner, since she has no heart failure. Continue metformin. I counseled her on smoking cessation for ten minutes and placed a quitline referral. Because she lives alone and cannot easily get to a supervised exercise program, I recommended a home walking program of 30 minutes three times a week, walking until moderate calf discomfort. I referred her to social work for help with transportation and to podiatry, and she will inspect her feet daily with a mirror. A clinic nurse will call her in two weeks to check on her progress, since she has no one at home to check in on her. She was given a written list of warning signs, including rest pain, a foot wound, or a cold or blue foot, and told to call the clinic or 911. Order an arterial duplex of the lower extremities. Follow-up in six weeks.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Geriatrics progress note, hospital day 2. This is a 79-year-old female who was readmitted two days ago with generalized weakness, poor oral intake, and continued weight loss. She was discharged from this hospital about three weeks ago after treatment of community-acquired pneumonia, and she completed her course of antibiotics at home. Since the earlier admission her poor appetite has persisted, she gets full after a few bites, and she says she feels tired and low most days. Her daughter reports she has lost about 5 kg over the past three months without trying. The patient denies dysphagia, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, and cough, and she has had no black stools.

Her history includes hypothyroidism and prior pneumonia. She was walking independently with a cane before the first admission but now needs help to get out of a chair. Home medications are levothyroxine 50 mcg daily and omeprazole 20 mg daily, which she has taken for years without a clear indication.

Overnight there were no events. Vital signs this morning: blood pressure 108/62, heart rate 72, respiratory rate 16, temperature 97.9 F, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Weight is 41 kg. She is thin with temporal wasting and decreased muscle bulk, her mucous membranes are slightly dry, her lungs are clear, and her abdomen is soft and nontender. Grip strength is weak and her gait is slow and unsteady. On screening, she scored positive for low mood. Labs show albumin 2.9 g/dL, hemoglobin 10.8, TSH 2.1, sodium 138, and creatinine 0.8. Chest x-ray this admission shows resolution of the earlier infiltrate.

My assessment is frailty with unintentional weight loss, most likely from moderate malnutrition after the recent pneumonia, deconditioning, and low mood. Her hypothyroidism appears adequately treated on the current dose given the normal TSH.

For the plan today, I am requesting a dietitian consult with a high-calorie, high-protein diet and oral nutritional supplements twice daily between meals. Start mirtazapine 7.5 mg at bedtime to help appetite and mood. Discontinue omeprazole, as there is no documented indication, and monitor for reflux symptoms. Continue levothyroxine 50 mcg daily. Physical and occupational therapy to evaluate and begin mobility work. Check vitamin B12 level and repeat complete blood count in the morning. We will discuss goals of care with the patient and her daughter, anticipate discharge to short-term rehabilitation in the next few days, and arrange geriatrics clinic follow-up two weeks after discharge.
"""

Endoscopy showed mucopurulent drainage in the right middle meatus without polyps, and the eye exam showed no orbital involvement or diabetic retinopathy. The impression was chronic rhinosinusitis with rhinitis medicamentosa. Oxymetazoline was stopped, fluticasone increased, doxycycline started with a culture sent, and follow-up planned in three weeks with teach-back instructions.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good morning. I see you're an 86-year-old male here for your memory follow-up. How have things been?
Patient: Pretty good, doc. My memory's about the same. I lose my glasses a lot, and sometimes I ask my daughter the same question twice.
Family member: He's also been skipping his blood pressure pills.
Doctor: Is that right? What's going on with the pills?
Patient: They got expensive. The lisinopril is about forty dollars now with the new plan. So I take it every other day to make it last.
Doctor: I'm glad you told me. That's lisinopril 10 mg for your high blood pressure, one tablet a day, correct?
Patient: Yes, 10 milligrams.
Doctor: Any getting lost while driving or at the store?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Any falls, or seeing things that aren't there?
Patient: No falls, no seeing things. And I still pay my own bills.
Doctor: Good. Today your blood pressure is 148/86, a little high, probably from the skipped doses. On the memory test, the MoCA, you scored 24 out of 30, the same as last year. That fits mild cognitive impairment, and it's not dementia. I want to repeat your vitamin B12 and thyroid labs, and we'll see you again in 6 months.
Patient: What about the pills? I can't keep paying that.
Doctor: Let's fix that. I'll send a 90-day supply of generic lisinopril 10 mg to the mail-order pharmacy, which should cost a lot less, and our social worker will check for help with the cost. Please take one tablet every day, not every other day. A pill box can help you remember.
Patient: Okay, a pill every day. That I can do.
Family member: I'll set up the pill box.
Doctor: Perfect. Keep walking daily and doing your puzzles, and call us sooner if the memory gets worse.
"""

His MoCA score was 24 out of 30, unchanged from last year, consistent with mild cognitive impairment rather than dementia. The plan was to repeat vitamin B12 and thyroid labs, switch to a 90-day generic mail-order supply with social work help for costs, take lisinopril every day with a pill box, and return in 6 months.

Patient: Pretty good, doc. My memory's about the same. I lose my glasses a lot, and sometimes I ask my daughter the same question twice.
Family member: He's also been skipping his blood pressure pills.
Doctor: Is that right? What's going on with the pills?
Patient: They got expensive. The lisinopril is about forty dollars now with the new plan. So I take it every other day to make it last.
Doctor: I'm glad you told me. That's lisinopril 10 mg for your high blood pressure, one tablet a day, correct?
Patient: Yes, 10 milligrams.
Doctor: Any getting lost while driving or at the store?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Any falls, or seeing things that aren't there?
Patient: No falls, no seeing things. And I still pay my own bills.
Doctor: Good. Today your blood pressure is 148/86, a little high, probably from the skipped doses. On the memory test, the MoCA, you scored 24 out of 30, the same as last year. That fits mild cognitive impairment, and it's not dementia. I want to repeat your vitamin B12 and thyroid labs, and we'll see you again in 6 months.
Patient: What about the pills? I can't keep paying that.
Doctor: Let's fix that. I'll send a 90-day supply of generic lisinopril 10 mg to the mail-order pharmacy, which should cost a lot less, and our social worker will check for help with the cost. Please take one tablet every day, not every other day. A pill box can help you remember.
Patient: Okay, a pill every day. That I can do.
Family member: I'll set up the pill box.
Doctor: Perfect. Keep walking daily and doing your puzzles, and call us sooner if the memory gets worse.

Clinical note:
"""
The patient is a 42-year-old male seen in the outpatient psychiatry clinic for follow-up of panic disorder, which has worsened over the past month. He returned about ten days ago from a three-week trip overseas to visit relatives that included two long-haul flights. He ran out of his sertraline early in the trip and was unable to refill it afterward because the copay was more than he could afford. Since then he has had recurrent panic attacks, about four per week, including one on the flight home, with sudden pounding heart, sweating, shortness of breath, trembling, chest tightness, and fear of dying that peak within ten minutes. He also reports dizziness, nausea, and brief electric-shock sensations in the head that began a few days after the sertraline ran out, which fits SSRI discontinuation symptoms. He initially told me he had been taking sertraline 100 mg daily, but later in the visit he clarified that for the last two months he had been splitting the 100 mg tablets and taking only 50 mg daily to stretch the supply.

While overseas he bought alprazolam 0.5 mg tablets from a pharmacy without a prescription and has been taking one up to twice daily for the past week, with only brief relief. He also takes pseudoephedrine 60 mg every 6 hours as needed for nasal congestion since the flight. He completed a course of atovaquone-proguanil, one tablet daily, for malaria prophylaxis, finishing seven days after his return. He denies fever, diarrhea, and cough since returning.

Other history includes HTN treated with lisinopril 20 mg daily, hyperlipidemia, and GERD treated with omeprazole 20 mg daily. He has not taken his atorvastatin 20 mg daily for about two months because of cost. He drinks about two beers per week, drinks three cups of coffee a day, and uses no recreational drugs. He denies suicidal ideation, homicidal ideation, hallucinations, and decreased need for sleep.

Last week his primary care physician obtained an ECG showing normal sinus rhythm with normal intervals, TSH 1.9, hemoglobin 14.6, and glucose 94. Today his BP is 136/88, HR 88, RR 16, and SpO2 99% on room air. On mental status exam he is anxious but cooperative, with normal speech, an anxious affect, linear thought process, no psychotic symptoms, and good insight. PHQ-9 is 6 and GAD-7 is 15.

My impression is panic disorder with recurrent panic attacks that worsened after he interrupted sertraline, with SSRI discontinuation symptoms, and contribution from unprescribed alprazolam use, pseudoephedrine, and caffeine. He also has HTN, hyperlipidemia, and GERD, and the missed doses of medication were driven by cost.

Management: Restart sertraline at 50 mg daily, with a plan to increase to 100 mg daily after one week if he tolerates it; the clinic pharmacist will use a low-cost generic program so the monthly cost is minimal. Discontinue alprazolam, because it is not prescribed and risks dependence; he will discard the remaining tablets. Stop pseudoephedrine and limit caffeine to one cup daily. Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily and omeprazole 20 mg daily, and ask his primary care physician to address the generic atorvastatin. Refer to the clinic social worker for help with medication costs. Start weekly cognitive behavioral therapy for panic disorder, with breathing retraining and interoceptive exposure. Because he recently traveled, I advised him that any fever in the next three months needs prompt medical evaluation. Return in two weeks, sooner for worsening symptoms or any thoughts of self-harm.
"""

reference: A 42-year-old male with panic disorder, HTN, hyperlipidemia and GERD returned from overseas travel after running out of sertraline because of cost, then developed recurrent panic attacks and SSRI discontinuation symptoms. He had been taking only 50 mg daily, not 100 mg as first reported, and used unprescribed alprazolam and pseudoephedrine. He denies suicidal ideation, and ECG, TSH, hemoglobin and glucose were unremarkable. The impression is worsened panic disorder after interrupting sertraline. Sertraline is restarted at 50 mg daily with a plan to increase to 100 mg, alprazolam and pseudoephedrine are stopped, social work and cognitive behavioral therapy are arranged, and follow-up is in two weeks.

He remains anxious and asked many questions during today's visit, including whether he would have a seizure, whether the medications could make him addicted, how long he would need to stay, and whether his employer would find out. Each question was answered and he was reassured that his symptoms are improving.

On initial interview he told the team that he drinks about six beers a day and that his last drink was yesterday. On collateral history from his sister and review of the admission documentation, both statements are corrected: he drinks about twelve beers daily plus a half pint of vodka most evenings, and his last drink was four days ago, before admission. When asked again today he acknowledged under-reporting because he was embarrassed. His CIWA-Ar score has fallen from 18 on admission to 9 this morning. He still reports tremor, sweating, and mild nausea, but he denies visual or auditory hallucinations, seizures, chest pain, vomiting, black stools, and thoughts of suicide or self-harm. He has slept poorly.

Past medical history includes hypertension, GERD, and hepatic steatosis seen on imaging this admission. He has no known drug allergies. He works in logistics, lives alone, and denies other substance use.

Current inpatient medications are lorazepam 1 to 2 mg by mouth every four hours as needed per the CIWA protocol, which was discontinued today because he has required no doses in the last 18 hours; thiamine, which was changed today from 500 mg IV three times daily to 100 mg by mouth daily; folic acid 1 mg daily; a multivitamin daily; pantoprazole 40 mg daily; and amlodipine, increased today from 5 mg to 10 mg daily because his blood pressures have been in the 140s to 150s. He also received magnesium sulfate 2 g IV once yesterday for a low magnesium level.

Vitals today: blood pressure 148/90, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 18, temperature 98.9 F, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. He is alert and oriented to person, place, and time, with a fine tremor of the outstretched hands and mild diaphoresis. Speech is normal, thought process is linear, and mood is anxious with a congruent affect. There is no asterixis. The abdomen is soft and nontender with the liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. Lungs are clear and there is no peripheral edema.

Labs this morning: sodium 134, potassium 3.6, creatinine 0.9, AST 98, ALT 62, MCV 102, platelets 138, hemoglobin 12.9, and magnesium 1.9 after replacement. A right upper quadrant ultrasound showed hepatic steatosis without ascites or biliary dilation.

We completed a 20-minute motivational interviewing session, and he agreed to consider residential treatment, so social work will be consulted for a program referral and Alcoholics Anonymous information was provided. Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good morning. I am using a professional Spanish interpreter on the video line, so please use short sentences and we will pause for the interpreter. I have you down as an 88-year-old male here about problems passing urine. Is that right?
Patient: Yes. I have trouble to start the urine, the stream is weak, and I go all the time. At night I get up four times.
Doctor: How long has this been going on?
Patient: More than two years, but now it is worse. I feel like the bladder never empties.
Doctor: Any burning, blood in the urine, or fever?
Patient: No burning. No blood. No fever.
Doctor: Have there been times when you could not pass urine at all?
Patient: No, never completely stopped.
Doctor: Have you fallen recently?
Patient: Not fallen, but when I stand up fast at night I get dizzy and I have to hold the wall.
Doctor: I see. Tell me about your medicines.
Patient: I take tamsulosin 0.4 mg once a day, lisinopril 10 mg once a day, amlodipine 10 mg once a day, metformin 500 mg twice a day, aspirin 81 mg once a day, and a pill for the bladder, oxybutynin, 10 mg twice a day.
Doctor: Let me check, because the pharmacy list in your chart says oxybutynin 5 mg twice a day. Can you look at the bottle?
Patient: Ah, yes, the bottle says 5 mg. I said it wrong. It is 5 mg twice a day.
Doctor: Thank you, that is helpful. So oxybutynin is 5 mg twice a day. Any allergies?
Patient: No allergies.
Doctor: And who helps you at home?
Patient: I live alone since my wife died. My daughter lives in another state and calls on Sundays. A neighbor checks on me sometimes, but not every day. I take the pills out of the bottles by myself. I do not have a pill box.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me. We will work on that. Now your vitals. Lying down your blood pressure is 150/82 with a heart rate of 72. After standing for three minutes it falls to 122/70, and you felt dizzy, right?
Patient: Yes, very dizzy.
Doctor: On exam, your belly is soft and I can feel fullness above the pubic bone, so the bladder is not emptying well. On the rectal exam, the prostate is large, about 60 grams by feel, smooth and firm, with no hard nodules. Your IPSS score today is 24, which is severe. The bladder scan after you urinated shows 180 mL left behind. Your urine test today had no blood and no infection. The blood tests from last week show creatinine 1.4 and a PSA of 2.9. The ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder showed no swelling of the kidneys, and the prostate measured about 62 grams.
Patient: Is it cancer?
Doctor: The PSA is not high for a man your age with a large prostate, and the rectal exam did not feel suspicious. My impression is benign prostatic hyperplasia with lower urinary tract symptoms and incomplete bladder emptying. The oxybutynin is probably making it worse, and the tamsulosin together with the amlodipine is causing low blood pressure on standing. You also have hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and coronary artery disease, which your primary doctor manages.
Patient: What do we do?
Doctor: Here is the plan. Stop the oxybutynin, because it can trap urine in the bladder. Start finasteride 5 mg once a day to shrink the prostate slowly, and it can take about six months. Keep the tamsulosin 0.4 mg once a day, but take it after dinner. Lower the amlodipine from 10 mg to 5 mg once a day because of the dizziness when you stand, and I will send a note to your primary doctor. Keep the lisinopril, metformin, and aspirin the same. Because your creatinine is 1.4, your primary doctor will watch the metformin. We will repeat the bladder scan and the standing blood pressure in four weeks. Because you live alone, I am asking our social worker to call you with an interpreter, to arrange a home health nurse to fill a weekly pill box, and to ask about a medical alert button. Stand up slowly, sit on the edge of the bed for one minute first, keep a night light on, and use a urinal at the bedside. If you cannot pass urine at all, or you have a fever, or you fall, go to the emergency room.
Patient: I understand. Thank you, doctor.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good afternoon. I understand you've been having back and leg pain. Tell me what's been going on.
Patient: Yeah, my lower back started hurting about ten days ago, and now there's this pain that runs down my right leg into my foot. It's no big deal, I can manage.
Family member: It is a big deal. I'm his wife. He hasn't slept through the night in a week, he's been limping, and he can barely get out of his chair.
Doctor: Okay, thank you for coming with him. So this is a 52-year-old male with right-sided low back pain radiating down the leg for ten days. Did anything trigger it?
Patient: I was moving boxes in the garage. I felt a pull when I lifted one.
Doctor: Is it worse with any position?
Patient: Sitting and coughing. Bending forward is bad too. Walking around is a little better.
Doctor: Any numbness or tingling?
Patient: A little tingling on top of my foot, by the big toe.
Doctor: Any trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, numbness in the groin or inner thighs, or trouble passing urine?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Any fever, chills, or weight loss you can't explain? Any history of cancer?
Patient: No fever, no weight loss, no cancer.
Family member: And he hasn't fallen, but his right foot kind of catches when he walks.
Doctor: Alright. I see in your chart type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and reflux, is that right?
Patient: Yes, that's right.
Doctor: What are you taking for the pain?
Patient: Just some ibuprofen, 200 mg, maybe once or twice a day.
Family member: That's not right. He's been taking his old 800 mg ibuprofen tablets from his knee surgery, three times a day, for the past week. I counted them.
Patient: Okay, okay, she's right. It's the 800 mg tablets, three times a day.
Doctor: Thank you for clearing that up. What are your other medications?
Patient: I take metformin 500 mg twice a day, lisinopril 20 mg once a day, atorvastatin 40 mg at night, and omeprazole 20 mg in the morning for the reflux. My regular doctor also started gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime four days ago, but it hasn't done much.
Family member: His metformin was bumped up to 1000 mg twice a day last month, so that's the dose now.
Patient: Oh right, 1000 mg twice a day. I forgot.
Doctor: Good. Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Alright. His blood pressure is 146/88, heart rate 84, temperature 98.2, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He weighs 112 kilos, BMI 35. A fingerstick glucose is 212. On exam, there's no midline spinal tenderness, but there's mild paraspinal muscle spasm on the right. Straight leg raise on the right reproduces the pain down the leg at about 40 degrees, and the left is negative. Strength is 5 out of 5 everywhere except the right big toe extension, which is 4 out of 5. Sensation is decreased over the top of the right foot. Knee and ankle reflexes are 2+ and symmetric. He has an antalgic gait but can walk on his heels and toes. I got a lumbar X-ray here and it shows mild disc space narrowing at L4-L5 and L5-S1, no fracture, and no spondylolisthesis. His creatinine from his regular doctor last month was 0.9 with an eGFR of 88, and his A1c was 8.3%.
Family member: So what does that mean?
Doctor: This looks like a right L5 lumbar radiculopathy, most likely from a disc herniation at L4-L5 pressing on the nerve root, and there are no red flags like cauda equina symptoms. Because of his diabetes, his kidneys, the reflux, and the lisinopril and metformin, I want him to stop the ibuprofen completely. High-dose NSAIDs can hurt the kidneys and the stomach. Start acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours on a schedule. Increase the gabapentin from 300 mg at bedtime to 300 mg three times a day. I'm avoiding oral steroids because his sugars are already high. Continue the metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin, and omeprazole as they are. I'm referring him to physical therapy. He should walk short distances several times a day and avoid prolonged sitting and heavy lifting. If he is not improving in four to six weeks we'll get an MRI of the lumbar spine, sooner if he has more weakness. Go to the emergency room right away for numbness in the groin, trouble with bladder or bowels, or worsening leg weakness. And see your regular doctor about the blood sugars.
Patient: Okay.
Family member: Thank you, I'll make sure he takes the right pills.
"""

Patient: My period has been going on for about twelve days now. It started out normal, but then I had really heavy bleeding, and for a few days I was soaking through a pad every two hours. It's lighter today, but I'm still passing small clots.

Doctor: Are your periods usually irregular?

Patient: Pretty irregular for the past year. Sometimes they're six weeks apart, sometimes closer.

Doctor: Is there any chance you could be pregnant?

Patient: I mostly use condoms. I took a home test last week and it was negative.

I'm ordering a TSH and a pelvic ultrasound, which you can get this week, and I want you to see a gynecologist within one to two weeks.

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 2 for this 89-year-old female admitted with symptomatic hyponatremia. Her daughter, who lives with her and manages her pills, is at the bedside and is providing part of the history.

Overnight she had no seizure, no falls, and no vomiting. She received a single 3% saline 100 mL bolus in the ED yesterday evening and has been on a 1.2 L fluid restriction since then. This morning she says her nausea is gone and she feels clearer, although she is still slow to answer questions. She denies headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, and ongoing diarrhea.

The daughter reports that they returned six days ago from a three-week trip overseas to visit relatives, ending with a long-haul flight home. During the trip the patient had about three days of loose stools that resolved on their own before the flight. The daughter says she drank a great deal of water and tea on the flight to stay hydrated, and over the next two days she became progressively confused, nauseated, and unsteady. There has been no alcohol use and no new supplements. The daughter first told me the patient takes hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. This morning she brought in the pill bottles and, correction, the label reads hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily, and that is the dose the patient has actually been taking. Her other home medications are sertraline 50 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, and apixaban 2.5 mg BID. Past medical history includes hypertension, hypothyroidism, atrial fibrillation, depression, and CKD stage 3.

Vitals this morning are BP 152/84, HR 76, RR 16, temp 36.8 C, and SpO2 96% on room air, with a weight of 54 kg. She is alert and oriented to person and place but not to time. Mucous membranes are moist, neck veins are flat, lungs are clear, and the heart rhythm is irregularly irregular with a controlled rate. There is no peripheral edema, and the neurologic exam is nonfocal with no asterixis. Sodium was 118 mEq/L on admission, 121 after the bolus, and 124 this morning, a rise of 6 mEq/L over about 15 hours. Serum osmolality is 254, urine osmolality 420, urine sodium elevated at forty-eight mEq/L, TSH 2.4, random cortisol 19, potassium 3.7, glucose 98, and creatinine 1.1 with an eGFR of 44. Noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute abnormality and CXR showed clear lungs without infiltrate.

Symptomatic hyponatremia, euvolemic on exam, is most likely thiazide-induced with contribution from sertraline and excess free water intake during the trip. TSH and cortisol are normal, which argues against an endocrine cause. I am discontinuing hydrochlorothiazide and she should avoid thiazide diuretics going forward. I am reducing sertraline from 50 mg to 25 mg daily. We will continue the 1.2 L fluid restriction, repeat a BMP every six hours today and then daily, and keep the goal rise to no more than eight mEq/L per 24 hours. If her confusion worsens or the level falls, I will repeat the 3% saline bolus.

For hypertension, BP is above goal, so I am starting amlodipine 2.5 mg daily in place of the hydrochlorothiazide. For atrial fibrillation, the rate is controlled without a rate-control agent and she will continue apixaban 2.5 mg BID, which is appropriate for her age over 80 and weight of 54 kg. For hypothyroidism, continue levothyroxine 75 mcg daily. For CKD stage 3, creatinine is 1.1, so I will avoid nephrotoxins and dose medications for her eGFR. Her confusion is improving, so delirium precautions continue and PT and OT will evaluate her today. If the level is stable we expect discharge in about two days with a BMP at the primary care office within one week. The daughter was updated at the bedside and understands the medication changes.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Gastroenterology clinic follow-up for a 72-year-old female referred by her primary care physician for progressive dysphagia.

History: She reports difficulty swallowing solid foods that began about 4 months ago and has progressed from occasional trouble with bread and meat to difficulty with most solids. Food sticks at the lower breastbone, and she sometimes regurgitates undigested food shortly after swallowing. She can still drink liquids without trouble. She has lost about 10 pounds over 4 months. She also describes pills sticking in her chest. She denies odynophagia, hematemesis, melena, hoarseness, cough with meals, and chest pain. She has never had esophageal dilation or surgery.

Past history includes atrial fibrillation, HTN, T2DM, GERD for many years, hypothyroidism, and osteoporosis. She has no known drug allergies.

Medications: She first stated that she takes apixaban 5 mg once daily. Her daughter, who fills her weekly pillbox, clarified, and the pharmacy list confirms, that she takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily; correction, the dose is 5 mg twice daily, not once daily. She also takes omeprazole 20 mg daily, alendronate 70 mg weekly, amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, and metformin 500 mg twice daily. Her over-the-counter supplements include fish oil 1000 mg daily, turmeric capsules, and calcium carbonate with vitamin D.

Vitals today: BP 134/78, HR 72, temperature 98.0 F. Weight is 132 pounds, down from 142 pounds 4 months ago. She has mild conjunctival pallor. She is thin and in no distress. There is no supraclavicular adenopathy, the abdomen is soft and nontender, and there is no hepatomegaly.

Data: Barium esophagram last week showed a smooth tapered narrowing of the distal esophagus about 3 cm in length with mild proximal dilation and delayed passage of a 13 mm tablet. Labs 2 weeks ago showed Hgb 11.2, MCV 78, ferritin 14, creatinine 1.1, eGFR 58, and A1c 6.9%.

Impression: Progressive solid-food dysphagia with weight loss and iron deficiency anemia, most consistent with a distal esophageal stricture, likely peptic from long-standing GERD, with possible contribution from alendronate. Malignancy must be excluded.

Recommendations: Schedule EGD with biopsies and possible dilation within 1 week under monitored anesthesia care. Hold apixaban for 2 days before the EGD, no bridging is needed, and resume 24 hours afterward if there is no bleeding. Stop fish oil and turmeric capsules 7 days before the procedure. Discontinue alendronate, and her primary care physician will arrange a different osteoporosis therapy. Increase omeprazole from 20 mg daily to 40 mg daily, taken 30 minutes before breakfast. Advise a soft diet with small bites, sitting upright for meals, and taking pills with a full glass of water. Recheck CBC and ferritin at the post-procedure visit, since iron replacement is deferred until after the EGD. Return to the emergency department for inability to swallow saliva, food stuck in the chest, vomiting blood, or black stools. Clinic follow-up after the EGD to review the biopsy results.
"""

TSH 2.1 and a basic metabolic panel from last month were normal.

Impression is essential tremor. This is not Parkinson disease because there is no rest tremor, rigidity, or bradykinesia. Plan is to stop the gabapentin and start primidone 25 mg at bedtime, increasing to 50 mg at bedtime after one week if he tolerates it. I warned him about drowsiness, dizziness, and nausea with the first doses and asked him to take it only at night to start. He should cut his coffee to one or two cups a day, and I will refer him to occupational therapy for weighted utensils and handwriting aids. No imaging is needed. We will see him back in six weeks.

Patient: No, only one day each week, always the same day.
Doctor: Good. What about folic acid?
Patient: The small yellow pill, 1 mg, every day.
Doctor: And the prednisone?
Patient: Prednisone 20 milligram every morning.

Doctor: Good morning. I understand you're an 87-year-old male, here about pain in your legs when you walk?
Patient: That's right, doctor. For about six months my right calf cramps up when I walk about a block. I have to stop and rest, and after a couple of minutes it goes away.
Doctor: Does the pain ever come on when you're sitting or lying in bed?
Patient: No, only when I walk. Nothing at night.
Doctor: Any sores on your feet that aren't healing, or numbness?
Patient: No sores and no numbness. My feet do feel cold sometimes.
Doctor: Any chest pain or shortness of breath with walking?
Patient: No, just the legs.
Doctor: What medicines do you take?

Patient: Is that serious?
Doctor: It means the arteries in your legs are narrowed, but your symptoms are mild and stable, so we don't need a procedure right now. Patient: All right, thank you.

"""
Nephrology consultation.

Reason for consult: Acute rise in creatinine in a kidney transplant recipient.
Requesting service: Hospital medicine.

History of present illness: The patient is a 73-year-old female with a deceased donor kidney transplant six years ago, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes who was admitted three days ago with four days of watery diarrhea, poor oral intake, and lightheadedness. Her baseline creatinine is 1.3. On admission her creatinine was 2.4, and it has improved to 1.9 after intravenous fluids. The diarrhea is now less frequent. She denies fever, dysuria, blood in the urine, pain over the graft, and new leg swelling. She reports no prior rejection episodes and no known drug allergies.

Current medications: Tacrolimus 2 mg twice daily, mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily, prednisone 5 mg daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily.

Examination: Blood pressure 108/64, heart rate 88, temperature 98.0, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Mucous membranes are dry, the lungs are clear, and the abdomen is soft with a nontender graft in the right lower quadrant. There is no peripheral edema.

Data reviewed: Creatinine 2.4 on admission and 1.9 today. Potassium 5.3 and bicarbonate 19. Tacrolimus trough level 14.2 ng/mL, with a goal of 5 to 8. Stool testing for Clostridioides difficile is negative.

Impression: Acute kidney injury in a kidney transplant, most likely from volume depletion due to diarrhea together with an elevated tacrolimus level, since diarrhea increases tacrolimus exposure. Rejection and obstruction are less likely given the ultrasound and urinalysis, although the BK virus result is still pending. Mild hyperkalemia and a low bicarbonate should improve with fluids.

Recommendations:
1. Reduce tacrolimus from 2 mg twice daily to 1.5 mg twice daily and recheck a trough level in 48 hours.
2. Continue mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily and prednisone 5 mg daily. Do not stop the prednisone.
3. Hold amlodipine while she is volume depleted and her blood pressure is 108/64.
4. Continue isotonic saline at 100 mL per hour for 24 hours, then reassess volume status.
5. Avoid NSAIDs, IV contrast, and other nephrotoxins, and dose all medications for her kidney function.
6. Check a basic metabolic panel daily and follow up the BK virus PCR.
7. If creatinine does not return toward baseline in 48 to 72 hours, we will reassess for further rejection work-up. The transplant nephrology team will follow daily.
"""

Family medicine inpatient progress note, hospital day 2, for a 59-year-old female with type 2 diabetes mellitus and a rising HbA1c who was admitted with symptomatic hyperglycemia. She denies abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, blurry vision, and chest pain. She says she has been taking her pills but admits she often skips dinner and eats larger portions of rice and bread at lunch.

Her HbA1c was 7.6% six months ago and is now 9.1%. Her home medications have been metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily for hypertension, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly for hyperlipidemia. She has no known drug allergies.

Her heart rhythm is regular, her lungs are clear, and her abdomen is soft and nontender. Monofilament testing of both feet was intact and pedal pulses are palpable. Laboratory results show fasting glucose 212, creatinine 0.9, eGFR 78, and negative urine ketones. Her LDL was 96. Her admission glucose was 380 with a normal anion gap.

Impression is type 2 diabetes mellitus with poor control and a rising HbA1c, with the recent symptomatic hyperglycemia resolving after fluids. Hypertension is acceptable at 138/84 today and hyperlipidemia is at goal with an LDL of 96.

For the diabetes, I will start insulin glargine 10 units at bedtime and continue metformin 1000 mg twice daily. A diabetes educator will teach her insulin injection technique and glucose monitoring, and a dietitian will see her tomorrow about meal timing and carbohydrate portions. Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly unchanged. I am ordering a urine albumin-creatinine ratio and a retinal exam referral. Clinical note:
"""
Family medicine inpatient progress note, hospital day 2, for a 59-year-old female with type 2 diabetes mellitus and a rising HbA1c who was admitted with symptomatic hyperglycemia. Over the past month she has noticed increased thirst, frequent urination, and fatigue, and her home fasting readings have been running between 220 and 260. She denies abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, blurry vision, and chest pain. She says she has been taking her pills but admits she often skips dinner and eats larger portions of rice and bread at lunch.

Her HbA1c was 7.6% six months ago and is now 9.1%. Her home medications have been metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily for hypertension, and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly for hyperlipidemia. She has no known drug allergies.

This morning her temperature is 98.6 F, heart rate 82, blood pressure 138/84, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She looks comfortable and well hydrated. Her heart rhythm is regular, her lungs are clear, and her abdomen is soft and nontender. Monofilament testing of both feet was intact and pedal pulses are palpable. Laboratory results show fasting glucose 212, creatinine 0.9, eGFR 78, and negative urine ketones. Her LDL was 96. Her admission glucose was 380 with a normal anion gap.

Impression is type 2 diabetes mellitus with poor control and a rising HbA1c, with the recent symptomatic hyperglycemia resolving after fluids. Hypertension is acceptable at 138/84 today and hyperlipidemia is at goal with an LDL of 96.

For the diabetes, I will start insulin glargine 10 units at bedtime and continue metformin 1000 mg twice daily. A diabetes educator will teach her insulin injection technique and glucose monitoring, and a dietitian will see her tomorrow about meal timing and carbohydrate portions. Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg nightly unchanged. I am ordering a urine albumin-creatinine ratio and a retinal exam referral. Plan discharge tomorrow if fasting glucose is improving, with a family medicine clinic visit in one week to review her glucose log and titrate the insulin.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
75-year-old male, new pt visit geriatrics clinic for wt loss and decline. Accompanied by daughter (primary caregiver), who provides part of Hx.
CC: wt loss ~12 lb over 4 mo per daughter. Pt says 'maybe a few pounds.' Chart wt 166 lb 6 mo ago, today 154 lb (clinic scale).
Poor appetite, eats about half of each meal, skips breakfast. Daughter notes he is more withdrawn and stopped cooking since his wife died 8 mo ago. Pt c/o fatigue and mild early satiety. Denies dysphagia, abd pain, N/V, diarrhea, melena, hematochezia, cough, night sweats, fever.
Daughter reports 2 near-falls when rising from a chair; pt denies any falls. Dentures ill-fitting x months w/ chewing difficulty.
PMH: HTN, T2DM, hyperlipidemia.
Meds: metformin 500 mg BID, lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily. Daughter fills pillbox weekly, no missed doses.
Vitals: BP 126/72 sitting, 118/68 standing, HR 70, Temp 36.6 C, SpO2 96% RA. BMI 21.4.
Exam: thin, temporal wasting, ill-fitting dentures, oral mucosa moist w/o lesions, lungs clear, abd soft NT w/o mass, no LAD. Slow gait, TUG 16 sec, gait speed 0.6 m/s, reduced grip strength.
Screens: MoCA 23/30, GDS-15 score 6.
Data from last wk: albumin 3.2 g/dL, A1c 6.4%, TSH 2.1, Hgb 12.4, Cr 1.1; CXR no acute findings.
Impression: frailty w/ unintentional weight loss, likely multifactorial: grief/low mood, poor dentition, reduced intake. A1c 6.4% w/ wt loss, metformin may be contributing to poor appetite.
Rec:
- Stop metformin (A1c at goal, anorexia)
- Start mirtazapine 7.5 mg qhs for appetite + mood
- Cont lisinopril, atorvastatin
- Dietitian referral, oral nutrition supplement BID between meals
- Dental referral for dentures
- PT referral for strength + balance
- SW referral: meals on wheels, grief counseling
- Labs: CMP, CBC, ferritin; FIT for colon ca screening
- Wt check + RTC in 4 wk
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Hi, thanks for coming in today. I see you're a 15-year-old female with asthma, and you've been having more trouble breathing. Tell me what's been going on.
Patient: For about four days I've been coughing a lot, especially at night, and I get wheezy walking between classes. I woke up three nights this week coughing.
Doctor: Any fever, sore throat, or runny nose?
Patient: No fever and no sore throat. My nose is stuffy, but that's my allergies.
Doctor: Any chest pain, or trouble finishing a sentence when you're short of breath?
Patient: No chest pain. I can talk okay, but I get winded climbing the stairs.
Doctor: What do you use for your asthma right now?
Patient: I have albuterol, and I use it when I'm wheezy, about once a day. Actually, no, that's wrong, it's more like four times a day this week. And I take a controller inhaler, fluticasone 110 micrograms, one puff twice a day, but I forget it a lot. I also take montelukast, the 5 mg one. Oh wait, I just looked at the bottle in my bag, it's the 10 mg tablet, once at night.
Doctor: Okay, thanks for checking. Any side effects from the montelukast?
Patient: I've been having really bad dreams since I started it a couple of months ago.
Doctor: That's important to know. What other medicines do you take?
Patient: Cetirizine 10 mg every day for my allergies. I also have eczema, but I haven't needed any cream lately.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Do you smoke, vape, or use any tobacco? This stays between us unless there is a safety issue.
Patient: I smoke about five cigarettes a day. I started vaping last year and switched to cigarettes a few months ago. I know it makes my breathing worse.
Doctor: Thank you for being honest with me. Have you ever been to the ED or hospital for your asthma?
Patient: Once, when I was twelve, I stayed overnight.
Doctor: Okay, let me tell you what I found. Your temperature is 37.0 Celsius, heart rate 98, respiratory rate 22, and SpO2 95% on room air. I hear wheezing throughout both lungs when you breathe out, and breathing out takes longer than normal, but you are not using your neck muscles and air is moving well. The lining of your nose looks pale and swollen. Your peak flow today is 280, which is about 70% of your personal best. The chest x-ray we took this morning shows hyperinflation and no pneumonia. After four puffs of albuterol through a spacer here, your peak flow went up to 340, the wheezing is much lighter, and your SpO2 is 98%.
Patient: So what is going on?
Doctor: You have a moderate asthma exacerbation. Your tobacco use and your allergic rhinitis are both making it worse, and we also know about your eczema. Here is the plan. I am starting prednisone 40 mg once a day for five days. Use albuterol, four puffs with the spacer, every four hours for the next two days, then only as needed. I want you to increase the fluticasone 110 micrograms to two puffs twice a day, and rinse your mouth afterward. Because of the bad dreams, I am stopping the montelukast. Keep taking the cetirizine 10 mg every day. I also want you to quit smoking. I will refer you to a teen quit program and give you a quitline number. We will repeat spirometry at a follow-up visit in one week, and I am giving you a written asthma action plan. Go to the ED if you need albuterol more often than every four hours or you cannot speak in full sentences.
Patient: Okay. Can I still do cross-country practice?
Doctor: Not until you are back to normal, and we will recheck you in a week.
"""

reference: A 15-year-old female with asthma, allergic rhinitis and eczema presented with four days of cough, night waking and wheezing, with no fever, sore throat or chest pain. She disclosed smoking about five cigarettes a day and reported frequent albuterol use, missed controller doses and bad dreams on montelukast. Exam showed diffuse expiratory wheezing, SpO2 95% on room air and a peak flow of 280, with hyperinflation and no pneumonia on chest x-ray, and she improved after albuterol. The assessment is a moderate asthma exacerbation worsened by tobacco use and allergic rhinitis. Prednisone 40 mg daily for five days is started, fluticasone is increased, montelukast is stopped, and tobacco cessation support, an action plan and one-week follow-up with spirometry are arranged.

Doctor: Hi, good to see you again. I have you down as a 37-year-old male here for kidney stone follow-up, right?
Patient: Yes. Two weeks ago I had terrible pain in my left side and went to the ER. They said I had a 6 millimeter stone. I took the tamsulosin, 0.4 mg every day, and drank a ton of water, and it passed five days ago. I caught it in the strainer like you told me.
Doctor: Great. How have you felt since it passed?
Patient: Much better. I get a little dull ache in my left side sometimes, but that's all. No blood in my urine anymore. No fever, no burning when I pee, and no nausea.
Doctor: Good. The stone analysis came back, and it is a calcium oxalate stone. That is the most common kind. Let's go over what you take. Any medicines or supplements?
Patient: I took ibuprofen 600 mg for the pain, but only during the attack. For supplements I take vitamin C, 1000 mg every day, for my immune system, a calcium pill, 500 mg, a fish oil, and protein powder, two scoops a day after the gym.
Doctor: Okay, that helps a lot. Vitamin C in that dose can turn into oxalate in the body and make the urine more likely to form stones, so I want you to stop the vitamin C. The calcium is fine. It actually helps if you take it with meals, because it binds oxalate in the gut. The protein powder, I would cut down to one scoop a day, because too much animal protein raises stone risk.
Patient: Wow, I didn't know that. I thought all that stuff was healthy.
Doctor: It is easy to do. Let me check you. Blood pressure is 126/78, pulse 70. There is no tenderness over your kidneys. Your creatinine from today is 0.9, so your kidney function is normal, and your urinalysis is clean, with no blood. The renal ultrasound we did today shows no hydronephrosis and no leftover stones.
Patient: That's a relief.
Doctor: Yes. So my impression is a calcium oxalate kidney stone that has passed with no complications. To lower the chance of another one, I want you to drink enough to make about 2.5 liters of urine a day, cut back on salt, and stop the vitamin C. I am also ordering a 24-hour urine collection to look at the chemistry, and we will see you in 3 months with another ultrasound. If you ever get severe pain, fever, or blood in your urine, come in or go to the ER.
Patient: Okay, got it. Stop the vitamin C, drink more water, less salt, one scoop of protein, the 24-hour urine, and see you in 3 months.
"""

"""
Doctor: Good afternoon. I have you down as a 44-year-old male with ulcerative colitis who came in because of some bleeding. What's been going on?
Patient: Hi, doctor. I'm really worried. About four days ago I started having loose stools, four or five times a day, and twice there was blood in my stool. Is this a flare? Is it going to get worse? Do I need to go to the hospital?
Doctor: Let's take it one step at a time. How many stools do you usually have?
Patient: One or two, formed. I've been in remission for about two years on my mesalamine. Could it have stopped working?
Doctor: What dose do you take?
Patient: 2.4 grams once a day. I haven't missed any doses, I promise. Why did this happen?
Doctor: Good question, we'll get to that. Any fever or weight loss?
Patient: No fever. I get some mild cramping before I go, but no severe pain, and no weight loss that I can tell. I'm not waking up at night to go either. Should I be worried about cancer? Or an infection?
Doctor: I understand why you're anxious, and I'll explain everything. Have you taken any other medicines, like pain pills or antibiotics?
Patient: Well, I took ibuprofen, 400 mg, a few times last week for my back. No antibiotics. Is the ibuprofen a problem?
Doctor: It can be. Ibuprofen and similar pain relievers can trigger flares in ulcerative colitis. Let me examine you. Blood pressure is 124/78, pulse 84, temperature 98.6, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Your abdomen is soft, with mild tenderness in the left lower area, no guarding, and normal bowel sounds. Your quick blood test here shows hemoglobin 14.1 and white count 7.9, both normal.
Patient: So I'm not bleeding a lot? What does that mean? Should I get a colonoscopy right now?
Doctor: Your hemoglobin is normal, so you haven't lost much blood, and a colonoscopy is not needed today; your GI doctor can decide later. My impression is a mild flare of ulcerative colitis, likely triggered by the ibuprofen, and there are no signs of severe disease. Here is the plan. Stop the ibuprofen completely. For your back, use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed. Increase your mesalamine to 4.8 grams once a day, and add mesalamine suppository, 1 gram at bedtime for two weeks. I'll send a stool test for C. diff and a fecal calprotectin to make sure it's not an infection.
Patient: How long until it gets better? What if it gets worse? Can I call you?
Doctor: Most people improve within one to two weeks. Go to the emergency department if you have more than six stools a day, heavy bleeding, fever, severe belly pain, or feel dizzy. Please see your GI doctor within two weeks.
Patient: Okay. Thank you for explaining. I feel a little better now.
"""

Family member: Yes, I'm here with her.
Patient: I'm so nervous. Please just tell me straight.
Doctor: Of course. The biopsy of the lump in your left neck shows diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. It's an aggressive lymphoma, but it is one we treat with the goal of cure. The PET scan shows involved lymph nodes in your neck, chest, and abdomen, above and below the diaphragm, so this is stage three. Your bone marrow biopsy result is still pending.
Patient: Oh my God. Okay.
Doctor: Tell me how you've been feeling.
Patient: So tired. The night sweats soak my sheets, and I've lost about ten pounds in two months without trying.
Doctor: Any fevers or itching?
Patient: Some chills, but no real fevers. No itching.
Doctor: Any chest pain, cough, trouble breathing, or belly pain?
Patient: A little dry cough, but no chest pain, no trouble breathing, and no belly pain.
Doctor: I see you recently traveled.
Patient: Yes, we spent a month in Brazil visiting his family and got home three weeks ago.
Doctor: Any diarrhea, rash, or fevers while you were there?
Patient: I had some stomach upset the first week, nothing since. No rash.
Doctor: Good. Because treatment includes steroids, I'm ordering a blood test for Strongyloides, a parasite from travel that can flare on steroids. We'll also check hepatitis B and HIV before starting rituximab.
Doctor: Now your medicines. What do you take?
Patient: Levothyroxine 75 micrograms every morning for my underactive thyroid, and lisinopril 10 milligrams daily for my high blood pressure. And supplements: turmeric 500 milligrams twice a day, and St. John's wort once a day for my mild depression.
Family member: It's actually three times a day. She's been taking the 300 milligram capsules, I fill her pill box.
Patient: Right, three times a day. Sorry.
Doctor: Thank you for clarifying, that matters. St. John's wort speeds up how your liver clears many chemotherapy drugs, so it can make treatment less effective. Please stop it today, and stop the turmeric too. Please don't start any new supplements without asking us. Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 3, endocrinology consult service, following this 74-year-old male admitted with symptomatic hypercalcemia from primary hyperparathyroidism.

Interval events: He was admitted two days ago with several weeks of fatigue, constipation, increased urination, and nausea, and became confused the evening before admission. The confusion has resolved since fluids were started. He denies chest pain, vomiting, bone pain, and fractures, and has had no fever. On admission he said he drinks "a couple of beers" in the evening; after repeat questioning today he clarified that he drinks 6 to 8 beers every night, and his last drink was the night before admission. He works rotating overnight security shifts, which makes his sleep and meal timing irregular. CIWA scores have stayed low and he has had no tremor or hallucinations.

Medical history includes hypertension, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, osteoporosis, and a kidney stone 5 years ago. Home medications on admission were hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and over-the-counter calcium carbonate 500 mg three times daily. Hydrochlorothiazide and calcium carbonate were discontinued on admission because both raise calcium. Lisinopril is on hold because of the acute kidney injury. Normal saline was reduced today from 200 mL/hr to 125 mL/hr as calcium improved. He received calcitonin 320 units subcutaneously every 12 hours for the first 48 hours. Cinacalcet 30 mg twice daily was started yesterday. He is also receiving thiamine 100 mg daily and folic acid 1 mg daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily was started for blood pressure after hydrochlorothiazide was stopped.

Today temperature 98.1 F, BP 142/84, HR 74, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air. He is alert and oriented to person, place, and time, with moist mucous membranes, no palpable neck mass, a regular rhythm, a soft nontender abdomen, and no tremor.

Data: calcium 11.4 mg/dL today, down from 13.8 on admission after correction for albumin. PTH 142 pg/mL, inappropriately elevated. Phosphorus 2.2, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 24, magnesium 1.6, potassium 3.9, sodium 136. Creatinine 1.6 (1.9 on admission, baseline 1.4), eGFR 43. AST 62, ALT 38, and lipase normal. Neck ultrasound showed a 1.8 cm hypoechoic nodule posterior to the left lower thyroid lobe consistent with a parathyroid adenoma, and a sestamibi scan showed concordant uptake in the left inferior position. Renal ultrasound showed a nonobstructing 4 mm stone in the right kidney. A bone density study last year showed a T-score of -3.1 at the distal radius.

Impression: primary hyperparathyroidism with symptomatic hypercalcemia from a left inferior parathyroid adenoma, improving. Acute kidney injury on stage 3 chronic kidney disease from hypercalcemia and volume depletion, improving. Alcohol use disorder with heavy nightly drinking and no withdrawal so far.

Plan: continue normal saline at 125 mL/hr and check calcium and creatinine every 12 hours. Continue cinacalcet 30 mg twice daily. No thiazides, calcium supplements, or vitamin D supplements. Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily and keep lisinopril on hold until creatinine returns to baseline. Continue thiamine and folic acid with CIWA monitoring. Endocrine surgery will see him tomorrow to plan parathyroidectomy. Addiction medicine consult and alcohol cessation counseling today. Social work will help schedule follow-up around his overnight shifts and give him a written medication schedule. Discharge when calcium is below 11 and he is eating and drinking well, with endocrinology follow-up in 1 week.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
This is a hospitalist progress note dictated on hospital day 2 for a 56-year-old female admitted with an upper gastrointestinal bleed. She came in yesterday with 2 days of black tarry stools and one episode of coffee-ground emesis, felt lightheaded when she stood up, and arrived with a heart rate of 112 and a blood pressure of 98/58. Hemoglobin on arrival was 7.4, correction, 7.1, I misread the first printout, and she received 2 units of packed red blood cells with a post-transfusion hemoglobin of 8.9 this morning. Overnight she had no further black stools or vomiting, and she denies chest pain, shortness of breath, syncope, and abdominal pain at this time.

Social history is important here. She works night shifts as a certified nursing assistant on a rotating schedule, so she eats and sleeps at irregular times and often misses doses of her medicines. She told the team she stopped taking her omeprazole 20 mg about 3 months ago because she could not afford it, and she has been stretching out her metformin for the same reason. For back pain from work she has been taking over-the-counter naproxen, she first said 220 mg once in a while, correction, she takes two tablets, 440 mg, twice a day for the past 2 months. She does not drink alcohol, does not smoke, and takes no blood thinners, and she has no prior history of ulcers.

Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and GERD. Home medications before admission were metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, the omeprazole she was not taking, and the naproxen. No known drug allergies.

Current inpatient medications: pantoprazole, which was 40 mg IV once daily after the 80 mg bolus on admission and was increased this morning to 40 mg IV twice daily after the endoscopy findings, and sliding scale insulin. Lisinopril and metformin are being held and the naproxen has been stopped.

Vital signs this morning: temperature 98.4 F, heart rate 88, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On exam she is comfortable, the conjunctival pallor is improved, the abdomen is soft and non-tender with no guarding, and there is no hepatosplenomegaly. The rectal exam yesterday showed melena. Labs today: hemoglobin 8.9, platelets 312, INR 1.0, BUN 38 down from 52, creatinine 1.0, glucose 210, and A1c 8.4%.

Upper endoscopy this morning showed a 1.2 centimeter gastric ulcer in the antrum with a visible vessel, treated with epinephrine injection and two hemoclips with good hemostasis. Biopsies were taken for H pylori and the result is pending.

Assessment and plan by problem. Problem one, upper GI bleed from a gastric ulcer, most likely related to the naproxen. Continue pantoprazole 40 mg IV twice daily for 72 hours, then switch to 40 mg by mouth twice daily for 8 weeks. Permanently stop naproxen and avoid all NSAIDs. Keep her NPO today, then clear liquids this evening and advance the diet tomorrow. Check hemoglobin every 8 hours and transfuse for a hemoglobin under 7. Follow up the H pylori biopsy and treat if positive. Repeat endoscopy in 8 weeks to confirm healing. Problem two, acute blood loss anemia, as above. Problem three, type 2 diabetes with an A1c of 8.4%, continue to hold metformin while inpatient, continue sliding scale insulin, and resume metformin 1000 mg twice daily at discharge. Problem four, hypertension, blood pressure is now normal, continue to hold lisinopril today and restart it tomorrow if her systolic pressures stay above 130. Problem five, medication cost and adherence. Social work and pharmacy are consulted for low-cost generic options, 90-day supplies, and meds-to-beds delivery so that she leaves with her pantoprazole in hand, plus a pill organizer and dosing times lined up with her sleep schedule, taking the pantoprazole 30 minutes before the first meal after she wakes. Follow up with primary care in 1 week and the GI clinic in 8 weeks. Likely discharge tomorrow if the hemoglobin is stable.
"""

"""
The patient is an 82-year-old male seen in the geriatrics clinic for follow-up of osteoporosis after a fragility fracture. Four months ago he slipped on a wet kitchen floor and fractured his left distal radius, which was treated in a cast. A bone density scan done after the fracture showed a T-score of -2.9 at the femoral neck. He has never been treated for osteoporosis and takes no regular medications. He does not smoke and drinks one beer a week.

Today he reports mild aching in the left wrist when he lifts heavy pots, but the fracture has otherwise healed well. He denies any new falls since the injury, hip pain, back pain, and loss of height. He also denies dizziness on standing.

On examination, blood pressure was 128/76, heart rate 72, and weight 70 kg. The left wrist showed a healed fracture with mild tenderness over the distal radius and full range of motion. The spine was non-tender, and his gait was steady without an assistive device. Labs from last week showed calcium 9.4 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 18 ng/mL, which is low.

My impression is osteoporosis after a fragility fracture of the distal radius, with vitamin D insufficiency. I started alendronate 70 mg once weekly and vitamin D3 1,000 units daily. We reviewed how to take alendronate with a full glass of water and to stay upright for 30 minutes afterward. I advised him to see his dentist before starting long-term therapy, and I ordered a repeat bone density scan in two years. He will return in three months to review how he is tolerating the medication and to repeat his vitamin D level.
"""

Visit modality: secure video visit. The patient joined from home with good audio and video, and identity and location were confirmed.

Reason for visit: Follow-up of pulmonary embolism on anticoagulation in a 76-year-old female.

Interval history: The patient was diagnosed with a pulmonary embolism three months ago and has been taking apixaban 5 mg twice daily since the initial treatment phase. Since the last visit she traveled internationally for ten days, with an 11-hour flight each way, and returned four days ago. She wore compression stockings and walked the aisle during both flights. Because of the time zone change she missed two doses of apixaban on the outbound trip. She reports mild right calf achiness since the return flight, which is slowly improving. She took naproxen 220 mg twice daily for about three days during the trip for the achiness. She also gets winded climbing one flight of stairs, which is unchanged from before the trip. She denies calf swelling, chest pain, hemoptysis, lightheadedness, and fainting. She also denies black stools, blood in the urine, nosebleeds, and bleeding gums. She takes amlodipine 5 mg daily for hypertension.

Home measurements: blood pressure 134/78, heart rate 76, oxygen saturation 96% on room air by home fingertip oximeter, and temperature 98.2 F.

Limited video examination: She appears comfortable, speaks in full sentences, and has no visible respiratory distress or audible wheeze. She showed both lower legs to the camera; there is no visible swelling, redness, or skin change, and the calves look symmetric. No bruising is seen on her forearms or hands.

Recent results: Labs from last month showed hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL.

Impression: Pulmonary embolism three months into anticoagulation, clinically stable after international travel but with two missed apixaban doses. Right calf achiness after prolonged air travel, and deep vein thrombosis needs to be excluded because anticoagulation was interrupted. Naproxen use on top of apixaban raises bleeding risk. Hypertension, stable by home readings.

Recommendations: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily without interruption and set phone alarms for dose times. Stop naproxen. Start acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for the calf discomfort. Right leg venous duplex ultrasound within 24 hours at the hospital imaging department. Repeat complete blood count and basic metabolic panel this week at her local lab. Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily. In-person visit in four weeks to decide on the duration of anticoagulation and reassess her exertional breathlessness, with an echocardiogram if it has not improved. She should go to the emergency department for chest pain, coughing blood, fainting, or heavy bleeding.
"""

"""
Telehealth video visit for endocrinology follow-up. The patient is a 61-year-old male with T1DM on an insulin pump and a continuous glucose monitor, connecting from home by video with good audio and picture. His identity was confirmed and he agreed to a video visit.

He reports frequent low glucose readings over the past month, mostly between 2 and 4 AM and again in the mid-afternoon after his walks. He feels shaky and sweaty with the lows and treats them with glucose tablets. He denies passing out, denies seizures, and denies ever needing glucagon or emergency help. He also denies chest pain and palpitations. He still feels the warning symptoms before a low. Current pump settings use insulin aspart with an overnight basal rate of 0.9 units per hour and a lunch insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio of 1 to 8. He also has HTN and hyperlipidemia, for which he takes lisinopril 10 mg once daily and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. He has no known drug allergies.

Home readings today are BP 126/74, heart rate 66, and weight 84 kg. The CGM report shared through the clinic portal shows time in range 71%, time below 70 mg/dL at 9%, and time below 54 mg/dL at 3%, with an average glucose of 138 mg/dL. His A1c from last week's lab was 6.4%. On video he looks well, speaks in full sentences, has no tremor, and the infusion site on his abdomen looks clean without redness. No hands-on exam was possible.

My impression is T1DM with recurrent hypoglycemia, mostly overnight and after exercise, driven by basal and carbohydrate ratio settings that are too aggressive. His HTN and hyperlipidemia are stable on current medications.

I am reducing the overnight basal rate from 0.9 units per hour to 0.75 units per hour and changing the lunch insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio from 1 to 8 to 1 to 10. I am also raising the CGM low alert from 70 to 80 mg/dL. I am prescribing nasal glucagon 3 mg to keep at home, to be used as needed for severe lows, and I reviewed how to use it with him. He should eat 15 to 20 grams of carbohydrate before his afternoon walks. Continue lisinopril and atorvastatin unchanged. He will upload his CGM data in two weeks for review, repeat the A1c and a lipid panel in three months, and return for a video visit in six weeks.
"""
