Clinical note:
"""
HD#3 - 73-year-old male w/ symptomatic hyponatremia
Admitted 2d ago w/ confusion, nausea, unsteady gait x4d. 1 fall at home, no head strike per pt. Na 116 on arrival. ED gave 3% saline 100 mL bolus x1, confusion improved after.
PMH: HTN, T2DM, CAD s/p stent, BPH, CKD 3a.
Social: lives rural, no car, relies on neighbor for rides, has missed 2 clinic appts this yr. Poor access to labs near home.

Home meds (per pt + pharmacy fill hx):
- pt first stated "water pill 50 mg" daily. CORRECTION: pharmacy list shows HCTZ 25 mg daily, started 3 wks ago by PCP
- lisinopril 10 mg daily
- metformin 1000 mg BID
- atorvastatin 40 mg qHS
- aspirin 81 mg daily
- tamsulosin 0.4 mg qHS
OTC: St John's wort 300 mg TID x2 mo, fish oil 1000 mg daily. Pt never told PCP about the OTC supplements.

Interval: no overnight events. Slept ok. AAOx3 this AM. Appetite poor, eating mostly tea and toast at home (low solute intake).
Denies: CP, SOB, vomiting, seizure, abd pain, dysuria. Mild nausea persists. Still some lightheadedness on standing.

Vitals: Temp 98.2 F, BP 118/70 lying -> 100/62 standing, HR 82 -> 96, RR 16, SpO2 96% RA. Wt 71 kg (3 kg below clinic wt).
Exam: dry MM, JVP flat, no edema, lungs CTAB, RRR, abd soft NT, neuro nonfocal, no asterixis.

Labs/imaging:
Na 116 (admit) -> 123 (HD2) -> 127 today. K 3.3 -> 3.9 after repletion. Cr 1.4 (baseline 1.2), BUN 28, eGFR 49, glucose 142, Hgb 13.4.
Serum osm 248, urine osm 410, UNa 48. TSH 2.1, AM cortisol 18.
CT head: no acute process. CXR: no infiltrate. ECG: NSR, no acute changes.

A/P:
1. Symptomatic hyponatremia, hypovolemic, thiazide-induced (HCTZ) +/- low solute intake +/- St John's wort. Improving, near asymptomatic.
- HCTZ DC'd permanently, avoid thiazides in future
- St John's wort stopped, counseled pt and neighbor to stop it at home
- NS 75 mL/h x 12 h then reassess
- Na q6h, goal rise < 8 in 24h; watch for overcorrection (aquaresis) - call MD if UOP > 100 mL/h w/ fast Na rise
- liberalize diet, high-solute foods, no fluid restriction
2. HTN: BP low-normal off HCTZ w/ orthostasis. Lisinopril held tonight, resume at 5 mg daily at d/c (dose decreased from 10 mg) once Cr back to baseline.
3. T2DM: metformin decreased to 500 mg BID while inpt w/ poor PO and eGFR 49. Check FSBG before meals.
4. Hypokalemia: KCl 20 mEq PO x2 given, K now 3.9. Repeat BMP in AM.
5. AKI on CKD 3a, prerenal: Cr 1.4 vs baseline 1.2, should improve w/ volume.
6. CAD: continue aspirin 81 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg qHS.
7. BPH: continue tamsulosin 0.4 mg qHS, fall precautions.
8. Dispo/transport: SW and case mgmt consulted for medical transport vouchers. Home health RN to draw BMP at home in 3 days, PCP tele-visit in 1 wk instead of clinic visit. Written instructions w/ large print given to pt and neighbor. Med rec letter to PCP re HCTZ. Anticipate d/c in 24-48h if Na >= 130 and stable.
"""

"""
ED provider note - 54-year-old female brought in by spouse
CC: sudden severe HA

HPI:
- c/o sudden onset severe HA x ~2 h, "worst HA of my life", maxed out within seconds, occipital then diffuse
- onset while lifting boxes at work; works rotating night shifts w/ irregular sleep (avg 4-5 h/day)
- assoc w/ nausea, vomited x1, neck stiffness, photophobia
- denies fever, denies vision changes, denies focal weakness, denies numbness, denies speech difficulty
- no seizure, no syncope, no head trauma or fall
- hx migraines but "this is totally different"; usual migraine is unilateral/throbbing and builds over hours
- last migraine ~3 months ago, sumatriptan 50 mg PRN helped

PMH: persistent AFib, HTN, T2DM, HLD, migraine
Meds per pt: apixaban 2.5 mg BID, metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, sumatriptan 50 mg PRN

NKDA. No tobacco, no EtOH, no drugs.
ROS: neg except per HPI. no chest pain, no SOB, no palpitations, no abd pain

Exam:
VS: BP 188/104, HR 94 irregularly irregular, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA, Temp 98.4 F, FSBG 172
- uncomfortable, photophobic, lying still in dim room
- GCS 15, A&Ox3
- neck: mild meningismus, nuchal rigidity
- PERRL 3 mm, EOMI, no visual field deficit, fundi not visualized
- CN II-XII intact, no facial droop
- strength 5/5 x4 ext, sensation intact, no pronator drift
- heart irreg irreg, no murmur; lungs CTAB; abd soft NT
- no scalp hematoma or signs of trauma

ED course/results:

- WBC 10.4, Hgb 13.2, Plt 244, Na 139, K 4.1, Cr 0.9, glucose 176, INR 1.3
- troponin negative
- anti-Xa level (apixaban-calibrated) 118 ng/mL, elevated
- ECG: AFib rate 92, no acute ST changes
- CT head w/o contrast STAT: diffuse SAH in basal cisterns and R sylvian fissure, no midline shift
- CTA head/neck: 6 mm saccular aneurysm at ACom, no other aneurysm, no dissection
- BP 188/104 -> nicardipine gtt started 5 mg/h, titrated up to 10 mg/h, goal SBP <140. BP now 142/82
- apixaban HELD. 4F-PCC 50 units/kg IV given for reversal (last dose ~10 h ago, anti-Xa elevated)
- ondansetron 4 mg IV x1 for nausea
- acetaminophen 1000 mg PO x1 for HA
- nimodipine 60 mg PO q4h started
- lisinopril and metformin held (contrast load, NPO)
- sumatriptan discontinued - contraindicated w/ SAH, do not resume
- HOB 30 deg, seizure and aspiration precautions

Dispo:
- Neurosurgery consulted, recs transfer to neuro ICU, endovascular vs surgical repair of aneurysm to be decided
- neuro checks q1h
- repeat CT head in 6 h
- spouse updated at bedside, understands dx and plan
- critical care time 45 min

Endocrinology clinic follow-up dictation for a 69-year-old male with primary hypothyroidism, seen today for levothyroxine adjustment. For the past two months he has had increasing fatigue, feeling cold, and constipation, and he says these started before the trip but got worse while traveling. Clinical note:
"""
Psychiatry follow-up dictation on the medical ward, hospital day 2, for a 19-year-old female with panic disorder who was admitted overnight after an episode of chest tightness, palpitations, shortness of breath, tingling in both hands, and a sense of impending doom. This is her third such episode in the past two months. The attacks leave her exhausted and peak within about ten minutes, they come on without a clear trigger, and she now fears another attack and avoids driving. She denies suicidal ideation, hallucinations, and manic symptoms, and she denies alcohol or drug use. She drinks two to three energy drinks a day, and I advised her to cut back.

Her cardiac workup in the emergency department was reassuring. The ECG showed sinus tachycardia that resolved, troponin was negative, TSH was 1.8, and the urine drug screen was negative. The urine pregnancy test today was negative. She is sexually active, uses condoms inconsistently, and is not on hormonal contraception, so pregnancy status matters for what I prescribe. She received lorazepam 0.5 mg once in the emergency department with good effect. At home she takes melatonin 3 mg at bedtime. She has no other medical history and no known drug allergies.

Vitals this morning are blood pressure 118/70, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and temperature 36.8 C. On mental status exam she is calm, makes good eye contact, speech is normal in rate, mood is described as anxious, affect is congruent, thought process is linear, there is no psychosis, and insight is good.

Impression is panic disorder, with caffeine from energy drinks likely contributing. Because pregnancy is possible, I am choosing sertraline, which has the most reassuring safety data in pregnancy among the antidepressants, and I am avoiding paroxetine and ongoing benzodiazepines. Start sertraline 25 mg daily for one week, then increase to 50 mg daily. No benzodiazepine prescription at discharge. I counseled her that sertraline takes two to four weeks to work and may cause jitteriness at first. Continue melatonin 3 mg at bedtime. I counseled her on contraception, asked her to repeat a pregnancy test if she misses a period, and told her to tell her prescribers right away if she becomes pregnant. Refer for cognitive behavioral therapy, reduce caffeine, discharge tomorrow if stable, and see psychiatry in the clinic in two weeks.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 3 for this 87-year-old male admitted with generalized weakness, poor oral intake, and a ground-level fall without injury, in the setting of progressive unintentional weight loss. His daughter, who is his primary caregiver and lives with him, is at the bedside and provides much of the history because the patient has mild dementia and has difficulty recalling details.

Overnight he slept well and had no falls, no fever, and no vomiting. This morning he reports poor appetite and feeling tired, and he says he gets lightheaded when he stands up. The daughter first reported that he had lost about 10 pounds over 3 months. After reviewing the clinic weights she brought from home, she clarified that he has actually lost 22 pounds over 6 months, from 168 pounds to 146 pounds, which is about 13 percent of his body weight. She says he eats about half of each meal and now needs help with bathing and meals. He denies difficulty swallowing, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, black or bloody stools, cough, night sweats, and chest pain. The daughter denies any choking with meals.

His history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, BPH, and mild dementia. Home medications were reviewed with the daughter. She first stated that he takes lisinopril 5 mg daily, but the pharmacy list she brought confirms lisinopril 20 mg daily. He also takes apixaban 2.5 mg twice a day, metformin 500 mg twice a day, tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, and donepezil 5 mg daily.

On examination his temperature is 97.9 F, heart rate 76 and irregular, respiratory rate 16, and SpO2 96% on room air. Blood pressure is 104/62 sitting and 88/54 standing. Weight is 66 kg. He is thin and frail-appearing with temporal wasting, and his mucous membranes are slightly dry. His dentures fit poorly. Heart rhythm is irregularly irregular without a murmur, the lungs are clear, and the abdomen is soft and nontender without masses. He walks slowly with a walker, grip strength is weak, and his Clinical Frailty Scale score is 6.

Labs show sodium 138, potassium 4.4, creatinine 1.6 with an eGFR of 38, hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, WBC 7.2, albumin 2.9, TSH 1.8, and hemoglobin A1c 6.4 percent. Chest x-ray shows no mass. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no mass or lymphadenopathy. The speech therapy swallow evaluation found no aspiration.

Frailty with unintentional weight loss, which is likely multifactorial: reduced appetite, poorly fitting dentures, mild dementia, and polypharmacy, with no malignancy found on imaging so far. He also has orthostatic hypotension, likely worsened by lisinopril and poor intake. Chronic kidney disease limits metformin use.

For the weight loss, I am starting mirtazapine 7.5 mg at bedtime to help appetite and sleep, adding an oral nutrition supplement twice daily between meals, and requesting a dietitian consult, a dental referral for the dentures, and staff assistance with meals. For the orthostatic hypotension, I am reducing lisinopril from 20 mg to 10 mg daily. I am discontinuing metformin because of his reduced kidney function and poor intake, and his A1c does not require another agent. I will continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice a day for atrial fibrillation and donepezil 5 mg daily, with delirium precautions. We discussed goals of care with the patient and his daughter, who prefer to avoid colonoscopy or other invasive testing, and I am requesting a palliative care consult. Physical and occupational therapy will see him, and I will repeat a basic metabolic panel tomorrow.
"""

Doctor: Good to see you again. I have you down as a 60-year-old male here for follow-up of your interstitial lung disease. How have your breathing and cough been?
Patient: Worse, honestly. I get winded just walking to the mailbox now, and I have this dry cough that never goes away.
Doctor: How long has the shortness of breath been getting worse?
Patient: About four months. It used to be only on the stairs.
Doctor: Any fever, coughing up blood, or chest pain?
Patient: No fever, no blood, and no chest pain.
Doctor: Any leg swelling or wheezing?
Patient: No swelling in my legs, and no wheezing that I notice.
Doctor: How is your acid reflux, and what do you take for it?
Patient: Fine on the pantoprazole 40 mg every morning. I also take lisinopril 10 mg daily for my blood pressure.
Doctor: Do you still smoke?
Patient: No, I quit about ten years ago.
Doctor: Tell me about your home situation.
Patient: I live alone. My brother lives two states away, so there is nobody around to help if something goes wrong, and I worry about managing all of this by myself.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me. We will build some support into the plan. Now, your vitals today: BP 128/78, heart rate 84, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air at rest. When you walked the hallway for six minutes your saturation dropped to 87%. On exam you have fine crackles at both lung bases and mild clubbing of the fingers, with no leg edema. Your breathing test from last week shows an FVC of 68% of predicted, down from 76% six months ago, and a DLCO of 44% of predicted. Your high-resolution CT shows basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing, which is a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern.
Patient: So what does that mean?
Doctor: It means you have fibrotic interstitial lung disease that is progressing, most consistent with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. I would like to start nintedanib 150 mg twice a day to slow the scarring. It can cause diarrhea and liver test changes, so I am ordering liver function tests today and then monthly for three months. Because your oxygen drops with activity, I am also prescribing supplemental oxygen at 2 liters per minute with exertion. Continue the pantoprazole and lisinopril. I am referring you to pulmonary rehab and to our social worker, and I am arranging a home health nurse to set up the oxygen equipment and teach you how to use it, since you live alone.
Patient: I can give you my brother's contact information for emergencies.
Doctor: Good, please do that. Follow up with me in six weeks. Call us sooner if your breathing suddenly gets worse, or if you have a fever or cough up blood.
Patient: Okay, thank you.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
The patient is a 77-year-old male seen in the urology clinic for evaluation of a rising PSA. He was referred by his primary care physician after a screening PSA of 6.1 ng/mL, compared with 4.4 ng/mL one year ago. His only urinary symptom is long-standing mild nocturia twice per night. He denies gross hematuria, dysuria, fever, back pain, bone pain, and unintentional weight loss. He has had no urinary retention, recent urinary tract infection, or instrumentation.

His history includes BPH, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, stable coronary artery disease with a coronary stent placed several years ago, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a. His daughter came with him and brought all of his pill bottles. Prescription medications are finasteride 5 mg once daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg once daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg once daily, atorvastatin 40 mg at bedtime, and aspirin 81 mg once daily. His primary care physician increased the lisinopril from 10 mg to 20 mg two weeks ago because of elevated home blood pressure readings. The patient initially told me he had started finasteride only a few weeks ago, but after reviewing the pharmacy labels with his daughter he clarified that he has taken it every day for about three years. This matters because finasteride lowers the PSA by roughly half, so his measured PSA of 6.1 ng/mL corresponds to an adjusted value of about 12 ng/mL.

He also uses several over-the-counter supplements to support prostate health: saw palmetto 320 mg, which he first said he takes twice daily but then corrected, after reading the bottle, to once daily; fish oil 1000 mg twice daily; and zinc 30 mg once daily. I explained that saw palmetto has not been shown to reduce prostate cancer risk and that fish oil adds to the bleeding tendency of aspirin around the time of a biopsy.

On examination, blood pressure is 148/82 and heart rate is 72. The abdomen is soft without suprapubic tenderness. On digital rectal examination the prostate is enlarged to about 50 grams, smooth, and nontender, with no discrete nodule. Laboratory results today include a repeat PSA of 6.3 ng/mL with a free PSA of 12%, hemoglobin A1c 7.2%, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, and eGFR 49. Urinalysis showed no blood, nitrite, or leukocyte esterase. A multiparametric MRI of the prostate obtained two weeks ago showed a 1.2 cm PI-RADS 4 lesion in the right posterior peripheral zone, with a total prostate volume of 52 mL.

My impression is an elevated PSA, about 12.6 ng/mL after adjustment for finasteride, with a PI-RADS 4 lesion that is suspicious for clinically significant prostate cancer. He also has BPH, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, stable coronary artery disease, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a.

We discussed MRI-targeted transperineal prostate biopsy with systematic sampling, including the risks of bleeding, infection, and urinary retention, and he wishes to proceed. I advised him to stop the saw palmetto and the fish oil now. I will contact his cardiologist to confirm whether aspirin 81 mg can be held for seven days before the biopsy. He will continue finasteride 5 mg once daily, tamsulosin 0.4 mg once daily, lisinopril 20 mg once daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg at bedtime. Metformin 500 mg will be held on the morning of the biopsy. I will see him two weeks after the biopsy to review the pathology.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
A 73-year-old female was seen in the gastroenterology clinic for heartburn that has persisted for about two years despite daily omeprazole 40 mg taken thirty minutes before breakfast. She confirms good adherence. She describes a burning sensation behind the breastbone several times a week, worse when lying down at night, along with regurgitation of sour fluid into the mouth. Over-the-counter antacids give only brief relief. She denies difficulty swallowing, painful swallowing, vomiting, black stools, and unintended weight loss. She has no chest pain with exertion. She reports no other chronic conditions and takes no other regular medications. She does not smoke and drinks little alcohol.

On examination, blood pressure was 126/74, heart rate 72, and weight 64 kg, stable over the past year. The abdomen was soft and nontender with no masses.

Impression is refractory gastroesophageal reflux disease despite once-daily proton pump inhibitor therapy. Given her age and persistent symptoms, I recommended an upper endoscopy to look for erosive esophagitis or Barrett esophagus, with biopsies if needed. In the meantime, omeprazole will be increased to 40 mg twice daily, taken before breakfast and before dinner. She was advised to raise the head of the bed, avoid eating within three hours of bedtime, and limit caffeine and large meals. If the endoscopy is normal, we will consider ambulatory pH monitoring. She will follow up in eight weeks, after the endoscopy.
"""

This 52-year-old male was seen in the infectious disease clinic for fever that began three days ago, two days after he returned from a two-week business trip to Thailand. Test results today: dengue NS1 antigen positive, malaria blood smear negative, white blood cell count 3.1, platelets 98, hematocrit 44%.

Assessment is dengue fever without warning signs. Plan is supportive care with oral hydration and rest. Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for fever and aches; he should avoid ibuprofen and aspirin because of the bleeding risk with low platelets. Repeat CBC with hematocrit in 48 hours in the clinic. Return precautions were reviewed: severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, or drowsiness should prompt immediate emergency evaluation.
"""

19-year-old male, walk-in. CC: chest pain. Hx per pt, no interpreter needed.

Initially said onset 3 d ago -> corrected on further q: URI sx (sore throat, cough, low-grade temps) 3 d ago, CP started ~18 h PTA. Sharp, central, pleuritic, worse lying flat, better leaning fwd. 6/10 now. Radiates to L shoulder. No exertional component. Took naproxen 220 mg x2 today w/ minimal relief. NSAIDs tolerated before, no bronchospasm hx.
Denies SOB, palpitations, syncope, diaphoresis, n/v, leg swelling, hemoptysis. No fever today. No recent travel, no hx DVT/PE. Denies cocaine or stimulant use.

PMH: asthma, GERD, anxiety. No hx CAD, no FHx early CAD or sudden death.
Meds PTA: albuterol HFA PRN, sertraline 50 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, cetirizine 10 mg daily, naproxen 220 mg PRN (OTC).
NKDA.
Soc: no tobacco, EtOH rare. Lives w/ roommate, no car, relies on bus (2 transfers, last bus ~9 PM).

Vitals: BP 124/76, HR 92, RR 16, Temp 99.1 F, SpO2 98% RA.
PE: NAD, anxious but nontoxic. RRR, friction rub heard at LSB w/ pt leaning fwd. Lungs CTAB. No JVD. Abd soft, NT. No calf tenderness or edema.

ED course/results:
- ECG: NSR 88, diffuse concave ST elevation I, II, aVL, V2-V6 + PR depression, no reciprocal ST depression, no Q waves
- hs-troponin 4 ng/L at 0 h, 5 ng/L at 3 h (neg x2)
- CBC: WBC 11.2, Hgb 14.6, plt 262. BMP: Na 139, K 4.0, Cr 0.9. CRP 48 mg/L
- CXR: clear lungs, normal cardiac silhouette, no pneumothorax
- Bedside echo: trace pericardial effusion, EF grossly normal, no tamponade
- ASA 324 mg chewed at triage
- Ibuprofen 600 mg PO given, pain 6/10 -> 2/10

ACS unlikely: age, atypical features, no reciprocal changes, trop neg x2 (0 h/3 h), no cocaine. PE unlikely (low risk, no tachycardia, no hypoxia, no leg sx). Pneumonia/pneumothorax r/o on CXR. - Start ibuprofen 600 mg PO q8h x 2 wks then taper per f/u, take w/ food
- Start colchicine 0.5 mg PO BID x 3 mo
- Increase omeprazole 20 mg -> 40 mg daily while on NSAID (GERD hx)
- STOP naproxen (OTC), don't combine NSAIDs
- Cont albuterol PRN, sertraline 50 mg daily, cetirizine 10 mg daily

This is a dictation on the hospital ward for gastroenterology follow-up. The patient is an 84-year-old female admitted yesterday with progressive trouble swallowing. History per the patient and her daughter, food has been sticking in her chest for about three months, first with meat and bread, now even with soft food and sips of water. She says she thought it was just old age. She has lost weight, about ten pounds, correction, eight pounds, over that time and her daughter says her clothes are loose. She denies chest pain, denies vomiting, denies coughing or choking when she swallows, no black stools, no vomiting of blood, and no fever. She does have some heartburn at night that has been going on for years.

Past history is GERD, hypertension, and hypothyroidism. Home medicines by the bottles are omeprazole 20 mg once a day, amlodipine 5 mg once a day, and levothyroxine 50 mcg once a day. No known drug allergies.

Vitals this morning blood pressure 138 over 76, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 16, temperature 98.2, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Weight 52 kilograms. She is thin with dry mucous membranes. Abdomen soft, nontender, no mass. No neck masses or enlarged nodes. Lungs clear.

Assessment, progressive dysphagia with a distal esophageal narrowing, concerning for esophageal cancer versus peptic stricture, along with dehydration with prerenal azotemia, and microcytic anemia, plus her chronic GERD, hypertension, and hypothyroidism. Plan, clear liquids today and nothing by mouth after midnight, EGD tomorrow with biopsies, normal saline at 75 mL per hour, repeat basic metabolic panel and iron studies in the morning. Increase omeprazole to 40 mg once a day. Continue amlodipine 5 mg and levothyroxine 50 mcg. Speech therapy swallow evaluation and dietitian consult for a pureed diet after the procedure. I explained the plan again with teach-back, and her daughter will be present for the consent. End of dictation.
"""

This is a dictation on the hospital ward for gastroenterology follow-up. The patient is an 84-year-old female admitted yesterday with progressive trouble swallowing. She lives alone and does not read well, so I used plain words and asked her to repeat things back to me, and her daughter brought in all of her pill bottles because the patient could not name her medicines, she just called them the little white one for the stomach and the pink one for the pressure.

History per the patient and her daughter, food has been sticking in her chest for about three months, first with meat and bread, now even with soft food and sips of water. She says she thought it was just old age. She has lost weight, about ten pounds, correction, eight pounds, over that time and her daughter says her clothes are loose. She denies chest pain, denies vomiting, denies coughing or choking when she swallows, no black stools, no vomiting of blood, and no fever. She does have some heartburn at night that has been going on for years.

Past history is GERD, hypertension, and hypothyroidism. Home medicines by the bottles are omeprazole 20 mg once a day, amlodipine 5 mg once a day, and levothyroxine 50 mcg once a day. No known drug allergies.

Vitals this morning blood pressure 138 over 76, heart rate 88, respiratory rate 16, temperature 98.2, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. Weight 52 kilograms. She is thin with dry mucous membranes. Abdomen soft, nontender, no mass. No neck masses or enlarged nodes. Lungs clear.

Labs this morning hemoglobin 10.9, MCV 76, creatinine 1.3, BUN 28, sodium 138, potassium 3.9, albumin 3.1. Barium esophagram today showed irregular narrowing of the distal esophagus about four centimeters long with dilation above it, concerning for malignancy versus a peptic stricture.

Assessment, progressive dysphagia with a distal esophageal narrowing, concerning for esophageal cancer versus peptic stricture, along with dehydration with prerenal azotemia, and microcytic anemia, plus her chronic GERD, hypertension, and hypothyroidism. Plan, clear liquids today and nothing by mouth after midnight, EGD tomorrow with biopsies, normal saline at 75 mL per hour, repeat basic metabolic panel and iron studies in the morning. Increase omeprazole to 40 mg once a day. Continue amlodipine 5 mg and levothyroxine 50 mcg. Speech therapy swallow evaluation and dietitian consult for a pureed diet after the procedure. I explained the plan again with teach-back, and her daughter will be present for the consent. End of dictation.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Endocrinology telephone visit. Audio-only, no video, patient at home and verbally consented to the phone visit. This visit follows a hospitalization within the past month.

Reason for visit: follow-up of primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia in a 61-year-old male.

Interval history: He was hospitalized about three weeks ago with a left kidney stone and was found to have hypercalcemia. He was treated with IV fluids and ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy and was discharged after two nights. Since discharge he reports persistent fatigue, increased thirst, frequent urination, constipation, and bone aches in his hips and back. He denies confusion, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, flank pain, and blood in the urine. He takes calcium carbonate 500 mg three times daily over the counter for bone health and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily for hypertension. He is not taking any vitamin D.

Home measurements: blood pressure 128/78 and pulse 70 on his home cuff this morning.

Exam: no physical exam is possible by phone. His speech is clear, he is oriented, and he answers questions appropriately.

Data reviewed from the hospitalization and recent outpatient labs: calcium 11.6 mg/dL at discharge, PTH 88 pg/mL, 25-hydroxy vitamin D 22 ng/mL, and creatinine 1.1 with an eGFR of 72. A sestamibi scan showed uptake consistent with a right inferior parathyroid adenoma. DEXA showed a T-score of -2.6 at the distal radius.

Impression: primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia and a recent kidney stone, with osteoporosis at the distal radius, which meets criteria for surgery. Hydrochlorothiazide and calcium supplements are contributing to the elevated calcium.

Next steps: stop hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily and stop calcium carbonate. Start amlodipine 5 mg daily for blood pressure. Start vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) 1,000 units daily for the low vitamin D. Drink at least 2 liters of water daily. Refer to endocrine surgery for parathyroidectomy. Repeat calcium, PTH, and creatinine in 2 weeks. I will call him again in 3 weeks. He verbalized understanding of the plan.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
The patient is a 71-year-old female with stable exertional angina who returns to the cardiology clinic for follow-up. She reports substernal chest pressure when walking uphill or climbing more than one flight of stairs, lasting three to five minutes and relieved by rest. Over the past month the episodes have increased from about once a week to three or four times a week at the same level of exertion. She reports no rest pain and no pain that wakes her from sleep. She denies palpitations, syncope, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and leg swelling.

Her history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a. She is allergic to aspirin, which causes hives and wheezing, and she has never taken it. For that reason she uses clopidogrel 75 mg once daily as her antiplatelet agent. During medication reconciliation she first said that she takes metoprolol succinate 25 mg, but after checking her pill bottle she corrected this and confirmed that it is 50 mg once daily. Her other medications are atorvastatin 40 mg once daily, lisinopril 20 mg once daily, and metformin 500 mg twice daily. She stopped amlodipine 10 mg once daily on her own two weeks ago because of ankle swelling, and the swelling has since resolved.

On examination, blood pressure is 142/84, heart rate is 76, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Hi, thanks for coming in. I understand you're a 70-year-old male here because of some trouble with your memory. What's been happening?
Patient: Well, my daughter made me come. A couple of days ago I got lost driving home from the grocery store, one I've gone to for twenty years. I figured it out after a while, but it scared me.
Family member: He's been forgetting things for about a year, Doctor. He repeats the same questions and misplaces his keys and wallet. He's also missed a couple of bill payments, which he never used to do.
Doctor: Has it been getting worse quickly, or slowly over time?
Family member: Slowly. It's more noticeable this last year.
Doctor: Any head injury or falls recently?
Patient: No falls, and I haven't hit my head.
Doctor: Any headaches or weakness?
Patient: No headaches, no weakness.
Doctor: What about your mood? Any sadness, or seeing things that aren't there?
Patient: I'm a little down about this, but I'm not depressed, and no, I don't see things.
Family member: And he sleeps poorly, so he takes something every night to help.
Doctor: What do you take?
Patient: Diphenhydramine, 50 mg at bedtime, the store-brand version of Benadryl. I also take lisinopril 10 mg every morning for blood pressure and tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily for my prostate.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Your vitals today are blood pressure 136/78, heart rate 72, temperature 36.8 Celsius, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Your fingerstick glucose is 104. On exam you're alert and pleasant, your heart and lungs sound normal, there's no weakness, your speech is fluent, and your walking is steady. On the memory screen, the MoCA, you scored 23 out of 30, with most of the points lost on delayed recall and the clock drawing.
Patient: Is that bad?
Doctor: It's mildly low. A slow decline over a year with you still mostly independent in daily activities fits mild cognitive impairment. That is not the same as dementia. Some things can make memory worse, and diphenhydramine is a big one in older adults, so I'd like you to stop it. You can try melatonin 3 mg at bedtime instead. Continue the lisinopril and tamsulosin. Urgent care isn't the place for the full workup, so I'm ordering blood tests today, a vitamin B12 level, TSH, a complete metabolic panel, and a CBC, and I'm referring you for an MRI of the brain and to our geriatrics clinic for a full memory evaluation. Until then, please don't drive alone on unfamiliar routes, and have your daughter help with the bills.
Family member: Okay, we'll do that.
Patient: All right. Thank you.
"""

Ambient scribe transcript. Urgent care visit for a 7-year-old female with wheezing and trouble breathing, accompanied by her mother.

Doctor: Any rash, lip swelling, or choking on food before this started?

Doctor: Does she have other medical problems?
Family member: Asthma since she was little, eczema, and allergic rhinitis.
Doctor: What medicines does she take?
Family member: For asthma she uses fluticasone, the 220 micrograms, two puffs twice a day with the spacer, and albuterol when needed. She takes cetirizine 5 mg every day for her allergies. She was on montelukast 5 mg at night, but we stopped it two months ago because she had nightmares.

Family member: She looks so much better.

75-year-old male, urgent care. Professional Spanish interpreter (video) used for the entire visit; hx obtained through interpreter.

CC: rash on R flank x 5 days, tick bite.
HPI: found a tick on R flank ~1 wk ago after working in his garden, removed it himself. Rash noted 5 days ago, now ~10 cm, slightly warm, mild itch. Mild HA, fatigue, and R knee ache x 3 days. No fever, no neck stiffness, no facial weakness, no palpitations, no syncope, no joint swelling, no vision changes.
PMH: A-fib on warfarin, HTN.
Meds: warfarin 5 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily. NKDA.

VS: BP 132/78, HR 76 irregular, Temp 99.0 F, SpO2 97% RA.

Impression: early localized Lyme disease w/ erythema migrans. A-fib, rate controlled.

- doxycycline 100 mg BID x 10 days w/ food and water, sun protection
- doxycycline may raise INR, so repeat INR in 4-5 days at nurse visit
- continue warfarin 5 mg daily and metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily
- bleeding precautions reviewed

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 3 progress note for a 91-year-old female admitted with acute kidney injury due to dehydration.

Overnight events and interval history: She was admitted after 4 days of poor oral intake, watery stools that have now stopped, and lightheadedness on standing. She had also been drinking a dandelion herbal tea several times a day for leg swelling, in addition to her prescribed furosemide. Overnight she had no fever, no chest pain, no shortness of breath, no vomiting, and no diarrhea since yesterday. She says she feels less dizzy today and drank 600 mL of fluid yesterday. Her daughter reports that the patient also takes over-the-counter supplements: vitamin D3 1000 units daily, a calcium carbonate tablet, and turmeric capsules 500 mg twice daily.

Past medical history includes atrial fibrillation, HTN, T2DM, CKD stage 3a with a baseline creatinine of 1.0, and HFpEF. On admission her apixaban dose was recorded as 2.5 mg twice daily, correction, the pharmacy fill history confirms she was taking 5 mg twice daily. She has no known drug allergies.

Current medications and infusions: lactated Ringer's at 75 mL per hour, insulin lispro on a sliding scale before meals, apixaban, amlodipine 5 mg daily, and vitamin D3 1000 units daily. Held since admission are lisinopril 20 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, and metformin 500 mg twice daily. The turmeric and the dandelion herbal tea have been stopped.

Vitals and data: temperature 36.6 Celsius, heart rate 74, blood pressure 112/64 lying and 104/60 standing, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, weight 52 kg compared with 51 kg on admission. Net intake exceeded output by 1.1 L over the last 24 hours, with urine output of 0.8 mL/kg/hr. Creatinine was 2.4 on admission, 1.9 yesterday, and 1.6 today. BUN has improved from 52 to 38. Sodium was 148 on admission and is 142 today, potassium is 3.8, and bicarbonate is 22. Hemoglobin is 11.4. Urinalysis was bland with no protein or blood, and urine sodium was low. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis.

Exam: frail elderly woman, comfortable, alert and oriented. Mucous membranes are now moist and skin turgor has improved. JVP is not elevated, the heart is irregularly irregular without murmur, the lungs are clear with no crackles, the abdomen is soft, and there is no leg edema and no costovertebral angle tenderness.

Acute kidney injury, prerenal from dehydration (poor oral intake, watery stools, diuretic, and herbal diuretic tea), improving with creatinine down from 2.4 to 1.6. Decrease lactated Ringer's to 50 mL per hour given HFpEF and the rising weight, and stop it once oral intake is adequate. Continue to hold lisinopril and furosemide, avoid NSAIDs and contrast, and repeat BMP in the morning. Discontinue turmeric and the dandelion herbal tea.

Hypernatremia, resolved with fluids.

Atrial fibrillation: rate controlled without a rate-control agent. Reduce apixaban from 5 mg twice daily to 2.5 mg twice daily because she is over 80 years old, weighs 52 kg, and has a creatinine above 1.5.

HTN: blood pressure is low-normal. Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily and hold lisinopril.

T2DM: continue insulin lispro on a sliding scale and hold metformin until the creatinine is near baseline.

HFpEF: daily weights and a daily lung exam, with furosemide on hold for now.

Disposition: PT evaluation today. Likely discharge home with her daughter in 2 days if the creatinine continues to fall.
"""

Doctor: Hello. I see we have a 7-month-old male here for a cough and fast breathing. Tell me what has been going on.
Family member: He has had a runny nose for about four days, and for the last two days he has a bad cough and he breathes fast. He is wheezing a little at night.
Doctor: Any fever?
Family member: No fever. I checked a few times and the highest was 99.
Doctor: Any vomiting? Has he turned blue or stopped breathing at any point?
Family member: No vomiting, and no, nothing like that. He is eating less though, about half of his usual bottles, but he still has wet diapers. Four or five today.
Doctor: Good. Does he have any medical problems, or take any medicines?
Family member: No, he was born at term and has been healthy. No medicines.
Doctor: Okay, let me examine him. His respiratory rate is 48, oxygen saturation is 97% on room air, and temperature is 99.2. He is alert and playful. I hear scattered wheezes and crackles in both lungs, with mild nasal flaring but no chest retractions. His ears and throat look normal and he is well hydrated. This is bronchiolitis, a viral infection of the small airways. Antibiotics and inhalers do not help this, so we treat the symptoms. Use saline nose drops, then gently suction his nose before feeds. Offer smaller, more frequent feedings. Go to the emergency room if he breathes very fast or hard, his lips look blue, he has fewer than three wet diapers in a day, or he takes less than half of his feeds.
Family member: How long will this last?
Doctor: The cough can last two to three weeks, and the worst days are usually days three to five. I would like to recheck him in two days.
Family member: Okay, thank you.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Hi there. I see you are a 30-year-old female coming in with pelvic pain. What has been going on?
Patient: I have had pain low in my belly for about two years, but the last month it has been worse. It used to be mostly right before and during my period, but now I feel it most days.
Doctor: How bad is it?
Patient: Usually a 5 out of 10, and an 8 during my period. I also have pain with sex and pain when I move my bowels around my period.
Doctor: Any fever, vaginal discharge, or burning when you urinate?
Patient: No fever, no discharge, and no burning when I pee. No blood in my urine either.
Doctor: Any bleeding between periods, or vomiting?
Patient: No bleeding between periods and no vomiting. I do get nauseated when the pain is bad.
Doctor: Could you be pregnant?
Patient: I took a home test last week and it was negative.
Doctor: What have you tried for the pain?
Patient: My gynecologist put me on norethindrone acetate 5 mg daily four months ago, and it helped a lot. But I ran out about six weeks ago. It costs too much with my insurance and I could not afford the refill, so I just stopped. The pain came back within a couple of weeks. I have been taking ibuprofen 400 mg when it is bad, but it only takes the edge off.
Doctor: I am sorry the cost got in the way. Let me check your numbers and then examine you. Your blood pressure is 118/72, heart rate 84, temperature 98.4, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Your belly is soft with mild tenderness low on both sides, but no rebound and no guarding. On the pelvic exam your uterus is tender and does not move easily, there is tenderness behind the uterus, no mass, no cervical motion tenderness, and no discharge. The urine pregnancy test we did here is negative, and the urinalysis shows no blood, no leukocytes, and no nitrites.
Patient: So what is it?
Doctor: My impression is chronic pelvic pain, most likely from endometriosis that flared after the hormone treatment stopped. Nothing today points to an infection or an emergency. For the plan, we will restart norethindrone acetate 5 mg once daily, and our pharmacist will find a generic discount program so the refill is affordable. Increase the ibuprofen to 600 mg every 6 hours as needed, taken with food. I am also ordering a pelvic ultrasound, and I want you to see your gynecologist within two weeks to talk about longer term options. Come back right away for severe pain, fever, heavy bleeding, or fainting.
Patient: Okay, thank you. I will do that.
"""

Patient: I have had pain low in my belly for about two years, but the last month it has been worse. It used to be mostly right before and during my period, but now I feel it most days.
Doctor: How bad is it?
Patient: Usually a 5 out of 10, and an 8 during my period. I also have pain with sex and pain when I move my bowels around my period.
Doctor: Any fever, vaginal discharge, or burning when you urinate?
Patient: No fever, no discharge, and no burning when I pee. No blood in my urine either.
Doctor: Any bleeding between periods, or vomiting?
Patient: No bleeding between periods and no vomiting. I do get nauseated when the pain is bad.
Doctor: Could you be pregnant?
Patient: I took a home test last week and it was negative.
Doctor: What have you tried for the pain?
Patient: My gynecologist put me on norethindrone acetate 5 mg daily four months ago, and it helped a lot. But I ran out about six weeks ago. It costs too much with my insurance and I could not afford the refill, so I just stopped. The pain came back within a couple of weeks. I have been taking ibuprofen 400 mg when it is bad, but it only takes the edge off.

The urine pregnancy test we did here is negative, and the urinalysis shows no blood, no leukocytes, and no nitrites.

Doctor: My impression is chronic pelvic pain, most likely from endometriosis that flared after the hormone treatment stopped. Nothing today points to an infection or an emergency. For the plan, we will restart norethindrone acetate 5 mg once daily, and our pharmacist will find a generic discount program so the refill is affordable. Increase the ibuprofen to 600 mg every 6 hours as needed, taken with food. I am also ordering a pelvic ultrasound, and I want you to see your gynecologist within two weeks to talk about longer term options. Come back right away for severe pain, fever, heavy bleeding, or fainting.
Patient: Okay, thank you. I will do that.

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Good morning. Please have a seat. I have you down as a 67-year-old female here to go over your blood sugar and cholesterol results. Is that right?
Patient: Yes, doctor. I'm so nervous. My sister got diabetes last year and I keep thinking I'm next. Am I going to get diabetes? Will I need insulin? Can I ask a few questions before we start?
Doctor: Of course, ask as many as you like. Your A1c came back at 6.1 percent, which is in the prediabetes range, so you do not have diabetes right now. Let's go through your history first. Any increased thirst, passing a lot of urine, or blurry vision?
Patient: No, none of that. No extra thirst, no blurry vision. I do feel tired sometimes. And my feet tingle a little at night. Is that from the sugar?
Doctor: Tingling can have several causes, and with an A1c of 6.1 it is less likely to be from sugar. We will check your B12 level. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or swelling in your legs?
Patient: No chest pain. No swelling. I get a bit out of breath on stairs, but I think that's just my weight. Should I worry about that?
Doctor: We will keep an eye on it. Tell me which medicines you take.
Patient: Let me think. Lisinopril 20 mg for the pressure, once in the morning. Atorvastatin, I take 10 mg at night.
Doctor: Is that right? Your chart says 20.
Patient: Oh, wait, let me look at the photo of the bottle on my phone. You're right, it says 20 mg. I misread it, sorry. And aspirin 81 mg every day, omeprazole 20 mg for heartburn, and vitamin D, 2000 units.
Doctor: Thanks for checking. So lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg at night, aspirin 81 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily, and vitamin D3 2000 units daily.
Patient: Yes. Oh, and I stopped the amlodipine last month because my ankles were puffy. My other doctor said that was okay.
Doctor: Good to know, and the swelling is gone now?
Patient: Yes, it's gone. Is it dangerous that I stopped it?
Doctor: No, your pressure is acceptable today. Now your numbers. Fasting glucose was 112, A1c 6.1 percent. LDL 138, HDL 38, triglycerides 210. Blood pressure today is 138/84, weight 196 pounds, BMI 33, and waist 99 centimeters. On exam your heart is regular, lungs are clear, there is no swelling in your legs, the sensation in both feet is normal on the monofilament test, and you have some darkening of the skin on the back of your neck called acanthosis nigricans.
Patient: Oh no. What does that mean? Is it my fault? Could I have prevented this?
Doctor: It is not your fault. Genes matter a lot. Putting it together, you have prediabetes and metabolic syndrome, which means a cluster of belly weight, high triglycerides, low HDL, and borderline blood sugar and pressure. It raises the risk of diabetes and heart disease, but it is very treatable, and you can lower that risk by up to half with lifestyle changes.
Patient: Half? Really? What do I have to do? Do I have to give up all sugar? Can I still eat fruit?
Doctor: Fruit is fine. Here is the plan. First, aim to lose about 14 pounds, which is 7 percent of your weight, with walking 150 minutes a week, and a Mediterranean style diet. I will refer you to the diabetes prevention program and a dietitian. Second, I am going to increase your atorvastatin from 20 to 40 mg at night because your LDL is 138. Third, I want you to stop the aspirin 81 mg. At your age, with no heart attack or stroke before, the bleeding risk is bigger than the benefit. Continue lisinopril 20 mg, omeprazole 20 mg, and vitamin D3.
Patient: Stop the aspirin? Are you sure? My neighbor takes it every day.
Doctor: I am sure. The guidelines changed, and your risk of stomach bleeding is higher than the benefit. We will also check a B12 level, a liver panel in 6 weeks after the statin change, and repeat your A1c and lipid panel in 3 months.
Patient: Okay. Let me say it back. Walk 150 minutes, lose 14 pounds, atorvastatin goes up to 40, no more aspirin, keep the pressure pill and the others, and blood tests in 6 weeks and 3 months.
Doctor: Perfect. Come back in 3 months, and call sooner if you notice excessive thirst or urination, chest pain, or leg swelling.
Patient: Thank you. I feel better knowing the plan.
"""

She denied thirst and blurry vision, chest pain, and leg swelling, but reported tiredness and tingling feet. Fasting glucose was 112, LDL 138, HDL 38, triglycerides 210, BP 138/84, BMI 33, and exam showed acanthosis nigricans. She was diagnosed with prediabetes and metabolic syndrome. Atorvastatin was increased from 20 to 40 mg and aspirin was stopped, with lifestyle changes, a diabetes prevention program, a dietitian, B12 and liver testing, and repeat A1c and lipids in 3 months.

Clinical note:
"""
Geriatrics clinic dictation on a 93-year-old male seen for follow-up of mild cognitive impairment. He says he left school after the sixth grade and has trouble reading the labels on his pill bottles, so I used plain language, short sentences, and teach-back throughout the visit. He has noticed memory problems over about two years, including misplacing his glasses, repeating questions, and occasionally forgetting appointments. He still manages his own bathing, dressing, and meals. He denies getting lost in familiar places, denies falls, denies hallucinations, and denies feeling sad or hopeless. His sleep is poor and he takes diphenhydramine 25 mg at bedtime, which he has used for years. Past history includes hypertension, for which he takes amlodipine 10 mg daily, correction, 5 mg daily, as confirmed on the bottle he brought in.

Vitals today are blood pressure 142 over 78 and heart rate 68, and his weight is stable. On examination he is alert and cooperative and follows conversation well with his hearing aids in place. Heart and lungs are normal and his gait is slow but steady without a device. His score on the MoCA today was 22 out of 30, with losses mainly in delayed recall and attention. TSH from last month was normal at 2.1, and his vitamin B12 level was low at 190.

Impression is mild cognitive impairment, with possible contributions from the nightly diphenhydramine and low vitamin B12, along with insomnia and hypertension that is near goal.

Plan is as follows. I am stopping diphenhydramine because it is anticholinergic and can worsen memory, and I reviewed simple sleep habits with him. I am starting vitamin B12 1000 mcg daily by mouth. Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily. I ordered a non-contrast head CT. I gave him a large-print picture medication list and a weekly pill organizer, and I asked the home health nurse to set up his pills for the first month. Teach-back confirmed that he understands to stop the sleep pill and take one B12 tablet each day. Follow up in three months with a repeat B12 level, sooner if his memory worsens or he has a fall.
"""

93-year-old male with mild cognitive impairment who left school after the sixth grade and has trouble reading pill labels; plain language and teach-back were used. About two years of memory problems including misplacing his glasses, repeating questions and occasionally forgetting appointments, while still managing bathing, dressing and meals. Denies getting lost in familiar places, falls, hallucinations and feeling sad or hopeless. Sleep is poor and he takes diphenhydramine 25 mg at bedtime. History of hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg daily, confirmed on the bottle after he first stated 10 mg.

OBJECTIVE:
Blood pressure 142 over 78, heart rate 68, weight stable. Alert and cooperative, follows conversation well with hearing aids in place; heart and lungs normal; gait slow but steady without a device. MoCA 22 out of 30 with losses in delayed recall and attention. TSH 2.1, normal; vitamin B12 level low at 190.

ASSESSMENT:
Mild cognitive impairment with possible contributions from nightly diphenhydramine and low vitamin B12; insomnia; hypertension near goal.

PLAN:
1. Stop diphenhydramine because it is anticholinergic and can worsen memory; reviewed simple sleep habits
2. Start vitamin B12 1000 mcg daily by mouth
3. Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily
4. Order a non-contrast head CT
5. Give a large-print picture medication list and a weekly pill organizer; home health nurse to set up pills for the first month
6. Teach-back confirmed understanding to stop the sleep pill and take one B12 tablet each day
7. Follow up in three months with a repeat B12 level, sooner if memory worsens or he has a fall

Clinical note:
"""
Visit type: Video telehealth visit, urology, new complaint. A professional Spanish medical interpreter joined the video call for the entire visit, and the patient agreed to proceed by video. The patient is a 66-year-old male located at his home, alone in the room. Identity and location were confirmed verbally.

Reason for visit: Difficulty with erections for about one year.

History reported by the patient through the interpreter: Over the past year he has had difficulty getting and keeping erections, and they are no longer firm enough for intercourse. He has noticed reduced morning erections. His sexual desire is still normal. The problem happens in every situation and has worsened gradually. He denies penile pain, denies penile curvature, and denies any pelvic or penile trauma or surgery. He denies chest pain, denies shortness of breath with exertion, and denies lightheadedness. He denies depressed mood and reports no unusual stress. He has no urinary hesitancy or weak stream and denies blood in the urine. He does not use nitrate medicines.

Alcohol and social history: He drinks about six to eight beers every day, mostly in the evening, for more than ten years. The interpreter clarified that he meant every day and not every week. He denies withdrawal seizures and has never been hospitalized for alcohol. He is a former smoker and quit ten years ago. About two months ago he bought tadalafil 20 mg from an online site and took it about four times; the effect was poor and it gave him headaches each time.

Chronic conditions: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia.

Medications reported: At first he said he takes metformin 500 mg twice daily. When the interpreter asked him to show the bottle to the camera, the label read metformin 1000 mg twice daily, so the correct dose is 1000 mg twice daily. He also takes lisinopril 20 mg daily, which his primary care doctor increased from 10 mg three weeks ago, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and amlodipine 5 mg daily.

Home measurements: BP 148/92 and HR 80 on his home cuff this morning, fasting fingerstick glucose 156, home weight 94 kg.

Limited video exam: He appears comfortable and in no acute distress and speaks in full sentences without shortness of breath. Mild facial flushing is noted. He is alert and oriented, mood is appropriate, and no tremor is seen. No jaundice is visible on camera. A genital and prostate exam was not possible by video and will be done in person.

Data reviewed from primary care labs one month ago: A1c 8.4%, LDL 96 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0, AST 58 and ALT 44, which are mildly elevated, total testosterone 262 ng/dL drawn in the afternoon, and PSA 1.1 ng/mL.

Impression: Erectile dysfunction in a 66-year-old male, likely multifactorial from type 2 diabetes with suboptimal control, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and heavy alcohol use. A low afternoon testosterone needs confirmation with a morning level. Mildly elevated liver enzymes are consistent with his alcohol intake. Erectile dysfunction was also discussed as a marker of cardiovascular risk.

Recommendations:
1. Stop the online tadalafil 20 mg because the source and contents cannot be verified.
2. Start sildenafil 25 mg by mouth as needed about one hour before sexual activity, no more than once in 24 hours. He may increase to 50 mg if the effect is inadequate after three attempts. He was told never to take it with nitrates and to go to the emergency department for an erection lasting more than four hours.
3. Counseled on cutting back alcohol with medical supervision because of withdrawal risk, referral to his primary care doctor and addiction medicine, and start thiamine 100 mg daily.
4. Order a morning total testosterone and a hepatic panel.
5. Message his primary care doctor about diabetes and blood pressure control.
6. In-person visit in six weeks for the genital and prostate exam and to review the response to sildenafil.
Teach-back was completed through the interpreter and the patient understood the instructions.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Nurse: Triage summary for the doctor. This is a 69-year-old female with known polymyalgia rheumatica who came in with worsening shoulder and hip pain. Blood pressure 138/82, heart rate 84, temperature 98.4 F, oxygen saturation 97% on room air.

Doctor: Thank you. Good afternoon. I understand the pain has come back. Tell me what has been going on.

Patient: It feels just like last year. My shoulders and hips are so stiff in the morning that I can barely get out of bed. It lasts about two hours, and I can't lift my arms to comb my hair. It started about ten days ago.

Doctor: Last year you were diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica and started on prednisone. What dose are you taking now?

Patient: Prednisone, 5 mg once a day, I think. I was tapering because my rheumatologist said I was doing so well.

Doctor: Okay, 5 mg. When did you last lower it?

Patient: About two weeks ago, and the pain started soon after. I have also been taking ibuprofen, 400 mg twice a day, just to get through the days.

Doctor: I see. Any headache, jaw pain when you chew, or vision changes?

Patient: No headache, no jaw pain, and my vision is fine. No fever either.

Doctor: Any rash, black stools, or stomach pain with the ibuprofen?

Patient: No rash, no black stools, and no stomach pain. It is the muscles. They ache and feel heavy.

Doctor: What other conditions do you have, and what else do you take?

Patient: I have high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and thin bones. I take lisinopril 20 mg once a day, metformin 1000 mg twice a day, alendronate 70 mg once a week, omeprazole 20 mg once a day, and calcium with vitamin D.

Doctor: Thank you. Let me examine you. Lifting your arms out to the side hurts and stops at about shoulder height, and lifting your knee against my hand is painful at the hip. There is no joint swelling in your hands, wrists, or knees, and no temporal artery tenderness. Your labs came back while we were talking. The ESR is 58 and the CRP is 31 mg/L, hemoglobin is 12.1, creatinine is 0.9, and your blood sugar is 196.

Patient: Wait, I need to fix something. My daughter just sent me a photo of my bottle, and it says 7.5 mg, not 5. I went down from 10 mg to 7.5 mg two weeks ago.

Clinical note:
"""
Telehealth video visit, neurology follow-up for persistent symptoms after a concussion. The patient is a 37-year-old male connecting from home on a smartphone with good audio and video, and he agreed to a video visit after we discussed its limits. His sister helped him open the link. He has limited health literacy, so I used plain language, short steps, and teach-back, and I asked him to hold each pill bottle up to the camera so we could read the labels together.

He fell off his bicycle 6 weeks ago and hit his head on the pavement. He did not lose consciousness, and a head CT in the emergency department that day showed no bleeding or fracture. Since then he has had daily headaches that feel like a tight band, worse in the afternoon and when he looks at screens, along with dizziness when he turns his head quickly, sensitivity to light, trouble concentrating at work, poor sleep, and irritability. He denies vomiting, double vision, weakness, numbness, seizures, neck pain, and new confusion, and the headaches are not getting worse. He denies thoughts of harming himself.

His history includes migraine without aura since his twenties, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea treated with CPAP most nights, and acid reflux. When I asked about his blood pressure pill he first said lisinopril 20 mg daily, but when he held up the bottle he read it as lisinopril 10 mg daily, so the correct dose is 10 mg daily. He also takes omeprazole 20 mg every morning for reflux, sumatriptan 50 mg as needed for migraine, which he has used once since the injury, and amitriptyline 10 mg at bedtime, which another provider started 3 weeks ago for sleep and headache. For the past 5 weeks he has also taken ibuprofen 400 mg three to four times a day for the headaches. He has no known drug allergies.

He measured these at home with his own cuff during the visit: blood pressure 128/82, heart rate 76, and temperature 36.8 C. On video he looks comfortable, is alert, speaks fluently, and follows multi-step commands. He squints in the room light but has no facial droop. His eye movements look full and smooth, finger-to-nose testing was accurate on both sides, and he walked in a straight line with a steady turn. I could not do a fundus exam or check reflexes over video. A PHQ-9 read aloud to him was 6, which is mild. Labs from his primary clinic 2 months ago showed TSH 1.9 and hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL.

My impression is post-concussion syndrome after a mild head injury, with headaches, dizziness, light sensitivity, and sleep problems, and with a risk of medication-overuse headache from near-daily ibuprofen. His hypertension looks controlled on the home reading, and his migraine and OSA are stable. For the plan, I told him to stop ibuprofen completely because daily use can make headaches worse and raise blood pressure. He should take no pain pills on more than 2 days a week, and on those days he may take acetaminophen 500 mg. I increased amitriptyline from 10 mg to 25 mg at bedtime. He will continue lisinopril 10 mg daily, omeprazole 20 mg every morning, sumatriptan 50 mg as needed, and CPAP nightly. I referred him to vestibular physical therapy for the dizziness. He should rest from cycling and sports until cleared, take a screen break every 20 minutes, and keep a regular sleep schedule, and I gave him a work note for reduced hours for 2 weeks. I asked him to mark headache days on a simple calendar, and he repeated the plan back correctly. Video follow-up in 3 weeks. He should go to the emergency department for repeated vomiting, a headache that keeps getting worse, confusion, weakness, or a seizure.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
Doctor: Hello, and thanks for coming in. I have you down as a 46-year-old male referred for trouble with erections. Tell me what has been going on.
Patient: For about eight months I have had trouble getting and keeping an erection firm enough for sex. It happens maybe two out of three times. It is embarrassing, to be honest.
Doctor: Do you still wake up with morning erections?
Patient: Yes, most mornings, so I know things still work.
Doctor: That is useful to know. Any pain, bending, or curvature of the penis during an erection?
Patient: No pain and no curve.
Doctor: Any chest pain or shortness of breath when you exert yourself, or any fainting?
Patient: None of that. I jog twice a week with no chest pain and no trouble breathing.
Doctor: How are your mood and stress level?
Patient: Work has been stressful, and I worry about performing, but I do not feel depressed. Sleep is fine.
Doctor: What medications are you taking?
Patient: Lisinopril 20 mg once a day for blood pressure. That is my only prescription.
Doctor: Anything over the counter, like supplements?
Patient: Yes. I bought an herbal vitality product with yohimbe bark extract, two capsules before sex, and I take L-arginine 3 grams a day. I also take a multivitamin.
Doctor: Do you use nitroglycerin or any other nitrate medicine, or recreational poppers?
Patient: No nitrates and no poppers.
Doctor: Good, that matters for safety. What about alcohol and tobacco?
Patient: Two beers on weekends, and I quit smoking three years ago.
Doctor: Your vitals today are blood pressure 146/92 and heart rate 78, and your BMI is 29. Your heart sounds regular without murmurs, your leg pulses are normal, and the penis and both testicles are normal with no plaques or masses. The morning total testosterone from your primary care doctor was 412 ng/dL, hemoglobin A1c 5.6 percent, and LDL 128.
Patient: So what is going on?
Doctor: My impression is erectile dysfunction, most likely from a mix of blood vessel changes and performance anxiety. Your hypertension is also above goal today. Yohimbe can raise blood pressure and cause palpitations, and neither supplement has been shown to help, so please stop the yohimbe and the L-arginine.
Patient: Okay. Is there something that works?
Doctor: Yes. I am starting sildenafil 50 mg, one tablet about an hour before sex as needed, no more than once in 24 hours. Headache, flushing, and a stuffy nose are common. Call us if an erection lasts more than four hours, and never combine it with a nitrate. Keep taking the lisinopril, and I will message your primary care doctor about the blood pressure. I also recommend counseling for the performance anxiety, regular exercise, and limiting alcohol. Let us meet again in six weeks to see how the medicine is working.
Patient: Sounds good. Thank you.
"""

Nurse: This is a 45-year-old female with known multiple sclerosis, here with numbness and weakness in her left leg for four days. Blood pressure 124/76, heart rate 80, temp 98.4, oxygen sat 99% on room air.

Doctor: Hi there. Tell me what has been going on.

Patient: Four days ago my left foot started tingling, and it has crept up to my hip. Now the leg feels heavy and it drags when I walk. I'm also exhausted.

Doctor: Is that how your relapses have felt before?

Patient: Yes, this is just like the one I had three years ago, when my right leg went numb.

Doctor: Any vision changes, double vision, or eye pain?

Patient: No, my vision is fine.

Doctor: Any trouble controlling your bladder or bowels?

Patient: No. No accidents.

Doctor: Burning with urination, fever, or chills?

Patient: None of that.

Doctor: Any back injury or back pain?

Patient: No, no back pain.

Doctor: What medications are you on?

Patient: Dimethyl fumarate 240 mg twice a day for the MS, and baclofen 10 mg three times a day for leg stiffness. No medication allergies.

Doctor: Thanks. On exam, your cranial nerves and vision are normal. Strength is 4 out of 5 in the left hip flexor and ankle dorsiflexion, and normal on the right. You have reduced pinprick sensation in the left leg below the hip, and the reflexes are brisker at the left knee. Your gait is mildly unsteady but you can walk without help. Your urine test here is negative for infection, your white count is 6.2, and your blood sugar is 104, so this does not look like an infection making your old symptoms flare. This is consistent with a multiple sclerosis relapse.

Patient: What do we do about it?

Doctor: We treat relapses with high-dose steroids. I'm giving you the first dose of methylprednisolone 1000 mg IV here today, and the infusion center will give you the next two doses on the following two days. I'm also starting pantoprazole 40 mg once daily while you are on steroids to protect your stomach. Keep taking the dimethyl fumarate and baclofen. We need an MRI of the brain and cervical and thoracic spine with and without contrast, and I'll have your neurologist's office see you within a week. Steroids can raise your blood sugar and affect your sleep. Go to the emergency room right away if you lose vision, if the weakness spreads, or if you can't pass urine.

Patient: Okay, I understand.
"""

Dictating a cardiology clinic follow-up on a 43-year-old male referred for exertional chest discomfort. He reports about six weeks of chest pressure when he climbs two flights of stairs or walks briskly uphill. It lasts roughly three minutes and goes away with rest. The pattern has been the same each time and has not worsened. He denies chest pain at rest, syncope, palpitations, orthopnea, and leg swelling. He also denies lightheadedness during the episodes.

He drinks heavily, about eight beers a day for several years, with the last drink yesterday evening. He denies tremor, sweating, or other withdrawal symptoms today. He does not smoke and uses no recreational drugs.

Past history is significant for hypertension that has not been treated and hyperlipidemia. His father had a heart attack at 52, correction, at 54. He takes aspirin 81 mg daily and atorvastatin 40 mg daily, and that is all.

On exam, blood pressure 148/92, heart rate 84, weight 232 pounds, BMI 32. Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, no gallop, lungs clear, no jugular venous distension, no peripheral edema, and the liver edge is palpable and mildly tender. Resting ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with no ST changes and no Q waves. Labs from last week: LDL 142 on atorvastatin 40 mg, AST 62 and ALT 48, hemoglobin A1c 5.7, creatinine 0.9.

Impression, one, stable exertional angina, probable obstructive coronary artery disease given the typical symptoms and his risk factors. Two, heavy alcohol use, with probable alcohol-related liver injury given the elevated AST and ALT. Three, hypertension, untreated, and hyperlipidemia not at goal.

Management. Start metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily for angina and blood pressure. Increase atorvastatin from 40 mg to 80 mg daily. Continue aspirin 81 mg daily. Prescribe nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingual as needed for chest pain; I reviewed how to take it and to call 911 if the pain does not resolve five minutes after one dose. Start thiamine 100 mg daily. Order a treadmill nuclear stress test and a transthoracic echocardiogram. If the stress test is abnormal we will proceed to coronary angiography. I counseled him at length on cutting back on alcohol and offered a referral to an addiction medicine clinic and counseling, which he accepted; he should not stop drinking abruptly without medical advice given his daily intake. Avoid heavy exertion until testing is complete. Return to clinic in two weeks after the stress test, and sooner for any rest pain, syncope, or worsening symptoms.
"""

Doctor: Good afternoon. I see you're an 83-year-old female and you came in about a letter regarding your kidneys. Tell me what happened.

Patient: No swelling, and I'm passing urine like always.
Doctor: Any nausea, itching, or foamy urine?
Patient: No, none of that. I do get tired sometimes in the afternoon.
Doctor: Okay. I reviewed your records. You have chronic kidney disease stage 3b. Your blood test last month showed a creatinine of 1.5 and an eGFR of 33, and it was the same six months ago, so it is stable and not a new problem.
Patient: What do I take for it? I take losartan 50 milligrams once a day for my blood pressure, and sometimes ibuprofen for my knees.

Patient: What should I use for my knees?
Doctor: Warm compresses and gentle walking, and check with your primary doctor before taking any pain medicine.
Doctor: So my impression is stable chronic kidney disease stage 3b, with your hypertension well controlled. Here is the plan. Stop ibuprofen, continue losartan 50 mg once a day, and drink fluids normally. Ask your primary doctor to repeat the kidney labs in three months and to refer you to a kidney specialist. Patient: Thank you, I feel better knowing it's stable.

Clinical note:
"""
Hospital day 2 progress note. The patient is a 39-year-old female admitted with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and elevated liver enzymes. She reports that the pain is mild this morning, about 2 out of 10, and she has had mild nausea without vomiting. She denies fever, jaundice, itching, dark urine, and pale stools. She drinks about one glass of wine per month and uses no other substances. Home medications are limited to an over-the-counter turmeric supplement 500 mg daily, which she started three months ago for joint aches, and acetaminophen as needed. She has a documented allergy to codeine, which caused hives.

Overnight there were no events. Vitals this morning: blood pressure 128/78, heart rate 74, temperature 98.2, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Her BMI is 34. On exam she is comfortable and anicteric, the abdomen is soft with mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant, and there is no rebound and no guarding. There is no peripheral edema and no stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Data: AST 118 and ALT 164 on admission, alkaline phosphatase 112, total bilirubin 0.8, INR 1.0, platelets 245, and hemoglobin 13.1. Hemoglobin A1c is 6.9% and fasting glucose is 131. A right upper quadrant ultrasound shows diffusely increased liver echogenicity consistent with hepatic steatosis, no gallstones, and a normal common bile duct. Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody are negative.

Impression is elevated liver enzymes most consistent with fatty liver disease in the setting of obesity, with newly identified type 2 diabetes. The turmeric supplement may be contributing. Given the codeine allergy, we will avoid opioid analgesics.

Plan is to stop the turmeric supplement and to start metformin 500 mg twice daily with meals. Continue acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed, not to exceed 2 grams in 24 hours. Order autoimmune markers, iron studies, and transient elastography before discharge or as an outpatient. Dietitian consult for a weight loss goal of 7 to 10 percent and carbohydrate reduction. Repeat a hepatic panel in two weeks and see her in hepatology clinic in four weeks. We expect discharge tomorrow if her pain remains controlled.
"""

"""
Dictating a follow-up visit in the celiac clinic for a 70-year-old male with celiac disease diagnosed two years ago. He lives alone, he has no family in the area, and the only help he has is a neighbor who occasionally drives him to appointments. He does his own shopping and cooking, he relies a lot on canned soups and frozen dinners, and he is not sure which of them contain gluten. He estimates that he gets glutened about once a week. He denies diarrhea, abdominal pain, and blood in the stool, and he has had no rash and no unintentional weight loss. He feels a bit more fatigued than last year. Past medical history includes hypertension and osteopenia found on his last bone density scan. Current medications are lisinopril 10 mg daily, vitamin D3 1000 international units daily, and a calcium supplement 500 mg twice daily. No known drug allergies. On exam his blood pressure is 132/76, heart rate 68, and weight 68 kilograms, correction, 72 kilograms, which is up from 70 kilograms at his last visit. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, and not distended with normal bowel sounds. There are no oral aphthous ulcers, no skin rash, and no edema. Labs from last week show hemoglobin 12.1, ferritin 14 which is low, and vitamin D 22 which is low. The tissue transglutaminase IgA was 38, correction, 58, down from 120 at diagnosis but still elevated. My impression is celiac disease with persistent serologic activity from ongoing inadvertent gluten exposure, iron deficiency anemia, vitamin D insufficiency, osteopenia, and hypertension that is stable. Because he is a 70-year-old male with iron deficiency anemia, I also want to exclude a colonic source of blood loss. For the plan, I am starting ferrous sulfate 325 mg every other day, increasing the vitamin D3 to 2000 international units daily, and continuing the calcium and lisinopril. I am referring him to a dietitian who specializes in celiac disease, and to social work for help with gluten-free meal delivery and transportation, since he lives alone with limited support. I am ordering a colonoscopy, and social work will also help him arrange a ride and an escort for the procedure. We will repeat the tissue transglutaminase IgA, hemoglobin, and ferritin in three months and I will repeat the bone density scan in one year. Return to clinic in three months, sooner if he develops diarrhea, black stools, or weight loss. End of dictation.
"""

She has had irregular, prolonged vaginal bleeding for about 3 weeks, which became heavy over the last 4 days with her soaking a pad every hour, along with lightheadedness, fatigue, and palpitations. Her history includes polycystic ovary syndrome, obesity, and asthma. She smokes one pack per day, correction, she smokes half a pack per day, about 10 cigarettes, for 6 years.

In the emergency department she was tachycardic with a heart rate of 118 and a blood pressure of 96/58. Hemoglobin was 6.8 g/dL, platelets 312, INR 1.0, TSH 2.4, and ferritin was very low. Urine hCG was negative. She received 2 units of packed red blood cells and her hemoglobin this morning is 8.6 g/dL. Pelvic ultrasound showed a normal-sized uterus with an endometrial thickness of 9 mm and no fibroids or polyps, and the ovaries have multiple small peripheral follicles consistent with polycystic ovary syndrome.

Her home medications are metformin 500 mg twice a day, an albuterol inhaler as needed, and naproxen 500 mg twice a day for cramps. I discontinued the naproxen on admission while a bleeding disorder is being excluded. She has mild cramping but denies pelvic pain. She denies fever, chest pain, fainting, nosebleeds, gum bleeding, and easy bruising.

On admission she was started on norethindrone acetate 5 mg three times a day, and the bleeding has slowed to light spotting. This morning her blood pressure is 112/68, heart rate 86, temperature 98.2 F, respiratory rate 16, and SpO2 99% on room air. She looks less pale. Her abdomen is soft with mild suprapubic tenderness and no rebound, and there is light spotting on the pad. Pelvic exam was deferred.

Impression. Abnormal uterine bleeding most likely from ovulatory dysfunction related to polycystic ovary syndrome, with symptomatic anemia from blood loss and iron deficiency, improving. A bleeding disorder is less likely, but a von Willebrand panel has been sent. Tobacco use.

For the plan, one, reduce norethindrone acetate to 5 mg twice a day starting tonight, and 5 mg once daily at discharge for 3 months. Two, start ferrous sulfate 325 mg twice daily, and I will recheck the hemoglobin tomorrow. Three, continue to hold naproxen. Four, start a nicotine patch 14 mg daily based on half a pack per day, and I counseled her on quitting for 5 minutes and she accepted the patch.
