"""
The patient is a 28-year-old female, gravida 2 para 1, at 34 weeks of gestation, seen in the obstetrics clinic for evaluation of possible preeclampsia after an elevated blood pressure at a routine visit earlier this week. She reports a mild frontal headache for the past two days and new swelling of her feet. She denies blurred vision, spots in her vision, right upper abdominal pain, nausea or vomiting, shortness of breath, vaginal bleeding, and leakage of fluid. She reports good fetal movement. Her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated, and her blood pressures at all earlier visits were normal. She takes a prenatal vitamin daily and aspirin 81 mg daily, which she started at 12 weeks, and she has taken ibuprofen 400 mg a few times this week for the headaches. She has no known drug allergies.

On exam her blood pressure is 148/94, and after 15 minutes of rest the repeat is 144/92. Heart rate is 84 and temperature is normal. She appears comfortable. She has 1+ pitting edema of both feet and ankles. Reflexes are normal without clonus, and there is no right upper quadrant tenderness. Fundal height is 34 cm and the fetal heart rate is 142 beats per minute. Urine dipstick shows 1+ protein. The urine protein to creatinine ratio is 0.42. Platelets are 198, creatinine is 0.7 mg/dL, AST is 26, and ALT is 21. A non-stress test was reactive. Ultrasound shows an estimated fetal weight at the 45th percentile and a normal amniotic fluid index.

My impression is preeclampsia without severe features at 34 weeks. Her blood pressures are below 160/110, her labs are normal, and her symptoms are mild, so she can be managed as an outpatient with close surveillance.

I am starting labetalol 100 mg twice daily. I asked her to stop ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for headaches instead, and to continue aspirin 81 mg daily and the prenatal vitamin. She will check her blood pressure at home twice a day and keep a log. We will repeat the labs weekly and repeat the non-stress test twice weekly, with a growth ultrasound in two weeks. Delivery is planned at 37 weeks, or sooner if severe features develop. I reviewed warning signs, and she should go to labor and delivery triage right away for severe headache, vision changes, upper abdominal pain, shortness of breath, a blood pressure of 160/110 or higher, or decreased fetal movement. Follow-up in the clinic in three days.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
This is a dictation for a follow-up visit in the oncology clinic for a 66-year-old female with stage one invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast, estrogen receptor positive, progesterone receptor positive, HER2 negative, status post lumpectomy and whole breast radiation, now fourteen months into adjuvant anastrozole. She came in anxious and had a long list of questions written on a notepad. History of present illness, she tells me she has been taking the anastrozole only twice a week, correction, every other day, for about the last three months because the copay went up and she is trying to stretch the bottle, and she had not told anyone until today. She also reports aching and stiffness in both hands and both knees that is worse in the morning, which she attributes to the medicine, and she has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg twice a day for it. She denies a new breast lump, nipple discharge, bone pain, cough, shortness of breath, headache, abdominal pain, and weight loss.

Past medical history includes hypertension and hypothyroidism. Medications are anastrozole 1 mg once daily as prescribed, amlodipine 5 mg once daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg once daily, calcium with vitamin D, and the ibuprofen I mentioned. She has no known drug allergies.

On exam blood pressure is 154/92, heart rate 78, and weight is stable at 164 pounds. She looks anxious but is in no distress. Breasts are symmetric with a healed lumpectomy scar on the left without nodularity, and there is no axillary adenopathy bilaterally. Lungs are clear and the abdomen is soft and nontender. There is no bony tenderness over the spine. Labs this week, CBC with hemoglobin 12.8, WBC 5.6, platelets 232, creatinine 0.9, and TSH 2.1. Her diagnostic mammogram six months ago showed no evidence of recurrence. A DEXA scan this month shows a lumbar spine T-score of minus 2.6, which is osteoporosis.

During the visit she asked many questions. She asked whether skipping doses raises the chance the cancer returns, and I explained that missed doses reduce the benefit of the treatment so taking it every day matters. She asked whether she should switch to tamoxifen, and I explained that it is an option if the aromatase inhibitor cannot be tolerated, but that her joint symptoms may be partly treatable and we should first fix the cost problem. She asked whether the joint pain means the cancer has spread, and I told her that is very unlikely given the normal exam, the normal labs, and the pattern of the pain. She asked whether she needs more scans, and I said no routine scans are needed beyond her yearly mammogram.

For the assessment, one, hormone receptor positive invasive ductal carcinoma on adjuvant anastrozole with partial adherence because of cost. Two, aromatase inhibitor arthralgias. Three, osteoporosis. Four, hypertension above goal. Five, hypothyroidism, stable. For the plan, continue anastrozole 1 mg once daily and take every dose, and I referred her to our financial counselor and pharmacy to apply for manufacturer assistance and to move to the lowest cost generic. Stop ibuprofen because it can raise blood pressure, and start acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for joint pain. Start alendronate 70 mg once weekly and continue calcium with vitamin D, and a dental check is advised before long-term alendronate. Increase amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg once daily, with a home blood pressure log. Repeat the mammogram in six months, follow up with me in eight weeks, and she can call the nurse line with any questions between visits.
"""

"""
Visit type: telephone only, no video. Patient identified with two identifiers, agreed to a phone visit, and was at home. 57-year-old male referred to pulmonology for chronic cough.

History: Cough for about 4 months, dry and tickling, worse when lying down at night and when talking, with no sputum. Patient is quite anxious and asked many questions during the call, including whether this could be lung cancer because his father died of it, whether the cough is contagious, and whether he needs a CT scan. He denies fever, denies hemoptysis, denies shortness of breath, denies wheezing, denies night sweats, and denies weight loss. He reports occasional heartburn. Former smoker, about 10 pack-years, quit 20 years ago. Medications are lisinopril 20 mg daily, started about 5 months ago for hypertension, and atorvastatin 20 mg nightly. He tried over-the-counter dextromethorphan syrup with no benefit. No known drug allergies.

Home measurements: pulse oximeter 98% on room air, BP 134/84, heart rate 78.
Exam: none by phone. He speaks in full sentences with no audible wheeze or stridor and coughed twice during the 15 minute call.
Results reviewed: chest x-ray 2 weeks ago was clear with no mass or infiltrate. Spirometry last week was normal.

Impression: Chronic cough, most likely ACE inhibitor-induced cough since it began after starting lisinopril, with possible contribution from reflux. Hypertension, controlled at home. His anxiety about the cough improved after discussion.

Plan:
Stop lisinopril today.
Start losartan 50 mg daily for blood pressure.
Start omeprazole 20 mg daily before breakfast for 8 weeks and raise the head of the bed.
Dextromethorphan is not helping, so he can stop it.
Explained that the cough usually improves within 1 to 4 weeks after stopping an ACE inhibitor but can take up to 3 months. Answered his questions at length: the normal chest x-ray and spirometry are reassuring, the cough is not contagious, and a CT scan is not needed unless the cough persists 8 weeks after stopping lisinopril or red flags develop. He verbalized understanding and sounded calmer by the end of the call.
BMP in 2 weeks to check potassium and creatinine after starting losartan.
Keep a home BP log. Phone follow-up in 4 weeks.
Call or go to the ED for coughing up blood, shortness of breath, fever, or weight loss.
"""

Clinical note:

Doctor: Welcome. I see you are a 19-year-old female here about pelvic pain. Tell me what is going on.

Patient: I have had really bad period pain since I was about fifteen. It keeps getting worse, and now I have pain in my lower belly even on some days when I am not bleeding.

Doctor: How bad is the pain during your period?

Patient: Eight out of ten. I miss one or two days of school every month. It hurts when I have sex, and it hurts when I go to the bathroom during my period.

Doctor: Is there blood in your stool?

Patient: No blood. Just pain.

Doctor: What have you tried?

Patient: Ibuprofen, 600 mg when it starts. It takes the edge off, but I still cannot function. My mom's sister had endometriosis, so I wonder if that is what I have.

Doctor: Any fever, vaginal discharge, burning when you urinate, or weight loss?

Patient: No fever, no discharge, no burning. My weight is the same.

Doctor: Your vitals today are blood pressure 110/68, heart rate 78, and temperature 98.4 F. The urine pregnancy test we did is negative, and the tests for chlamydia and gonorrhea are negative. Your pelvic ultrasound last month was normal, with no cysts. On exam your belly is soft with mild lower abdominal tenderness and no masses. On the pelvic exam, with a chaperone, you had tenderness behind the uterus on the left side, and the uterus moves freely.

Patient: So what does that mean?

Doctor: Based on your story, I think this is most likely endometriosis. A normal ultrasound does not rule it out, because the small spots do not show up on it. We can start treatment without surgery. I want you to start norethindrone acetate 5 mg once a day, taken every day without a break, which should lighten your periods and reduce the pain. I would also like you to switch from ibuprofen to naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food, starting two days before your period and for the first five days of it. Please stop the ibuprofen so you are not taking two anti-inflammatory pills together. A heating pad can help too.

Patient: Okay. What if it does not work?

Doctor: If your pain is not clearly better in three months, we will talk about other hormone options or a small surgery called laparoscopy to look inside and confirm the diagnosis.

Patient: The hard part is I live about two hours away and I do not have a car. I take two buses.

Doctor: I understand. Let us make it easier. We will do your follow-up by video in three months, and I will send a three-month supply of the pills to your pharmacy near home. If your pain suddenly gets much worse, you have a fever, or you faint, go to the nearest emergency room.

Patient: That works. Thank you.
"""

Reason for consult: Evaluation and management of neutropenia in a patient receiving chemotherapy. Requesting service: emergency medicine.

HPI: 63-year-old female with breast cancer, 10 days after cycle 3 of docetaxel 75 mg/m2 and cyclophosphamide 600 mg/m2 given every three weeks, who came to the emergency department with 2 days of fatigue and a sore mouth. She did not receive growth factor support with the prior cycles. She has been eating less because of mouth soreness but is tolerating liquids. She denies fever, chills, cough, dysuria, diarrhea, and rash. No sick contacts.

Pertinent history: Breast cancer on adjuvant chemotherapy through a right chest port. Hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg daily. No known drug allergies.

Exam: Temp 99.1 F, BP 118/70, HR 92, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air. Fatigued but nontoxic and in no distress. Mild grade 1 oral mucositis of the buccal mucosa without thrush or ulceration. Port site is clean with no erythema or tenderness. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft and nontender. No rash.

Data reviewed: WBC 1.1 with ANC 480, hemoglobin 10.4, platelets 142, creatinine 0.8. Lactate normal. Urinalysis negative. Chest x-ray clear. Blood cultures from the port and a peripheral vein are pending.

Impression: Chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, grade 3, after docetaxel and cyclophosphamide, afebrile and hemodynamically stable with no identified source of infection. Mild oral mucositis. Hypertension, stable.

Recommendations:
- Give the first dose of filgrastim 300 mcg subcutaneously in the ED, then daily at home until ANC recovers above 1500, with self-injection teaching.
- Reasonable to discharge home with neutropenic precautions if she remains afebrile on observation and blood cultures stay negative.
- Repeat CBC with differential in 48 hours at the infusion center.
- Hold the next cycle until ANC is above 1500 and reduce docetaxel to 60 mg/m2.
- Salt and baking soda mouth rinses four times daily.
- Return immediately for a temperature of 100.4 F or higher, or shaking chills.
- Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily.
- Oncology clinic follow-up within one week.
"""

Clinical note:
"""
The patient is a 28-year-old male seen in the family medicine clinic for sneezing, a runny nose, and itchy eyes that return every spring and have been much worse for the last three weeks. He works outdoors on a landscaping crew. He has limited health literacy, so I used plain language, short sentences, and the teach-back method throughout the visit and used his pill bottles to check his medicines.

He describes clear runny nose, fits of sneezing, itchy watery eyes, and an itchy throat, with a mild cough at night. Symptoms are worse when he is mowing or working in tall grass and better on rainy days. He has had the same pattern every spring since his teens. He denies fever, facial pain, wheezing, and chest tightness. Since his last visit he denies leg swelling, calf pain, bleeding, and black stools.

His history includes a DVT in the left leg two years ago, asthma, GERD, and anxiety. When I asked about his blood thinner, he first said he takes apixaban "one pill a day." His bottle reads 5 mg twice a day. After we counted the pills left in the bottle and went over his morning and evening routine, he confirmed that he takes one pill in the morning and one at night, so the correct dose is apixaban 5 mg twice daily. Other prescribed medications are an albuterol inhaler 2 puffs as needed, used about twice a week, omeprazole 20 mg daily, sertraline 50 mg daily, and fluticasone nasal spray, 1 spray in each nostril once daily, which he uses only on bad days and aims straight up the middle of his nose. Over the counter he takes pseudoephedrine 60 mg every 6 hours for stuffiness, diphenhydramine 25 mg at night, and ibuprofen 400 mg twice a week for sinus headaches.
